                       The "CHALLENGER" - Her Challenge




nI'm a spar decked corvette, built of wood, not of iron,
I am good under steam, under sail,
No Sheffield plate dead weights my topsails environ
As I ride like a duck throW a gale.
By my Lords I'm about to be put in commission
For a cruise of three years, if not four,
and for all I'm short-handed, I carry provision,
Such as corvette ne'er victualled before.


"Mines's no cruise to train officers, boys or blue-jackets
Or Brittania's old flag to display,
To observe or report South American rackets
Or enjoy life in hapless Blue Bay.
To practice manoeuvers, or study steam tactics
Hunt down pirate junk or slave dhow,
The "Challenger" now aims at higher ~ates_ ~d~
And on different quest sets her prow.




                                        3
(8)
Her task,s to sound ocean's, smooth humour or rough in
To examine old Neptune's sea-bed.
                                             )4/
Dredge up samples precise of his mattress~· stuffing.
And the bolsters that pillow his head,
To study the dip and the dance of the needle
Test the currents of ocean and air,
In a word, all her secrets from nature to wheedle
And the great freight of facts homeward bear.



And by way of a treat when the fauna and flora
Of all lands and all seas I've run through,
And learnt if the Austral Antarctic Aurora
Our Boreal in beauty outdo.
In the Isle of Kerguelen with nothing between us
But the thinnest of clouds, - Oh what fun!
I'm to lurk and look on at the Transit of Venus,
Across the broad blush of the sun.




(9)
For this I bear science and seamanship plighted
In Thomson and Nares and Maclear1
While from highest to lowest aboard all invited
To serve both alike volunteer.
Broadside guns have made room to ship's batteries magnetic
Apparatus turns out ammunition,
From maindeck to ground-tier I'm a peripatetic
Polytechnic marine exhibition.

( 13)



H.M.S. "CHALLENGER"
Sheerness.    Nov. 22nd '72


Dear Tom


        We came into this ship on Monday morning 175 all told,     including 19
Privates and one Sergeant of Marines, and the same evening one of the Marines
was drowned, walked right over the ship's gangway into the dock basin which is
27 feet deep, and was drowned in sight of several of his shipmates.        It was
about seven o'clock at night and pitch dark, and there was no light to direct
anyone walking on shore from the ship or anything round the edge of the basin
to prevent them falling in.     As soon as the alarm was raised all the ship's
company went out on the jetty with lights, etc., and the dock yard police went
for the drags (14) and dragged for two hours, but were unable to find him so
had to desist for the night.


        In the morning a diver was fetched and all the seamen from the barracks,
a crowd of dockyard men assembling to see the diver go down.      As soon as he
had his dress on with about 50 Ibs of iron hung round his waist, his mates
began pumping air, and down he went to the bottom, and was there about three
minutes walking over the whole space between the ship and the side of the
basin without finding him when just as he was coming up - he saw him standing
bolt upright against the side of the basin, and after    ~ a rope round his
waist, he came up, and hauled him out of the water head first.       He had only
been immersed about ten hours but his features were so altered,          (15)   his
shipmates could scarcely recognize him.


        He was buried yesterday afternoon with all the honours allowed by the
service, the .f.iag ship's brass band playing the "Dead March" and the Blue
Jackets and Marines of the "Challenger" following with arms reversed.           The
poor fellow's mother and sisters came down from London to his funeral.




                                       6
     Another Marine has come today from Chatham Barracks in his place, and he
turns out to be an old shipmate of mine, who was in the "Invincible" and
"Audacious".     I have about eight old shipmates on board.


     We are to have 50 boys when we get to Portsmouth, which will make the
complement 0,<!.,~30All the officers are on board except Lord George Campell,
who, I expect is waiting until all the (16) dirty work is done.       We have two
steam boats on board, and about 30 miles of deep sea line, and dredging line.
The other six boats we shall take in when we go into the river next week.      All
the scientific chaps are on board, and have been busy during the week stowing
their gear away.      There are some thousands of small air tight bottles, and
little boxes about the si.ze of valentine boxes packed          in iron tanks for
keeping specimens in, insects, butterflies, mosses, plants etc.        There is a
photographic room on the main deck, also a dissecting room for carving up
bears, whales, etc:


     We had a grand funeral here on Sunday morning last, a Pruss ian fr igate
came in to bury one of her seamen, the greater part of the officers (17) and
her crew followed him to the grave.         Their band was composed of all seamen,
playing a funeral march, and the coffin was' drawn on a field piece by the
seamen.   They were dressed much the same as ours, but were not such good
looking men, the Marines wore a black and silver uniform, and helmets, which
had a fine appearance.     The ship left again on Monday after saluting the flag
ship with 18 guns •.


     We are to go out in the Medway on the 28th and expect to leave Portsmouth
about the 2nd.


     The Crest is a facsimile of the ship's figure head which is gilded.


     Believe me,
     Very Truly Yours
     Joe Matkin

(18)


H.M.S. RCHALLENGERw
Portsmouth,
Dec. 17th 1872


Dear Tom
       We left Sheerness last Saturday week, and had awful weather round, having
to put back three times, once into Deal on the Monday,       into Folkestone on
Tuesday, and into Dungeness on the Wednesday, arriving here on Thursday: the
distance is 105 miles and we were 109 hours steaming full speed all the way.
The wind was dead against us, and it commenced to increase as soon as we had
passed Dover on the Saturday night.    In the morning it had increased to a gale
and we found ourselves close into the coast of France.         At 10 o'clock on
Sunday the (19) Captain gave orders to put back for the Downs, but the wind
rose to a hurricane and we could make no headway against it.     At midnight the
ship passed through a cyclone, which caused the sea to come right over her
and go down into the engine room, through the hatchways, nearly putting out
the fires, the lifeboat cutter was smashed to atoms, and the jib boom carried
away with all the head sails, so that the ship drifted along under a single
storm staysai1.     She rolled fearfully all night.    I was pitched out of my
hammock two or three times, and think it was the most fearful night I ever
passed in my life.       Several ships were wrecked close to us,     and it was
considered the roughest night on the southern coast (20) for the last eight
years.


       We reached Deal on the Monday and waited until the storm abated.    There
were hundreds of vessels of all nations at anchor in the Downs.      Directly we
dropped ours the scientific blokes made a rush for the railway station and
came on to Portsmouth by train arriving two days before us.       They lay about
sea sick during the gale and the sailors did make game of them.      The damages
are nearly all repaired except a new lifeboat, which is to be sent out to the
Cape Verdes in a month's time.




                                       8
       The chief engineer made a sketch of the ship dur ing the gale on Sunday
night which is to be printed, this week's "London News" and "Graphic" are also
expected to contain plates of (21) the "Challenger". Since we came in here we
have been very busy drawing extra stores for the cold weather.         The Lords of
the Admiralty were on board on Saturday inspecting the ship, and ordered
extras, such as wines, pickles, jams, cranberries etc.        We are to have warm
clothing sent out to the Cape of Good Hope in a year's time, and it will be
issued before going down amongst the ice, or rather lent, for it will be taken
away as soon as we reach the latitude of Melbourne, and again issued at
<P';~·ropavlovsk-Kamch~tsk~Jbefore going through B~hring Straits.      We are also
 to have extra p~Y-~~~e cold .~~,

                     c(~
       The Marquis of ~ was on board on Saturday, he is not as handsome as
his picture.     We also had Admiral       (22)   Sir Leopold McClintock of Arctic
notoriety, and I can't tell you who has not been to look over the ship since
we came here.


       The Queen passed us today in her yacht on her way across to Osborne, and
all the Marines were drawn up under arms.


       Portsmouth is a very fine town larger I      think than Hull.   We expect to
sail on Saturday next for Lisbon, and if we make haste shall most likely be
there for Christmas.
       Yours Very Sincerely
       Joe Matkin.



(23)


H.M.S. "CHALLENGER"
Lisbon Roads,
January 7th 1873


Dear Tom,
       We left Portsmouth on Saturday the 21st of December, and only arrived in
Lisbon on the 3rd of this month. True, we were three days dredging in the Bay



                                       9
of Biscay, but it was the weather that delayed us so, gales of wind all the
way, and always dead against us.     We burnt nearly the whole of the coal coming
this 700 miles.


     We had a miserable Xmas day as far as the weather went, but we managed to
enjoy ourselves a   1itt1e~   on xmas eve we made a nice plum pudding in my mess.
We all had a (24) hand in its manufacture, and it was highly successful.


     We had a short service in the morning by the Captain, as we had no
Chaplain, but no Xmas hymns or anything, for the ship was rolling too much to
cast the harmonium adrift.


     In the evening the Captain gave each one in the ship 1/3 of a pint of
sherry, which went down high among the ship' s company, and they all agreed
that if the four ensuing Xmas's that we are to spend on the "Challenger" only
pass off as comfortably, we shall have no cause to complain.


     On the 27th inst. we passed in the Bay of Biscay a vessel bottom upwards
in the water, but it was too rough to lower a boat although (25) we passed her
quite close.   Again on the 29th we passed the remains of another vessel, and a
great quantity of oranges floating on the water~ it was evidently one of the
many fruit schooners running between here and England, and had foundered in
the gale with all hands on board.


     It was a very solemn light to see that first vessel bottom upwards in the
sea, with the waves breaking over her.       She was quite entire too, and had not
been many days in the water ~ every man in the ship came on deck to look at
her, and it made our company quite dismal for a time.


     I have not time to send you particulars of the deep sea dredging this
time, but I have it all in my diary,         and shall send it   (26)   in my next
letter.    The dredge was cast in four different places, the lowest bottom was
nearly a mile and half, and the highest not quite three miles, the strain on
the line is something wonderful as the dredge gets close to the bottom, and
they have lost already in heaving it in, nearly two miles of line, and two
dredges.



                                        10
       Only one dredge came up as it ought to, and contained mud, and some very
rare   species of        fish,     as   well   as   a common crab.      These    have     all   been
preserved.         They were brought from a depth of 1500 fathoms or nearly 2 miles.
The mud also contained numerous insects, and was successfully analyzed.


       The weather here in the daytime is very hot, and we have all (27) kinds
of fruit very cheap, and I have eaten an enormous amount since we came in.


       Our    Captain     and     Professor    Thompson   dine   with   the   King   of   portugal
to-night.


       They have been coaling ship today, and we sail for Gibralter on Thursday,
leaving there again about the 25th of January for Madeira.


       Our letters now have to be franked by the Commander, who is now busy with
some hundreds and the mail closes in 5 minutes.
       Believe Me
       Yours Very Sincerely
       Joseph Matkin



(28)


H.M.S. "CHALLENGER"
Gibralter,
January 20th 1873


Dear Tom,
       I     had   no   further    opportunity of writing again from Lisbon,               so must
conclude my account of there as briefly as possible in this letter.


       I had a run on shore the day after I wrote you, went with a shipmate in
the afternoon and had a nice walk out into the country among the orange
groves.       We had a look at the King's Palace, which is a very fine one, built
on the top of a hill overlooking Lisbon, from there we had a stroll round the




                                                    11
city, and were very much surprised at the dirt and (29) squalor in all parts
except the principal streets and squares,            in which   are   some   really   fine
buildings.     Still there is no bustle and business like you see. in an English
town.    The shops have no windows or fronts and are dingy looking holes, those
only which can compete with the English are the confectioners and they beat us
hollow in the varieties of sweets and pastry, and the style in which they
display it.


        The Cathedral is the most magnificant building in the city after the
style Of~) Paul's in London, with dome and towers, and being built of white
stone, looks of course cleaner.


        There is also a very beautiful ~nvent there, built like Westminster
Abbey on a small scale, and the peal of bells, in that, and the (30) Cathedral
were the best I ever heard.


        At 6 in the morning and evening they play opera tunes, which sounded
beautiful from the ship.         In the evening we went to the opera, which was
really grand.    The singing was all in Italian.       The opera house is the finest
(of the sort) I was ever in - seated 20,000, and there was a magnificant box
for the King and Royal Family.          The opera was "Ruy B1as" and the singing was
truly splendid,     there were    250    in the orchestra, after      the opera came a
Ballet, and it was nearly 1 0' clock in the mor ning when we came out.                 The
Portuguese ladies are very handsome 1 so are the Spanish, but about one in
every five is marked with small pox.


        The Captain and Professor Thompson (31) dined with the King at the Palace
soon after we came in, and just before we sailed, the King and several of his
officers came on board to have a look over the ship, and dredging apparatus
etc.     He was a fine looking man, about 35 and dressed in military uniform.           He
came in his barge, a very handsome boat, pulling 26 oars, but I can't say the
same for his boat's crew who looked as if they had been whitewashed, although
they were from the pick of his navy.             Our men were all in their best, and
manned the yards for him, and the ~ficers were in full uniform for the first
time.




                                            12
     While we were on shore we had a look in at a masquerade ball, which is a
sort of national (32) affair and lasts for ten days after Christmas, according
to the style of the ~rnival at Rome and Venice.


     Most of the dancers were in fancy dresses, some of the most grotesque
character1 and very costly, each one wore a domino, or black velvet mask which
conceals the upper part of the face, so that it is impossible to recognize any
one except from their dress.   Some of the ladies were rigged as men and "vice
versa" so that it was a mixed up affair altogether.


     The Channel Fleet brings a great deal of custom to Lisbon, wintering
there, for there are 3,500 men in it, they had just left for Gilbralter when
we arrived.   One of their sailor boys belonging to the "Sultan" died in the
English hospital (33) while we were there, and half of our men attended his
funeral.   There are a great many buried in Lisbon cemetry who belonged to the
Channel Fleet and they all have nice gravestones erected by their mess-mates.


     We took in 150 tons of coal there, and were to have sailed on the lOth,
but it came on to blow, and we were not able to start until the 12th (Sunday).
We steamed down the Tagus just as the sun was setting over Lisbon, and very
pretty the city looked as we slowly passed it1 I should like to call there on
my way home again, but think "Ascension" is the last place we stop at on our
return.


     We were five days on the way to Gibralter, distance from Lis-(34)bon 400
miles, but the best part of each day was spent in dredging, sounding, etc.
with fishing, which on the whole was very successful.     No more line was lost,
and a great deal has been done by the scientific party, when the dredge is
hauled up they stand round in their shirt sleeves, and commence overhauling
the mud for fish, etc. and as soon as they get any, down they all go to
dissect and pickle them in glass jars.     The sea bottom between Lisbon and here
varied from 400 to 2,500 fathoms at which depth the dredge brought up mud and
shell fish, one, a regular common Sheerness crab.       The mud was analyzed and
some baked in the oven in bread tins, numbered and put away for the Museum
(35) when we return.




                                      13
      A boat was lowered everyday and a fishing party told off, which went a
considerable distance from the ship, and succeeded in obtaining some very rare
species, but the choice kinds were by means of the trawl net, which is the
same as a common herring net, and is paid out from the stern by a line of the
requisite length to reach the bottom and towed along by the ship1 it was only
cast once and took about 6 hours hauling up from a depth of 1900 fathoms, and
contained several fish varying from 1/2 lb. to 4 1/2 Ibs. and of the most
wonderful form and shape, heads larger than their bodies, and eyes in the
middle of their backs, of course the scientifics (36) were in rare good humour
and took them down to the analyzing room, where they christened them over some
bottles of champagne 1 I forget the name with which they were honoured but
should know it by sight, as i t was composed of about forty letters.              The
scientifics keep all their information and specimens to themselves and I dare
say you will know as much about the expedition from the papers, by and bye, as
we do who are in the ship.


      We sighted the coast of Africa on Tuesday night          (the 17th)    at the
entrance to the Straits, and during the night we passed right through into the
Mediterranean Sea where we hove to until Saturday morning early, then steamed
into the (37) Bay of Gibralter.


      The rock looks very grand and imposing from the sea, it is 1500 feet
high, and has 1873 guns mounted, varying from 9 pounders to 18 and 25 ton guns
(which command the Straits).     The small guns protect it ~rom the Spanish side,
and there is one for each year, the one for 1873 is now being mounted - a 25
ton gun.


      The Channel Fleet were at anchor in the bay, and left the same afternoon
for Madeira and Teneriffe, where we shall see them again.        It comprised the
ironclads "Minotaur", "Agincourt", "Sultan", "Hercules",       "Bellerophon", and
"LivelY"1 the other one, the "Northumberland", has gone to Malta to be docked
for   repairs,   having   been accidentally rammed   by the   "Hercules"    and   (38)
seriously damaged.    We came alongside the jetty on the south mole as soon as
the Fleet had gone ready for coaling, and today, Monday, all hands are busy
filling up with it.




                                        14
      On Sunday morning we all went on shore         to the English church;      the
 congregation was nearly all soldiers, and officers, with their families.         In
 the afternoon I went on shore and had a long ramble - first to the top of the
 rock, the guns are mounted nearly to the top, some small ones are on it, and
 the rock is regularly honeycombed all round for them; the Royal Engineers have
 done a good deal of this, but the heaviest part was done by the Spaniards,
 before it was taken from them in 1704.


      The view from the summit of the rock was magnificant, opposite (39) lay
 the coast of Barbary, an awfully rugged and mountainous country; some of which
 are twice as high as Gibralter.       The only towns in sight are Tangiers and
~ and on the Spanish coast across the bay is Algerias, a very pretty
 place, and higher up the Mediterranean is Malaga.     The artist made a sketch of
 the former town as we came in, and the photographer took the south side of the
 Rock, he also took views of Lisbon; we are to be allowed to purchase any we
 like at l/each.


      From the top of the rock I      had a walk into Spain, past the line of
 British pickets across the 500 yards of neutral territory, past the Spanish
 pickets and into the ajoining towns.     The Spanish soldiers (40) are worse than
 the Portuguese, they wear blue coats, green trousers, and cocked hats, and
 look about as fierce as maggots; you enter the town by a gate, at which stand
 about twenty beggar~, the most wretched looking objects, you ever saw, most of
 them -deformed,    and the stench from them is     something- fearful,   they   stop
 everyone for alms and the Reis come in handy, there being twenty to an English
 penny.   There are any amount of Moors here from the Barbary States, dirty
 looking beggars most of them, and dressed like Arabs.       I like the Portuguese
 the best after all and Lisbon is 10 to 1 to Gibralter.


      There   are   two towns,   English town,   and Spanish town both under      the
 English governor.     There was plenty of gambling going on yesterday morning
 (41) among the Spaniards.




                                         15
        We received a mail as soon as we came in, and I had one letter from
W.      Blackwood,    congratulating   me   on   being   selected   to   accompany   the
·Challenger- on her wonderful expedition.


        This letter goes to-morrow and you may expect another from Madeira or
Teneriffe.
        Believe me ever,
        Sincerely yours,
        Joe Matkin.

Santa Cruz
Feb. 7th 1873


Dear Tom:
        We left Gibralter on Sunday the 26th of January, intending to call at
Tangier, Morocco, but it was blowing too hard, and we had to get up steam to
keep clear of the African Coast.        On the following Sunday we were just ready
to drop anchor at Madeira after a very pleasant passage with sounding and
dredging every day, the deepest bottom was 2,600 fathoms, or rather more than
3 miles, obtained off the Islands of the Desert (belonging to Madeiras) •


        We also had some good trawling (43) in the passage, very rare species of
fish being obtained on the 28th of Jany., and on the following day a turtle
was caught and eaten by the Officers.


        Off Porto Santo we picked up a large bale of cotton, which was very
slightly damaged by the salt water.          We did not run into Madeira on Sunday,
but the Captain decided on having some trawling, and the result was that the
trawl net (worth £100) and 2,000 fathoms of dredging line was lost overboard,
being as the sailors' said, a judg~ment on fishing on the Sabbath.




                                            16
        On the Monday early we anchored off Funchal, the chief city of Madeira,
and made preparations for coaling.       The Madeira Islands (44) are in Lat. 32°
N. and Long. 17° W.        They all belong to Portugal and are distant from Lisbon
540 miles.       They consist wholly of mountains 6,000 feet high, and we could see
them 45 miles away, the productions of the islands are grown at the foot of
these mountains, and consist of dates, plantains, pomegranates, bananas, figs,
alligator pears, sugar canes, coffee, grapes, arrowroot, etc.


        The climate is the best in the world, and there were a great many English
visitors staying the winter there of whom we had several on board, including
the Mayor of Edinburgh and his family.         The islands have an area of 336 sq.
miles, and a population of 120,000.       Funchal is a very clean and pretty place,
built something after the (45) style of Lisbon.       I had a fine run on shore at
Madeira, walked nearly to the top of the island, and drank some of the wine as
well.     We expect to call there again in July, when of course it will be much
hotter.


        We coaled on the Monday, ~~ailed on Tuesday at 3 o'clock, just as we
were leaving H.M. Troop Ship Qwu,tes (1-) came in from England, and brought us
some packages.       As soon as we got clear of the island, we picked up a splendid
breeze, the fires were put out, and every stitch of canvas set, dr iving the
ship 12 miles an hour •


    . The Canary Islands are distant from Madeira 250 mil~s, and we sighted the
Peak of Teneriffe, at 3 p.m. yesterday, exactly 24 hours from Madeira.


        (46)     We remained out sounding all night and came into Santa Cruz early
this morning.        Being so misty we are unable to see the beach today, but I
think some of the Scientifics are going to try and reach the summit before we
leave, it is 12,300 feet high, or nearly 2 1/2 miles, and on the top, is at
present covered with snow, although here at the bottom it is quite hot and
sultry.        Teneriffe is not such a pretty island as Madeira, and Santa Cruz is
not to be compared with Funchal for cleanliness.




                                          17
        The population is 300,000 and it has an area of 878 sq. miles.                 Palmas
one of the other Canar ies        is nearly as large.           They all      belong   to   the
Spaniards, and one of their gun boats is (47) at anchor close to.


        The productions   are   the   same   as   at Madeira,    with   the    exception of
cochineal, but I think the bananas are finer.             Santa Cruz is very strongly
defended, and there are a great many Spanish soldiers here.                It is famous as
being the only place Nelson was unable to take, but he failed in consequence
of the great surf which runs here capsizing the boats before the men could
land.     He lost his right eye, and a great many men here.             An Ironclad of the
present day could knock the place into ashes in about 2 minutes.


        The Spaniards fired a salute for us at 12 o'clock today, but as this ship
is not fitted out as a Man (48) of War she did not return it.



Sunday, Feb. 9th
        The mail for England closes in five minutes, so must cut this short.                   I
am going on shore this afternoon so must describe the place in my next letter.


        We can see the famous peak quite plainly today, a party of three Officers
and Scientifics with four seamen went away yesterday to scale the mountains.
They have taken five days provisions, etc.           To-morrow we are going to cruise
round the other islands, and are to come back on Thursday, for the surveying
party, when we shall start for St. Thomas.


        Last night one of the men caught a shark, about 6 feet in length.                   (49)
He was a long time dying, for after his tail was cut off, and his entrails
(including 14 young ones) taken out of him, he was as lively as ever.                       The
young ones were all alive and the Scientifics took charge of them.                     The old
gentleman is now being eaten for dinner in the mess of the men who caught him.


Believe Me
Your ever Sincerely
Joe Matkin.

H.M.S. nCHALLENGER n
At Sea, Feb. 27th 1873


Dear Tom:
       As I have time to spare this afternoon I will get the ·S. Thomas's· let-
ter under weigh.       We left Teneriffe before the mail came in from England so
have had no letters yet, but shall expect to receive some at S. Thomas, and
Bermuda.    The last I posted to you just before I went on shore at Teneriffe.
I went on the following Sunday afternoon, and had a splendid walk over the
mountains from Santa Cruz to La Laguna, the Spanish capital, 5 miles in the
interior.     At Santa Cruz the heat was tremendous, but on climb- (51) ing the
mountains the air got gradually cooler,           and when I     left La Laguna,      after
sunset it was quite chilly.          I could not make it out, at first, why the men
and women coming down from the mountains all wore a large blanket each for a
cloak, and on arriving at Santa Cruz took it off, but found out it was through
the change in the climate.           The men and women all went barefooted, and the
latter appeared to do the best part of the work, some of them were carrying
enormous baskets of fruits from the country into Santa Cruz.                 La Lag una was
the largest place of the two, but the Cathedral was the only building worth
looking at in it, in which there was a very fine group of statuary. (52)                The
sides of the hills were covered with a pretty shrub called the prickly pear on
which the cochineal insect feeds.         That is the principal export, the fruit of
the P!ickly pear is"not up to much, but alligator pears are very fine eating;
Santa Cruz or the "City of the Holy Cross·               is where the Spanish Governor
resides, but is not such a nice place as Madeira.           The next day after going on
shore we got under weigh early for a four day cruise round the other Canary
Islands, with occasional sounding, dredging, etc.


       After we got clear of the islands we had a fine view of the Peak of
Teneriffe, and could see it from all the other islands.                They are all of vol-
canic origin, and most of them (53)          rise for 8 and 9000 feet above the sea
level;     some   of   them   rise    perpendicularly,    and   have    a   very   wonderful
appearance.




                                            19
     We steamed round palmas,auert~:~~and two or three smaller ones and
were away four days.     The soundings varied considerably, in one place it was
only 75 fathoms, a little farther on it was 1900, then 2,500, and so on, show-
ing the bottom to be as varied in depth as the islands in height.     The dredge
brought up a sort of petrified cinders, which had every appearance of being
thrown up from volcanoes ages ago.      Off the island of S. Christopher we fell
in with a Spanish fishing boat,        and bought all the fish they had for     3
dollars.     There were 3 large baskets full, and (54) they were of the most won-
derful color I ever saw, being gold and silver, green, violet, blue and every
shade you could mention.      I   never thought the sea contained such beautiful
creatures.     We were away four days, after which we anchored off Santa Cruz,
and picked up the exploring party, who had been away five days attempting to
scale the peak, but they only reached 9,000 feet in height out of the 12,360,
when the cold was so intense that the Spanish Guide refused to go any higher,
so down they came again.      For 1200 feet the peak was covered in snow, which
lies on the summit all the year round.


     The day after we returned we took in all the coal there was in Santa
Cruz, 25 tons, and got ready for sear the (55) same evening one of the boys
fell from the mainyard into the sea, but was immediately picked up by one of
the seamen who jumped overboard after him, he was stunned at first, but soon
recovered, the distance was 37 feet from the mainyard.


    -The next day Saturday, Feb. 15th we got under weigh for S. Thomas, dis-
tant 3,100 miles and to-day we are 1300 miles from Tener i ffe, and have 1800
more to go.     The peak could be seen the best about 70 miles away, rising above
the clouds like a pillar of snow.


     We have had the trade winds all the way, and might have been close there
by this time, if it were not for the sounding and dredging, etc. every day,
which occupies 8 and 9 hours each day, besides the labour of furling, and mak-
ing (56) sail after it is allover.




                                         20
        The scientific operations, I believe, have been very favorable, the low-
est bottom has been 1900 fathoms, and the greatest depth 3,650, or rather more
than 4 miles.     Several thousand fathoms of line, and a few dredges have been
lost, but of course that counts as nothing.       In some places the dredge brought
up black coral and beautiful sponges, in others, shell fish, mud, gravel and
various experiments have also been made by the Scientifics, such as tele-
graphing down to the bottom of the sea, and finding out the strength of the
electric fluid at such great depths.        By means of a certain instrument water
is also brought up from the bottom; at the greatest depth (57) it was quite
fresh    and drinkable,   the temperature was 34 degrees or      2 above   freezing
point.     Boats' have been lowered occasionally with an instrument for testing
the strength of the current; yesterday it was ascertained to set at the rate
of 4 1/2 miles per hour in a N.E. direction, or in the direction of Barrowden;
of course this is at some distance below the water that the current is felt.
We entered the Tropics on Sunday last, and it is hotter now than in the middle
of summer in England.     The time slips away though much quicker than with you,
and the health of the ships's company is excellent at present, though our
living is far from flattering, and I should enjoy some fresh butter, as from
one week's end to another it is biscuit, salt horse, (58) pork, and Australian
meat, which is very far from gay living.         The Officers had their meat-safe
broken open last night, and everything it contained was eaten before 4 o'clock
this morning, so they had a short allowance for breakfast, I expect it was


                   '=-)
taken and ate up aloft, like the turkey at xmas.
(as Artemus Ward          in a few days.

March 12th


        Within 250 miles of S. Thomas, W. Indies, and expecting to get in on the
15th.


        The dredge has just come up full of mud etc. from 3000 fathoms of water,
and all hands are making sail again for the night.        We had a most interesting
lecture given last week by (59) Professor Thompson to the Ship's company, on
the object of the expedition which I have written as well as I can remember,
and send for your perusal.     The Professor has promised to lecture again on the
same subject ere long.



                                           21
        Our brass band comes along very well, and plays every night now,     two
marches, and "God Save the Queen".


        We passed a Spanish schooner, called the "Virgin Mary" while we were in
church on Sunday, she was bound to Cuba, and had one lady on board7 great ex-
citement on board the "Challenger" to have a look at her, not having seen one
of the fair sex for a month.


        We have had an enormous shark following us for the last 1100 miles, and
the men say he won't leave until (60) some one dies, and is thrown overboard.
They have tried everything to catch him, and the Officers have fired at him
with rifles, but to no effect, he only goes under the ship's bottom for a
time.     Our future dates have just been posted up, Bermuda letters to arrive
there by April 8th, those for New York to reach there by the 25th and Bermuda
again to May 15th after which it will be Madeira.


        We shall stay about a week at S. Thomas, but the mail that takes this
leaves there the day after we arrive.


March 16th
        We have been delayed by the fog, but are just about to drop anchor in
S. Thomas' Harbour, and the mail leaves in about 2 hours so I must wind up,
and descr ibe the place in my next letter.     We shall soon have some English
news _ now, and letters too,   also something to eat I    hope in the shape of
bananas and alligator pears.


        We caught three sharks yesterday about six feet in length, but the mon-
ster one is not yet caught, and is most likely under the bottom of the ship
now.     The young ones were eaten for breakfast this morning, I   tasted a small
quantity, and thought it very good indeed, though rather dry.      We were sound-
ing yesterday off the island of Sombrero and the dredge brought up a young sea
serpent, which was collared by the Scientifics.      The bottom wi thin the last
120 miles, ran up from 3,075 fathoms to 400, a difference of 3 milies.
Yours as Ever.
J. Matkin.

H.M.S. "CHALLENGER",
Bermuda, Dockyard,
April 17, 1873


Dear Tom:
       I   received two letters from you at S. Thomas, the day after       I   wrote you
from there, one being addressed to "Madeira", and the other "Tener iffe" so
that they always manage to reach us finally, and none the less welcome for the
delay.      I   am   expecting another or two by the same mail which br ings this to
you.       I read in the papers about the "Northfleet" catastrophe.            We lay at
Dungeness on our bad passage down Channel, and I should think (63) there were
300 vessels at anchor in the Downs.            We get most of the newspapers sent out,
and a great many magazines. ·Good Words· will soon receive accounts of our do-
ings from Professor Thompson.        Did you see the picture in the "Graphic" of the
King of Portugal in our ship.           I have given instructions for a letter sent
home to be forwarded to you to read, containing an account of the island and
the colored persons, and about our picking up a large Iron Merchant ship be-
longing to Greenock, that had been dismasted in a gale soon after leaving New
York for Liverpool.         We left S. Thomas on the evening of March 24th under all
plain sail, and the dredging and sounding at once commenced, and has continued
(64) up to our arrival here.        On the 25th we obtained the deepest soundings we
have had hitherto,. and I believe the deepest on record, 3,875 fathoms, or
about 4 1/2 miles.         The dredge was hove overboard, and the strain on the line
was so great when it reached the bottom, that when they commenced hauling it
in, it carried away an iron block that was screwed in to the deck, and had all
the strain to bear.           The block as it flew up struck a sailor boy, named
Stokes, on the head, and dashed him to the deck with such terrible force, that
his thigh was broken, and spine dreadfully injured.             He was car r ied to the
sick bay and attended to by the surgeons, but he was insensible the whole
time, and only lived two hours.         (65)




                                               23
     At 5 p.m. the next day the bell tolled for his funeral, all the Ship's
company and the Officers and Scientific gents, attending on the main deck.
The captain read the service, and at the appointed place in it, the body was
lowered into the sea, by the lad's messmates, three 36 lb shots were attached
to it, to sink it, the depth was over four miles.          The boy carne from Deal
where his father is a Channel pilot.     All his clothes and effects were sold,
and the money, with his wages, a few photos, letters, and his bible will be
sent to his friends by this same mail.       We had soundings right across and the
average depth was 2,800 fathoms, nothing of any importance was brought up in
the dredge.    On the evening of the     (66)   1st of April they pipe RHands to
BatheR and about 80 of us went overboard and had a fine swim.      A boat was low-
ered to keep away sharks, etc., the water was over 3 miles in depth.        A few
sharks have been caught and eaten since we left S. Thomas and the other morn-
ing one of the men harpooned a dolphin, which is the most beautiful fish in
the sea, and best eating.     When dying they keep changing color, but after they
are dead they are of an ordinary color.         They are about 3 ft long and live
chiefly on flying fish, which are about the size of a herring, and skim the
water like a swallow1 but have not very good times for they are pursued in the
water by the dolphin and other fish, and in (67) the air by gulls and sea
birds.   On a dark night if a lighted candle is placed in the Ship's port they
will often fly in.   At 2 p.m. on the 3rd of April the Bermuda Islands hove in
sight, the land being wonderfully low for islands in the middle of the ocean,
and looks very blea~ and bare from the distance, but when we arrived in close
it had a better appearance.


     We dredged round the islands all day on the 4th and in the evening the
pilot (a darkie) brought us in.


     The navigation on entering is very intricate and difficult, as there are
so many shoals and rocks1 the pilot had to stand in the foretop, where he
could see the rocks, and give orders for          the steering, etc.   The Bermuda
Islands all (68) belong to Great Britain, and are about 300 in number, but the
whole lot are no larger than S. Thomas.         Bermuda itself is the largest, and
Hamilton the chief town is built on it, the whole population is about 12,000,
and the greater portion are colored people.         The islands were discovered in
1527 by Bermudez a Spaniard, who named them after himself.        In 1609, Admiral



                                        24
Sir George Somers, was wrecked on the islands and ,founded the colony~ and have
belonged to the British ever since.      There is a fine fortified dockyard on one
of the islands, and an immense iron floating dock, for the convenience of re-
fitting the fleet stationed in North American waters, without sending them
home.     This immense dock was built      (69)   at Woolwich, and towed across the
Atlantic a few years ago by four of our largest ironclads.          This place would
be of great importance as a rendezvous for the fleet, etc., in case of a war
with America~ it is 5 days sail from New York, and 800 miles from the nearest
land, Cape Hatteras in North America.


        The governor of the islands is Major General Lefroy, and there are plenty
of soldiers here for its protection.       The climate is not nearly so warm as at
S. Thomas, but we are able to bathe every evening.        The greater portion of our
North Amer ican Fleet     is here,    including the    "Royal Alfred"    flag   ship of
Admiral Fanshawe, for whom we brought a heavy mail from S. Thomas.


        Their head station is Halifax, but (70) they generally winter here.         The
Governor with a party of ladies and Officers are at present on board lunching.


        On the night of April 4th we had another awfully sudden death on board.
I left the upper deck at 10 p.m. to go down into my hammock, leaving the
ship's schoolmaster, Mr. Ebbe11s and the writer (who sleeps next to me) wa1k-
ing the upper deck together.         Soon after I turned in, they also came down,
after which I went to sleep, I had not been asleep ntQre than half an hour
before the writer woke me, and said that the schoolmaster was dead.              He was
heard to be breathing hard, and one of the men tr ied to rouse him, but not
succeeding went for the Doctor, before they came he was dead.             On Saturday
morning (71) they held an inquest, the verdict being "died from apoplexy".           In
the afternoon, and less than 7 hours after he died, he was buried in Bermuda
Cemetry.     Nearly all the ship's' company attended his      funera1~   I should have
gone but could not be spared, the band of the "Royal Alfred" played the "Dead
March in Saul", to the     grave~   our band not having practiced it yet.        A very
singular and affecting scene occurred at the funeral,           the Chaplain of the
dockyard buried him, and did not know just at the time whose corpse it was,
but happening at the conclusion to glance at the coffin plate, read the name
backwards, as he stood at the head of it.         "Adam Ebbe1s, born April 4th, 1837,




                                          25
died April 4th, 1873-, and for some time was so much affected (72) that he was
unable to continue the service.


        After he had finished, on addressing the men at the grave, said he had
sailed round the world with the deceased in H.M.S. -Liffey-, and had been in-
timate with him for 3 or 4 years, during which time he had always found him an
honourable man, and was never so surprised before, as he was on reading that
coffin plate.        The deceased was a very strong and healthy man, and clever and
intelligent.     He was not marr ied and only had one sister living at Woodbury
near Xeter, and what was very singular, died on his 37th birthday.


        The Captain has his only son on board, a little lad of 10 years, he in-
tended taking him as far as Sydney with us where he was going to school.       (73)
The schoolmaster was educating him in the meantime, but now he is dead, I hear
the Captain will send his son back to England from New York.         This made the
fourth sudden death on board since we commissioned, and hope we shall have no
more.     The 1st Lieutenant played the harmonium yesterday in the Schoolmaster's
place, he is a splendid player, and has a fine little instrument of American
invention, I think it is called a melodian and much sweeter than a harmonium.


        H.M. Ship,               a troop ship sailed for England yesterday morning
with time expired troops, their band playing -Auld Lang Syne- as they steamed
past us.


        I went on shore yesterday afternoon, and had a fine walk on 5 or 6 dif-
ferent (74) islands, which are connected either by a bridge or ferry boat, and
have some splendid walks on them.        The flowers here are beautiful, and there
are plenty of English singing birds, as well as native ones of most brilliant
plumage.     The walks are shaded by trees on each side, and there are several
churches, schools, etc., on the islands.       Hamilton, the chief town is 2 miles
from here, I walked nearly there yesterday, and intend going all the way be-
fore we leave, about the 20th inst.




                                          26
                            J~~
        I had a look in at bel1ierSeh church while the service was going on, there
was a good organ, and the chanting and singing excellent, the congregation was
nearly all black, and some of the ladies, "Ohl they just was dressed", would
beat Barrowden all to smash.     The best (75) bit of fun was the morning after
we arrived, at about 6 a.m. about 50 black washerwomen came on board, and

you'd have thought it impossible to get their mouths shut again, asked "Any
Vashing Sare" (answer) "go to the Devil" -- "Yes, Sare, after you Sarene      They

        We returned on board about 7 p.m. and nearly half the men were intoxi-
cated, and all but capsized the boat coming off, fighting all the way.        When
they get on board, they drop down on the deck and sleep sober before morning.
We came into the dock basin this morning, and (76) are now close to the iron
floating dock.

H.M.S. "CHALLENGER"


Out at Sea.       May 7, 1873


Dear Tom:
       "While my shipmates are dredging the sea, I'll indite a letter to thee"
(one of their poetical specimens and quite extempore).                         Your   last letter
reached me on April 9th and being the only one by that mail was all the more
welcomeJ on Good Friday the other mails came in "via Halifax" and brought me
some epistles, all yours have reached me quite safely.


       On Good Friday we had church in the morning, and in the afternoon I went
in the ship's steam launch over to Somerset, and Hamilton, the capitol of the
Bermudas.     (78) The distance is 18 miles, and we passed about 80 islands on
the way, most of them covered with forest and shrub.                         The shops were all
closed so I went for a walk into the country, and saw two cricket matches be-
ing played, which made it seem more like Old England.                        One was between the
soldiers, and the other the negroes, I liked the niggers best, they made such
a sweet row, and stopped the balls with their hands occasionally, but they are
very weak about the shins.           I had SQme tea with half a dozen eggs, etc. before
coming back, some of our men who were having tea, ate a dozen eachJ but I did
not feel equal to that.             The landlady's daughter who waited upon us was a
trifle blacker than a crow, the sailors called her Miss Julia Snowball.                          We
arrived (79) on board again about 8 p.m. and found the Halifax mail had just
arrived from England, it brought us Halifax papers containing accounts of the
loss of the Atlantic Steamer, but think the one I                      read was greatly exag-
gerated, so am anxiously awaiting for news from England about it.                        We shall
pass the scene of the wreck in another 2 days.                  Easter Sunday was very wet at
Bermuda and I never left the ship.                On the 14th inst. a seaman belonging to
the "Royal Alfred" Ironclad, fell from the main rigging to the bottom of the
great iron floating dock, a distance of 70 feet, and was picked up dead.                         On
the 17th we took in 100 tons of coal.                  I caught an octopus, or devil fish in
the bathing place.         This fish has 8 arms of feelers capable of clinging to
anything,     a    man,   or    a   rock,   and    is    the   most   (80)    horrible   thing   to




                                                  28
look at in the world.     His eyes and mouth are in the middle of his body, and
he looks something between a dragon, star fish, and the devil.     A large octo-
pus is capable of holding a man under the water until he is suffocated, they
are not often met with, but there is one living in the aquarium at Brighton,
our specimen died.


     On Sunday 20th all hands went to the Dockyard church, and in the after-
noon I had a walk to the Dockyard cemetry~ I spent nearly two hours reading
the inscriptions on the stones, etc.        You would be surprised to see what a
quantity of seamen and naval officers have been buried there during the last
80 years.   There are 80 or 90 different ship's gravestones~ each ship has a
large stone with the names of all the (81) officers, seamen, and marines, that
they have buried engraved thereon.    Drowning, falling from aloft, and yellow
fever appear to have caused the most deaths; some of the stones were beauti-
ful, and had the Ships' crests carved on them.       There are 3 Admirals buried
there, and a large monument to the 350 officers and men belonging to H.M.
Ships "Acorn" and "Supply"~ which foundered with all hands between Halifax and
Bermuda about 40 years ago. But the prettiest stone of all is one dated 1809
to the memory of 2 midshipmen, brothers belonging to the same ship, one 17
years old, the other other only 13, who died within 3 days of each other from
yellow fever.


     We are to bring a stone back with us from Halifax to Bermuda, in memory
of our schoolmaster, and the sailor boy who was killed off S. John.     The sub-
scription was made for it the other day and over £15 was obtained.     On Monday
April 21st we left Bermuda for Halifax, but remained off the island dredging
and sounding on what is called the Great Bank of Bermuda, extending out to sea
for more than 50 miles.     A few days after the Captain decided going to New
York, but when we were within 80 miles of Sandy Hook, he again altered his
mind, and are now within 220 miles of Halifax.     Expect he was afraid of losing
some of our men at New York.    One of our surgeons and the chemist went in the
mail boat from Bermuda to New York, and are there still, from where they will
bring our letters, and go on to Halifax by train.




                                       29
     On the 25th we passed a French barque      (83)   and a few days later an
American.   On the 26th and 27th we had a heavy gale of wind again, the ship
pi tching and tossing fr ightfully and scudding before the wind under close
reefed top sails, the weather was bitterly cold, but has improved within the
last few days.    During the gale one or two accidents happened, on Sunday 27th
a seaman fell from the foreyard arm down on to the deck and was very severely
injured.    For a long time they thought he could not recover, but is improving
now, and will go to the hospital at Halifax.     On the day following, another
accident occurred by the wheel taking charge a tremendous sea struck the rud-
der suddenly and caused the wheel to vibrate with great velocity; 2 men and 2
boys were steering and the latter were dashed insensibly to the deck, the men
were not hurt as they (84) let go.    The boys are still in the sick list but
getting better fast.    During the gale there were hundreds of brother Carey's
chickens about, but they disappeared with the wind, we also had several land
birds come on board the ship in an exhausted condition, and died soon after.
They were a species of lark, and had been blown out to sea from the coast of
America, a distance of 280 miles.


     On the 28th we lost overboard while sounding 2,100 fathoms of line.     The
average depth up to yesterday was about 2,500 fathoms, but we are getting
shallow again now.   We spent 2 days taking temperatures in the Gulf stream and
trying to sound; the water on the surface was 10 degrees warmer than the at-
mosphere but there was such a tremendous undercurrent      (85)   flowing in the
direction of England, that no soundings could be obtained, although the water
had not the appearance of being so deep as off the West Indies; 2,500 fathoms
found no bottom.     One or two experiments were made as to the effect of the
pressure of a column of water on any substance at 2,800 fathoms; 2 large iron
buoys were sent down and came up twisted and smashed out of all shape, after
that an empty ginger beer bottle was sent down carefully corked, it came up
full of water with the cork forced inside.




                                      30
            On May 2nd, the dredge brought up a live star fish and mud, on the 3rd,
       more star fish and 2 small sea serpents.     On Sunday we had church in the morn-
       ing and kept under sail all day, we sang Hymn 222, A and M, which we have
       every Sunday (86).      Today the sounding and dredging is allover, but don't
       know with what result.     All present 7 p.m. the band is playing splendidly, and
       the ship steaming away for Halifax, and the shaking caused by the engines is
       such that you would be unable to write.


       May 9th Halifax Dockyard.


            All day yesterday we were fishing and some scores of          fine cod were
       caught, which we had for dinner, tea and supper.    We sighted the coast of Nova
       Scotia early this morning and steamed up the harbour mooring, alongside the
       dockyard at twelve o'clock.     The passage down the river was spendid, regular
       English scenery, lighthouses, forts and batteries, and Halifax itself is quite
       like one of our towns at home.       It is the principal Naval station (87)    in
       British North America and the dockyard is very extensive.     The harbour is con-
       sidered one of the finest in the world, and the fish market more plentifully
       supplied than any other known, cod, salmon, halibut and mackerel are very
       abundant, and lobsters are only 1d each.     The weather at present is very cold,
       more so than in England in MaY1 although it is in the same latitude as Paris,
....   the winter    is more severe than it is in the north of Scotland.         We saw
       naught of the   wrec~   of the "Atlantic· coming in, but nothing is spoken of on
       shore here but that at present, and bodies are being brought every day for
       identification or burial.     The walls on shore are placarded with descriptions
       of the drowned people, and very large rewards are offered for some of the of
       the bodies.

(88)
       May 13th I have not been on shore yet but am going in a day or two,
Sunday and Monday were wet, cold and miserable, today has been fine but is
still very hot.    Several of the Officers have gone to New York by train~ dis-
tant 400 miles.    On Monday one watch went on 48 hours leave, and are gradually
coming back again, they like the place much and say the people treat them
well, but the military and police are very smart on them when they get         3
part 7 eighths intoxicated.     One or two have been fined 7 and 8 dollars for
drunkness and assulting the police, and you would be surprised to see what a
quantity there are with broken noses and black eyes.     One man said it took 12
bobbies all night to take him to the lockup, he had a terrible cut across the
fore(89)head and was fined 7 dollars, which is paid by the Paymaster and
charged against his wages.     He says he rather thinks he shall give "em what
for" if he can get on shore again before we sail.      Another of our Scientific
.seamen brought a young Nova Scotia youth on board to see the "Mermaid" we have
caught, all alive 01    Today we have been taking in six months provisions etc.
We have had any amount of visitors off to see the ship already and the Halifax
papers are crazy about her.     Yesterday the diver went down and examined the
ship's bottom, which is done every quarter if we are in harbour.       We have 2
divers, a carpenter and a seaman, and 2 sets of diving gear.       The Flag Ship
"Royal Alfred" came in yesterday from Bermuda, and is moored just ahead of us,
she was only 3 days and a half (90) on the journey, while it took us. 19 days:
She brought the Adm.iral, his wife, family,     servants, carriages, etc. from
Bermuda.   An Admiral on a foreign station lives on shore and has his wife and
family with him, this one has a house here, and another at Bermuda where they
pass the winter.    An Admiral's pay is £6 per day, with an allowance of another
£6 for table money, servants, etc.    The "Royal Alfred" carries 750 men, and is
larger than the "Audacious".    We sent two seamen home from Bermuda, who were
invalided, also one to gaol, having three others in this place from the "Royal
Alfred", three more have deserted since we came here, which we shall have to
obtain others in place of.


       May 16th    We have taken in six (91) months provisions and 200 tons of
coal, and are to sail on Monday afternoon for Bermuda.     I   have been on shore
this afternoon and had a good walk out into the country, the place is very
strongly defended, and there are plenty of troops here for its protection.




                                       32
The town is about the size of Leicester but not such a business place.        The
streets are all laid with tramways but are very dirty and illpaved, and 9 out
of every 10 houses are built of wood, the chimneys only being of brick, and
you may not      be   surprised to hear   some day of Halifax being burnt    like
Chicago.     Living is pretty cheap, but the climate is much colder than England,
yesterday we had snow, and the other night the northern lights were very bril-
liant for about three hours.


     (92) "While on shore I saw the mail come steaming in from England, and she
dropped anchor an hour ago, so we shall receive the letters tomorrow.          We
shall only be 8 days on the way back to Bermuda.       I told Willie to lend you
his letter from S. Thomas, not having time to write you from there, so that
you will have a descr iption of each place we visit.      From the papers I see
Roger is in full swing again, one of our seamen says he will give all his pay
to hear the conclusion of the trial when we reach home in 76.     May 19, we sail
at 4, the mail closes at 3.       The ship is full of visitors who have come all
the way from New York to see it, one Yankee Professor wishes to go to Bermuda
with us but not sure if he will.      The dates for postage are from Bermuda to
Fayal in the Azores, and only 1000 miles from England, to arrive by the 28th
of June, after the S. Michael to Madeira, then to S. Vincent, Cape Verdes,
arriving there July 22nd, Bahia in Brazil until the 27th of August,          from
thence to the Cape of Good Hope, by mails leaving England every 10 days, the
last to write by being Nov. 5th.


     ~'le   are 3 weeks behind the time appointed for    leaving Bermuda by the
Admiralty and are to make up for it before reaching the Cape.       The Admiralty
having the whole voyage marked out for us, with dates for arrival and depar-
ture from each place, the time for arriving in England being Mayor June 1876.
Yours sincerely,

H.M.S. "CHALLENGER",
Out at Sea, May 27, 1873


Dear Tom:
       We shall soon be at Bermuda again so will get another letter under
weigh.     We sailed from Halifax at 4 p.m. on the 19th leaving our letters on
board the "Royal Alfred" for dispatch by the first mail.     Our departure from
there was of the gayest description, the wharves were crowded with people to
see us cast off from the dockyard jetty.       The Flagship "Royal Alfred" was
crowded with ladies and gentlemen, and the 750 seamen belonging to her all
stood in the rigging and cheered as we steamed past; while their band gave us
"Auld Lang Syne".    The weather was (95) bitterly cold when we left, but 3 days
after we were in the Gulf Stream, and the heat was almost unbearable, the iron
was all dripping with moisture and everything in the ship was damp, so much
that braziers of red hot coals had to be hung on the lower decks to dry them,
and being under steam all the time made it so much worse.    The sudden changes
in weather are very unhealthy and trying to weak constitutions, and we have a
great many on the sick list with rheumatics and sow fever.    The stone for the
schoolmaster came on board just before we left Halifax, a very nice one of
white marble; the day previous to starting, leave was given to go on shore for
seven hours,    which gave six more men chance to desert, so we were again
obliged to draw upon the "Royal Alfred·.


       (96) An American Scientific gentleman came with us from Halifax to see
how the dredging operations were carried on, he will leave at Bermuda, and go
to New York by mail boat.    We have had a head wind all the way and for 2 days
it was so rough that the soundings could not be taken; we have burned nearly
200 tons of coal coming from Halifax, and shall have to take in 300 more at
Bermuda, where coal is about £3.10 per ton.      We have come an entirely dif-
ferent course to what we steered when going, keeping further out into the
Atlantic, and dredging etc. every day; but the depth is not so great as the
sea is deeper in towards the Amer ican Coast -- the way we steered going to
Halifax.     The depths up today are - 80-200-1250-2,200-1800-2,800-2,200- and
today 2,675 fathoms.




                                       34
(97)
           On the 22nd the dredge brought up star-fish,        anemones,   insects,
etc. and on the following day, it and 1800 fathoms of line were carried away;
today the trawl net was sent down, and brought up a few insects -             which
Professor Thompson said were worth their weight in diamonds.       On the 24th be-
ing the Queen's birthday, the Captain issued to all hands one third of a pint
of sherry, and the band played selections during the evening.        This wine is
supplied to the ship as extra surveying stores, no other ship in the Navy is
allowed it.    It is issued at the discretion of the Captain to the men and boys
who are engaged in dredging, sounding, etc.       One-third of a pint for men, and
one-sixth for boys, about 40 are so employed, and they generally have it about
twice a week, and they (98) say that if nothing comes up in the dredge, no
wine given, though they work just as hard.     The Steward and I have to serve it
out - and being greatly interested in the dredging operations, generally drink
ourselves to its success.    -No more tonight-.


       May 30th, Dredging off the Bermudas.       On the 28th we sounded at 1760
fathoms,   and in the evening the revolving light on Bermuda islands hove in
sight, but they kept away all nigbt.        Yesterday we were dredging the whole
time on the west side of the island, depth varying from 1600 to 750 fathoms,
dredge brought up star-fish,     insects, etc.      We anchored last night in 30
fathoms of water about 2 miles from land, and all hands commenced fishing.
Several fine rock cod have been caught, but are not so fine eating as those
caught (99) off Halifax, the water being so much warmer.         We got up anchor
this morning and went round to the east side of the islands, soundings were
taken at 1700 fathoms the dredge brought up nothing.        After dinner the trawl
net was sent down, and after several attempts to haul it in, it carried away
wi th 1700 fathoms of line, so the men are of opinion that no wine will be
issued to night, as it has been about the most unluc'ky day we have had.


       May 31st, 9 p.m.   We took a black pilot on board at 6 a.m. this morning,
and stood in for the land, and at 4 p.m. we moored alongside the Dockyard
jetty in our old spot.      I told you before what a dangerous and intricate en-
trance existed here.      At present there is a large merchant ship        (100)   on




                                       35
shore at the north west of the islands which is not likely to be got off, and
in the Dockyard being repaired is a large steamer called the Petersburgh of
Leith, which also ran on a shoal.           These shoals exist 5 or 6 miles out at sea,
and lie between 8 and 12 feet beneath the water, their position is indicated
by the green water all round them, the deep being of a blue color.                  Standing
on the rising ground on shore, and looking seaward in any direction, hundreds
of these green patches are to be seen, especially when the sun is shining.
They are not visible unless you are some distance from and above the water,
for that reason the Pilot in charge of the ship, sits upon the foretop and
sings out "Starboard a point, a port" as the case may be.


(101)
        The "Royal Alfred" ran aground about 6 weeks ago, and had to go in dock
to have her false keel replaced.        She draws 25 feet of water, we draw 22.           One
of the Scientific party returned on board from New York, they have been on a
pleasure tour and the rest will return before we leave.                 The weather is twice
as hot, as when we were here before, and the flies and mosquitos are ravenous
on to strangers.


        June 2nd.     We all went to the Dockyard church yesterday norning, and in
the evening I went again alone.              It is a very long, cool building, with
Venetian windows opening to the sea, and the organ and singing was very fair
indeed, the parson was also pretty good.               The congregation was nearly all
Naval and Military, with a few colored ladies and gentlemen from Somerset
(102) Island.        The colored people are fond of imitating the whites in dress,
etc., but the negresses have rather a job about the chignon, as their wool is
scarcely two inches long, but they manage with a net and sundries in the way
of stuffing.        It was raining on the way to church, and the black ladies could
be seen half a mile from the church running with their small parasols wet
through, their white muslin over their heads, and skirts raised very consid-
erablY1 the chignon hanging rather limp by the time they arrived.                   We had a
regular storm while in church, and the skies after the sun went down were a
splendid light, such a sunset as is never seen in England.                  I have just been
to bathe, the water is beautiful, we go every morning and evening.                We had the
usual quantity of black washerwomen on board (103) this morning, and all ready
to   swear   they were      the   parties    who   washed   for   you   before,   and   finish



                                              36
up by hoping "You had pleasant passage, Sare, you remember me, Sare, Jemima
Tricker, Sare".     At present there are here H.M.      Ships "Terror",    "Vixen",
"Fly", and a large old line of battle ship called the "Irresistible", used as
a temporary domicile by the crews of ships that are being repaired in the
floating dock.    The "Challenger" is going in the great dock on Wednesday, and
all the ship's company, Officers, etc., will live on board the "Irresistible"
for a day or two.    The other men of war here belong to the North American and
West Indian Squadron.     The English Mail,    via "S. Thomas" came       in   at   12
o'clock, and has sailed again for Halifax.    I have sent a letter home by her,
but the mail which leaves on Friday (l04) next via New York, will be home as
soon, and very likely before this one, so shall not close yours.      The letters
which arrived in the mail have not come on board yet.


     June 5th - The mail closes at 4 p.m. so I must finish at once.            The S.
Thomas mail brought us no letters, so shall have no more until we reach Fayal
at the Azores.    All the curiosities, etc., that have thus far been obtained,
are going home in the same mail which brings this.      We are not going in dock
now before we get to the Cape of Good Hope, or Sydney.      The coal is coming on
this week, and 6 months biscuit next week.     Some of the old is quite mouldy
and contains maggots and weevils, etc., but of course it has to be eaten, and
I expect we shall get worse before we get better.


     The rest of th~ pleasure party, con-(105)sisting of Lord Campbell, 2 or 3
scientifics, and other officers returned from New York ~n the mail boat yes-
terday, some of them have been away nearly 2 months.      We expect to sail hence
to the Azores, about June 13th and shall most likely be at Fayal by July 8th,
Madeira the 18th and S. Vincent, the 30th.    But the Admiralty have the letters
altered at the Post Office when the dates are incorrect, so that if you ad-
dressed a letter to Fayal, Azores, and it was not likely to arrive there in
time to catch us, it would be crossed out, and put Madeira, so that you may
always depend on its arriving some time or other.




                                      37
     We had a letter in the last mail, addressed to a seaman, for H. M. Ship -
"Challenger" on her voyage round the world, Mediterranean, or elsewhere, and
it was (106) at Halifax as early as i f it had been directed there.       On the
3rd, H.M.S.     "Fly· sailed for England to payoff,     having been out here 4
years.     Our brass band played her out of the harbor, they have improved won-
derfully, and by the time we get back will be good musicians.     The same day a
merchant seaman belonging to the "Petersburgh" in dock here, was crushed be-
tween the ship and a boat, by which his thigh was broken in two places. One of
our surgeons attended him, and had him conveyed to the Naval Hospital.       The
same night one of our seamen came on board three parts, seven eighths, and
fell from the hatchway on to the iron cable, causing a dreadful cut across his
left eye.     The gravestone we brought from Halifax, went to the cemetry (107)
yesterday for erection, and I intend going to see it on Sunday afternoon.     It
is a large marble cross of pretty design, costing L16, it bears the following
inscription -- "This stone is erected by the Officers and Crew of H.M.S.
·Challenger", to the memory of Adam Ebbels, Naval Schoolmaster, who died at
Bermuda, April 4th, also to wm. H. Stokes, 1st Class Boy, who was killed March
25th,    1873 off the West India Islands.     "In the midst of life we are in
death".     The Governor of Bermuda and family were on board yesterday 1 and in
the evening they gave a ball to our Officers.       As these letters have to go
through New York Post Office, we have to put two stamps on them.    Bye the time
you get this we shall be in mid-Atlantic, and much closer to England 1 Fayal
and S. Michael, Azores, is where (108) most of the oranges come from that are
sold -in England, but I think we shall be too early for them.        The islands
belong to Portugal.     4:00 p.m. mail just going to close -- another man went to
hospital today with cholera, brought on through eating too many cucumbers,
tomatoes, bananas, etc.      Two other seamen are breaking their leave, and there
is L3 reward out for them, we think they have left the island in the steamer
"Petersburgh" which sailed this morning for New York, if not, we shall soon
have them on board again, as they can't walk off the island.


        Believe me to be -
        The Great Circumnavigator,
        Joseph Matkin
