(109)
H.M.S. ·Challenger"
Mid Atlantic, June 21st 73.


Dear Tom:
        You will be surprised to hear that I have been very ill since I wrote
last, and have got quite thin, but am improving every day, and have felt so
much better since, that on the whole I think it has done me good.      Bermuda is
a very unhealthy place in summer, and the south-west wind always brings sick-
ness with it at those islands.     With it came the dysentry about 5 days before
we sailed, and was blowing when we left, and nearly all our Ship's company had
it, officers and men, some only in a mild (110) form, others very severely, I
among the latter, but got rid of it soon after we were clear of the island.
For 5 days I ate nothing and was on Patent Beef Tea diet the whole time, and
after it left me, was as weak as if I had been laid up with fever for a month
or two.     We left two bad cases behind at Bermuda Hospital, and have still one
or two down with it.     It attacked the people on shore, as well as us, except
the negroes, who have passed out of it.     Unless the wind changes it frequently
pr9ves fatal, and the best remedy is to leave the island and push out to sea
for a breeze, which our Captain did as soon as we got the coal and all stores
in, and the repairs made good.     He said he should not like to leave a dog of
his on those islands, and am sure (111) I never wish to see them again.        We
did not leave our m~ring until the evening of the 12th June, and anchored in
10 fathoms of water to the east of the islands that night~     Early in the morn-
ing we got up anchor and sailed away to the Azores, with the wind right behind
us, and at present are more than half way to there, having had the counter
trades blowing us on the whole journey.     The distance was about 2,100 miles to
Fayal, and we are today 980 miles off, besides having obtained soundings,
etc. every day.    The passage thus far has been very pleasant and invigorating,
and I feel much better than I did, before being doubled up with the dysentry.
The depth thus far has been 2,700 - 2,875 - 2,700 and 3,000 fathoms.     At pres-
ent the dredge is overboard and (112) will be up in an hour's time.       This is
Saturday evening, and the band is playing away splendidly on the main deck,
the officers having dinner, and most of the men dancing, or mending their
clothes.




                                       39
        Several fine specimens of zoophytes have been obtained this week, and on
Thursday the dredge brought up a fine piece of pure amber, from a depth of
over 3 miles.    It was the best day we have had this passage, and-was the cause
of wine being issued to all hands.      We are to take enough wine at Madeira this
time to last us all the commission.


        The flies and mosquitoes that were so troublesome at Bermuda, all dis-
appeared as soon as we got to sea, and will sleep until we get in harbour
again.     Some of the men were covered with (113) mosquitoe bites, but I escaped
altogether, having been sucked dry by them some time ago in Australia.         The
depth today is 2,700 fathoms and the dredge has brought up mud, insects, etc.


        June 27th, 300 miles from Fayal.      Wind dropped again, but it has been
splendid up to today, and we shall most likely anchor at Fayal on Monday the
30th.     On Sunday, 22nd, we had church in the forenoon, and took soundings at
2,750 fathoms, after which made all plain sail again.      On the 23rd, sounded at
2,700 fathoms and made sail again, passing several ships during the day. On
the 24th sounded at 2,170 fathoms,       and sent down the trawl net, by which
several fine specimens of zoophytes etc., were obtained.      On the 25th sounded
at 2,200 fathoms and sent down the trawl again (114) which was 6 hours corning
up and was very rich in     rarities~   a large blubber fish 5 feet in length was
the first to be hauled out, and in the evening it was placed in water on deck,
and emitted a wonderful green phosphorescent light, but in the morning no fish
was to be seen, it 'had exploded or dismembered itself in some way, and the
atoms and pieces were floating about.


        Several other species of cuttle fish have the wonderful power of ex-
ploding themselves1 each separate atom still possessing life and motion in the
water.     But this was not considered such a rarity as a large prawn of a bright
scarlet colour, which was in the bottom of the net among smaller creatures.
It had a sort of spike protruding from its head, and further appendages in the
shape of wings.     I have (lIS) not seen it yet, but hope to by and bye, so the
25th was quite an eventful day for the Scientifics, and they were in rare
feather.     Yesterday we sounded at 1,675 fathoms, and trawled after dinner, a




                                         40
few small specimens were obtained but nothing of any consequence.                         A small
turtle was caught asleep in the water by the boat, which is generally lowered
for fishing purposes while the trawling and dredging are going on.                       Today the
depth was 1675 again, the trawl has been down, but has come up bottom upwards,
and   2000    fathoms of line carried away,          that was being used to test the
strength of the current.          We have been in the Gulf Stream for the last week,
and the air is very damp indeed.


      July 1st, 2:00 p.m.          We are just running     (116)      into Fayal, and in 10
minutes more the Commander will be singing out "Let to the starboard anchor",
the engines will cease turning, and the Portuguese boats will be swarming
round us with fruit, fish, and all manner of good things.                    We have been told
to have our letters ready tonight in case there should be a mail leaving, so I
must have this all ready for closing. On the 28th, Sunday, we had church in
the morning, and kept under sail all day~ yesterday we sounded at 1000 fathoms
and sighted the island of Flores, 70 miles N.W. of Fayal.                 We should not have
done so, only were blown out of our direct course on Sunday.


      The land was high but we never went nearer than 8 miles to it, and kept
under (117) easy steam all night.            This morning we sounded at 1000 fathoms and
caught several fish, we also passed out of the Gulf Stream, and the sea was
swarming with cuttle fish, blubber fish, nautilus, etc., of the most brilliant
colours and curious forms, some like snakes 8 and 9 feet ~n length, but quite
harmless, and as thick as bees, at night these creatures shine like stars in
the water, and the prow of the ship scatters them like fire.                   The Gulf Stream
separates into two parts between Florida and Bermuda, one part (the largest)
runs as far north as the Banks of Newfoundland, where it is met by another
current of icy water from the poles, and turned to the east right across the
Atlantic, past Land's End, and the Irish Coast, and raising the temperature of
the British (118) islands several degrees in winter, also the coast of Norway,
and it can be traced as far north as Spitzbergen, after which it cools and
returns again to the Equator, as an under current 2000 or more fathoms below
the surface of the water, you are aware I told you the temperature in the
tropics is only 2 degrees above the freezing point at 3000 fathoms.                        This is
the   Polar    current which gradually rises           to the    surface as        it nears the
Equator,      and   as   its   temperature   rises   through    the   heat    of   the    sun,   it
                                              41
commences its journey to the poles again, raising as it goes the temperature
of every country that is washed by its waters.            If it were not for the Gulf
Stream,    Scotland would   be    as    cold    as Labrador,    and England colder   than
Newfoundland, those countries being in the same latitude.               (119) The smaller
branch of the Gulf Stream flows across to these islands, passing to the north
of them into the Bay of Biscay, making Lisbon and Portugal so much warmer in
winter than New York, which is in the same latitude.                It is the Gulf Stream
which has kept us so long in the Atlantic (North) having followed its track
for so many miles, and I think Professor Thompson is to give another lecture
next week, chiefly about it, when of course I shall chalk him down, and send
it to you.        The islands of Fayal and pico hove in sight at 10 a.m. this
morning and we have been all this time coming up to them.             They are over 6,000
feet high, and similar to Madeira in appearance, the Peak of Pico is over 8000
feet high and at present is up in the clouds, the day being very hazy. The
Azores are a group of (120) islands 800 miles west of Portugal (to which they
belong) and 1100 from Southampton, are all fertile and inhabited.             Their names
are Fayal, Pico, Corvo, S. Jorge, Flores, Graciosa, Terceira S. Miguel, and
S. Maria.    Terceira is the seat of government, but S. Miguel, or S. Michael's
is the largest and most fertile, there the English Consul "Hon. E. Monson"
resides, and there we expect to find our letters.              The area of the whole group
is 1134 square miles, and the total population 252,000.             The exports are wine,
oranges, brandy, grain, etc., a great deal of which goes to England.               Neither
of the islands possesses a good harbour, and if it comes on to blow, ships
have to stand out to sea.        Our Channel Fleet generally come here and Madeira,
once a year, in winter.     Nearly all the oranges (121) that come to England are
from S. Michael's, the quantity sent last year amounting to 250,000 boxes.


     I hope we shall get some fresh meat and bread here, for I am a long way
behind in body yet,      and as thin as a rat.           We are now running      into the
anchorage off the capitol town "Horta" by name, and the boat is already to go
on shore to see for letters, and hope we may get some for we have had no
English news later than May 8th.           We heard a strange rumour just before we
left Bermuda, about "Sir Roger" that he was proved to be Arthur Orbon, and had
murdered    the   real Sir Roger       in South America 20 years ago,         and was now
indicted for it.      Considering that there is no submarine telegraph to Bermuda


                                           42
from any other place and no mail having arrived there (122) from England, or
any other place, I for one, did not believe itJ and expect to hear something
fresh about -The Claimant- by this mail, and think his career of deception
(which must have cost him many a sleepless night during the last few years) is
nearly played out.


     The corn fields on the islands look beautiful, and it appears to be ready
for cutting, the vineyards too have a fine fresh appearance.      We leave in the
morning I think for S. Michaels, so don't expect I shall get on shore here.
There goes the anchor in 15 fathoms of water, and I must go up and have a look
at the town of Horta, distant 1/4 of a mile.


     8 p.m.   Horta is an extensive place, much larger than Funchal, or santa
Cruz, and seen from the sea looks like Brighton built all along the beach, the
houses are all white, and it appears very clean, and the convents which are
built right up the mountains, shine in the sun splendidly -- At present the
bells are ringing for evening mass -- not in a peal like ours at Oakham, but
one deep tenor bell ringing     very slowly,   and   sounds   so solemn from   the
mountain heights.    As soon as we dropped anchor the quarantine boat came
alongside, and after a good deal of delay, gave us pratique, at the same time
informing the Captain, that the small pox was very bad on shore, so he allowed
no one to go on, except himself, with one or two officers and Scientifics.
The English vice-consul came off, and brought one or two letters for           the
Captain, which had come by the pOrtuguese mail from Lisbon, our letters are
either at S. Michaels (124) or Madeira.    The small pox was brought here by a
British merchant ship from Boston, America, and we are told all the other
islands have it, and Madeira alsoJ i f so our stay there will be very short
indeed.   The fruit boats are alongside with mackeral, bread, cheese, eggs,
green figs, apricots, pears, damsons, etc.     Apricots and figs are 12 for a
penny, ripe and beautiful, and have brought 6 dozen of each which will last me
to S. Michael.   None of the pOrtuguese are allowed on board, and we have to go
down to their boats alongside to purchase anything.

July 2nd. Between the islands of Fayal, pico, and S. George.       Dredging.     We

     The peak of pico has been visible all day right above the clouds, i t

July 3rd. The peak is in sight, still r ising high above the clouds and it

     The depth today was 900 fathoms and the dredge brought up a few sponges

Eggs are cheap, 24 a shilling, I won't tell you how many some of our men ate

        July 5th.   Nearly all hands are on shore, I hope to go tomorrow.              8 p.m.
They have nearly all returned, but most of them intoxicated, the wine here is

saW1 the climbing up the ship's side, and falling in on the quarter deck for

properly, so they were nearly all reported, and will have their leave stopped

        Sunday, July 6th, 9 p.m.        I was not able to go on shore, for which I was
very glad, but am going to-morrow.               We had church this morning and after
dinner leave was given to all hands, when the return was worse than last
night, and there have been several pitched battles on deck since they came

several are in such .a mad state that it requires 2 or 3 men to hold them.                   To
                                                                     -
get drunk with wine is worse than with beer, and requires 2 or 3 days before a

      July Bth, Tuesday.      I went on shore yesterd·ay afternoon with two of my
messmates and spent a very pleasant day.          We hired a donkey each for 1/6, and
went for a ride into the country, and should like you to have seen us making
the donkey gallop, and the boys who owned them about 2 miles astern, singing
out for us to stop, but the donkeys did not understand English and the more we
said "Woa, Woa" the faster they went.          Only their countrymen can stop them by
speaking to them.      The boys carry a big stick with a spike in it, and they
always stick it into one place, and we soon found out the sore one, and by
touching it with our fingers the animals would start off and never stop until
the boys could get near enough to make them hear.           It was fine sport and the
country was beautiful, there were whole (132) forests of orange trees, but the
fruit was quite green and will not be ripe before September.               We saw them

pulling the corn and    ~     treading it out in the open fields, they don't cut

but only a few ugly old women and Sisters of Mercy seemed to be going.          We saw

Dear TOm
        Through the Commander's impatience in closing the mail before the steamer
was ready to sail, I was unable to answer the Fayal and Madeira letters.
within 10 minutes after they were sent away I received two from you and six
others, and was then informed that the mail bag was again opened for           two
hours, so had time to write a short note home.      yours was the only one sent me
to Fayal, but it was no fault of yours I did not receive it there, as the
British Consul sent it with others onto         (138)   San Miguel and Madeira, by
H.M.S. "ADRIANE n •    I suppose the blackberries will be looking up by the time
this reaches you,      and I would rather have a walk along Barrowden pasture
again than at all the Madeira's, S. Michael's or Teneriffe's, we have been to,
or shall visit.       I was very pleased to read of Joe pepper's success in the
Mercury; he is certainly the best and most creditable pupil that Mr. Creaton
has turned out.       I read in the papers all about the Shah's visit, I should
have liked to have been in the "Audacious" at the time.           If ever the Shah
visits England again, I should think they won't make such a fuss about him, or
waste so much money, for I have never read or heard that he has done us any
good, and don't expect he ever will.        still I suppose like the Siamese Twins
and the two headed nightingale, (139) he was a novelty for about 10 minutes.
As regards Roger, I should think he will soon be in fashion again, and expect
by the time we reach Bahia it will be all up with him.         There is generally a
pitched battle among the sailors about him after we receive a mail.




                                       48
        We only stayed 24 hours at Madeira for the smallpox was very bad there,
so of course no leave was given, so am glad I went on shore when there in

fresh meat, vegetables, bread, fruit, etc. peaches, bananas, and figs were
very plentiful there.              The Captain gave a party just before we sailed, and
took them in the ship over to the Desert Islands, 25 miles off, but the ladies
were very sea sick and glad to return.                     Our (140) brass band was playing all
afternoon, and the ladies and officers were dancing on the upper deck.                                   At 1

northeast trade winds behind us and at present are only 570 miles from Saint
vincent, and expect to arrive there on the 27th.                         At present we are off the
Canary Islands, and have been dredging and sounding all the way.                            On Saturday
we were dredging close to the island of palma, and some fine black coral was
obtained at a depth of 1100 fathoms.


        We    shall       get   letters   at   Saint     Vincent.        We   are   to   have     a      fresh

        The Portugese send all their convicts and political prisoners there, I

been sent out, and a reward of £20 offered for information, but nothing has

        August 1st.   We have finished coaling having taken in 250 tons at £5
per ton, and I hear we are to sail for Bahia on Sunday evening the 3rd, inst.
On Monday     H.M. Troopship ftSmoonft came in for coal, sailing again on Tuesday
for Cape (144) Coast Castle, distant 700 miles.        She took in 500 tons of coal,
and was 10 days from Portsmouth, and has on board 300 mar ines and alot of
stores for the Ashantee War.


        No information concerning the fate of the missing schoolmaster has come
to light, but his clothes and effects were brought on board yesterday and
overhauled.     A more disgraceful affair I never heard tell of than the loose
manner he was sent off to join the ship, and the unchr istian treatment he
received on his arrival here from the British Consul.          From the date of his
appointment to this ship, he kept a daily journal, which closes on the day of
his disappearance.     I   read it all through last night, and this is what      I    was
able to deduce from it.        His name was Briant, and he came from near            (145)
Bristol, he was 33 years of age, and had been a schoolmaster in the Navy for
10 years.     Was a supernumary on board the Royal Adelaide, when he was ordered
to proceed to Southampton for passage to S. Vincent by mail boat for                   the
ship.     A second cabin passage was given him from the Admiralty, and he sailed


                                        50
from England early in July calling at Lisbon for some hours when he went
ashore, and of course spent some money.     He arrives on this barren island on
the 19th with only £2 in his pocket, and after describing the kind of people
on shore here in his journal; he goes on to say -- "Having such a small sum of
private money with me, and not being furnished by the Admiralty with any funds
to defray my expenses on disembarking, I consider my best plan is to (146)
consult the British Consul at once about it.     The Consul kindly informed me,
he says, that the "Challenger" might arrive in 10 days, or she might be a
month, he really could not say, but he told me I might manage to subsist at a
hotel until her arrival at the rate of about 8/ per day.       I then enquired,
"can you furnish me the means for subsistence until the ship's arrival for I
have only about £2 with me, and you shall then be reimbursed everything."    His
answer was -- "I have no instructions that would justify me in so doing, and
to me, you are no more than any other British subject."     After this pleasant
information (he says), I walked about the place to collect myself and consider
what was best to be done, and I have calculated that I shall be able (147) to
manage at least a week if I only sleep at the hotel.       I must pass away the
time during the day by walking about the island, and must do the best I can in
the town for food."


     This is the last entry in his journal, for on the same afternoon (eight
days before we arrived) he left the hotel to go for a walk, and was never
again seen alive.     He was wearing his watch at the time, and had his money
about him, and it is considered by people who know the place well, that he has
been murdered for his money and buried, which is no uncommon circumstance on
this island, for I have been told that six British subjects have disappeared
in the same manner during the time the present Counsul has resided here.     The
poor schoolmaster had seven or eight hundred pounds in shares at home, so that
his embarrassment was only temporary.     I suppose he considered he had funds
sufficient for his journey expecting to find the ship here on his arrival.     I
consider the Consul ought to be superseded at the least; he is getting £400 a
year for looking after the interests of British subjects, and that is the way
he treated one of his own countrymen.     Sub Lieutenant Harston came out in the
same mail boat, and was nearly in the same predicament on landing here, but



                                     51
the Consul invited him to his house and then kept him until our arrival,
merely because he was a commissioned Officer.      People say a Freemason can find
friends in any part of the world, but poor Briant could not though he was one
of the fraternity, and had been a considerable time.


      August 4th.   The mail boat sails in an hour's time and this will reach
you about the 15th.    If you write to Bahia by mail leaving Liverpool, August
27th, I shall receive it there, where we shall be by September 16th and stay a
few days, the distance is 3,100 miles.       I was on shore yesterday, and climbed
to the top of one of the highest mountains, where a flag staff has been
erected, upon which scores of names have been engraved, and of course added
mine to the number in letters one inch deep, also putting Oakham, Rutland, so
that if anyone else belonging to the large county ever ascends that mountain,
his eyesight will be gladdened.       The island is totally destitute of any sort
of vegetation, everything is scorched up by the sun.         The view from the top
was   grand,   nothing but mountains and sea to be seen.         The climbing was
difficult and dangerous, and very few would care to attempt it.         The people
are mostly negroes of a poor description and are nearly all employed in
coaling the barges, and getting out coals from ships, the women working at it
the same as the men, and smoke their pipes equally as well.          They are very
ugly, and not all bashful, thinking nothing of undressing on the beach and
bathing without any sort of gown whatever.        The children run entirely naked,
and can swim like fishes.     We sail in the morning for S. Tago one of the other
islands -- thence to Bahia.       Themail boat that brings this has come from
there,   where yellow fever    was very bad     indeed,   so at present she   is   in
quarantine.    I have another letter to finish so must conclude, wishing you to
observe that I am all serene and still unmarried.


      Believe me, Faithfully yours,
      Joe Matkin.

H.M.S. Challenger, Sierra Leone, August 16, 1873


Dear Tom
       It will be at least a month before this letter leaves the ship, but must
write it by installments as the information comes to hand.                         We left St.
Vincent on the 5th for another of the Cape Verde Islands, called S. Tago, 200
miles further south.      No more information concerning the fate of the missing
schoolmaster turned up, and everyone on board considers that he was murdered,
and bur ied long before our ar rival.               Between St. Vincent and S.            Tago we
sighted 2 or 3 islands belonging to the same group.                   One of them Fogo is a
volcano 9,200 feet high.        We were two days on the passage and found S. Tago
quite a paradise compared with St. Vincent.               We remained there two days and
quite enjoyed it.      The island is the largest of the whole group, and the chief
town is the seat of government, it was quite an extensive and well built
place, and we found more Portuguese than at St. Vincent, still the majority of
the population were     negro~s.      The island abounds with cocoanut and date palms
which grow close to the water's edge.              Bananas and plantain were the finest we
have yet. seen, and pineapples, mangoes, etc. were very plentiful.


       There is any amount of fish in the bay, a party of our seamen caught
enough to supply all hands for breakfast and dinner.                    Of course I went on
shore and spent a ve;y pleasant afternoon among the palm groves.                     I bought a
cocoanut off the tree for 1 d, but it was not so good as when kept some time.
When the green shell is on them they are twice as large as those you see in
England.     They grow in enormous clusters               at   the   top of   the    tree,       just
underneath the branches.       There were monkeys and parrots on the island, one of
our boys bought a monkey for 9/6, and let him run up the rigging, when he was
made   to chase   it    for   three   hours    until    he caught     it,   and    then    had     to
throw it overboard so it was not a good speculation for him. Monkeys, etc.,
are not allowed in the ship until we are homeward bound.


       The Governor of the Cape Verdes came on- board before we sailed and looked
over the ship.      We took in 2 bullocks, 300 cocoanuts and 5000 limes for the
ship's company and sailed on the 9th for St. Paul's Rocks.                        The Captain is
going to run the African coast down as far as Cape Palmas, then sail along the
equator to St. Paul's Rocks.            This is almost doubling the distance for we
                                              53
shall be fur ther away at Cape Palmas than we were at S. Tago.       Today we are
off Sierra Leone (or the white man's grave).     For the last two or three nights
the sea has presented a wonderful phosphorescent appearance in consequence of
certain minute animals flourishing most abundantly in this particular portion
of the Atlantic.    The ship appears to be literally ploughing her way through
fire, and the surface of the water is lighter than I have ever seen it on the
brightest moonlight night.


     August 29th.    Made fast to a rock in mid-Atlantic.      The depth between
S. Tago and these rocks of St. Paul is on the average about 2 1/2 miles and
some magnificant specimens have been obtained in the trawl net.        We sighted
these famous rocks on the 27th and have been here two days surveying and
sounding round them. When we first sighted them they looked like a railway
train rising out of the water and at 6 p.m. we steamed close up to them and
made the ship fast to one of the rocks by a hawser.      There are seven distinct
shapes of rocks, and rocks such as I have never seen before, for all the world
like rough pumice stone and the edges as sharp as a knife.      The whole surface
of them would not cover a square acre in extent.      They are 850 miles from the
African, and 650 from the American continent, and are only 90 miles from the
equator.   The sea all round them is 2 miles in depth.     They only rise 60 feet
out of the water and as it breaks allover them, landing is very difficult.


     There is not a particle of vegetation on them and with the exception of
thousands of sea birds, no animal life whatever, neither is there a drop of
fresh water.   They are out of the track of any ships, and as nothing is to be
obtained, no vessel ever comes, the last known to call here was a man-of-war
in 1845.   The birds are called boobies and are about the size of a goose, but
have very long sharp beaks and claws.      They make no nest but lay their eggs on
the bare rock, and feed the young ones on flying fish.      The rocks are swarmed
with them and are certainly their owners.        When the boat first landed they
were so. tame that the men could knock them over with their sticks, but are
much wilder now.    The sea round the rocks abounds with fish and some scores of
fine ones called cawalks have been caught, enough to last all hands two days.




                                      54
        Yesterday was a grand holiday on board, and all who wished could land and
go fishing.      Of course I went and stretched my legs and also had the skin
burned off my neck by the great heat of the sun.              But spent a pleasant
afternoon in fishing and teasing the old birds, and should think am about the
only Oakhamite who ever landed there.        Today the boats are away sounding, and
we sail tonight for the island of Fernando de Noronha, 400 miles distant. Pass
onto the next island - Sept. 3.        At anchor off the island of Fernando de
Noronha.


        We crossed the line at 1 p.m. on August 30th.         No shaving, etc., was
allowed, but the captain issued wine to all hands in honour of the event.        We
have now finished operations in the north Atlantic, having crossed it in three
different directions and visited most of the islands south of England.         I see
by a book I      am   now reading that the Canary Islands were the first to be
discovered by the Spaniards in 1390, next came Porto Santa and Madeira in
1410, after which the Azores and Cape Verdes in 1420, (page 160) all by the
Portuguese.     The Canary Islands was the final point of departure by Columbus
on his voyage of discovery and at that time Teneriffe was throwing out fire
and ashes from its peak.     On his second voyage he sailed from the Cape Verdes,
and the last land seen was the peak of Fuego, also an active volcano at that
time.     The town of S. Tago where we were the other day was burnt down by the
English under Francis, Drake in 1553.        This island hove in sight on the 1st of
September and we anchored off the town the same night.          -We sounded at 2000
fathoms just off the island.       It belongs to Brazil and is used as a self
supporting convict settlement. It is about 10 miles long and 2 1/2 broad ,and
has 2 or 3 high peaks on it.      The highest about 1500 feet, hangs over on one
side (161) and looks as if it would fall with a slight push.          The island is
very fertile, but we have been unable to get a single thing here, and all the
officers can manage to buy is a few turkeys, melons and bananas.         We came on
purpose to survey the island and harbour, and yesterday morning all the boats
were got out and provisioned ready.           Just as they were on the start, the
Governor of the Island, an obstinate old fool, took it into his head that we
had come to see what sort of an island it waS1 whether it would be a desirable
possession at any time for England, so he refused to allow the boats to land
or take a single thing from the island. The Captain went on shore and tried to


                                        55
explain what we had come for           (162), but the old fellow was too stupid to
understand, so the Captain returned on board.


        The boats are all in again and in half an hour we sail for Bahia, distant
700 miles.      It appears that everyone on the island is a convict, male and
female, except the soldiers and officials, and they have to support themselves
by cultivation, etc.      The nearest land is 500 miles distant, so there is no
chance of escaping.     The convicts live in houses of their own during the day,
but all sleep under a guard up at the fort at night, and anyone later than
eight p.m. is flogged.      They wear what clothes they like, and are allowed to
traffic    among   themselves    but   not    with   strangers   without   the   Governor's
permission.     Some of them are allowed to go fishing in tiny canoes made out of
hollow trees and propelled with a small paddle (163)              but they are not very
safe, and afford no means of escaping unless it is on board a ship.                For that
reason they don't care for a ship to come here at all unless it is a Brazilian
vessel with supplies, etc.       They speak the portuguese language but a few know
English.     One of them asked one of our boat's crew if he had any old European
newspapers, as he had seen none for 10 years.               Most of them are here for
life.     The murderers and worst criminals are strictly confined.


        Sunday, September 7th.     Five Hundred miles from Bahia.          We have had bad
winds and weather and at present are just this side of pernambuco under steam.
We s~ghted the Amer'ican continent last night off Cape S. Roque and saw the sun
set behind the land.      Several vessels about.          We expect to be at Bahia by
the 11th or 12th (164)      there to receive our letters and get in some fresh
provisions.


        Sunday afternoon, September 14th.         Just steaming in to Bahia.       We shall
be at anchor again in an hour's time, and this evening hope to be reading one
of your letters, and tomorrow have a look at the newspapers, etc.                  This has
been a long passage, 60 days from Madeira.              We have been steaming down the
coast of South America all the week, and in sight of it nearly all the way.
The land is not so high as the coast of Devonshire.                We sighted pernambuco
lighthouse the other night and have been sounding and trawling all the week,
depth sometimes 2000 fathoms, at others only 14.            Some splendid specimens have


                                             56
been obtained in the trawl.       We are burning the last ton of coal now, so shall
have to fill up here for the Cape, (165) where we expect to be about the 5th
of November and to remain until the 6th of December.                I hope there is no
sickness here as they had yellow fever when we were at Madeira.            The weather
is very hot although it is only the beginning of summer yet.               Bahia is in
lat. 130 south of the equator.       This morning many miles from land we had some
splendid butterflies come on board and at present the ship is swarmed with
them, and suppose we shall soon have the flies and mosquitoes round us.


     September 15th.      Anchored in the Bay of Bahia.    We had not enough coal to
bring us in, so had to sail in and were too late to get any letters last
night, but this morning the mail from England came in 30 hours before her time
and I received seven letters, two being from you.         I like to (166) hear of Joe
pepper's success.      YOU    can tell him that the Naval Surgeons are almost all
Irish and Scotch men of very doubtful abilities, promotion is very slow, and
the pay small until they are old men, but don't suppose he has any idea of
joining the Navy, as it is only fellows who can't get on anywhere else that
apply for an Assistant surgeon's commission in the navy.


     Regarding "Roger" I am more in a fog than ever, and shall read no more of
his trial until its culmination.


     rhe "Daily News'" sent is the latest I have seen, as the mail was only 18
                                                                -
1/2 days on     the   journey,    5,200 miles,   and calling at Saint Vincent and
pernambuco for    coal,      she stayed here 8 hours and      sailed again    for   Rio,
Montevideo and Valparaiso.       From the British Consul at St. Vincent she brought
news that the body of the missing schoolmaster had been found in a deep gully
at the foot of a mountain, but owing to its having lain there for a month
(167) they were unable to say whether the man was murdered or accidentally
killed.


     Bahia is a splendid city seen from the sea, looks very like Lisbon, and
is qui te as large, but shall tell you all about it after I have been on
shore.    The Bay is splendid and the harbour full of shipping.         The oranges and
cigars are beautiful and very cheap.          The city is the 2nd in Brazil, and was


                                         57
once the capital.         Rio De Janeiro which now takes that honor is 850 miles
further south and where the Emperor lives.        The country of Brazil is almost as
large as Europe but the population including negroes and native Indians is
only 12 million.


        September 21st.     The mail leaves to-night (168) so I must close up at
once.     I have been on shore and had a good walk about the town and into the
country.     I was more surprised at the luxuriant vegetation than with anything
else here.     The creepers and tropical plants grow as thick as a jungle, and
the flowers and trees are beautiful.         The banana tree is the most prolific of
all in the world, and I believe it bears 15 times more abundantly than wheat.
The cocoanut palm and bread fruit trees are most handsome, the latter also
bears most plentifully and the fruit is very pretty and about as large as a
child's head, the rind being irregular like maize when ripe.         Guavas, custard
apples and alligator pears also grow here to perfection and pineapples to an
enormous size.      The birds and butterflies are magnificent, I think humming
birds most attractive, they are (169)         like flying gems, and their plumage
shines like gold, perching on to flowers as bees, and some of them are no
larger if it were not for their tails.         I shall bring some stuffed ones home
with me from Rio De Janeiro, it is much larger than Bahia, having 300,000
inhabitants.     The latter has about 150,000 of whom four-fifths are negroes,
who are of the same species as those at the Cape Verdes, and originally came
from-the same part of Africa.       They are very ugly, the women coarse and fat,
the native indian women are much more handsome.


        The greater part of these negroes are slaves and are let out for hire by
their masters for about 6 d. per day.         We had about 60 of them getting in our
coal, while the ship's company went on leave and they (170) got in 200 tons in
a day.     They live chiefly on Manioc flour, the same root from which tapioca is
made.     Bahia is a well built town, the houses are of stone and 5 or 6 stories
high, but the streets are very narrow and stink fearfully.         The negroes empty
all their refuse, etc. into the streets from the top story and if ever you
corne here, be sure to walk in the middle of the street.       No wonder that yellow
fever makes such havoc in this country, when the streets are so narrow and
badly drained.     The negroes occupy the greater part of the town.     The European


                                        58
merchants, etc. all live at one end of the place facing the sea.                    Very few of
the people can speak English.               The money        is all paper,   excepting copper
pennies,       the loss is considerable in changing the money for English.                  The
principal streets are all laid down for tramways, the cars being drawn by
mules.     Instead of      cabs     and omnibuses        they use sedan chairs carried by
negroes; some of our seamen spent a good deal in riding about in these chairs,
one or two are absent and most likely deserted, as there is a tremendous lot
of shipping here, a great many from America.                  The town is not very wide, but
nearly 6 miles in length, and I never was in such a place for churches, which
of course are all Roman Catholic, and such gaudy rubbishy affairs inside, all
candles, pictures and gilding.             There is a cathedral which is a little better
than the churches inside and out as well, but even that is nothing compared to
one of our own at home.           I looked in at Evening Mass and it was crowded with
negroes, chiefly women, and in full evening dress of course.                  The singing was
very fair.       The shops all close at six and after that the town is very quiet.
There are very few amusements              here,      only one   theatre and opera house      I
believe.        The soldiers are almost all negroes about 4 1/2 feet high and are
three times worse to look at than the Portuguese.                 The Brazilians also have a
bit of a navy.       There is a turret ship of theirs here now, which was built on
the Thames, and the seamen are nearly all negroes and are thrashed a good deal
at    times.      Just   ahead of    us    is   a    large   Amer ican man-of-war   called the
"Lancaster" but their men are not allowed on shore, as half of them ran away
at Rio.        They are paid very irregularly and bolt at every good opportunity.
As far as we have gone in this ship the deserters have been the very worst
among the ship's company.


       The American Admiral was on board yesterday looking over the ship, and we
have had a great many visitors off to the ship.                   Our brass band plays "Hail
Columbia" after "God Save the Queen" every evening at 8 o'clock.                     We sail on
the    25th of September      for    the Cape and arrive about the 1st of November
remaining until the 6th of December.                 I enclose the latest instructions as to
future dates and addresses.               You will get this about the 12th of OCtober,
quite getting on for winter in England.                  The summer will be just commencing
there and finishing at Australia, but (174) there is a little cold weather



                                                59
between the two.     Must now conclude as the mail leaves in an hour and shall
write again by the next from where we are.


     Yours faithfully,


     Joe Matkin.



H.M.S. Challenger, Tristan d'Acunha, Oct. 15, 1873


Dear Tom:
     We are lying at anchor again, but at a far different place to where I
wrote from last.     The temperature at Bahia was 82 0 in the shade, and at this
wonderful snow covered island today it stands at 45 0 , rather a sudden change
in 3 weeks - a'nt it?     Still, the change has driven the yellow fever out of
the ship, which was the object of our captain in running so far south before
standing to the east.      However   I   will commence my letter from the date of
closing the last -- September 23rd.


     I   was not over-struck with Bahia (176) and did not care to make a second
visit on shore there 1 nearly every night while we remained we used to see a
display of fireworks, etc., in the Cathedral Square, and the cathedral itself
was generally illuminated, all in honour of the Saints - and to please the
niggers.    Our naturalists procured some large serpents and native minerals
before we left to practice on, but they are all dead now and preserved in
spir its of wine.     There was a large iguana, or      immense lizard, which the
negroes are very fond of in a stew, also a racoon, an ant eater and a large
sloth, which was the sleepiest looking customer you ever saw, more like a
bundle of old hay.     He has a very thick skin which protects him from the bees
when robbing their honey, is more active in climbing than at anything else.
We lost two of our worst characters at Bahia by desertion, and the day before
we sailed sent a man on shore to hospital suffering from yellow fever.       This
hastened our departure (177) for we should have had to go in quarantine, had
we stayed any longer.    On the 25th of September at 5 p.m. we steamed away from
Bahia, and steered due south for 1100 miles so as to get into cool weather as


                                         60
soon as possible.        One more man - a marine - was attacked, but by being kept
on the upper deck in his hammock soon recovered.                  Captain Nares had also a
severe attack of some sort of fever, but is all serene again now.                    We had a
pair of goats on board, that we were to land on the island of Tr inidad for
breeding purposes, but the old gentleman died before we arrived so they ate
the old lady and did not call at the island, but are to do so on our return
trip in 1876.      We kept down the South American (178) coast for some distance
below Rio De Janeiro, then stood across for this island, sounding, dredging,
etc., about every third day.           The average depth thus far - from Bahia - has
been about 2100 fathoms, but the dredging has been very unsuccessful and the
bottom must have been very rocky, for we lost a dredge, a trawl net, and 2100
fathoms of dredging line which costs 8 d. per fathom, and the trawl a lot of
money.    The coal also for each day's dredging amounts to about £10 besides the
time and labour lost.


       We have had some very rough weather too this trip, been under double
reefed topsail for 2 days.            Only 2 vessels have been passed since leaving
Bahia,    for   this par t    of   the ocean is not often crossed. The only living
companions we have had are albatrosses, cape hens, cape pigeons, petrels and a
host of other sea birds.             The albatross is the monarch of sea birds (179)
frequently measuring 17 feet from wing to wing, and in flying does not flap
its wings but keeps them spread out.                These birds will follow a ship for miles
in cold latitudes and have very powerful wings and beaks.                     Some years ago
H.M.S. "Rutledge" on her way to Vancouver's island, lost a man overboard in a
gale of wind; a boat was lowered but just before it reached him, an albatross
swooped down and drove its beak into his skull, killing him on the spot.


       Perhaps you have read Coleridge's quaint poem "The Rhyme of the Ancient
Mariner" describing the calamities which occurred to a ship among snow and
ice,     through   one   of    the    seamen    shooting     an   albatross   with   his   bow,
(quotation): "Is it he, quoth one, is this the man, by Him who died on the
cross - With his cruel bow, he laid him low, the harmless albatross".                      (This
is all (180) at present in reference to albatrosses).




                                               61
    At 4 p.m. yesterday morning the peak of Tristan d' Acunha hove in sight
being a mass of snow and ice, rising 8300 feet above the level of the sea.               We
were 80 miles away then.        In the early morning objects at sea can be seen much
plainer than in broad daylight.          We hove to and sounded at 2150 fathoms, then
dredged but obtained nothing.        At 5 p.m. we steamed in towards the land, but
only anchored this morning at about 1/2 a mile from the settlement.


     The island was discovered in, I believe, the year 1530 by a Portuguese
navigator named Tristan da Canta, but owing to its isolated position in the
midst of an unsheltered and stormy ocean, no one ever thought of settling on
it until the year 1812 -- a few English, Scotch and American families settled
there and have themselves (181) and their children remained ever since.              There
are two other islands forming the group, all three in sight of each other and
rising very abruptly out of the water, this one almost perpendicularly to the
height of 6000 feet.         A goat could not ascent it.       So of course there is no
sea beach at all, but a terrific surf breaks all along the shores making it
very difficult for a boat to land except in the finest weather.                It is about
3 1/2 miles in length and two in breadth, but nearly all mountains, except a
small tongue of land which runs about 1/4 mile to the west, here the settlers
have built their cottages and graze their cattle.              Corn does not thrive but
potatoes,    and many sorts of vegetable          are    plentiful,   sheep,   cattle,   and
poultry are the most profitable articles on the island and the principal in-
ducement for a ship to call.        Fish and seabird eggs are_very (182) abundant.
In the winter seals and sea elephants come to breed, from these they obtain
their oil.    Flour, tea, sugar, coffee, etc., they procure from any ships that
may call, which are chiefly whalers, and English men-of-war.              The inhabitants
are very primitive and sociable in their habits,                living   almost   like one
family.     The profits derived from bartering, etc., with ships are placed in a
common fund, and equally divided among the children when they are sent out in
the world to shift for themselves.           The island will not support many, and as
the population gets too numerous, some of the children are sent away to the
Cape in passing vessels.        Only three men of war have been here during the last
eight years,        the last one   in 1867, was    the    "Galatea" under      the Duke of
Edinburgh, she took some of the (183) children to the Cape and her captain
baptized      all      the    children     and   marr ied     what     eligible     couples


                                            62
there were, for no clergy man resides there.              As soon as we anchored the whole
male     population   came   off   in   their    boats,    bringing   with    them   potatoes,
albatrosses eggs, etc.        They were dressed in var ious costumes and all wore
sealskin shoes, and wove worsted stockings.               They were a fine healthy looking
lot of men, some of them born on the island and never having once left it.
The women had a gipsy looking appearance, several of them were Creoles from
the Cape and St. Helena, but the native born children were very handsome.
There are no marriageable couples -- or our Captain would have conducted the
ceremony, for as many as wished.         The chief man went by the name of Mr. Green,
he is over 60, and has his mother (184) living with him - aged 91 - to whom he
wanted our Captain to give a passage to the Cape, at the old lady's request,
but he declined fearing that she might die on the way.                One man from each of
the seamen's messes was allowed to go on shore and purchase provisions for his
mess.     Nearly all of them have sheep, pigs, potatoes, many of them geese and
fowls.     A bullock weighing 61 1/2 stones was procured for the ship's company
and in exchange we gave them 2 casks of flour, 1 of vinegar, 1 of madeira
wine, a case of sugar, 50 Ibs. of chocolate, 20 Ibs. tea, 30 Ibs. tobacco,
some salt, lamp wicks and flannel.


        They were out of all these articles, but expect a supply shortly from the
Cape.     The present population is 84, the men all answer to their chr istian
names        except   "~r.   Green".      Tristan d' Acunha      is   the    farthest   from a
continent of any inhabited island in the world, it is 1750 miles southwest of
the Cape and 1000 southeast of Bahia.


        About 8 months ago, a Portuguese vessel was wrecked on the other side of
the island, with all her crew drowned.              The present season is early spring
here, but the snow is plentiful on the hill tops.              The time is almost the same
as in England, but we gain 16 minutes per day when under sail, as our course
is due east.     The men here report that on one of the other islands, 22 miles
from here, there are two German seamen who have lived there two years.                  We are
just leaving Tristan to sound, etc., round the other two islands and may hear
or see something of the ·German Crusoes·.




                                            63
        October 16th, at Inaccessible Island.        We anchored this morning close
under the (186) lee of this wild looking island and in a small cove about 200
yards in extent, we saw the hut of the two Germans and themselves walking down
to the beach.     Directly our boat landed, they came off and asked the Captain
to remove them from the island for they had been living on it for two years in
great hardship and with no probability at present of being removed.              After
hearing their story he consented to give them a passage to the Cape, and has
given them some clothes, etc., for their own were quite worn out and they had
neither boots nor stockings.       I have heard them relate their adventures and
will give you the roughest particulars.         They are brothers, Prussian seamen,
named Gustave and Frederick Stoltenhoff, speak excellent English, and are very
intelligent looking men.    On   the breaking out of the Franco Prussian war, they
were enrolled and served in the army besieging Metz, the elder rose to be 2nd
Lieutenant.      In the early part of        '71,   they were discharged with    their
regiment, and joined an American whale ship, which arrived at this island in
October '71.    As is not unusual in whalers, they were, with there own consent,
victualled and left on the island for three months to catch seals, while their
ship went farther     south, whaling,   but she never      returned and was     in all
probability lost.      They had the misfortune to lose their boat soon after
landing, and the beach where they had built their hut was entirely surrounded
by cliffs, or rather mountains, so that there was no opportunity of getting to
the other side of the island.       The patch of land in question was only about
200 yards (188) in extent, and on it they had sowed potatoes and vegetables
which thrived very well.     The island covers about 3 square miles, and rises
for 2000 feet on all sides, more or less precipitous.          On their side it rose
almost perpendicularly but fortunately there were several streams of fresh
water running down the clefts in the rocks, caused by the melting snow and
rain.      They tried hard to scale the cliff but found          it   impossible,     and
resolved at last to swim round the island, in hope of finding an easier ascent
to the sununit.     This they at length found and managed to reach the top
which was comparatively level,       and covered with rough vegetation,         but    it
abounded with wild boars of such a fierce and ferocious description, that they
soon found they should have to return again to their old haunt under the
cliff.     However they managed to (189) seize two tiny sucking pigs, and drag
them to their hut through the surf, building them a stye, and feeding them on


                                        64
potatoes, etc.     They soon increased, but not fast enough to supply them with
food, and they had occasionally to swim round and ascend to - shoot a boar.
They had a good supply of matches and ammunition.               Seals came in the winter
and penguins in such numbers that the beach was covered with their eggs.
These they used to eat, and feed their pigs on them partly.              After this manner
they have existed during the last two years, occasionally seeing a ship at a
great distance, but never one near enough to attract notice, until last night
when they saw a vessel coming under steam straight for their island home, and
they never     lost sight of     its light until she appeared and anchored this
morning, and found her name was the "Challenger", and this is the conclusion
of the "Stoltenhoffw story.       (190).


       We have been sounding, etc., round the island all day, while the Germans
have    been   picking   up   their   traps,    seal   skins,   etc.,    digging   up   their
vegetables which they gave the ship's company, with the three remaining pigs
and some hundreds of penguins's eggs, which they had stored up, knowing the
birds would soon be leaving the island for a colder region.                 Their hut they
burnt down, and are at present on board with their goods and chattels.                   They
have a sum of money which the paymaster has taken charge of for them.                    They
kept a log of their voyage and adventures, but were a day ahead in their
reckoning, not having known it was Leap Year.            They are translating their log
into English, and some of the scientifics and officers are already concocting
a regular (191) romance about it for the newspapers~ which I have no doubt you
will see, and find far more interesting than my account.                We are anchored for
the night close to the still smouldering hut, but leave early in the morning
to sound etc., round the other islands.


       October 17th, Nightingale Island.         We steamed over here at 4 a.m. this
morning and landed the scientifics to explore while we sounded round it.                   It
eighteen miles from Tristan and eight from Inaccessible.                It is the pleasan-
tist looking of the lot, being covered with vegetation and rising gradually to
a height of about 1000 feet above the sea level.            There are three or four dis-
tinct hummocks of land, but th.e area of the whole is less than Inaccessible
and there are no animals on it whatever.           The great feature of the island is
its caverns, of which there (192) are a great number all round the shores.


                                           65
The artist and photographer have taken views of all these scenes.              We have
several penguins on board, for these islands swarm with them.             They are the
clumsiest looking creatures you ever saw, being half bird and half seal, hav-
ing the head and feet of a duck wi th a seal's body and habi ts, except that
they lay eggs.     They are covered with a fur-like feather very pretty to look
at.   Several of our men have skins but they are only good for making muffs.
We are laying off from the land and are to sound between the islands tomorrow,
sailing for the Cape at night.


      October 27th, 150 miles from the Cape and expecting to anchor tomorrow.
We left the islands at 7 p.m. on the 18th obtaining a fine view of the Peak of
Tristan, as (193) we stood away.            We have had a slashing wind thus far and
have sounded four times, depth over 2500 fathoms, dredging pretty fair. We
picked up a fine piece of timber which was covered with fine specimens for the
scientifics, but we have seen no vessel yet. The Germans are getting fat, one
of them is reading sketches by "Boz", the other "Nicholas Nickleby".


      OCtober 28th.     8 p.m.       Anchored in Simon's Bay, Cape of Good Hope.     At
4 a.m. this morning we sighted Table Mountain and the adjacent headlands down
as far as the Cape.      We were about 60 miles away then and hove to for sound-
ings, proceeding again at 9 a.m. under sail and steam.             At 4 p.m. we entered
False Bay and thence into Simon's Bay which is only a part of the former, but
the most secure for vessels (194) of any in this part _of Afr ica.             We found
H.M.S. "Rattlesnake" and a gun boat at anchor here as well as a Dutch frigate
that is refitting for sea.           Directly we had anchored the "Rattlesnake" sent
our letters on board and I            had the satisfaction of receiving yours dated
Sept. 16th.    Themail that brought yours has been here two days and we have
newspapers to September 27.          The next comes in November 5th.


      The "Rattlesnake", Flag Ship on this station, has just returned from Cape
Coast Castle     and   br ings   a   bad   account of   the   Ashantee War.   Commodore
Commerell lies on shore shot through the lungs and thigh, he is in a very bad
state, and several of his boat I s crew are badly wounded and some of them I
believe were killed.      You must have felt rather dull in returning to Barrowden
after your London visit, amid so much dissipation and wandering away from your
professed faith, among charming preachers, with strange doctrines1 but hope
                                            66
you are still sound and unmoved after all this search and curiosity to behold
these heterodox religions and preachers.          You know what Dryden says of these
sects and people -- "A rambling crew of dreaming lambs succeed of the true old
enthusiastic breed,       Garnel form and order they their power employ, Nothing to
build, and all things to destroy·.


        The   newspaper    paragraph    in    reference   to   Joe   Pepper   was   very
satisfactory. I also read it in the London News and expect we shall have him
Surgeon to the Queen, or something of that sort, before I get back.            You have
some quite noted cousins, can't you write a novel or invent something, so as
(196) to keep up the family credit, discover a planet, then there will be an
Astronomical Swann, as well as an Anatomical Pepper.


        In consequence of our having had the yellow fever since leaving Bahia, we
were placed in quarantine for 24 hours, so there is no communication whatever
between us and the shore yet.            We are to remain here until the 6th of
December, so I shall get at least one more letter from you, and I will write
again before we sail describing the country in general, etc.            Cape Town is 22
miles distant from here by land and about 60 by water.                It stands on the
shores of Table Bay and the celebrated Table Mountain (which we saw at sea)
lies just behind the town.         I   believe we are to go round to Table Bay next
week so as to give leave to the ship's company in Cape Town; we shall be there
about 10 days, and I believe the officers will give a grand Ball during the
time.     We shall return here to refit etc., for the Dockyard Arsenal is here
and we (197) have a great deal to do to the ship, preparatory to going down
south among the ice.       There is a small town here called Simon's Town, where is
the Commodore's house, in which he lies wounded at present.           This Bay is about
40 sq. miles in extent and entirely surrounded by immense mountains, shutting
out the sea view inland altogether.           The coast has the same barren uninviting
appearance it had off Barbary over 5000 miles further north, and from whatever
part of the African Continent you look at from the sea, the view is everywhere
the same, great mountains and sandy deserts until you get further inland.            The
Cape of Good Hope (198) lies just to the west of this, and is one of the
boldest headlands in the world, but is not, as is generally supposed the



                                             67
extreme southern point of Afr ica. Cape Agulhas, 80 miles to the southeast
extends nearly 40 miles further to the southward.


       Sunday, November 2nd.             Themail leaves us for England on the 4th and the
one from there is expected on the 3rd, tomorrow.                         I believe the Captain has
decided on not going to Table Bay, so in that case, I don't suppose we shall
see Cape Town for it is very expensive riding up from here and there is not
much to see for the money.               At present the ship is stripped for refitting, the
yards and top masts being on deck, the fore and mainyards are sprung and the
dockyard carpenter will have to make new ones.                       We were three days (199) in
quarantine and directly the yellow fever flag was hauled down, leave was given
to one watch for 4 days, and the greater part of them are up at Cape Town.
The ship is very quiet now for nearly all the officers and scientifics are
also on leave.         The new schoolmaster from England is on board, came out in the
same mail boat that brought your letter.                      He is a young man and had been
married       five    days     when   he   received    24    hours      notice    to   embark   for    the
"Challenger".          It has been very hot here today and I have landed on African
soil    for     the    first     time.      All   hands     went   to    church    today,   Catholics,
Presbyterians, Wesleyans and "Anglo Catholics" each going to his own church.
There is also a Dutch Reformed Church but we could not muster any for that, of
course we have some who profess no religion at all, who have to look after the
boats meanwhile.             (200)    We all went to the Dockyard Church and the color of
the congregation was even more mixed than at Bermuda.                            There were the usual
soldiers and sailors, with negroes, Kroomen, Hottentots, Malays, Creoles and
children belonging to the lot mixed.                      This afternoon we have had lots of
visitors on board, several from the "Rattlesnake" describing their exploits at
the war on the coast.            One of their men was killed on the very day that his 20
year's service expired, which circumstance caused a general laugh and the
remark that he had not been kept a day in the service beyond his time.                                There
are a good many Malays here who do washing and all sorts of such work~ one of
them has done mine better than I have had it anywhere since leaving England.


       9 p.m.         The mail has arrived -- 27 days from England.                      She came into
(201) Table Bay this afternoon, three days before her time, but there was



                                                  68
nothing of any sort for me, letters or newspapers, so must make up my mind to
wait for another ten days at least.


       November 3rd, I have read all the English news up to the 4th of October.
I   know more about the Ashantee war and the Rattlesnake affair from the news-
papers than I     knew from the   account of the men who were there.          I    see
Tichborne is not yet played out, and the pilgrimage to Paray-le-Monial Din the
face of a scoffing and unbelieving world D has been fully carried out.       I

should think i t has been very beneficial to the shopkeepers and hotels at
Paray.    You will get this about Dec. 2nd, my 20th birthday.   We are almost go-
ing out of the world for the next 4 months.
Yours as ever,
Joe Matkin.


                                                          H.M.S. Challenger
                                                          in Table Bay
                                                          December 4, 1873
Dear Tom:
       Your letter dated Oct. 21st reached me in Simon's Bay, Nov. 20th, having
been only 25 days from Southampton.     I   see by the flag staff up on the Green
Mountain another mail is in sight, about 50 miles away, so will be in by 2
p.m.     She is one day, before her time having left England on Nov. 5th.         It is
very hot here today and we can see the sunnnit of the famous Table mountain
quite distinctlY1 the sides are rugged and steep but the top is as flat as a
table, about 2 miles in length, it is 3600 feet high.     I shall go on shore to-
morrow and intend to ascend it.     Since I last wrote from Simon's Bay, a good
deal has been done to the ship1 has been newly rigged throughout,                 (203)
caulked inside and out, and fresh painted.       We have also filled up with six
months provisions, coaled, etc., and fitted up stoves in all parts of the ship
against cold weather.    As soon as we get to sea, each man will have issued to
him gratuitously -      one pea jacket, one pair pilot trousers, one pair mitts
and one pair flannel drawers.   About 10 days ago news came from Port Natal
that the Caffres had broken out, so t~e DRattlesnake D was sent round at once
with 300 troops to quell the disturbance.      Our Captain had orders to be ready
at a day's notice to take more troops round if any further assistance was


                                       69
required, but as we have heard nothing more I daresay it is all settled.
Natal is 700 miles from here and the "Rattlesnake" is not back yet.                          Commodore
Commerrel did not (204) go in his ship as he is not better yet.                              He was at
church last Sunday and looked very ill indeed.                 The Caffres are a more warlike
race   than    the Ashantees,         and are considered the           finest      colored    race   in
Africa, there is nothing of the negro about them, and are more like the North
Amer ican Indians or Maor ies than any other.                   They come down here to buy
rifles, ammunition, etc., and live chiefly by hunting.


       The    Malays   here    are    principally     fishermen      and    come    from   the   Dutch
settlements of Sumatra and Java, in vessels.               The Arabs trade along the coast
from Egypt and Abyssinia.              The Hottentots belong to this part of Africa and
are handsomer than negroes, and not quite so black, they are employed by the
Dutch farmers and speak that language.                The Kroomen are the blackest race of
people on the face of the earth, they come from (205) the country round the
river Gambia, not far from the Ashantees.                 These we see here belong to Her
Majesty's Navy on the coast of Africa, and never leave                      it~    they are lent to
any ships that may be in the station to do the duty of stokers, being able to
stand the great heat of the Tropics better than white men.                        They wear the same
dress as our men but mess by themselves in the ship, one of their own race
acts as foreman over them.             They are paid about 10/- per week, and have all
kinds of fancy     name~      as very few can speak English, so there is any amount to
answer- to Tom Teapot, Flying Gil, Tom Gridiron, Dixie Land, etc.                       Simon's Town
is not much of a place for going on shore, I went though, four or five times,
and Sunday evenings generally went to the Dutch Reformed Church, where the
service is conducted in (206) that language in the morning and in English at
night.       Great shoals of mackerel and salmon came into Simon's Bay last week
and you could catch 20 Ibs. in about 5 minutes, rather different to fishing in
the WeIland.      On December 2nd we steamed away from there, to come round here,
60 miles further north.              We had a party of ladies and gentlemen, friends of
our Commander, come round with us, and they were seasick, just like the party
we took for a cruise at Madeira.


       Our    Commander    belongs      here   (his   father    is    Sir    Thomas    Maclear,      the
Astronomer Royal at this place)~ he was appointed to this ship on purpose for
astronomical observations.            He has been on leave ever since he came here.                  The
                                               70
coast all        the way round from Simon's Bay was wild and mountainous.           We
anchored in Table Bay (207) at 8 p.m. same night, but the party of ladies
slept in hammocks in the Captain's cabin.              When they were just ready for
turning in, they found they were not able to do it, so called the Captain, and
he lowered the end of the hammock down until they got in them and hauled them
up, one at a time.          They had to be hoisted out of the ship into the boats
(like cattle)       as i t was blowing hard.       We have been more than a year in
conunission, and I have only slept out of the ship one night,              that was in
Lisbon.


        I think when we payoff I must bring my two hammock hooks away with me,
that I hung up to for 3 1/2 years.         They are fitting a stove close to mine, so
I shall be warm in the cold weather.            Table Bay is about as large as Simon's
Bay, and similarly surrounded by great mountains 1 there is an island at the
(208) entrance, upon which is a lighthouse.           The bay is not so land-locked as
Simon's Bay and does afford such good shelter for shipping unless they go into
the dock basin.


        There    is a breakwater under construction being made by convicts and
prisoners.       Four or five of our seamen are working on it, who preferred going
to Gaol for a month, and afterwards to a fresh ship, instead of going further
in the Challenger.         Five or six have gone to hospital and three have deserted
to   the diamond fiedds,          but we shall fill    up from the Guard Ship before
leaving.        Many will desert in Australia and New Zealand, as the men are very
dissatisfied at not getting extra pay for this cold weather trip, and the work
is so much harder for everyone than in an ordinary man-of-war when the ship
is in harbour six months at a time.             Men who were in this (209) ship's last
conunission say she used to lie in Sydney for months at a time, and was a very
happy ship then,        but now when we go in harbour         it's to refit, coal, or
provision, and the men get scarcely any leave.            Several of the officers are
great bullies, the most popular of the lot is Lord Campbell.           We are anchored
about     half a    mile   from   the city of Cape Town,     which has a    very clean
appearance, and looks something like Penzance in England, only larger1 it is
about four miles in length but not very broad, is well fortified, and there is
a railway which runs up the country, the first I have seen since we left


                                           71
England, though there were some at Lisbon, Halifax and Bahia.            We are to lay
in our Christmas stores here and on the 8th the officers give a grand ball in
the Royal Exchange on shore.        We shall (210) have any amount of visitors on
board here.


     Last night the cable parted with one anchor and all today the diver has
been at work picking it up and has now got it all right again.              One the 10th
we leave here for Simon's Bay again to fill up with coal, and also to take in
a deck cargo of it.       We leave there before the 15th December and are to
inspect a lot of islands in the Southern ocean, to report which would be the
most suitable for      an expedition to go to from England next December              and
observe the Transit of Venus.       Two or three parties are going from England to
observe it in different parts of the world, and our party will watch it from
some island in the China Sea. We call first at Pr ince Edward Island, and
probably spend Christmas there, before going on to Marion Island and thence to
the Crozet Islands      (211),   after    that to Kerguelen's Land,    a large island
discovered by Kerguelen, a French navigator in 1763.            Captain Cook was there
in 1774 and lay a long time in the only harbour -- which he called Christmas
Harbour.      The   island he called the Land of Desolation,         as there was      no
vegetation on it, neither any animals except seals, sea elephants, etc., but
there is ice and snow all the year round.           The island is 100 miles in length
and 50 in breadth~ it is 2200 miles south by east of this colony.               We are to
lie a month     in Chr istmas Harbour,       and thoroughly    suryey and   explore   the
island, which has never yet been done.           Leaving there we steer south until we
reach the great Antarctic ice barrier, then run up for Melbourne about the end
of March, and stay there a week or 10 days before going on to (212) Sydney to
stay five weeks, refitting etc.          From there we go to Wellington and Auckland,
after which warm weather and some far different islands.             New Guinea is the
first, then Timor, Borneo, Amboyna, and Manilla, Phillipine Islands~ thence to
Hong Kong, China and on to Yeddo, Japan, after which the Kurile Islands and
Petropaulopchy,     the cold capital of         Kamchatka.    Thence Aleutian    Islands,
Berring's Straits and down to Vancouvers,             about May/75 after     which begin
again.




                                           72
        December 9th.   We do not leave here for Simon's Bay until the 10th -- to-
morrow, and sail finally on the 16th.        The English mail has not yet arrived,
but is expected hourly as she is four days behind time.           She is a very old
boat, the worst the company has and is always late.         I dare say we shall re-
ceive another mail before the 16th and there is one sails for England on that
day which takes this, the Captain is going to send his little boy home by it,
as he is not strong enough for the next voyage, and has suffered very much
from bad eyes since he came in here.         The Officers' Ball came off last night
on shore and was a great success, over 400 being invited.           Our band was in
attendance and came off this morning quite drunk, and couldn't carry their in-
struments.     The inhabitants of Cape Town give a return ball to-night to our
officers and we sail tomorrow night.      We have been crowded with visitors since
we came in, the ship if full of them now (one young lady just asked me to whom
I was writing, I answering to you, my love).        There's some very handsome (214)
girls in this place, Dutch and English, very extensive about the bustle and in
the latest fashion.      We had the Governor, Sir H. Barkly and party on board on
Saturday, also Sir T. Maclear and party, and they danced with the officers on
the main deck, while the sailors dance on the opposite side.          Two more have
deserted since we came round to this bay.          I was on shore yesterday morning
until 7 p.m., and went to the top of Table Mountain.          It is 3500 feet high,
and I was 2 hours going up, the ascent was not half so difficult as that up
St. Vincent, but the view was far better.          Look ing south you saw the Dutch
town of Wynberg, and a level track of vineyard country until you came to the
mountains round Simon's Bay, and the city of Cape Town spread out under your
feet.     It was intensely hot climbing up, but on arrival at the summit you were
enveloped in a damp cold (215) mist which kept the sun off you completely, and
made it very chilly and cold until you descended about 800 feet -- where it
was as hot as ever.      Cape Town is a pretty good place for business, but noth-
ing to look at, not to be compared to Melbourne.        There is not a single strik-
ing building or church in the place, all after the same heavy Dutch style.
There are a great many Malays and Hottentots in it, about every 3rd house is a
hotel.     There are theatres, music halls, etc., here, and plenty of loafers,
and that sort of people, flash women, etc.        Peaches, apricots, oranges, straw-
berr ies are the cheapest fruits at present, but are not so nice as those at
Madeira and the Azores.      Two fine merchant ships have been here and gone since


                                        73
we came in, they were called emigrant ships, and had each on board about 500
coolies   from   Calcutta   for   Jamaica      and    Demerara,   to   work   in   the   sugar
plantations there. They go for five years and are paid (216) about 2 d. per
day and are supposed to be voluntarily emigrating, but it is really a quiet
way of importing slaves, for they are treated like those in the West Indies
and very few ever live to get back to India again.


     The ships lie a long way from the shore, and don't allow their emigrants
to land, neither permit anyone on board.             I was looking at them the other day
