through a telescope, they were dirty, miserable looking creatures, all wrapped
up in blankets, having had cold weather beating round the Cape of Good Hope.
They only remained here four days to take in water, fresh provisions, etc.


     December 15th.     In Simon's Bay.     We left Table Bay with a party of ladies
on board, and steamed round Robin's Island with them, returning the same night
and landing (217) the visitors, after which we steered for here and anchored
on the 11th.     We found here the "Rattlesnake" again from Port Natal, she sails
for England shortly having been out for four years.                We have filled up with
coal and have 70 tons on the main deck, as no ship could be procured to bring
us any down to Kerguelen Land.         We have 40 sheep, 5 bullocks and a large
quantity of poultry belonging to the officers, also several goats for breeding
purposes that are to be left on different islands.                The missing mail came in
on the 14th and brought me two letters, one being from you with two newspapers
and shall have no more news this side of Melbourne.                We sail tomorrow night
for the long voyage and shall be at Kerguelen by the time you get this.                    Did
you see the Illustrated London News for 1st November?                  It contained (218) a
picture of our ship at St. Paul's Rocks.


     I daresay you will hear of our arr ivaI in Melbourne, about the end of
March, as there is telegraphic communicaltion between there and England.                   Two
more men have deserted and three are now absent, one boy tried to swim ashore
last night, and has never been heard of since, the distance was 1 1/4 miles,
and i t was blowing hard and the boy had his clothes on.                 I have sent you a
ball programme with the new device of the Challenger, drawn by our artist,



                                          74
J.J. Wild.    I have laid in my Antarctic provisions and clothing and expect to
weather it admirably.    So must conclude for this side of Melbourne.


Yours sincerely
Joe Matkin


(219) H.M.S. "Challenger"
Off Prince Edward Island,
Christmas Day - 1873


Dear Tom:
     Our 2nd Christmas on board has arrived and finds us in sight of two snow
covered islands, but they are still 20 miles away, so we shall not anchor
until tomorrow1 the weather is just about the same as with you, and the day
has passed away    far   more pleasantly than   last Christmas   in   the   Bay of
Biscay, still the sea is very rough today, and the ship rolls a good deal, but
we are pretty well used to that now, it was too rough for the regular church,
but we had prayers as usual, and are now wearing our warm clothing for the
first time, as the thermometer now stands at 40 degrees, and was down to
freezing point last night1 rather a sudden change as it stood 70 degrees only
4 days ago.   We left the Cape on the 17th for this island, distant 1200 miles,
and had a good wind, we sounded 2 or 3 times, depth about 2 miles, and the
island hove in sight about 10 o'clock this morning_


     All hands were on deck looking out for land till dinner time, 12 o'clock,
when the band struck up -- "The Roast Beef of Old England" which sounded very
nice, though the dinner was salt port, and pea soup.       Of course we brought
private stores with us, and had a fine dinner consideringl the Captain walks
round just to see the tables laid out, and tests each messes' plum duff, a
very ancient custom in the Navy 1 there are 20 messes, but he only managed
about 5, after 1/3 pint of Madeira was issued to each man, and the band played
dance music, which they are (221) still doing, so I being no dancer have got
this letter underweigh with two or three others.         We were considering at
dinner time where we are likely to be next Christmas, and find that we shall
be somewhere in the neighbourhood of Hong Kong, and Christmas '75 close to


                                      75
Valparaiso.     December 21st was the anniversary of our leaving Portsmouth, so
the Captain issued wine to all hands.        Just before we left the Cape our
photographer deserted, so at the last moment Professor Thompson had to rush up
to Cape Town, and engage a young fellow there: who has been very sea sick
coming across here.     We are now standing between the islands until morning,
when we run up to Marion Island.


     January 3rd, 1874 - Off the Crozet Islands.


     On the day after Christmas we stood in to Marion, and landed an exploring
party while the ship sounded round the island.     It is (222) about four miles
in length, and three in breadth, and has mountains on it about 3000 feet high,
covered with snow nearly all the way down.


     There was grass on      it but no animals whatever    except Penguins,   Sea
Elephants, and hosts of great Albatrosses, some of them measuring 17 feet from
wing to wing.    All these creatures, as well as lots of other sea birds, were
there for breeding purposes, as the season lasts from November to May.        The
Albatrosses and Penguins are very fr iendly, the former generally makes his
nest between two Penguins, which make none, but merely a hole in the ground
and lay two eggs, but the Albatross has a regular nest of dirt and moss, and
raises it about 4 feet from the ground, they also lay two eggs which are
nearly as large as Ostrich's, after they are laid one -of the birds sits on
them until they are hatched.    The old man goes to sea and gets (223) his belly
full, then returns and sits on the eggs while my lady goes for a feed.    A good
many of these birds were killed for the sake of the breast of white down, and
the web of the foot which our men make tobacco pouches of.        They can't fly
from the ground on account of the great length of their wings, but must start
from some elevation.    They are very tame, and would never leave the nest until
toppled over with a stick.     A large sea elephant was shot on the beach, but I
did not see him.    On the 27th we stood across to Prince Edward's Island, which
is much smaller and rather higher, but no one landed.     We had dredging between
the islands and obtained some good specimens, and the same night we make sail
for the Crozet Islands distant 540 miles.     On the 31st of December we sighted
Hog Island, but could not go (224) in very close on account of the fog.


                                      76
        New Year's Day was terribly foggy,       but on the 2nd we sighted the 12
Apostles' rocks, Penguin Island, Possession Island, and East Island.            In the
evening we stood in for an anchorage off Possession Island, but found it was
blowing too hard, with a very rough sea, so we stood out again, and obtained a
good view of the island which was something like Marion, but larger.            As the
sun was setting the mountains in East Island came out right above the fog in
the most wonderful manner, of which the Artist made a fine sketch 7 today we
have been dredging, depth 700 fathoms but as it still keeps very foggy we are
just going to leave the Crozets, to make sail for Kerguelen Land, distant 700
miles.


        January 7th, 1874.     Anchored   in   (225)   Christmas Harbour, Kerguelen's
Land.


        We have only been 3 1/2 days coming the 700 miles, aild sighted this
island at 4 a.m., anchoring at 8, in this magnificant harbour, the best one we
have yet been in, it is about a mile in length, and 1/2 a mile in breadth, and
has deep water all round, it is surrounded on three sides by high lands, and
there are two or three small islands abreast of the entrance, the land has a
very dead appearance, the hills are covered in snow, and there is not a sight
of a tree to be seen.        There is a very peculiar rock at the entrance to the
harbour, it lies in the middle of the passage, and has a tunnel through it
large enough for a. train to travel.           This has been made by the ceaseless
        -
action of the water, and makes it look like a railway. bridge.               Christmas
Harbour is at the extreme north west of the island1 it is in lat. 49 degrees
south (226), long. 70 degrees east, the same latitude as the Scilly Islands,
and although this is the middle of summer down here, the hills are all snow
covered.     Several parties have been on shore during the day exploring and have
returned again, bringing with them various kinds of sea birds, sea elephants,
penguins, etc.     I shall tell you more of the sea elephants after I have been
on shore and seen them.        There are four different sorts of penguins on this
island, the largest and handsomest being the King Penguin, which stands about
3 1/2 feet high, and has a golden crest on its head.             Our men say they look
like the Russian Sentry's up the Crimea, for they. stand as stiff and immovable
as a soldier, with their flippers standing out straight.           They are of a white
and purple black colour, with yellow feet, and are perfectly harmless, and
look so helpless when they are being killed.           They stand on the (227) beach in


                                          77
droves,    and in the evenings go through all sorts of military evolutions.
Besides this kind there are the Jackass, Royal and common Penguin here, all
breeding on the beach and rocks of this island.                Then there are Petrels,
Albatrosses, Cape hens, Tern, Sea swallows, Rock pigeons, and carrion hawks~
the latter two kinds are land birds, but migratory and get their living along
the sea beach.       There are also plenty of wild ducks, but they like the rest
are only here for the summer.       Specimens of all these creatures, with a couple
of sea elephants, and a large seal were shot, and brought on board, and are
now stuffed and pickled for the museums.           The seal weighed about 40 Ibs., and
the sea elephants each 1100 Ibs. requiring a good number of men to hoist them
on board.        Bundles of the Kerguelen cabbage were also brought, which proves
very (228) palatable, and eats something like spinach though rather bitter.
It is the only plant to be seen on the island and grows close to the sea, is
in shape something between a lettuce and palm cabbage.           Captain Cook found it
very efficacious in curing the scurvy among his crew, so we shall eat plenty
of it.    We go to sea again to-morrow for a cruise round the island, but are to
come back here again before we leave it finally.            It is snowing now, and very
cold.     This island was discovered by Kerguelen, a French navigator, who, on
his     return    to. France   published   a    grossly   exaggerated   account   of   its
capabilities and extent.       In the year 1776 Captain Cook visited it, and called
it the "Land of Desolation", from its dead and inhospitable appearance~ it is
composed of igneous rocks, which rise into hills from 2 to 3000 feet high.
The island is 100 miles in (229) length, and 50 in breadth, there are a great
many 'smaller islands round it, and plenty of bays and- good harbours.                 The
interior of it has never been visited by man, and perhaps never will, for the
ground is frightfully irregular and boggy, so impassable that all progress is
debarred inland.        Captain Cook spent five weeks round its shores, and also
visited Marion Island before leaving for the south.            He started from the Cape
of Good Hope, and after visiting these islands, penetrated to 71 degrees
south,    then ran up to New Zealand in 110 days.              Captain Weddel in 1824,
penetrated to lat. 74 degrees south, and in 1840 Captain Ross got as far as 78
degrees, 4 minutes south, the farthest anyone has ever been, or is likely to
reach.      His ships were the IIErebus ll and· "Terror ll ,    afterwards lost in the
Arctic under Sir John Franklin.        In lat. 78 degrees Ross found an impenetrable
(230) barrier of ice, and also discovered land with burning volcanoes on it
10,000 feet high.       The French, Russians, and Americans have each succeeded in
sailing within the Antarctic Circle, but never reached so high as Ross.


                                           78
     Our Captain expects to reach Lat. 65 degrees south but his orders forbid
him from forcing his way through the outer ice barrier, for he will only have
three month's provisions left then, and dare not risk being frozen in.


        February 1, off Kerguelens Land, bound south.              We have finished surveying
and exploring the island, so will give you further particulars before leaving
it finally.       On the 8th of January we left Christmas harbour and anchored the
same night in Betsy Cove, a snug harbour, named after some whale ship.                          It is
about 40 miles from Chr istmas Harbour further east, there are several small
islands as you (231) steam along the coast, also plenty of rocks and shoals,
so that a very careful lookout has to be kept,                     and soundings continually
taken.     The coast as we came along to Betsy Cove, and indeed, all round the
island, presented the same dreary and desolate appearance, in some places the
hills were higher, and quaintly shaped, but were always covered in snow; and a
heavy     fog    hangs continually over        the   land,   so    that    the    view    inland     is
completely obscured.


     We remained in Betsy Cove eight days, while the boats went away surveying
the adjacent bays and harbours,              which were very numerous, and parties of
officers and scientifics went exploring, shooting and botanizing inland, but
they never succeeded in getting more than about 10 miles.                   Numerous birds, sea
elephants, etc., were shot, and enough wild ducks to supply all hands two days
for dinner.        I went on shore (232) once with the Paymast~r shooting ducks, and
we went about five miles inland to see some wonderful cascades of water which
come down from the mountains.            The walking was something frightful, the island
is one vast swamp.          At every other step you sink up to your knees in the boggy
ground.        What looked like grass from the ship turned out to be moss, and it
was the mossy ground which was the most treacherous.                  Not a tree or shrub was
to be seen anywhere, no animals of any sort, neither insects on the earth
though we looked carefully, except wild ducks and carrion hawks, we saw no
birds, so that we may call it truly a "Land of Desolation".                       Just abreast of
where     we    are     anchored,   on   a   prominent     hummock    of   land    were     7   or    8
gravestones.          We were greatly surprised to see them when first we entered the
harbour,        (233)    they   stand    upright,    and   being     painted     white    are      very
conspicious, long before a ship is near enough to see what they are.                               They


                                               79
have been erected by whalers who rendezvous in this harbour, to the memory of
their shipmates who have died or been drowned off the island.                         They are made
of ship's timber, well shaped, and painted and, I need not say how solitary
and desolate       they    look    in   this dismal    spot.     They    are    all    English   and
American, some of them dating back to 1840, and nearly all read after this
description -- "In memory of George Eccles, Second Mate of the Barque 'Julius
Caezar' who was drowned whilst whaling off Desolation Island, May 1863." "And
so he bringeth them into the haven where they would be".


       Great quantities of kelp abounded               in the sea round this,            and other
harbours, and (234) on one part of the beach we found an old ship's copper,
and a lot of iron hoops that had been left by whalers years ago, after boiling
down their whales.         The beach was strewn with whale bones, some of enormous
size -- much larger than an Elephants.             A day or two after we came into Betsy
Cove, we were surprised to see a small schooner standing into the bay, which
anchored the same night and proved to be the "Imogen" whaler of new London,
America.       During the rest of the time we lay there the whale men were always
on board our ship, telling us all about the island, their line of life, pay,
etc.    The Captain dined with our officers every night, and having been down in
this part of the world for a good many years, was able to give us a great deal
of information.


       Their    vessel    had     just come from Heard Island           further   south and was
waiting to be joined by (235) another schooner from America, to commence the
season's whaling.         The crew composed English, Scotch, Americans, Negroes, most
of whom came on board before we left.                 They join the vessel for four years,
and are paid according to their success, but the average was much less than
that of our men, while the hardship is something awful.                        They would gladly
have changed places with ours, for from the time they leave America, until
their return they scarcely see a strange face.                 These men have been here three
years, and the only inhabited place they have landed on is Tristan d'Acunha.
Once a year another vessel comes out to them bringing provisions, clothing,
etc., and taking back their oil and skins.               As yet they had none, having just
sent their stock off.           They carry casks, staves, and hoops as cargo, and when
they kill a whale, take the blubber to the nearest island, and boil it down,


                                              80
the Cooper goes on shore and sets up as many casks as may be required, after
which they are filled with oil, marked and left on the island until the store
vessel comes for them at the end of the year.               This one had a store of oil on
one of the Crozet Islands and when their annual store vessel was removing it,
one of the boats was capsized whereby the mate and three men were drowned.
This island is their great rendezvous and they generally winter in Christmas
Harbour.     They live very well for they eat wild ducks, albatross, penguins,
rock pigeons, sea elephants, sea leopards, and any amount of cabbage.                   Some of
our men have tr ied these animals and approve them all.                     I have tackled an
albatross and liked it, but don't care to try sea elephants.                     They have told
us all about the latter, so will describe the animal to you.                      He belongs to
the walrus and seal family, but is much (237)                larger, and not so valuable,
though the whalers often kill them for the sake of their oil.                    They weigh from
1200 to 1500 pounds: we killed one weighing 1100.                 They are covered with a
coarse furry skin, which is only of value to themselves.                They live in the sea
in winter, but come on shore in the summer to breed the same as seals and
penguins, etc. They live on the same food as seals and whales, and during the
time they are on shore they eat nothing, so get very thin during their three
months on land.           Their head is exactly like that of a lioness, they have
whiskers, but of course have no feet like animals, have large eyes, and two
large flippers where their forelegs should be, and two very strong ones where
their tail is situated, which he used to propel himself through the water, and
by raising himself on them manages to hobble along on              (13~)    land: they come to
the island in November, with the seals and penguins from the south, for the
purpose of breeding.              The males come a week or two before the females, and
wait on the beach until they arrive, who, on their arrival retire farther up,
while the gentlemen have a very long and fierce combat for the possession of
the best looking wives: after this little affair they choose their partners,
and settle down comfortably.                There is a sort of general confinement in May,
during     which   time    the     ladies    are very helpless,   and      the   gentlemen most
affectionate and attentive.             They are also very savage if anyone attempts to
intrude on the mother and infant, have been known to defend them to the last
extremity.     I read the other day Anson's voyages, in which was an account of a
sailor who had killed the mother and calf, and while engaged skinning the
latter, the male          (239)    animal came unperceived behind him, and getting his


                                                 81
head    in his mouth,     inflicted on him such frightful injuries that he died.
This was at Juan Fernandez.


        About a fortnight after the calf is born, the mother seizes it in her
mouth    and   throws    him   into   the   sea,   for   they do   not    take   to   the    water
naturally, but require preparatory lessons in swimming. After a few trials he
manages it, and at the latter end of May the whole herd leave the island for
the south again.        They are quite harmless if let alone, if you poke him with a
stick, he raises himself on his tail and makes a sort of helpless jump at you,
but of cour se falls down.            If you throw a stone in his mouth, he roars and
shows his great teeth, grinding the stone to powder.               An enormous quantity of
blood comes from them when they are            killed~   the whalers generally spear them
and (240) they tell us, that, like the elephant on land, they often shed tears
while dying, and look at you with such a pitiful and accusing gaze. Seals and
penguins have very similar habits.


        On the 16th January we left Betsy Cove for another harbour further east.
We had a severe gale during the night, which drifted us to the extreme east
end of the island.        We passed several small islands, and found the east coast
very mountainous and wild looking, the mountains generally being sugar-loaf
shape.


        At 7 p.m. on the 17th we steamed into Royal Sound,           a~d   after steaming for
about 8 miles where the navigation was very intricate (for the land was broken
up into hundreds of small islands, rocks and reefs), we came to an anchor
between three islands, and the boats were got out for surveying, the harbour,
etc.     Here we found another whaler called (241)            the "Charles Colcott", also
from New London, but in opposition to the "Imogen".                      The crew were mostly
living in a hut on shore, where they had their oil stored in casks on the
beach.     On a small island opposite their hut was another lot of tombstones,
all whalers but not belonging to this vessel.


        The crew were very much surpr ised to see a large man of war, steaming
into their harbour and fully expected that we should run on shore.                          Most of
the men came on board while we were there, but the Captain, who was a regular


                                              82
churlish Yankee, refused to come, or to give our Captain any information about
the island or harbour.


        He invited him to come to church on the Sunday morning, and to dinner in
the evening, but he wouldn't come.            No Captain he says -- I ain't been to no
church for     20 years,    and      (242)   I guess lain' t    going to begin now.    We
remained there three days, and on the 20th steamed out of Royal Sound, and
hove the dredge, some good specimens were obtained, but no fish have been
caught round the island.          We anchored off the land that night,          and after
dredging again on the 21st stood in, and anchored in Greenland Bay, which is
at the extreme south east of the island.               Several parties landed there, but
the island was exactly the same -- no animals or trees, and vegetation to be
seen.     On the 22nd we left and made sail for Christmas Harbour, distant 140
miles.     On the 23rd we had a tremendous gale, during which we were struck by a
very heavy sea which smashed the sounding platform, and went down the funnel
into the stoke hole.       On the 24th we anchored in Cascade Bay, and on the 25th
in Betsy Cove     (243)    again, where we rode out another heavy gale.            We had
landed a pair of goats on the island before we left, hoping that they would
find their way into the interior, and increase and multiply; but we found them
grazing among the grave stones, and as soon as they saw the ship, they came
down to the beach and commenced bleating.                However, we left them there but
whether they will live through the winter is a query -- no other domestic
animals could I'm sure.


        On the 26th we made sail again for Christmas Harbour, but were obliged to
anchor that night in Hopeful Harbour.              There we took in another good supply of
Kerguelen cabbage, and on the 27th made another start.                Our ing that day we
fell in with the "Imogen" and her partner the "Rossal King" also from New
London.     They were out on a (244) whaling cruise, and each vessel had two men
on the lookout for         whales.       They anchored with us that night       in Rhodes
Harbour, and the two Captains came on board our ship to dinner.


        Several of the crews of the vessels also came and we had the band under
weigh, and some good dancing.            On the 28th we got out the boats and surveyed
the harbour, which is a very extensive one.                There are plenty of good ones


                                              83
round Kerguelens Land but Chr istmas Harbour is the best.    We anchored there
again on the 29th and remained two days to get some specimens' of coal which
were found in the rocks and cliffs, and on the 31st we made sail from there,
intending to leave the island for good.      Previous to leaving, another good
supply of cabbage was taken on board and a paper recording the ship's visit,
and other particulars was buried on shore.    All today, Sunday, (245) we have
been sailing parallel with the land, and have just cleared the south point of
the island.   The west side we did not survey at all as Ross examined it pretty
well in 18407 the south side is as barren as the rest, I think the mountains
are higher, some quite 4000 feet, and shaped like church spires.   We have been
25 days round the island, and anchored in most of the principal harbours.   The
mountains are now almost out of sight, and we are under all plain sail for
McDonald and Heard Island, distant 300 miles, due south.


     February 6th - Anchored in Whisky Bay, Heards Island.     We have been 6
days coming this distance, owing to the frightfully foggy weather we have had,
and the uncertain information as to the correct position of the islands.     We
sighted them twice but were obliged to keep away on account of (246) the fog7
at 10 this morning we came up to McDonalds Island or rocks, which are a group
very similar, and as barren as S. Paul's Rocks, the highest point would be
about 400 feet •


    . Heards Island lies 20 miles further south, and is in the same latitude as
the Falkland Islands.    It is about as long as Marion Island and Whisky Bay is
the only anchorage.     The island looks like an immense iceberg, being covered
with snow and ice glaciers, which are formed all down the mountain slopes.
There are several men on it belonging to the "Imogen·, who are here for the
summer to kill sea elephants for the sake of their oil.     The Captain landed
and got what information he could from the men, and we leave for the south
tomorrow, as any exploring party is impossible, for the snow lies several feet
thick on the island.


     February 16th - Within the Antarctic Circle - Latitude 66°,39'5.   Off the
great ice barrier, and surrounded by icebergs.    We left Heard's Island on the
7th for the south, with a good breeze, which increased to a regular gale


                                      84
during the night; the ship was knocked about anyhow by the tremendous seas,
two of the main deck ports were stove in and men knocked out of their hammocks
by the sea, the carpenters were up all the night repairing the damage.               It was
considered the worst gale we have yet had, tho' not so dangerous as the one in
the Channel.


    We ran 214 miles during the gale, with         (248)   storm staysails only,         the
best part of the time, the gale moderated on the 8th Sunday, and we were in
the latitude of Cape Horn.


     On the 9th we were out of the track of navigation being in latitude 58°S
and on the 10th we were in latitude 60°, IS'S and no icebergs in sight.


     The thermometer stood at 33 1/2° in the shade, and the temperature of the
surface water    was exactly the same.        On the 11th at    4: 00 a .m.    the    first
iceberg hove in sight, and we lay to, close to it, and hove the trawl.                  This
iceberg was about a mile in length, and 400 feet high, it was quite square,
and the sununit was covered in snow.         We found the depth 1,275 fathoms, the
surface water was 32 1/2, only half a degree above freezing point for fresh
water, and from this depth we brought up living specimens, the best being a
large prawn, and a curious sharp-snouted fish about a foot long, and of a sort
(249) hitherto unknown.    We passed another large iceberg quite close the same
night.    On the 12th we were in latitude 62°, 40' S. ana sighted several more
icebergs; one we passed quite near which looked something like an ironclad
ship with a splendid ram in front,       it was a beautiful blue color,           and the
sununit was    frosted with snow,   giving   it the appearance of     a   lion's mane.
There was an opening in its centre large enough for a ship to sail through,
but the   two,   apparently separate masses,     were   joined together       beneath    the
water.


     According to Commodore Maury only one-tenth of a large iceberg appears
above the water, so the weight and total extent of some of those we have seen
must be enormous.


     Great quantities of small ice was floating in the wake of this iceberg,
which would have been invaluable to us had we wanted (250)           any fresh water;
                                       85
for, you doubtless know when salt water is at freezing point, the salt sinks
to the bottom, and the water frozen is fresh, and when thawed, fit to drink.
Captain Cook obtained several supplies when he was down here.                     27.2° is the
freezing point for salt water at rest, but if in motion 25.5 is the average,
this varies according to the degree of saltness.                      A strong under current
drifts the icebergs to the north from 5 to 8 miles a day, and the prevailing
westerly winds also drives them to the east, so that their course is about
N.E.


       By the time they arrive at latitude 50 0 S, they meet with a very warm
under current from the Indian Ocean, which rapidly melts them beneath the
water,   and as soon as         the submerged part        is lighter than that above the
surface, they topple over, and either sink or break up into small pieces.
They seldom (251) reach farther than latitude 40 0 S, although they have been
found as high as the Cape, latitude 34°S.           Those in the Arctic Ocean generally
drift down to latitude SOoN, where they are met off the banks of Newfoundland,
by the warm current of the Gulf Stream which very soon settles them.                      Those
banks have been formed of earth, rocks, etc., which the. icebergs bear away
with them from the land, and the sea above them gets shallower every year. The
vapour which this icy current causes to rise from the Gulf Stream is the cause
of the general fog to be met with off Newfoundland.                   The same meeting of the
warm current from the Indian Ocean with the Antarctic current, cause those
divers     fogs   we   found   off   Prince   Edward's,    Mar ion,    Crozets   and   Kerguelen
Islands.     After we were in lat 60 0 S, we lost those brave westerly (252) winds,
and are now in a region of light wind and calmJ if it were not for the very
cold weather we could fancy ourselves in the tropics.                   On the 13th we passed
numbers of icebergs, and on the preceding night nearly ran into one during a
snow squall, nearly all the sail is taken in for the night on account of the
icebergs, the latitude was 65°, 15' south and the weather mild for the region,
and we began to think we were going to the South Pole.                    But during the same
night we ran into the great outer ice barrier, for some distance, and had a
job to get out again and as soon as we did the ship hove to until morning.
Her course was much impeded by the great lumps of floating ice, and the roar
they made against the bows of the vessel dur ing the night, I shall never




                                              86
forget.     It was like thunder more than anything else, and the grinding noise
woke all who were (253) in their hammocks, and nearly everyone was on deck.
It was a beautiful sight to see the ship ploughing her way through it, and the
light emitted from the ice made it nearly as light as day.        This light is
called by polar voyagers, the "ice blink".     Twilight in these high latitudes
lasts until 12 o'clock, and daylight breaks at 1:00 a.m. so there is night in
one sense of the word.     Of course this is the middle of summer down here, for
7 months in the year the sun is seldom seen above 65°S.     The Aurora Australis
was visible dur ing the night, and the coruscations of light were much more
brilliant than the Aurora Borealis we saw at Halifax.       On the 14th over 30
large icebergs were in sight from the deck, and the great ice barrier about 5
miles away looking like lowland covered with snow, and a pale misty light
hanging over it. (254) The icebergs were of all shapes and sizes from a Gothic
cathedral to a haystack, and varied from 100 to 500 feet in height, and the
largest were about 4 square miles in extent.       Some had spires to them like
churches, others bays and harbours running into them, and many were honey-
combed with caverns extending through them in all directions.     These had been
formed by the restless action of the waves, and through these caves the sea
rushed and roared with tremendous force, the spray often rising quite 100 feet
alongside the bergs.     These caverns were of a dark blue colour, the iceberg
itself being of a starch shade.    Several of them looked exactly like the Spit-
head Forts, but the majority were more like haystacks with sloping snow cover-
ed rpofs.     Many of' them had great fissures through them, as if they had been
stricken with lightning, these rents were of a (255) dark blue colour.     Close
to the ice barrier we sounded at 1,675 fathoms~ the water temperature was 29°,
the latitude 66°S. only 30 miles from the Antarctic Circle.      After sounding,
sail was made to the west along the barrier, in hopes of finding an entrance,
the sea was as calm as a fish pond but covered with cakes of ice, the wind was
very light, and not much progress made~ a new kind of sea bird called the Snow
Petrel was first seen on the 14th, they are white, and about as large as a
dove, they breed on the icebergs but are never seen below latitude 65°S.      On
some of the icebergs we saw numbers of penguins, and on one we saw a large
rock and some earth, showing that the bergs are formed in bays and harbours
near the south pole.     The artist made sketches of most of the large icebergs.
We passed one on the night of the 14th, which looked something (256) like


                                      87
Windsor Castle, and had a large cavern through it which showed the daylight on
the other side.     Nearly all hands were on deck to see it, and one of the men
even said, he had often paid a penny in England to see not half such a sight.
At midnight it was light enough to see to read, and the sky was still scarlet
in the west where the sun had gone down.      On Sunday the 15th, we had church in
the morning, but only sailed 15 miles.        Over 30 icebergs were in sight at
once, and no two were alike.        The thermometer stood at 27 1/2°, water tem-
perature 29°.     During the night we ran into the ice barrier again, but the
ship was at once put about, and we sailed out until this morning when we were
about 8 miles from it.     The barrier extended from east to west as far as the
eye could reach, and looked like a marble wall 50 feet high.             We saw this
(257) morning the largest iceberg we have yet seen, it was about 4 sq. miles
in extent, and looked like a piece of ploughed land in winter covered in
snow. It was over 500 feet high, and sloped up very gradully; if I can get you
some photographs of these bergs will send some.         We saw another that was quite
blue, it having very recently turned over.


     At 9:00 a.m. the sails were furled, and steam got up, and we steamed as
far south as the barrier would allow us.      The latitude was 66°, 40' S. longi-
tude 78° E.     Sail was then made to the west in hopes of finding an entrance to
the southward, but, the wind was very light and not much progress made.           Wine
was issued tonight to celebrate our entry within the Antarctic Circle.              At
present the barrier is still in sight, and we are surreunded by icebergs of
all sizes and shapes.      There are also any (258) amount of great whales in
sight, blowing and having such a game among themselves.         It is now 10 p.m. and
the sun is still above the horizon, and the sky like fire, giving all the ice-
bergs to the west a scarlet tinge.      A fine breeze has just sprung up, but they
will have to shorten sail on account of the icebergs.          The Captain would have
tried to force his way through the barrier, but his instructions from the
Admiralty forbad him, and we have only 3 months provisions, and 80 tons of
coal remaining in the ship.     I   hope we shall reach latitude 70 0 S -- everyone
is in good health and spirits, and very few wish to turn back yet; and those
who do are recommended by the others to get out and walk.         We are all wearing
our polar clothing, large caps, with flaps to them to cover the ears and neck,
and great jackets, trousers, boots and mitts.       I    am considered to (259)   look


                                        88
like the Shah of Persia in my cap.    A great byword among the men at present is
"Do you think you shall weather it Bill? Yes, I think I shall go round in her
Bob".
        Sunday, March 1st, bound to Melbourne, blowing hard.           On the 17th of
February we were in latitude 65 Os and could find no opening                in the   ice
barrier.     We sailed through several fields of floating ice, and had some snow
squal1s~    it was one of the coldest days as the wind came from the south pole.
On the 18th it was still colder, the thermometer stood at 24 0 in the shade ~
salt water froze as it was thrown on the deck, and the surface temperature was
28 1/2°.     We passed through more fields of thick floating ice, which shook the
ship most terribly as she forced her way through         it~   her (260) sides leak in
several places, and she will require docking at Sydney.             Numbers of immense
icebergs were passed on that day,       one large one looked exactly like the
pictures we see of the Coliseum at Rome ~          another     like the great fort    at
Sheerness, and while we were all gazing at it, one of the natives of that port
sang out -- "Change here for Sheerness".


        The latitude was 64·, 30', and the longitude 84°E on that day.               The
Captain finding he could not get a passage through the ice barrier, made sail
for     Termination Land,   a discovery of   the    United States expedition under
Captain Wilkes in 1839-40.     This expedition sailed from Sydney for the south,
and consisted of 5 ships, but none of them could find their way through the
barrier of ice, latitude 67°S was their farthest, about 20 miles beyond us.
They discovered a few islands, and       (261)     this Termination Land.     A   French
expedition came down here at the same time, which consisted of 2 corvettes,
but they could not get beyond latitude 66·,40', where the barrier stopped
them.     The ships were nearly lost amongst the ice, and only discovered a few
islands.     Sir James Ross was starting from Tasmania just as the French and
Americans were returning; his ships were strongly protected against the ice,
and he forced them through the outer barrier which extended for 200 miles,
then he found an open sea teeming with whales, and free from icebergs.                He
reached to latitude 78°, 4' the first year, and wintered in New Zealand; the
second year he reached to 78·, II'S and wintered at the Falkland Islands, the
third he reached 71·, lOtS and sailed for England.           His ships the "Erebus" and




                                       89
"Terror" were much damaged, but were repaired and sailed again-with Franklin's
expedition to the Arctic (262)      region.     Ross discovered the north magnetic
pole, and found the position of the south which is in the interior of a range
of mountains discovered by him in Victoria land.        A Russian expedition under
Bellingshauser      penetrated to latitude 73°S and discovered Alexander      Land.
So we have been as far south as the French and Americans, and have been beaten
only by the Russians, and our own countrymen.          As some of our men say "We
shall be able to talk Antarctic with anyone in England when we get back."         On
the 19th February we passed numbers of icebergs, looking like the chalk cliffs
of Dover ~ the weather was very cold and the barometer stood at 28.5 inches,
lower than in any other part of the world.           We sounded that day at 1,650
fathoms and at night passed an immense iceberg, shaped like a castle on the
summit of a cliff, and we had to lay to all (263) that night, the icebergs
were so numerous.        On the 20th we were in latitude 63°,     20'S.,   longitude
88 °E.,   the thermometer    stood at   27 0, the barometer at 28.7 inches, decks
covered with snow.      On the 21st we were obliged to furl the sails and steam as
there was no wind, and the sea was quite calm, we were surrounded by immense
icebergs, 50 could be counted at once, the ship was steamed within 30 yards of
one, and a 9 pounder shot fired at it which brought down tons of ice.         On the
22nd, Sunday, there was no wind again, it was like being in the tropics only
the weather was freezing.      On the 23rd we were on the exact spot marked on the
chart as Termination Land, and no sign of land was to be seen; soundings were
taken, and the depth was 1300 fathoms which was a certain indication of no
land in these high latitudes, for all round Kerguelen and Heards Island, the
depth     (264)   was only about 100 fathoms.     We steamed for two days    in all
directions, but saw nothing but ice, so may conclude that Termination Land has
no existence,       and the Yankees were deceived by a large      iceberg, or well
defined cloud.       One of our men (quiped) it was low-water when they were down
here.     On several occasions land has been reported from out mast head, and had
it not been for our having steam, we might have marked new lands down on the
southern charts~ but, although we could all have sworn that we saw land on one
occasion, on steaming towards it, it proved to be a peculiar, and remarkably
defined vapour cloud.       We have passed over several spots marked on the chart
as "Indications of Land· without finding any, and I daresay a steam ship would
dispel several of the mythical discoveries in this part of the world.         We had


                                         90
a magnificant (265) sunset on the 23rd, and 45 icebergs were sighted at once,
besides any amount of penguins and whales jumping about all round us.                    On the
24th we sounded at 1300 fathoms and hove the dredge, when some good specimens
were obtained.    As soon as the dredge came up, it came on to blow, and all
hands were called to make sail for Melbourne.                The ship was steamed close
under the lee of a large iceberg to allow the topsails to be reefed, and some
undercurrent drifted her right on to the berg; the engines were turned full
speed   astern,   but   to   no   purpose    and   she   drifted    right   on   to     it;   but
fortunately struck it very gently, though with sufficient force to carry away
the jib boom, dolphin striker, and other head gear.                As soon as the ship got
free, the wreck was cleared away, and the carpenters set to work to make fresh
spars, which took (266) them 2 days, and delayed us about 300 miles.                   The wind
increased to a gale, and it was the coldest day we have had, snowing and
freezing all the time; the thermometer stood at 24 degrees, and the wind was
fearfully cutting.      The latitude was 64 0 , IS'S. and longitude 95 0 E.                   The
wind kept increasing, and the ship lay to under bare poles, the fog came on so
thickly that nothing could be seen 50 yards ahead, and the snow was blinding.
At three p.m., a large iceberg was discovered drifting right on to us; the
hands were called to make sail, but by the time they got on deck the berg was
only about 20 yards from us,          and rose right above the ships masts.                   The
confusion was something fearful nearly everyone was on deck, it was snowing
and blowing hard all the time; one officer was yelling out one order, and
another something else.       The engines were steaming full- speed astern, and by
hoisting (267) the main topsail, the ship shot past it in safety.                      A seaman
fell from the trysail while they were hoisting it, and was much hurt.                         The
gale still increased, and the fog was thick, three men were kept on the look-
out all day and night.        During that night the ship was put about 9 times to
keep her clear of the icebergs.        On the 25th there was 1/2 an inch of ice all
over the outside of the ship, and while she was forcing her way through a
large field of floating ice, the artist sketched her from a boat.                     It came on
to blow again that night, and most of the sails had to be furled as there were
such numbers of icebergs about.             While furling a boy fell         from the lower
rigg ing overboard f the life boat was manned, but was not required as he had
caught a stray rope and was hauled on board unhurt, but half frozen.                      On the
26th were in latitude 63-S. and (268) longitude 94-E. and there were plenty of


                                            91
icebergs to be seen.               The new jib boom etc.,            was got out that day and
re-rigged.        We    also sounded at 1,975 fathoms and hove the trawl, obtaining
some rarities.         It was the greatest depth since leaving the Cape, and a series
of bottom temperatures were also taken which showed a warmer current beneath
than at the surface.         It came on to blow a regular gale that night, with snow,
and a thick fog. The icebergs were so numerous that the Captain thought it
would be safer to lie to, under the lee of a large one, than to drift with the
wind: so for six hours we did so, until the wind shifted and blew us away from
it.      The ship was knocked about frightfully during the night by the great
rolling seas, and everyone was glad when morning appeared.                          It was considered
the worst and most dangerous night we have had, and the Captain never (269)
left the deck for hours.              Almost all the men's crockery was broken, and many
messes used Australian meat tins for basins.                       Although we were all eager to
see an iceberg, we are just as anxious to lose them now, it is so dangerous
sailing these foggy nights with such masses of destruction all round us.                            On
the     27th     it    cleared   up     a   little,    and    we     passed   numbers     more,    one
tabular-shaped was three miles in length, and was the very largest we have
seen.        Yesterday it blew very hard and snowed a good deal, and we only ran 60
miles.         If you give your         finger    a slight cut, or          knock,     in these cold
latitudes it takes weeks to get better.                 Today, Sunday, we ran 150 miles: we
are     in     latitude   58°S.,      longitude    102 0 ,   50'     E.   weather     rather   warmer:
thermometer standing at 35 0 , we have passed several icebergs but expect they
will-be the last. We shall sail all night after this, and shall soon (270) get
into the belt of westerly winds, we are only 2000 miles from Melbourne today,
and expect to be there by the 15th March, the day I told you some time ago.
We had church this morning as usual, and at present - 7:00 p.m. - the ship is
sailing 10 knots per hour.              I have got much thinner this trip, finding I have
lost 12 lbs. since leaving England.


        Sunday, March 8th - 960 miles from Melbourne, but a head wind.


        On the 2nd March we ran 118 miles but ran nearly into a large iceberg
during the night in a fog.              We were going 9 knots per hour at the time and as
soon as it was seen, the helm was put hard down, and the ship shot past it



                                                  92
close enough to allow a biscuit to be thrown on to it, and had we struck it
the ship would have gone down stern first: some of the men got so timid of
them, that they used to remain up all night (271) in case the ship ran into
one.     For my part, although I always slept as soundly as in harbour, I don't
care if I never see an iceberg again, except in a picture, as some of our men
say -     "We have had our whack of them".            On that day we caught the brave
westerly counter trades - the best winds for sailing to be found anywhere.
Australian Clipper ships coming across here in the depth of winter have been
known to average 334 knots per day, for eight days: one famous clipper the
"James Bains· with a gale of wind behind her ran 420 knots, or 462 miles in
the 24 hours.       On the 3rd we ran 119 miles, and furled sails for trawling,
etc., the depth was 2000 fathoms, the deepest since we left the Cape.                       It
brought up some beautiful specimens, fish of the most brilliant colours and
curious forms.      On the 4th at 1 a.m., we had a splendid display of the Aurora
Australis, and turned out of my roost (272) to see it: the flashes of light
varied     in   colour,   being    white,   orange,   yellow    and   purple.    It   was    a
magnificant sight, tho' rather chilly the way I was dressed.                We only ran 40
miles that day, but on the 5th, 175 miles and on the 6th 224: on the 7th 177
in 17 hours, when we sounded at 1800 fathoms and obtained some fine specimens
in the trawl,       notably a transparent star fish,           that looked like red silk
velvet.     The creature's heart could be seen beating and some young ones inside
it with the naked eye.            Some curious fish with long tails like rats were
brought up.      We ra~ 120 miles today, but have a head wind, and only 40 tons of
coal on board: unles the wind changes the Captain will put into Hobart Town
for coal.       The last two icebergs were passed on the 4th.             Today we are 960
miles from Melbourne in latitude 48°S. and longitude l30 0 E.


       Monday - March 16th - off King's Island, (273) 110 miles from Melbourne.
As the wind shifted on the 9th we did not put into Hobart Town.                 Should have
been there before this only had two days trawling - depth about 2,500 fathoms,
much deeper than any since leaving the Cape, and some rare specimens were
obtained.       It is much warmer now, the thermometer at 70 0 in the shade, and the
days much shorter, it being dark again now at 7 p.m.              Yesterday at our church
service, the Captain returned thanks for our safe delivery from the recent



                                            93
dangers in the ice country.      We sighted a ship last night: the first for 13
weeks, except the whalers.    We left the Cape, December 17th and shall arrive
at Melbourne March 17th, three months to the day.            We are now off King's
Island, 20 miles from Cape    Otway~   it is about the size of Marion Island.
There was a large passenger ship lost on it about 10 years ago, the passengers
reached (274) here in safety, and were soon relieved from Melbourne.       A child
was born on the island the same night the ship was lost.        As soon as they see
us from Cape Otway they will telegraph to Melbourne, and thence to England, so
that owing to the 10 hours difference of time, they will know there before
Melbourne (according to the clock).


     I hear the mail leaves to-morrow and on arriving at Melbourne hope to be
reading some of your home news.


     Concluding this long form
     Believe Me
     Faithfully yours,
     Joe Matkin.

                                            March 25, 1874


Dear Tom:
     The mail came on board the same evening we anchored, and brought me 7
letters, 8 newspapers, etc.    I enclose you a splendid specimen of the aborig-
inal ladies of this country: who neither wears chignon or bustle as you'll
see, still she has good pints about her, and in summer her dress is even less
expensive than at present, as it is the fall of the year.         However, I should
like the ladies opinion before I commit myself, and its just possible I may be
able to find a handsomer sort at New Zealand or the South Sea Islands, and one
that a'int so (276) fond of dress.      The first news we heard on arrival here
was that Tichborne had 14 years.       I think he has been dealt too leniently



                                       94
with, many better men than he have been hung for much smaller offences.                  We
also heard of Bazaine's conviction and sentence, and of the conclusion of the
Ashantee War.       The English cricketers went home the day before we arrived,
they were beaten on one or two occasions, and I believe quarrelled between
themselves on money matters.            I was very sorry to hear of Mr. Blackwood's
death, my last letter from him I received at Lisbon.                Soon after we anchored,
two gentlemen came on board to see me~i one an old schoolfellow at Oakham, he
is a Draper, and lives 200 miles up the country, had come down to buy goods
and wanted     (217) me to return with him for a few days, which I could not
manage, but spent two days with him and a friend of his at Melbourne, who was
a Danish gentleman and had a great dislike to Germans, but admired the English
because they were beaten at Copenhagen, under Nelson, and on other occasions.
We went about Melbourne a good deal and I visited all myoId favorite haunts
and walks.     It has increased wonderfully but must tell you more about it in my
next letter.       I also went out to Brunswick, three miles distant, to see some
old colonial friends that were very kind to me when I was out here before.
They are an elderly married couple, very well off, and I can go and live with
them whenever I am      ashore~    I am going on Sunday (278) to dinner.           They are
never tired of hearing about our voyage and Mrs. Appleby has been allover the
ship.    The have been out here 20 years, and made a lot of money, and are soon
coming back to England to spend the remainder of their days, but are first
going to France and Italy excursioning, etc.             They come from the neighbourhood
of Ely, and have been home once for 18 months, and came_ out again with me in
the "Essex", where I first made their acquaintance.


        Enclosed   is   my   portrait   taken    here.      until   July    16th    address
Singapore, China.


                                                         Yours sincerely,


                                                         Joe Matkin.
