                                                Sydney, April 10, 1874
Dear Tom:
      The English mail arrived here today from Melbourne and brought me only
one letter from yourself dated February 6th.         A mail leaves to-morrow for
England via San Francisco and the Pacific Railway, and think it will reach
England within a week of the last, posted a fortnight ago.          We remained in
Melbourne until April 1st and arrived here on the 6th, the distance is 580
miles, but we were sounding and dredging as we came along.         I enjoyed myself
very much in Melbourne, spent two or three days on shore with myoId friends
at Brunswick (280).      We had such numbers of visitors on board before we left.
The Officers gave a dance party on the 28th, over a hundred ladies and gentle-
men came off.       Our men say Melbourne is the finest place in the world, they
were so well treated by the people, the railway authorities gave them free
passes for travelling up the country.        Many went up to Ballarat, the great
gold mining metropolis and 6 of them never came back.          I spent a fortnight
there, when out here before, it is a fine town, over 90,000 inhabitants and is
100 miles from Melbourne.      We read an account of the university boat race in
the Monday papers after the event.       On the 30th, two seamen tried to escape
from the ship to the shore in one of the boats, but they were recaptured and
are now in irons waiting court martial.        On the 31st, I had to (281) go up
with the paymaster to Melbourne to fetch £800 from one of the banks to pay the
ship's company.      We left on the 1st of April and sailed-and steamed round, we
sighted the coast nearly all the way and passed several small islands.          The
coast    is moderately high,     and wholly covered in forest,. very unlike the
African coast.      We passed several ships and sounded once within 15 miles of
the   land   at   a depth of 2375 fathoms,    5 miles nearer     the depth was 100
fathoms.     This was our first sounding in the Pacific ocean.


        We spent our Good Friday and Easter Sunday at sea, so you may be sure we
were not over comfortable.      The German frigate "Arcona" came round with us and
arrived a few hours earlier.      We entered Sydney Heads at 1 p.m. Easter Monday,
and at 2:00 p.m. dropped anchor in Farm Cove, close to the "Arcona" and (282)
HMS "Dido".       It is 9 miles from the Heads to Sydney, and the scenery down the
bay is magnificent, and the harbour of Sydney is justly considered one of the


                                        96
finest in the world.       There are so many bays and creeks branching off from
Botany Bay, which afford fine shelter for shipping.          There are several small
islands close to the town, on one of them there is a large suburb like New
York and Brooklyn and steamers cross every few minutes.        We are lying nearly a
mile from Sydney and can't see much of it, but are within a stone's throw of
the public park, in a fine bay reserved for the anchorage of men of war only.
When we came in on Easter Monday, the park was crowded with people holiday
making,    picnicing,   etc.   The ladies saluted us      bravely with   their   hand-
kerchiefs and we were soon surrounded with pleasure (283) boats.          The houses
here are older than at Melbourne and the place has a more English appearance.
Some parts of the harbour are very similar to that at Plymouth.          This bay is
not one fourth as large as Hobson's Bay, but much better sheltered being per-
fectly land-locked, we are unable to see the sea from where we are lying, but
there is a fine view of the Pacific from the highlands of the town.                The
shores of the bay are covered with forest and park, with residences of the
gentry peeping pleasantly out between the trees.        There are some splendid mer-
chant ships here J the famous China Clipper "Thermopylea" is at anchor.            She
ran from London to Melbourne in 58 days, and in one 24 hours ran 420 miles,
but the finest and largest merchant vessel we can see is a new one,                the
"Samuel Plimsole" (284) from London.         I have not been on shore yet, but am go-
ing for 2 or 3 days next week.        All our men who have been, say that is in-
ferior in every way to Melbourne.      One watch is now on four days leave and re-
turns on Monday ne.xt and on Tuesday the ship goes in dry dock at Cockatoo
Island for some time and expect we shall lose more men during our stay.            The
weather is very hot although winter is coming on, the thermometer standing at
80·     in the shade,   but in the   summer months Sydney is often cooler         than
Melbourne and Adelaide.        I am anxiously looking out for English papers con-
taining the termination of the Tichborne trial, the people here always thought
him an imposter and rogue.


        You will receive this by the end of May and if you write at once, and
(285)    address Sydney,   it will be forwarded to us at the Fiji Islands. Put
"elsewhere" on it, and its bound to reach us sometime.         One of our men has his
letters addressed "Challenger" voyage round the world (or elsewhere).            After
the middle of June until the latter end of July, address Singapore, and it


                                        97
will reach us at Somerset, Cape York, by the end of August.      After leaving New
Zealand, the Fijis, New Caledonia, etc., we stand west towards Torres Straits
and New Guinea, calling at Cape York, the most northerly point of Australia,
further particulars in my next.


                                                      Yours sincerely,


                                                      Joseph Matkin.



(286)                                                 HMS "Challenger"
                                                      Sydney, May 15, 1874


Dear Tom:
        I   have only received a "Daily News· from you since last I      wrote, and
expect no more letters before we reach New Zealand.       Themail that takes this
starts tomorrow for Melbourne and England, being the last one homeward bound
before we leave, the date for which at present is May 27th, but it will prob-
ably be later.      We shall be 14 days going to New Zealand, as we have to take a
line of soundings across the Pacific from Sydney to Wellington or Auckland,
for a cable to be laid this year if possible.


(287L         We have taken in 230 tons of coal and at pres~nt all hands are busy
filling up with provisions, coaling, etc., to last us to Hong Kong, where we
are to arrive the 2nd of November.       We have lost about 24 men since we arrived
in this country and only three have been recaptured.       Two were tried by court
martial today for desertion, and each sentenced to 12 months imprisonment, the
third one only got 90 days.        There are 3 men of war here now: our ship, the
"Dido" and the "Pearl" -- Flag ship of Commodore Goodenough, which has just
come from the Fiji Islands, now under British protection.        The French man of
war, the "Chern is also close to us, she came in on Sunday morning from New
Caledonia to make enquiries concerning Rochefort, and the other three com-
munist prisoners who       (288)   escaped from there a few weeks ago and landed
here. Our officers gave a grand ball on shore the other night to the nobility,



                                         98
etc. of Sydney, and tomorrow our ship's company are invited to a Tea meeting
and Temperance lecture at the Masonic Hall on shore.     The Tea ~eeting will be
a great success, but the lecture won't allure many towards the teetotal breth-
ren. Your letter addressed Sydney will reach me at New Zealand or the Fij i
Islands, and I shall write you from both places.       I have been on shore here
several times, but don't like the place so well as Melbourne.        I have seen
some fine buildings, including the Governor's House, new post office, town
hall, university, museum and Protestant Cathedral, the bells of which are very
much like ours at Oakham1 the building is a (289) very pretty one, the windows
are all of stained glass and the organ cost 1500 pounds.    The sittings are all
free, but there is an offertory after each service.     It is soon full after the
doors are opened, and the lady part of the attendance dress very smartly and
fashionably.


     The children of Australia are not such strong healthy looking children as
the English, but the colony of Victoria is healthier than New South Wales.
They are very fast children generally, much like the American juveniles, but
speak better English here, although they call a cow, a keow.      We were only 5
days in dry dock at Cockatoo Island, as the ship's bottom was in very good
condition; the ice did us but little damage, and when a ship sails through
water of such varying (290) temperatures no barnacles or other secretions can
accumulate on her bottom.


     An English bargue (sic) arrived here the other day with the Captain's
wife lying dead on board, having died the day before the ship came in -- in
childbirth.


     Professor Thompson and some of the scientific party are gone to Brisbane
for a three week tour into the inter ior of Queensland.      The rainy season or
winter has commenced here, but it is quite as hot during the day as summer in
England.   We have had some magnificent sunsets here for the last month, and
for rainbows I never saw a place like Sydney.   A fine iron vessel called the
"City of Benares· sailed hence yesterday for London, via Cape Town, but should
not care to have taken the voyage in her, as (291) she was laden deeper than
any ship I ever saw and it is the worst time of year for doubling the Horn.


                                    99
The fine ship "Samuel Plimsole" sailed for London a fortnight ago.                  She is
supposed to be a faster vessel than the "Themopyla".              Wigram's fine steam ship
"Northumberland" arrived at Melbourne last week from Plymouth in 51 days, 18
hours, via the Cape of Good Hope, which is faster than the mail boats do it
from SOuthampton via Suez.    Our officers have been feted a great deal since we
came here,     but the men have      not    been so well     treated as     they   were   at
Melbourne. We have had the Governor and any amount of visitors on board, but
we shall all be glad to get to sea again for a change.                 We shall have been
nearly 8 weeks here before we leave for (292) New Zealand where we do not stay
long.    The time slips away very quickly with us, it seems as if we shall be in
England again in almost less than no time.             It takes us a rare lot of cash,
which one is unable to see the wonders of the world without spending, and some
more will have to fly in purchasing curiosities at Japan. Most of our men have
drawn their money out of the ship's savings bank since we arrived here and
talk of commencing afresh after leaving New Zealand.               until July 30th address
Singapore, via Southampton.        I expect it, will be Hong Kong after August, and
to Manilla I don't think there is any mail.


                                                           Your Sincerely,


                                                           Joe Matkin.


                                                  HMS "Challenger"-
                                                  South Pacific
                                                  June 21, 1874


Dear Tom:
        Your last letter reached me on the 2nd June, which was dated March 9th,
and must have been delayed in England for some time, for the paper you sent on
the 4th of April reached me on May 22nd.


        We left Sydney at 4 p.m. on the 8th June for Wellington distant 1180
miles, S by E and we were to take a careful line of soundings across, to sound
every two hours in the shallow water, for the cable that is to be laid from
Sydney to New     Zealand   next    year.     We    are still     25 men short of     (294)


                                            100
complement, although we shipped 8 new hands as stokers, cooks, etc., and took
those out of prison that were sentenced to three months for deserting.       There
was quite a crowd of people on the wharves and shores of the harbour to see us
depart, and as we steamed past the "Dido" and "Pearl", their crews mounted the
rigging and cheered us while their bands played "Auld Lang Syne".      Our men re-
turned the cheers and our band gave 'em "The Girl I Left Behind Me".       We had
been nine weeks in Sydney and were getting tired of it.


       Until March 1875 our address will be Singapore, the letters to be for-
warded from there to wherever we are, mails leave England every fortnight, so
you can't make much mistake.       We do not expect to be home before July /76 as
we are a month behind time already.      The Melbourne (295) Illustrated paper for
June 13th had a picture of our ship at Kerguelen's Land and also amongst the
ice.       They were taken from our photographs, but have not been able to get you
any of them, but daresay you will see the same pictures in the London papers.
On the 9th of June we sounded in sight of Sydney Heads at 50 fathoms and 75
fathoms but a gale sprang up that night which stayed any further sounding and
obliged us to run back and anchor in Watson's Bay for two days until the
weather moderated.       On the 12th we started again and sounded several times
from 70 to 900 fathoms, on the 13th sounded from 400 to 700, and ran back to
the land to verify the line of soundings. On the 14th (Sunday) it blew very
hard and was too rough for church, but not for sounding the Captain (296)
thought, so he sounded at 2275 fathoms, about 2 3/4 miles, the sea had deep-
       -
ened nearly two miles in that run of 40 miles.        In hauling in the line 1500
fathoms were carried away which the men attributed to sounding on the Sabbath
and not having had any surveying wine lately.         The same night it came on a
regular gale, the upper yards were sent down and everything prepared for it,
the cutter was stove in and the patent life buoy carried away by a heavy sea
in the night and a good deal of the men's crockery broken.


       This life buoy is a new patent, there is a place for the man to put his
feet in if he understands it and can reach it and a receptacle for 7 days pro-
visons, and on being let go by means of a common bell handle and wire, a mag-
nesium light ignites and burns for 20 minutes, water not affecting it.          We
(297) had only that one, though we have several old fashioned buoys.        On the


                                        101
15th it was rough, but on the 16th, we sounded at 2550 fathoms and carr ied
away 2500 in hauling in, which line costs 9 d per fathom.            On the 17th the
depth was 2700 fathoms -- over 3 miles, and we obtained a few living specimens
in the dredge.        On the 18th and 19th it was a dead calm, and we had to steam
   depth 2600 fathoms.          To-day, Sunday, we had no church again as it was too
rough, but we sounded at 1975 fathoms -- nearly a mile shallower since yes-
terday.        It is now blowing hard and the barometer falling.



                                                         Saturday night, June 27th.


        Anchored under Long Island, Cook's Straits.       Last Sunday night the gale
increased and the foretop mast staysail was carried away.          The ship stood it
first rate, it was a frightful          (298) night, every now and then a heavy sea
would strike the ship and make her quiver again.           On the 22nd, it cleared a
little and we sounded at 1100 fathoms, a difference of two miles in a run of
about 80. On the 23rd we sailed 141 miles and sounded at 275 fathoms only,
(another mile shallower).          We were then 240 miles from the nearest land, Cape
Farewell, N. Zealand.          From there to Cape Farewell the depth varied from 450
to 45 fathoms.           At 1 p.m. on the 24th we sighted Mount Egmont 65 miles dis-
tant.     It is 8200 feet high and of course was covered in snow,      ~s   it is mid-
winter here, still there is no snow on hills under 3000 feet high. The wind is
fri~htfully      cutting and we all are wearing our winter clothing.


        There are several mountains in New Zealand over 8,000 feet          high~   the
highest Mount Cook, is 13,200 feet above sea level, and is a fine landmark
(299)    for    ships.     The 2 large and 5 or 6 small islands of New Zealand are
nearly as large as Great Britain and Ireland together, and most of the land is
cultivable.        There are only about 8 towns larger than Oakham, the 4 largest
are Dunedin and Christchurch on the south island, and Wellington and Auckland
on the north.        Dunedin is the youngest and most go ahead place, there are some
rich gold diggings there about.


        Christchurch was formerly the capital and a nice English sort of town I
am told.         It gave place to Auckland, which although the largest place was


                                           102
superseded by Wellington on account of its more central position, which is at
the south point of the North island, and Auckland is 580 miles- north of it by
water and Dunedin 630 miles.         There are under 300,000 white people on N.Z. as
yet (300) so there is plenty of room for emigrants.            There are 40,000 Maories
partly civilized left now, and all are on the North Island except 1,000 who
are scattered about the south.        They speak the same language as the South Sea
Islanders, but were intermixed ages ago with the Papuans of New Guinea, who
are supposed to have come from some of the Polynesian Islands about the year
1550.     This supposition is borne out by their own traditions and war songs,
which relate how they sailed here in their canoes and conquered and exter-
minated the original natives; with the names of their chiefs.                   The original
natives were probably of the same race as the aboriginals of Australia.                  The
Maories are the finest and bravest race of savages in the world and are good
seamen.     Although they were cannibals they lived in houses and tilled the
ground when Cook (301) visited and explored the island in 1776.


        On the 25th June at 1 p.m. we were close into the land and as it came on
to blow, and we could not get through Cook's Straits, the ship was anchored in
Amnesty Bay on the South Island.        The coast was mountainous and something like
Kerguelen's, especially coming through the Straits, except the hills being
covered in forest.       We had to remain all day on the 26th, caught lots of fish
and got plenty of fine shell fish from the rocks.             This morning at 3 a.m. the
anchor was got uP' and we steamed out of the Bay for Wellington, distant 45
miles.     We found the wind and sea as rough as ever on getting outside and the
wind was right in our teeth.          In 8 hours we only steamed 20 miles and were
obliged to run under the lee of Long Island, and anchor until the weather mod-
erated.


(302)      We   passed   lots   of   islets   and   rocks   today   and   the   coast   looks
frightfully bleak and wild, the mountains on each side are covered in snow.
The straits are about 20 miles wide just here and there is a fearful sea
running.    The Captain is in a great hurry to reach Wellington but the men are
not while this weather lasts, and until further orders would rather lie here
nice and snug catching fish.         When we left the Cape on our long voyage we had



                                           103
280 tons of coal, and had 10 tons left when we reached Melbourne.     On leaving
Sydney we had 220 tons and have burnt it all but 10, so what with the coal and
the sounding line carried away, this will be a very expensive trip.



                                        Sunday Night, June 28th, at Wellington.
        The passage is over at last and so is the long voyage for one poor fellow
who was drowned at 12 o'clock today, while everyone else was dining (303) in
comparative comfort, drowned in broad daylight, whilst performing his duty and
not one of us to see him go, or to throw him a life bUOY1 the ship went steam-
ing on for Wellington, and he to his last long home.


        Although it was blowing as hard as ever this morning, and a frightful sea
running, the Captain had the anchor got up and started full speed on the last
25 miles of the journey.    We had no church as it was too rough.   The ship was
cutting an awful caper but still riding like a duck on the water, the fore and
aft sails were set and as the water is shallow in the straits a leadsman was
in the chains sounding.     At 10 o'clock we passed a dismantled ship at anchor
under the lee of the land and at 12 o'clock they piped dinner.      The officers
then go to lunch, and all the rest of the (304) ship's company to dinner, ex-
cept the lieutenant in charge of her, the 4 men steering, the leadsman and the
boatswain's mate.    The leadsman stands on a platform outside the ship to heave
the lead.     Just after the crew went to dinner, the man sounding got his lead
and line fouled round the anchor, and was seen to climb up to clear it by a
marine.     Just at that time a frightful sea struck and broke over the fore part
of the ship shaking her from stem to stern.       It capsized lots of plates and
basins on the mess deck, but only caused a general laugh1 one facetious fellow
said: "who's that knocking at the door", and another told the sea to "come
in", that was all that occurred there, but on the upper deck the sea had come
in and gone out again taking with it the poor leadsman from off the anchor, in
all his thick winter clothing, sea boots and oilskins.     Then the ship righted
(305)    herself again and went ploughing away for      some 10 minutes1   at the
expiration of that time, the marine who saw the man go out to clear his line,
happened to look out of the port and saw the line still round the anchor, but
no leadsman there, when he ran and told the lieutenant of the watch, who at


                                       104
once informed the Captain and Commander 1 the Captain telegraphed the engine
room to stop and all hands were called to put the ship about, and in 2 minutes
she was steaming fast back over the original track.      Some of the officers went
aloft with glasses and nearly every soul in the ship was in the rigging
looking out for some sign of him. After a few minutes some dark object was
seen right ahead and about a dozen sang out, "there he is, right ahead", but
on steaming up it proved to (306) be only seaweed, and nothing more of the
poor fellow was seen.       The ship then stood on again for Wellington and we
dropped anchor half an hour ago, about half a mile from the town.         The de-
ceased Edward Winton was one of the finest and steadiest seamen in the ship,
was about 25 years old and married just before we left England.      He was an ex-
cellent swimmer, but had on an enormous lot of clothes, and no one knows
whether he was stunned against the ship's side by the sea, or he might have
been struck by the fans of the screw as he drifted under the stern.       No   boat
could have lived in the sea that was running but the ship could have steamed
up close enough to throw him a rope, had he been seen.       No blame attaches to
anyone.


        June 30th.   We have just made a subscription (307) on the lower deck for
the widow of the poor fellow, and £20 were obtained from the crew alone, and I
daresay the officers will raise another £30.


    -There were no letters here for us.


        The Bay of Wellington is something like Table Bay, and the place is not
unlike Cape Town.      It is about as large as Stamford, but the houses are mostly
of wood and it is as dirty as Halifax.        Meat is 3d per lb and is better than
the Australian1 provisions are generally cheap, but rent and clothes are very
dear.     We are now coaling to last us to the Fiji Islands, and I hear we are
not going to Auckland being so much behind time.




                                        105
July 1.


       The English mail has just arrived and brought me 3 letters,               two from
yourself, the last dated May 4th and addressed Auckland.          It has not been long
on the way and is the latest news I have from England. (308) We shall be at
the Fiji islands about the 1st August and shall write you from there~ they are
in the tropics,      the distance is 1250 miles,       so we shall soon be in warm
weather again. Any later letters you have written will be kept there until we
arrive, or i f after we have gone,          they will be forwarded to Cape Yorke,
Australia.


       I have not been on shore yet, but am going on Friday.          We expect to leave
here on Monday the 6th, and will tell you more about the place in my next let-
ter.


       I have not yet told you of the loss of the "British Admiral" on King's
island close to Melbourne.          It has happened since we left there and 80 lives
were lost.


       Meat, potatoes, flour and bread are cheap here but clothes, house rent
and drink are very dear.          (309)


       Wages are even better than in Australia, but are not so steady: a jobbing
man won't work under 8 (shillings) per day and mechanics, etc., get 12 (shil-
lings) ~ still there are plenty of idlers and loafers from England, America,
and    Australia,    some   are    continually   travelling   about   to   the   different
Australian colonies, and never work for a week together.              After we leave the
Fijis you will not get a letter for 2 months.          We shall be dredging round the
Malayan Islands and Polynesia, until March /76, when we go to Japan.              The let-
ters must be addressed Singapore and the Consul or other authorities there
will forward them by private ships to wherever we are.


       Yours faithfully,


       Joe Matkin.

                                           HMS "Challenger"
                                           Tongatabu, Friendly Islands (now Tonga)
                                           July 23, 1874


Dear Tom:
     We are now with the savages of Polynesia, so will write up our adventures
amongst them.     We have only 210 men on board now, instead of 244, for we lost
6 more men at Wellington.     I think I told you of my going on shore there, and
what a dull place it is compared to Melbourne or Sydney.        I saw some of the
Maories and they are exactly like these natives, though more savage in their
manner and appearance through being tattoed.       We left Wellington on the 6th
for these islands, distant about 1250 miles, N by E.       (311) We kept close into
the New Zealand coast for three days, sighting Poverty Bay and the East Cape,
but we did not go to Auckland, as we were so much behind time.        Our greatest
depth thus far has been 2925 fathoms, and this is the deepest since we left
the North Atlantic.     Some wonderful marine curiosities, sponges, coral, etc.,
have been obtained in the dredge and trawl net.      We passed the 180th degree of
longitude on the 10th when the difference of time was exactly 12 hours between
us and you.     As we are losing time again now by going back towards Australia,
we did not have the usual extra day but shall have it between Japan and
Vancouver.      We passed through the Kermadec group of islands on the 14th and
sounded off SundaY,Is1and, but did not land.       They looked fertile, but don't
think   (312)   they are inhabited.    On Sunday 19th we sighted Eoa, the first
island of this group, and after coming up to it sighted Tbngatabu and anchored
there at 1 p.m.     This group received the name of Friendly Islands from Captain
Cook, who was the first to communicate with the natives, but Tasman the Dutch
navigator discovered them in 1642.       They are just inside the tropics and ex-
tend from 300 miles each way.         There are over 150 islands of all sizes but
only about 30 are inhabited.     The total population is 25,000 and Tongatbu is
the largest island and the residence of the king.          It is about as large as
St. Thomas, but much more level, and its population is about 5000, and there
are some 30 or 40 white people from Australia and New Zealand who are car-
penters, coopers, bakers, traders, etc., and also a few missionaries.




                                         107
(313) There are about 50 small islands in sight from here, they look like
small gardens afloat, some are scarcely out of the water and not 10 feet above
the water's edge.     You seem to step out of the ocean into a paradise.   There
are several islands not as large as your back garden, but they are covered
with vegetation down to the water's edge, Palm trees and bananas principally.
Of course there are no inhabitants on these little oases, and it was suggested
by one of our forecastle philosophers that the Captain should serve out an
island to each man who cared for one, and after providing him with a wife,
some rum and tobacco, leave him for the remainder of his days in virtuous re-
tirement.     We found 3 large Amer ican whale boats at anchor here, waiting a
week or two until the humpbacked whales arrive, and they can commence their
fishing season. They are after the sperm whales, and have no such hardships to
undergo as those whalemen down at Kerguelen's Land, after the cold water
whale.     Several (314) boats of natives came out to meet us and we towed them
in with us. They were fine able-bodied looking men of a light copper colour,
almost red, and they had black curly hair standing up straight from the head.
This they dye with a sort of lime until it is of the same colour and as stiff
as tarry oakum.     They were naked but as soon as they were fairly alongside,
they put on a white linen sheet that reached from the waist to the knees, with
great satisfaction and complacency.       They could speak a little English and
asked for tobacco.     They looked over the ship and seemed much struck with the
engines and the    s~eam,   for they don't (315) often see a steam ship at these
islands.     There was an Englishman in the boat with them, who does a sort of
small export trade with any shipping that may call.      He informed the Captain
that King George had an Englishman imprisoned on one of the small islands for
attempting to murder a native whilst drunk and that the King was waiting for a
ship of war to arrive and try him, so our Captain investigated the matter and
ordered the man to be sent to New Zealand or Australia at the first oppor-
tunity.     He had been 5 years on the island and came from Yorkshire.       The
natives told us they would bring off fruit, etc., on Monday but they never
traded on the Sabbath Day and always go twice to church. Some of our men told
them they were ftfools and should trade whenever they could get the chance ft ,
and were answered by the heathens, ·You (316) no good, you too much devil, you
no missionary·.     Well, on Monday morning swarms of canoes came alongside to
trade.     The canoe is made out of the hollow tree, and has a log framework to


                                       108
balance it on the lee side.     There are generally two natives in it -- one on
the bows and another in the stern who paddles, in it there is a large bunch of
bananas, a basket of cocoanuts, one of limes, one of lemons, one of figs and
another of shells, coral, etc., a few fowls, and in the centre of the lot, a
small black and very quiet pig, which gentleman makes no noise and looks as if
he had come out for a cruise in his own trough.    The natives asked a shilling
for each article and basket of fruit, etc., upon hearing which, the sailors
cursed the missionaries and said they would soon (317) spoil the whole world,
some of   them were expecting to pass buttons for money, and think of getting
to some islands by and by, where they can buy pearls, etc., for beads, and
where a cold missionary is always kept on the table.     However, as the natives
didn't know the difference between a 3d piece and half a crown, things might
have been worse they said.    Only when the small money began to get scarce, the
poor ignorant savages would not give change at the usual rate -- not 10 3d
pieces for half a crown.       I bought a large bunch of bananas, some melons,
shells, etc., a fish hook made out of a shark's tooth for 3d, a paper collar
and an old tie.    About 50 native priests and instructors came on board on
Monday and were very partial to collars and ties, they were dressed in the
most grotesque rigs imaginable, some had old black (318) suits too large for
them, relics of departed missionaries, some had a coat and a sheet, others a
pair of trousers and sheet, and several had college caps but none shoes or
stockings, and each had some little article to trade with.


     Photographs of the native men and women were taken on Monday.    The ship's
band also landed and played selections outside the King's palace to the great
delight of the whole island.     Last night the chief missionary, the Rev. Baker
(Wesleyan), his wife and 2 daughters, the three American whaling captains and
their wives, and the King's 2nd son came on board and dined with our officers.


     King George, who is nearly 80 years old, and his eldest son governs the
northern island.   The other son was a fine looking man, over six feet, he was
dressed in European costume and could speak good English, and also play the
harmonium and violin.    He played and sang some     (319) sacred hymns, to our
officers and the whaling captains' great delight.       The missionary seems to
have more power than the King and is more looked up to: his cottage is a very


                                      109
pretty one, the best on the island.      The royal palace is built of wood, with a
thatched roof, and is one story high, and looks very much like a large stable.
r went on shore yesterday afternoon and had a long walk inland.           There is no
landing place and you have to be carried on shore from the boat.           The island
is like an enormous garden covered with palm trees, etc., and overrun with a
jungle of creepers and tropical vegetation.          The roads are like the green
avenues in our woods at home, only shaded with the palms.          There are no rocks
or stones but the ground is covered with sea-shells right inland, showing that
these islands have not existed above the ocean for many hundred years.         It was
(320) a very hot afternoon and I had on my straw hat.           water is very scarce,
the natives seem to drink cocoanut milk instead, which by climbing the trees
you can get as many as you want, or by asking at the huts, which is the
easiest plan, as they have the milk ready and it is rather a difficult matter
to get the outer shell off a cocoanut.            They       wi th melons and bananas
flourish all the year round -- but oranges and other sorts of fruit are out of
season just now for it is mid-winter.         Nothing appears to be cultivated, for
everything the natives require grows spontaneously and they won't do any reg-
ular work for more than 2 days together.       They pay a small tax to the King and
missionary.


        I   believe there are some Roman Catholic missionaries on some of the
islands, but the two sects are at variance, though they do not actually fight
with each other.      There are (321) plenty of flies and mosquitos, a few pretty
birds, some gorgeous butterflies and lizards, but there are no wild animals or
snakes, but any amount of pigs, cats, dogs, horses and fowls, which were orig-
inally imported and have greatly increased.              There are not many sheep or
cattle.      We took in one day's fresh beef, but the men threw it away as it was
so fat and oily through the cow having been fed on cocoanuts.          On the highest
point of land, facing the sea, is the principal church.          It is built of wood,
painted and thatched, is well seated and has a very clean and neat interior
and would hold about 800.       There is a nice organ and the singing was first
rate.       There are other places of worship and several schools, etc., which the
native teachers instruct under the missionary.           Nearly all the younger people
can read and a great many write. (322) Some of the young women are very hand-
some and have fine long black hair, but they get fat as they grow old. They


                                        110
have fine teeth and good figures, and like most ladies are very fond of dress
on Sundays. Some of them have silk gowns, in one of the huts I entered the
girls were ironing their Sabbath muslins.            On week days they wear nothing but
the usual sheet, from the waist to the knees, the children wear a palm leaf.
They    smell    rather    disagreeably owing   to    their   anointing   themselves   with
cocoanut oil, which is very unpleasant under a tropical sun.                 This oil is
about the only export.         Copper money is not taken on the island.        The native
huts are framed of bamboo and thatched with palm leaves, etc.             There is a hole
in the roof for the smoke to escape and another in the side to enter by.
There is no furniture (323), a few mats to sleep on and some rough cooking
utensils.       They are very hospitable and delighted if you will come and sit
down in their huts, where you generally find the whole family squatted on
their hams on the floor and gr inning a welcome as you enter.                 The hostess
invariably tells the girls to bring you a cocoanut (a large one holds over a
pint of cool milk), and they also give you yams roasted in plantain leaves.
It is a large root like an old tree stump to look at, and is like a potato
when boiled, and eats between that, an artichoke and a turnip.               This and the
banana is the principal food of all the South Sea islanders and the natives of
many tropical countries.        I like bananas as well as any fruit I know and they
are wonderfully plentiful in the Tropics.            The ladies are very fond of tobacco
and I made presents (324) to all those who entertained me.            Some years ago the
Chief of one of      th~   Polynesian islands offered to sell all his missionar ies
for    a keg of tobacco.     The natives invariably ask you if-you are a missionary,
by which they mean a Christian, and bring you their Bibles and hymn books to
look at.        They have also almanack for 1874 hanging up in their huts, with
local chronological events recorded for each day.             All these books are printed
in London by the Wesleyan Missionary Society in the native Tongan language.


        In these 40 or 50 years the Wesleyans have instructed and civilized the
natives of these and many other groups of islands far more than the Roman
Catholics have done the negroes of Brazil, and other countries, in the course
of 200 years.       This island and the people- is a credit to them and speaks well
for the zeal       (325)   and care of the missionaries, they do their work thor-
oughly, and I doubt whether the Church of England missionaries would have made
as much progress in the time, but shall be better able to judge when we


                                          111
get to some of the islands under the evangelism of the Established Church.
The Wesleyan Missionary Society deserves the support of all denominations in
England, and I should think their faith is the simplest and best for these
primitive people.     They have made great progress with the Maories.         We are
just outside of Tongatbu now, under sail for Kandavu, Fiji Islands, where we
expect letters.      There are plenty of flying        fish,   and several humpbacked
whales to be seen.     At night the sea is alive with beautiful sparkling phos-
phorescent creatures invisible to the naked eye, but emitting a bright light,
and making the foam look like         (326)    fire as it is dashed from the ship's
bows. The sunrise and sunsets, too, are beautiful in the extreme, more so in
the Pacific I believe, than in any other part of the world.         We are now in the
S. East Trade Winds region and this will be favourable to us until we cross
the line in Malaya, and we shall have some 4 or 5 months cruising in the
tropics again now.


        Sunday, August 2nd, at sea.    On the 23rd we passed Turtle Island, and on
the 24th stood in to Matuku Island belonging to the Fiji group.          It was about
5 miles long, and 3 broad, and some 1200 feet above the sea level.         A party of
officers and men landed and explored the island.         There were about 600 natives
on it and like those of all the Fiji Islands, they are black and ugly.           They
are not to be compared to (327) the Friendly Islanders in strength or dis-
position, and have a fierce, morose look about them and there is more New
Guinea blood in their veins than in the Maories or Tongans.            On the 25th we
arrived at Kandavu and found that our letters had been sent on to Levuka.
Kandavu is an island about 29 miles long and 6 broad, and some 1500 feet above
the sea level, and pretty fertile, though mountainous.             There are not many
natives on it and only a few white people.         There is no town to speak of, but
as there is a pretty good harbour, formed by a cay reef extending across the
entrance and acting as a breakwater.          The San Francisco mail boats call here
for coal, and are met by the branch mail boat from Sydney and New Zealand.
These mail boats, will I expect, eventually make Levuka their place (328) of
call.    We remained two days at Kandavu surveying, etc., and sailed on the 27th
for the island of Obalan, distant 120 miles.            We arrived the next day and
anchored off Levuka, the capital of the Fiji group and received our letters --
old ones from Sydney.      Obalan is about as large as Kandavu and mountainous.


                                         112
The Fiji group numbers over 220 islands, the two largest are 300 miles in cir-
cumference and there are several larger than Tongatbu.            Of course they are all
in the tropics and vegetation is remarkably luxuriant.                  The bread fruit,
banana, plantain, arrowroot, nutmeg, capsicum, teaplant and sugar cane will
all grow here, but the first three, with the coocanut are the principal pro-
ductions.     Cotton also grows wild, though it is a great object of cultivation
by the white colonists settled (329) on the banks of the river Renvi on the
largest island of Vanu Levu.          The whole native population is not less than
200,000.     There are several different tribes and great chiefs, but Thakombau
is the supreme governor of the whole group.            He lives on the large island but
has a house at Levuka.        In the interior of the large island the natives are
still very savage and uncivilized, and fighting frequently takes place amongst
them.      There are several missionaries of all denominations, but they don't
find the natives so tractable as those of the Friendly Islands.             Of course you
read     in the   papers of   the    Fijis being     annexed   to Great Britain.          King
Thakombau has gradually contracted a debt of over £80,000, and finding himself
unable to pay it handed over the kingdom to England (330) on the understanding
that our government should be responsible for his debt and also pay him a
pension of £3,000 a year, besides several smaller pensions to minor chiefs.
He is to govern the natives, etc., but all financial matters will be under
British management.     The treaty is not concluded yet, but it is only a matter
of time,     and the ,transaction will ultimately prove            profitable   to   us    and
beneficial to the natives.          Just before we left Kandavu, we heard the French
ship "Chern that was at Sydney with us, had run on a reef some 300 miles
north, and become a total wreck.          She was taking Catholic missionaries round
the Fij i    islands. We passed several good sized islands before we sighted
Obalan. Levuka stands at the foot of a range of hills, the houses are all
built of wood (331)    and the place is not unlike Wellington.              There are no
natives living near the town so I did not go on shore.


        The white population numbers about 500 who are from all the colonies and
America, and not of the most honest description, they are generally shop and
hotel keepers, and call themselves the pioneers of the Fijis.              There is a post
and     newspaper office and a German,           French,   American,   and British Consul
there.     We had fresh meat and bread while we stayed and also took in 150 tons


                                           113
of coal that was sent from Sydney on purpose.      HMS "Dido" arrived on the 31st
from Sydney.     King Thakombau was not at Levuka, or we should have had him on
board.   I saw one of his war canoes, a wooden house built on a double canoe,
had a mast and a large angular sail made of native fibre (332) and it also
pulled with oars.     It was steered by an oar at the end of each canoe and was
about 70 feet long.    On it there were some 80 natives and they sang a sort of
war song as they sailed past us beating time on their drums or tom-toms.       On
July 31st, the ship's barqe with a crew of 7 men, 7 officers and scientists,
under the charge of the First Lieutenant left the ship for a long cruise round
the larger islands, and are going up one of the rivers into the interior of
Vanu Levu.     They have a tent, rifles, cutlasses, etc., and a week's grub, and
are to join us at Kanadavu next week.       On August 1st, leave was given to all
who wished to go for 4 hours, and more than half of those who went came back
so hopelessly drunk that they had to be hoisted on board like cattle.         The
liquor sold to them by the "Pioneers of the Fij is" was such (333) poisonous
stuff, that some of them were raving mad for hours.


    We shipped at Sydney, as a chartroom servant, a young man of about 24
years of age, who had scarcely a rag to his back, and the Captain took him out
of charity.     It appears that his father is a Church of England clergyman and
this son was such a wild scamp, that they were glad to get rid of him, and he
came out to Australia with £400 some 5 years ago and has spent the lot.        He
has been the round of all the colonies, tried the gold fields and lots of
speculations.     He is an inveterate drunkard and has had the delirium tremens
several times, so much that, when he is perfectly sober his hands are all of a
shake, and his gait that of a decrepit old man.        He is a good scholar, and
when sober has the (334) manners of a gentleman, is not at all proud and very
liberal in standing "glasses round" when on shore, so is rather popular with
the sailors.     He says he wants to save enough money by the time he gets back
as will enable him to clothe himself decently before showing up at home.


     Welll he went on shore at Wellington, and came on board beastly drunk, he
went again at Levuka yesterday, and was the worst and most incapable of the
lot, broke 17 shillings worth of glass, etc., on shore, that the paymaster had
to payout of his wages, and he smuggled 2 pints of rum into the ship by means


                                      114
of a bladder tied round his waist.     It was taken away from him and he got so
excited that he went mad for several hours, tried to stab one of the ship's
police, broke 3 large lamps and did much other damage         (335)    until he was
dragged down to the cockpit and put in irons just outside my door.         His rav-
ings were of the most blasphemous kind (worse than any drunken sailor) I ever
heard, and he said that he had once been in irons for 6 months in Australia,
and that they always treated him well in gaol.


     This morning he is pitiful to look at, his one suit of clothes all torn
to rags, his limbs too weak to keep him up, and one of the worst blackeyes I
ever saw.    He has no recollection of anything, is very willing to apologize to
all, and says he will drink no more, which resolve I am afraid will be only
very temporary, and it is easy to see that his years are numbered for this
world.    He calls himself "Dawson" but I doubt whether that is his real name.


     We left Levuka at 4 p.m. last night (336)      for Kandavu again, where we
are to remain until the English mail arrives from San Francisco, surveying the
harbour in the meantime.    We are under sail at present and shall be there to-
morrow.     The British Consul, Mr. Layard, is accompanying us.       He is a stout,
jolly old man and has been out here several years.     We have also on board 10
natives of the New Hebrides who have been working at the Fiji's for the white
people for 3 years, on the cotton plantations.     They each have a small chest
of clothes and a rifle, with other arms, given to them_as wages.           We are to
take them back to the New Hebr ides to where we go from Kandavu.           They are
something like the Fijians, but not to be compared to the Friendly Islanders.
Probably they were kidnapped in the first place by some British (337) vessel,
for this system of slavery has been much resorted to by white people at the
Fijis and in Australia.    There are several men-of-war schooners fitted out at
Sydney to prevent this cheap labour traffic, for it had become so dangerous,
that it was unsafe for a peaceable ship to go near to many of the South Sea
Islands, as the natives retaliated by murdering any white people who they come
across. A short time ago the whole of the crew of a peaceful (barque) were
murdered and eaten at the Soloman Islands, and to this system of revenge may
be attributed the murder of Bishop Patterson some time ago.



                                      115
        August 4th, at Kandavu.     We have had scores of native canoes alongside
today, and I have invested my (3d bits) in shells.         Some of the native women
are     (338) good looking, but not like those at Tongatbu, and wear even less
clothing.     A lamb was born on board this morning and is at present the centre
of attraction with the sailors.


        August 7th.   Themail is not in yet but expected every minute.        We are
not going to sea until Tuesday now.      We had several great chiefs on board yes-
terday and took their portraits, they were fine looking men.           Our barqe has
not yet returned from her weeks cruise and the Captain is getting very anxious
about her.

(339)                                              HMS "Challenger"
                                                   New Hebrides, August 18th, 1874


Dear Tom:
        As we are just about to make sail for Cape York, -I will get a letter
underweigh which I hope to send from there via Torres Straits and Singapore.
My last letter I had to close at a moments notice, and the San Francisco mail
never came in with ours, so shall not receive them until we reach Hong Kong or
Manilla.


        On Sunday, August 9th, I went on shore at Kandavu, Fiji Islands, and had
a long walk, but not such a pleasant one as at Tongatbu.          The roads were not
so good, nor the island so fertile, neither were the natives as (340)          hand-
some, and very mercenary.         There were missionar ies, but they have not made
such progress there as at Tongatbu.       We heard from Sydney that our government
had refused to annex the Fiji Islands, if so, I believe one of the colonial
governments will see what can be done.         We left Kandavu on the lOth of August


                                         116
for these islands distant 450 miles west and sighted them last night.                 The
depth across was about 1500 fathoms.          We were caught in a heavy squall the
other night and lost a spar, and some small sails before the sail could be
shortened, but it was allover in half an hour.


       I told you we had 10 natives of this group of islands on board, brought
from Levuka: this morning we took their portraits and landed them on their
native shore on the island of Assi.            This group of (341)     islands was dis-
covered in 1606 by Jurros, the Spanish navigator.            It consists of about 20,
most of them of good size, for their area is almost as great as the Fij i
group, like which they are of volcanic origin, but are more mountainous and
there are several active volcanoes.           The largest islands are Espirita Santa
(200   miles   in   circumference),   Tomna    Erromango,    Assi,   Aurora,   Mablicolo,
Amboyna, Penticost, Santa Maria and Vanua Lava, and are about 300 miles north
of New Caledonia.      The inhabitants are something like the Fij ians but more
slender, are broken up into many different tr ibes and are always fighting,
their weapons being clubs, spears, bows, and poisoned arrows and they have a
very bad name.      We sighted several peaks on the different islands last night,
and lay (342) to, until this morning, when we steamed into Assi Island to land
the natives.     It is about as large as Tongatbu and has a beautiful appearance
being covered with trees to the very top of the mountains, which are about
2000 feet high.     There are not many palm trees and of course the island is not
so fertile as Tonga~bu.     There are several reefs in the vicinity and the ship
did not go in very close.     We sent 3 boats in containing the 10 natives, their
arms, clothes, etc., and several officers and scientists with fancy articles
to make presents and barter with the natives.               The boat's crew, officers,
etc., were all armed in case of an emergency.          The natives came down to meet
them and were all armed, but as soon as they saw their returning countrymen
they yelled with delight.      Our 10 natives (343) belonged to several different
tribes and each claimed their own men with their arms, etc., and marched away
into the bush.      Only one of them could speak English and the sailors called
him Toby.      When his tribe came down to claim him, he said to our men "All
those men belong to me", and he and the chief stood on the beach and laughed
at each other for about 10 minutes.           The boats brought back yams, plantains,



                                        117
cocoanuts,    curiosities,   etc.,    and are all hoisted on board again, and we
are now under sail for Cape York, distant 1500 miles northwest.              The natives
of Assi wore no clothing, merely a nominal wreath of leaves -- both sexes.
There are no missionaries for they ate one at Erromango a short time since.


(344)     Sunday, August 30th.       Anchored in the Coral Sea off Raine Island. Our
greatest depth on this trip has been 2,450 fathoms and we have had good trade
winds and pleasant weather.      We entered the Coral Sea today and are about 120
miles from the Australian continent.


        The water was 1400 fathoms yesterday and tonight we are at anchor owing
to the great number of reefs all round us.          The great barrier of coral reefs
extends for more than a thousand miles along the east coast of Australia, and
runs for more than 100 miles out from the land.          We sighted Raine Island this
morning and can just see it from where we are anchored.          It is not two square
acres in extent and destitute of           trees,   being scarcely   (345)   out of   the
water.     Of course there are no people on it, but there is a large stone
beacon, 60 feet high on it, that has been erected as a landmark by the Board
of Trade.     Like St. Paul's Rocks, there are thousands of birds living on the
island.    We are 8 miles from it now and anchored off a long reef.          It is some-
thing wonderful to see the number of reefs all round us. The Captain was up at
the foretop with a glass as we came in.          I believe Captain Cook ran on one and
was repaired at Batavia.      There are enormous quantities-of sharks here about,
as well as other fish, all hands are busy catching them now and over 20 have
been already caught, some of them 8 feet long.             The men cut off the tail,
slice open his belly and let him go again: he generally swims (346) about then
for half an hour, then dies and is eaten by his mess-mates.            Other good fish
have been caught, one was pulled up and just as he was level with the water's
edge, a shark came and took half of him. We had no church on board today owing
to the great number of reefs we were among.          To-morrow we are going to land a
party on Raine Island, and shall anchor again at night in the open sea.


        September 4th.   Somerset, Cape York. On August 31st we stood into Raine
Island, and landed a party to overhaul it, etc.           There was nothing on it but
sea birds, and they were thicker than at St. Paul's Rocks,              the ground was


                                           118
literally covered with them, their eggs and young. The soil was sandy but
there was little vegetation to be seen, and in the course of time a soil will
be formed from the deposit of the birds, and cocoanuts, etc., will wash on
shore and spring up as they have done at other Pacific Islands. The island is
of coral formation, and will probably rise higher out of the water, and en-
large every year.     The stone tower was sadly in want of repair.    On the top
there was a cistern for catching fresh water, so that if anyone was wrecked
there, they would find a supply and be able to live on birds, eggs, etc., un-
til succouredJ but this cistern and the whole roof of the tower had fallen
in.     On the doors were records of the visits of different ships, but there had
been none there for the last six years.      A record of our visit was added and
the party returned, after which the boats were hoisted in and (348) we made
sail for Cape YorkJ but owing to the reefs we anchored again the same night in
sight of three other small islands.      Lots more sharks were caught, I should
think there is no sea in the world where they are more abundant.      It came on
to blow that night, and over 120 fathoms of cable were paid out to ease the
strain on the anchor, this took three hours getting up in the morning when we
made sail again for Cape York.     We sighted the Australian continent again at
11 a.m.     and anchored the same night, September 1st, off the settlement of
Somerset and the coast here presented the same flat sterile appearance that it
did towards Melbourne, more than 2,200 miles further south.       There is not a
hill to be seen over 600 feet high, and yet on the opposite side of Torres
(349)- Straits within 120 miles there are mountains on the island of New Guinea
over 13,000 feet high, in sight half way across the Strait, and in the in-
ter ior are some whose peaks are over 16,000 feet above the sea level.       This
mountain system may be traced across the Pacific from the Rocky Mountains in
North America.      It rises at the Sandwich Islands over 13,000 feet, again in
Japan higher still -- still higher in New Guinea.


        It does not touch the continent of Australia but stretches more to the
east.     It appears moderately high at the New Hebrides and Fiji Islands, and
extends through the New Zealand Islands rising over 13,000 feet on the south
island, and was found by Ross in the Antarctic Circle in Lat. 76°S where burn-
ing mountains were seen over 13,000 feet high.       Everywhere along its course
earthquakes are prevalent and owing to its near vicinity they have occasional
shocks here that are felt in no other part of Australia.
                                       119
        The land here is covered with bush and trees and on the night we came in
there was a large bush fire inland that could be seen by us out at sea before
the land was visible. The colonists say these fires are caused by the great
heat of the sun, and the excessive dryness of the grass, etc.                      A glass bottle
has been known to act as a magnifier sufficient .to set fire to the grass in
Victoria, and here it is much hotter for it is only ten degrees south of the
equator.        The aboriginals of Australia are thicker here than in any other por-
tion of the continent, and are very treacherous and troublesome.


        This place belongs to the colony of (351) Queensland, which is a tropical
colony and one-fourth the size of Europe, and west Australia a little larger.
The     whole    colony     is    only one-fifth        less   than   Europe.     As   soon   as   the
Queensland mail was started via Torres Straits, Somerset sprang into exist-
ence.     There are not many white people even now, but still they are all work-
ing men.        The land is being cleared for cultivation and there is the nucleus
of a town in the shape of a dozen substantial white verandah'd cottages, a
barracks for the mounted police, a post office and some missionaries to keep
the natives in order, and no doubt Somerset will improve during the next 20
years, for it is in one of the main thoroughfares of ocean traffic between
America, Queensland and the East Indies.


(352)           We took in a bullock today and shall have fresh meat while we are
                                                                           -
here.      The two missionaries are on board now dining with the Captain, they
call themselves Cameronians.                 I   believe we go from here to Timor,             thence
through     some    small        islands   into the     Indian Ocean,     after   which we    return
through the Lombok and Bali Channel to Amboyna,                       the Dutch capital of the
Molucca Islands, thence to Celebes and Borneo to Manilla, after which Hong
Kong where I have heard we shall be detained refitting until after Christmas,
and that owing to this delay we shall leave out the trip to Vnacouver's Island
and go from Japan direct to the Sandwich Islands, but this is not decided on
yet.     After January 25th, our address is Yokohama, Japan via Southampton.




                                                  120
(353)        From Hong Kong, we go to New Guinea, New Britain, New Ireland and
Caroline Islands before going on to Japan, where we are to spend three months
surveying in the inland seas, etc.        It is also decided that we go to Monte
Video instead of Rio Janeiro on our way home,        for which I    am sorry,    par-
ticularly wishing to see what Rio was like.


        Soon after we anchored here our letters came on board, I receiving some
from home, with one of yours, and was sorry you did not appreciate my mahogany
colored charmer: you must please to remember she a'nt dressed, which makes a
considerable difference,      but she   is not a circumstance to the females of
Tongatbu, and wish I could send you the portrait of one I have (354)            in my
"mind's eye" now.        You would find me much altered since I left England, am
much thinner and as pale as Hamlet's Ghost, with hair getting quite grey.         You
see I get very little exercise and my work lies below the water line, where
fresh air and daylight never penetrate, having to do all my writing by candle
light, the "Challenger's" accommodation is very poor for all except officers.


        September 7th.    We expect to leave here tomorrow, but this will not go
before the 18th.     We had a party of native men and women on board the other
day, they were similar to those of Victoria and New South Wales, and as thin
as rats, the ugliest race we have yet seen: the Ashantees are handsome com-
pared with them.     We (355) had one of the missionaries on board yesterday to
conduct our Church service.      In the afternoon I went on shore with 5 mates and
got lost in the bush, for the land is one great forest and there are no roads,
or animals, and but little fresh water.       Parrots, cockatoos, etc., were very
plentiful,    there were some magnificent     butterflies,   also   lots of   snakes,
centipedes, lizards, mosquitos, flies and ants, the latter are the pest of the
settler.     We got entangled in a mangrove swamp, up to our knees in mud, it
came on dark, with the tide rising into the swamp in which lizards and even
alligators abound.        I separated and struck off into the bush,      arriving on
board at 8 p.m., the others coming in this morning by way of the shore, having
slept in a tree all night until the tide went down.


                                                      Yours sincerely,
                                                      Joe Matkin.
