(356)                                       HMS "Challenger"
                                            Arra Islands, Sea of Arafura
                                            Sept. 15, 1974
Dear Tom:
        We are now wi thin 5 degrees of the equator again, and are undergoing a
sort of mild roasting, which is aggravated by the ship being continually under
steam and there being no wind to speak of, I need not say that this does not
improve my health, being shut up all day between decks and getting no exer-
cise.     Do you see the pictures in the "London News" of the ship at Kerguelen
and amongst the ice?


        Great alterations have been made in our cruise since last I wrote.     We
are proceeding to Manilla by an entirely different (357) route to that origin-
ally laid down.      We do not go to Timor or Borneo, Celebes or any of those
islands, and after leaving Hong Kong, do not again visit New Guinea or New
Britain, Solomon Islands, etc., but go direct from the Caroline Islands to
Japan.     This alteration is owing to our being so much behind time, and to the
refusal of the Admiralty to extend the voyage beyond April 1876, so that you
may expect me home about May.      After leaving this group of islands now in
sight, we go to New Guinea, thence to Amboima, Mollucca Islands, and on to
Manilla, reaching there the 1st of November, from thence to Hong Kong, arriv-
ing about the 15th, to refit and do not leave before the 27th December, so
that-we shall have a Christmas in China.      From Japan in end of June we proceed
direct to the Sandwich Islands and do not go to (358) Vancouver's at all. The
remainder of the voyage is the same except one part we go to Monte Video in-
stead of Rio Janeiro, but this arrangement may possibly be altered again.       We
left Somerset on the 8th and steamed out through Torres Straits for          these
islands distant 500 miles J the straits are about 100 miles across in their
narrowest part.     We did not sight New Guinea but called at two small islands
for a few hours,     there are several situated in the straits, some are in-
habited, but those we called at were not.       As soon as we cleared the Straits
we were in the Sea of Arafura, as this part of the Pacific is called.          The
depth is only about 40 fathoms and we have dredged and trawled every day with
great success.     We passed a Singapore mail boat the other morning bound to
Brisbane (359) but she had no letters for us.      The same day we passed a large


                                      122
Dutch merchant ship under full sail for Batavia, the Dutch have many valuable
possessions in this part of the world.      Thunder storms and vivid flashes of
lightening are very prevalent after sunset in this part of the world.           The
southern island of this group is now in sight but our place of call is farther
north.   The doctor is now serving out quinine to the boat's crews who have to
land tomorrow as a preventive of fever, ague, etc.


October 2nd, at Banda, Nutmeg Islands.
     We were a week round the Arra Islands, they are a group of small extent
lying about 90 miles west of New Guinea.      The population is about 60,000 and
is a mixture of the Malay with the Papuan or Austral negro (360) family.     They
are good seamen and were formerly great pirates -- the terror of the old China
Sea clippers and other merchant ships that came this way, but our steam gun
boats have stopped all that sort of thing.     On the night of the 14th September
we anchored about 7 miles from the island of Tronyan, the largest of the Arra
group and the next evening we steamed in for the island of Dobba and anchored
off the town of that name.     It was a beautiful island, but rather low, but
covered with a dense vegetation and forest abounding in parrots, cockatoos,
birds of paradise,     and enormous butterflies and lizards.       Soon after    we
anchored, three large praus or native canoes came alongside with the principal
chief of the island.    These canoes and several flag staffs on shore flew the
Dutch flag.     All the groups of islands hereabouts either belong (361) to the
Dutch, or are under their protection.       Our men of war _seldom come this way,
and they go through the Straits of Malacca to China.       This route to China is
called the Molucca Passage, and is little frequented by any but Dutch ships,
so here they reign supreme and have it all their own way.        There was not a
sign of a European in the island, but lots of Chinese trading and scraping a
fortune together.    All the rest were natives.   Those in the canoes came along-
side in great style, singing their war songs and beating their tom-toms or
native drums.    The singing was something frightful, all in one key, and sounds
very doleful and monotonous.    The chief with a few Chinese came on board and
were received by the Captain and Professor Thompson in the cabin, leaving
again after having refreshment and cigars. The chiefs were dressed in Chinese
costume, but the other     (362) natives had only a cloth round the loins, and
were the ugliest race of people we have yet seen, except the abor iginals of


                                      123
Australia.   They were slender, ill shaped, with irregular features and hor-
rible mouths: this latter deformity is caused by their chewing         a root called
betel nut which rots their teeth away altogether, destroys their voices and
their mouths look like a piece of raw liver.          They are Mohommedans and live
chiefly on fish, eggs and vegetables, they are very chary about letting you
see their wives or females of any sort.            Cocoanut trees and bananas grow
there, but not abundantly, and fruit was very scarce.         The town consists of a
lot of bamboo huts, two storys high, thatched, and open at the gable ends to
admit a current of air right through.       I went on shore one afternoon and had a
fine swim (363) in a salt water lake, the water of which was hotter than any I
ever before bathed in.       The people and houses were very dirty.      Some of the
Malay children were pretty, those who had never chewed the betel root, or been
scorched in the sun.       The betel root is a shrub common to the East Indies and
China and is a species of pepper vine.         The lower story of the huts is used by
the pigs and fowls, a bamboo ladder leads into the upper loft, and as soon as
the women and girls saw us coming, they bolted up this ladder like a shot,
while the men and boys stood below and laughed.          Those women we did see were
very ugly.       The Chinese do all the trade, keep stores, and sell rice, rum,
tobacco, etc., and they buy all the birds of paradise and pearls the natives
can get (364).      I saw two or three Chinese women, but they were very shy about
showing themselves, though they were very fair looking.         In the middle of the
streets were wells of fresh water and the Chinese community bathe at the mouth
of th~se wells by drawing buckets of water and pouring _over themselves, so
that the water finds its way back into the well again, this way of bathing is
economical, but not our style.          The Chinese brought off lots of birds of
paradise, ready stuffed and cured and sold them each at 10/ (shillings).            I
did not buy any but may do if we go to New Guinea, where they are natives of,
but a few of them find their way to these islands.         They are about as large as
a thrush, but have golden tails over 2 feet long.          They look beautiful while
flying but are very timid and difficult (365) to shoot.         Our officers went to
several of the other Arroo Islands in the steam pinnace and shot a few birds
of paradise, as well as other splendid parrots, etc.             They also shot some
large   flying    foxes,   caught   a young cassowary or    emu and several snakes,




                                         124
butterflies, lizards, etc.             Some of the butterflies were as large as English
sparrows.        The native canoes of the larger sort are thatched over and look
like floating haystacks.             When they go to sea the whole family -- fowls, pigs,
etc., go also -- and they make voyages of 11 to 1200 miles at a stretch, for
the sea about here is as calm as a mill pond generally, and gales of wind are
unheard of.       On arrival in port they draw the canoe upon the beach and live in
it the same as at sea.          These are the migratory Malays.          Their sails are made
of cocoanut fibre, and also their ropes, and they live on fish when at sea.
The natives gamble and play at cards to a great extent.                     The Chinese have
taught them to gamble, and the Dutch to play cards.                 The real natives of the
islands are PapuansJ the Malays and mixed races being emigrants.                  On (366) the
21st September, the sun crossed to the side of the equator, and the southern
summer commenced.         On the 23rd, we left Dobba for another group called the Ki
Islands, about 80 miles farther west.                We sighted the largest of the group,
called Great Ki, the next day.              It was about as large as St. Thomas and much
higher than any we had seen since leaving the New Hebrides.                 Off these the sea
deepened to 800          fathoms.       Lots of natives    (367)   came off there in their
canoes, drum-beating and singing the same old tunes.                 They were very similar
in appearance to those of the Arroo Islands, but not quite so ugly.                   All that
day we steamed through the Ki group, which is very numerous though of small
extent, and anchored at night in a bay surrounded by beautiful islands.                    The
sunsets     in    this   p~rt   of    the world   are   splended   and   nearly   every   night
lightening, without either rain or thunder.               We had a whole tribe of natives
off that night, and they were allowed to climb the rigging and ramble allover
the ship.        After dark they were had on the quarter (deck) to dance and sing
their war songs.          All hands stood round them and the Captain burned a blue
light to illuminatae the scene, after which they had a feed of biscuit and de-
parted.


     We left on the 25th and anchored again at night (368) at another beauti-
ful island of the Ki group.              On the 25th we left for the Nutmeg Islands dis-
tant about 330 miles and passed numbers of others on the passage.                  On the 28th
we sighted Banda and took soundings at the enormous depth of 2875 fathoms, the
next day we anchored there.             It is the largest island and capitol of the group



                                               125
called Banda or Nutmeg Islands, which consist of nine, all belonging to the
Dutch.   Banda is a very clean little town, and is used as a convict settlement
for the natives of all the Dutch possessions in the East Indies.       There were
many women convicts, and they were employed in making roads, etc.      There is a
large fort and barracks built by the Portuguese before the year 1700 after
which the islands were taken by the Dutch.     Banda and nearly all Dutch posses-
sions in the east were taken by the British in 1775 but they were nearly all
(369) given back again at the conclusion of the war, except Ceylon, the rich-
est island in this part of the globe.          The natives of Banda are Malays,
Papuans and all sorts of mixed races and a few Chinese merchants; but there
are not many Dutch or white, except soldiers and officials.       We saluted the
Dutch flag with 21 guns, and are to do so at all their possessions we visit.
The governor dined on board one day.        Fruit, fowls and eggs were plentiful,
but other provisions were dear.   The sight of the town is the volcanic mount-
ain of Goomong-assi, 2,200 feet high and still active.        There is a book on
board written by an American-professor Beckford -- describing his visit to
these islands and his perilous ascent of the burning mountain.     He relates how
he had native guides, and all sorts of appliances for making (370) the ascent,
and that it took him 2 days.   There is also a picture of him hanging on to his
eyebrows to the side of the mountain with all the blocks of lava cinders roll-
ing from under his feet.   The mountain rises very abruptly, and the ascent is
certainly difficult. and dangerous, several people have lost their lives in the
attempt at different times, and not long ago an Englishman was suffocated
while looking over into the crater.     On the day after we arr ived several of
our officers ascended with guides, and were only five hours absent from the
ship, and had had a rest in the town.         On the following day, myself and a
messmate went on shore, and after having a look over the town, started to go
up the mountain, without guides or anything.     We were 2 1/4 hours going up and
50 minutes coming down.    The last half (371) of the ascent is very dangerous
as the surface of the mountain is nothing but a mass of loose cinders, which
rolled down with us 2 feet for every three we ascended.        On arriving at the
summit we saw a flagstaff erected by our officers at the mouth of the crater,
which was about 100 feet deep, and a mass of sulphur inside.        The ground is
hot enough on the surface to cook eggs and dense volumes of smoke and vapour
rose from the crater and numerous cracks in the earth.      It is always smoking,


                                      126
and we were obliged to cover our faces whilst we looked over into the crater,
for the whole air round the summit is suffocating.      We made the ascent in the
heat of the day, and forgot to take any water with us, but we soon got some
from a Malay hut at the foot of the mountain.         We descended at a rattling
pace, for there was no walking down the first half of the way.        It is nearly
100 years since the last great eruption which was accompanied by an earthquake
that divided the island asunder, and separated the mountain from the town, and
the sea is now a 1/4 of a mile wide between the two islands and very deep --
we had to cross in a native canoe.


     The Dutch fleet was left high and dry for some hours during the earth-
quake, by the waters retiring from the bay, but as the sea returned again to
its former position, they received very little damage.      I had a fine bathe   at
the foot of the mountain, then we visited the spice plantations.         The clove
tree is very pretty and the buds that grow in clusters at the top of it form,
when dr ied , the spice called cloves.       The nutmeg tree is very like a pear
tree, and (373) the fruit when ripe resembles an apricot, and nearly as large:
the outer shell is yellow and is allowed to rot off as a walnut, leaving the
nutmeg enveloped in a thin membramous, sweet scented substance, which when
dried, forms the spice called mace.      Yesterday we went out to sea to look for
a disabled Dutch mail boat, but found nothing of her so returned at night.       We
are not going to    Ne~   Guinea until we return from Hong Kong, as this is the
rainy and sickly season.     This evening we leave Banda for _Amboina, distant 150
miles north.     We are only about 200 miles from the line and the weather is
roasting.


     Sunday, October 25, at Zamboanga.        We anchored off the town of Amboina
on Sunday, October 4th, and remained until the 10th, coaling, etc.      Amboina is
the capitol of the Molucca Islands       (374)   and has about 30,000 inhabitants.
The town has 16,000, mostly Malays, Papuans, mixed races, Chinese, Arabs and
Europeans.     There was a large fort and lots of soldiers there, and we had the
Dutch governor and numerous visitors on board.       I went on shore several times
and also played cricket, the first time for two years.         The island is moun-
tainous, but fertile, is a large size and has a good bay.         It was intensely
hot there, 140· in the sun and over 90· in the bottom of the ship.


                                       127
        Cloves and spices are the principal export and fruit of all kinds was
cheap and plentiful.      The colored people are all Mohammedans, I looked through
the windows into one of their Mosques, which was built of wood and shaped like
a Chinese pagoda: the interior was quite bare and (375) the floor of stone:
the natives stood up to pray and went through all sorts of antics.          The Malay
people do washing beautifully, they use no soap, but beat the clothes on the
stones in the river beds.         They are very fond of wearing white garments when
they do have any clothing, and some of the children who had not been scorched
in the sun, were very pretty, had splended eyes and teeth and long black
hair.     They paid us a month's money at Amboina in Dutch dollars at 4/2 each.
We had fresh meat, vegetables and bread there for two days for our health's
sake.     The meat was 2/5 per lb., vegetables 1/6 and bread 1/ per lb.           The
Admiralty allow 2/6 per lb. to be paid for fresh meat and vegetables when a
ship has been long at sea and the doctor reconunends it.           I was reading the
other day the voyages (376) of Cook and other English navigators amongst these
islands over 100 years ago: they used to bury 2 or 3 men each day at the Arroo
Islands.     In those days lime juices and quinine were unknown in the navy.       We
left Amboina on the 10th for Temati, another of the Molucca Islands, 50 miles
north of the line.        We passed several others of the group and crossed the
equator on the 13th at 10 p.m. in longitude 127°30' east.


        On the 13th we anchored off the town and island of Temati, on which was
another volcano 3000 feet high and very active.               On one of the adjacent
islands there is another 5000 feet high.         The town of Temati was not so large
as Amboina but much cleaner and prettier.         There was a fort and barracks and a
Dutch man-of-war at anchor off the town.          I went on shore there and spent a
pleasant    (377)   evening.      Fruit was very plentiful,    especially pineapples,
which sold 1 1/2 each.         Fowls were 6d each, and eggs 1/2.   On the 17th we left
there for the Phillipine Islands, passing lots more on which were volcanoes,
and sighting the large Dutch Island of Celebes, on which were 3 active vol-
canoes.    The Dutch Islands and possessions are very quiet, dead and alive sort
of places, there is no enterprise or progress to be seen anywhere: no railways
or improvements of any kind and the people are the same as they were 100 years
ago.     I wonder what the Spaniards, Dutch, or any other people think when they
visit Melbourne, Sydney or any English colony.         We sounded in the Celebes Sea


                                           128
Sea at 2,375 fathoms and 2,675 fathoms,              and on the 22nd sighted the large
island of Mindanao, Phillipine group, which group is large                 (378)    and very
valuable 1 they are in the North Pacific and belong to the Spaniards.                     They
were discovered in 1521 by Magellan, and taken possession of in 1570, in the
reign of Philip II after whom they were named.


       They number nearly 1000, but only about 150 are inhabited.                Luzon is the
largest island and is only one-fifth smaller than England. Mindanao Island is
only a trifle less.        They are rich, abounding in all sorts of fruits and min-
erals1 even gold and diamonds have been found and there are also coal mines in
Mindanao.     They are mountainous, volcanic and subject to earthquakes.                  They
export rice,    tobacco, cigars, hemp, etc., and Manilla is the capitol.                   The
whole population is over 8 million and about 2 million are either Spanish or
of Spanish descent,         that   (379)    portion are Roman Catholics,     the    remainder
Mohammedans, or Idolaters.          There are two tribes of natives, the Aboriginals,
called Karasoras,         of Papuan origin,     and the Malays and mixed races.            The
Karasoras are nearly yellow, small, ugly, with long black hair, something be-
tween the Maor ies and Papuans.             There are also great quanti ties of Chinese.
On the 23rd we anchored off the town of Zamboanga, which is the capitol of the
large islands of Mindanao.           The town stands at the foot of a range of high
mountains, which are clothed to their summit in dense forests of ebony and
sapan wood. There is a large Spanish man-of-war at anchor here, and we have
had most of the officers as well as the Spanish governor on board.                   The town
looks something like Amboina, but is much larger, stronger fort,                   (380) more
soldiers and is much dirtier.              There are great quantities of cocoanut trees
here   and   fruit   is    very plentiful,      especially oranges,    guavas,    pineapples,
shaddocks and bananas, as well as the bread fruit.               There are lots of wild
creatures, serpents, etc., wild buffalos, and small half-wild horses, called
mustangs, inland.         The buffaloes have been tamed and crossed with the domestic
ox and are used for all sorts of heavy draught labor.                 The small horses are
very fleet and pretty and were to be hired, with a native attendant,                      for a
dollar per day.      Lots of our men had them and astonished everyone, as well as
themselves, by their riding.          This morning we had Church and after the heat of
the day was over I went on shore and had a good walk and look about.                        The
Spanish half-caste women are very handsome and have beautiful                     (381)   black


                                              129
hair, almost reaching the ground.    The natives here are far mqre industrious
than at the Dutch islands, in cultivating the soil and any manual work.       The
town trade appears to be in the hands of the Chinese, but the principal export
trade in the management of the British and American merchants. I looked into
one of the Roman Catholic churches during service, there was an organ and the
singing good.   Just opposite the church was the Spanish officers' quarters.
They invited all our officers this evening to come and see a native dance.
The dancers were natives, with Chinese girls, women, and some men, and were
dressed in Chinese fancy silks and all sorts of costumes, the music was hor-
rible and the dancing peculiar.


     They build the houses two story's high with open verandahs, so from the
street we could see (382) all that was going on.     The native houses are built
of bamboo on piles, and were similar to those at the Arroo Islands.     We leave
here tomorrow for another large town further north and shall pass very close
to the island of Borneo, but shall not touch it.      The weather is still roast-
ing and we are almost always under steam, the decks have to be kept constantly
wetted to keep the pitch from melting.      Mindanao is very rich in minerals and
coal, but the Spaniards are too lazy to work the mines, and all the coal used
by steamers here comes either from Sydney, or the British Island of Labuan, to
the north of Borneo.   We hope to get some letters and English newspapers at
Manilla next week. .



November 11th, off Luzon under steam for Manilla.
     We left Zamboanga on (383)     the 26th and on the 27th sounded at three
miles in depth, and that night there was lightning from every quarter of the
heavens, such flashes as I never saw before and neither rain or thunder.       On
the 28th we sighted the island of Panay in this group and anchored at night
off the capital town of Iloilo (pronounced Elo Eli).       It is much larger than
Zamboanga having 60,000 inhabitants and is the second city of importance in
the Phillipine Islands.   It stands on a river in a wide marshy plain, at the
foot of a chain of mountains, is notoriously unhealthy and very dirty my mess-
mate said, so I did not go on shore, there being nothing to see different to
Zamboanga.   We had the Spanish governor on board and also took in fresh meat,
vegetables and bread, the meat was only 6d per lb.         We also took in (384)
                                      130
50 tons of coal, English coal.       We heard news from the English merchants of
Banzaine's(?) escape, and of a terrible typhoon near Hong Kong, and that some

Manilla, distant 350 miles and on our passage, saw scores of fine fertile
isles, all mountains.     Are now off the large island of Luzon, which is nearly
the size of England, and tomorrow expect to be at anchor at Manilla by 3 p.m.
hoping to receive some welcome letters.


Sunday, November 15, in the China Sea.


       We anchored at Manilla at 4 p.m. on the 4th and received our letters at 9
p.m.    Mine numbering nine, besides newspapers.


       We anchored nearly 2 miles from the city of Manilla, which stands on a
flat peninsula at the bottom of the bay, which is as large (385) as Table Bay,
and    surrounded   by high lands.    Nothing but the spires and domes of       the
churches could be seen from where we lay, but the city had a very pleasant
appearance especially at sunrise and sunset, when the great chains of moun-
tains situated some 15 and 20 miles inland came out very distinctly.       Luzon is
the seat of government for all the Phillipine Islands, its capitol, Manilla,
stands on a river, which is navigable up as far as the town and was full of
shipping,   I   think even more than Bahia, which town it somewhat resembles,
though a much busier and gayer place, and quite equals     i~   in dirt.


       We saluted the Spanish flag with 21 guns and the same number was returned
from Fort St. Philip, which defends the city.      Manilla is the oldest European
city in this part of the world, it was founded in 1571 and was formerly much
more important than it is now.       The Spanish treasure ships used to sail from
Acapulco in Mexico across the Pacific to Manilla and home to Spain by the Cape
of Good Hope.


       Commodore Anson took one of these galleons worth over one million pounds
sterling.


       Its present population is about 230,000 of all colors, but the majority
are Malays, Papuans and Chinese.      Of course there are Spaniards and there is a
                                        131
Spanish squadron always stationed at Manilla, as well as lots of troops, but
the principal foreign trade is in the hands of the British and American mer-
chants, the chief exports being cigars, rice, indigo, tobacco, hemp, coffee
and sugar.


        The British Consul gets £1100 a year.   He, with his wife and family, were
often on board during our stay.     Fruit, eggs, were (387) plentiful and we had
fresh meat, bread and vegetables all the time we were there.


        A month's money in Spanish dollars at 4/ each was paid to the ship's com-
pany, and leave was given every night from 4 till 10 p.m.       The steam pinnace
did all the boating as it was a long pull for a rowing boat.      The weather was
much cooler at Manilla and we had plenty of rain.      We had the Spanish Governor
and Admiral,     with lots of military and naval officers      and men,   Catholic
pr iests, ladies, etc., on board dur ing our stay, and the day before we left
the Captain gave a lunch and dance party.       The ladies were tolerably handsome
and well dressed.      I like their style of dancing better than the English.    I
went on shore one evening but it so soon got dark that I did not see much of
the town, which is lighted by oil lamps.


(388)        There is a fine cathedral, and several large churches, and also some·
enormous government cigar manufactories, employing thousands of native women.
Most of our men have laid in a stock, but beinq no great smoker, I did not go
in for a bargain.     The price of the very best is 8d per hundred, and you could
buy the same quantity for 3d.     The houses are built of stone two storeys high,
with flat roof and open balconies, but there is nothing pretty about the best
streets and the back ones where the Malays and Chinese reside were something
horrible.     There was a bit of a park, full of well dressed people, for it was
Sunday night, and the military bands were all playing.         The ladies wear no
bonnets only lace veils, and many of them smoked cigars in their carriages.
Horses were very (389) plentiful, and vehicles of all descriptions were to be
seen driving about the fashionable streets, carriage exercise is the principal
amusement.     The natives were about the same as at the other islands, they and
the Chinese seemed to be the only hard workers in the place.         Altogether, I
think Manilla is the finest place we have visited except Lisbon, Melbourne and
Sydney, but everything is very dear there.        At 2 p.m. on the 11th we got up

anchor and left for Hong Kong, distance 700 miles.       We were two days getting

weather, the worst since we left Wellington.     We were only 170 miles from Hong
Kong today at 12 o'clock, and expect to reach there tomorrow night.       We have
been two years in commission today.         Are expecting the weather to be com-

November 17th at Hong Kong.

                                                      Hong Kong, Dec. 16th, 1874
Dear Torn:
     From my last you are aware we arrived here on November 16th and expect we
do not leave until the middle of January.


     We have taken in all our provisions, etc., to last us until April 15th,
when we are due at Yokohama.    We have coaled and they have almost finished re-
fitting; we are not going in dock.



                                      133
        The island of Hong Kong or "Fragrant Streams" belongs to the Ladrone
group of islands, and is only 29 square miles in extent.          It   is mountainous
and barren, although it is in the Tropics, it is about 15 miles from the mouth
of the "Pi Kiang" or "River of Pearls", generally called the Canton River.
(392)The city of Canton is 85 miles from Hong Kong, and the Portuguese settle-
ment of Macao is 40 miles up the river before you reach Canton.            Macao has
been a Portuguese possession over 200 years.        The island is separated from the
mainland by a narrow intricate strait called the Ly-ce-moon Pass, about a mile
wide in its narrowest part.        It is shaped like a half-moon 1 the two ends of
the island approaching the peninsula of Kowloon, and forming one of the most
magnificant harbours in the world.        The capital town of Victoria stands in the
hollow of the harbour, at the foot of a range of hills terminating in Victoria
Peak, which is 1875 feet above (393) the sea level.           The town has at least
200,000 inhabitants, besides an immense floating and migratory population num-
bering many thousands.       From the harbour of Hong Kong nothing of the sea can
be seen, it is surrounded by mountains both on the island and mainland.         These
mountains have a very bleak sterile appearance but present a beautiful scene.
Looking at the splendid landlocked harbour, you would wonder how the recent
terrible typhoon could cause the damage it did to shipping1 over 1,000 lives
were lost in this little harbour.         This you would not be surprised at if you
saw the myriads of Chinese junks and sampans in which the floating population
live and die.     Live~    count for nothing in this country.     It was the dollars
      -
absorbed by the typhoon that made it such a terrible calamity.          (394) The sea
rose many feet into the town, which stands off on a steep slope, the water was
as high as the 2nd story in those houses facing the bay, ships were dr iven
from their anchors, and thrown almost into the town.        Two steamers are now ly-
ing one on the top of the other close to the wharf with their masts only above
the water.      The captain of one of them,        a Spaniard,   with his wife were
drowned,    and their     bodies washed   into the 2nd street from the bay.       The
typhoon extended as far as Macao up the river, and no one knows how many
Chinese lives were lost up there.         There was not a single man of war damaged
although there were three or four lying here.


(395)         Hong Kong was ceded to us in 1842 and the opposite peninsula of
RKowloon" in 1851.      Of course it was not taken for its richness or fertility,


                                          134
for nothing grows on it, but as a military and naval station for the pro-
tection of our commerce and as the centre of an immense expOrt trade,                                  its
value cannot be over-rated.            The amount of shipping that comes into Hong Kong
in the course of a year, on their way to Japan, and the sea ports of China, is
something enormous.          Hong Kong was the base of operations during the long
Chinese war between 1848 and 1859, and from its position at the mouth of the
great Canton River, its possession by us is of the greatest importance.                                We
have a dockyard and victualling yard here to accommodate our numerous fleet on
the Chinese station, and its fine harbour (396) is the admiration and envy of
all other European naval powers.                   At present there are at least 300 vessels
here of all nations and flags, and myriads of Chinese coasting junks.                                There
are     10   British    men-of-war         lying    here,       two    American,   one    Russian,     two
Portuguese, one Siamese and three Chinese.                       Every vessel and junk carries a
light at night and the bay looks like a town.                         Hong Kong is well lighted with
gas (or rather Victoria), and it has a very brilliant appearance at night for
the streets rise one above another for 800 feet.                         There is a Governor here, a
General, a Commodore in charge of the dockyard and the Admiral in command of
the fleet.       There are not many European merchants or people of any sort except
(397) soldiers, the white civilian population is under 1000.                             All the trades
people are Chinese, the whites are either merchants, chemists, doctors, hotel
keepers,       etc.,   the   minor    trades        and   all    branches     of   manual   labour     are
monopolized by the Chinese, and no European could compete with them in prices,
etc;     Seen from the water, Hong Kong is something bet~een Lisbon, Levuka and
Wellington in appearance, the climate is generally healthy and dry, there has
been no rain since we have been here.                     We had two cold days and nights: the
rest of the time has been as warm as an average English summer.                               There are
three    old    three deckers        and    line of       battle       ships here; one      the   "Victor
Emmanuel" was a hopsital ship at the Ashantee war and has just come out, the 3
decker, the "Princess Charlotte" was flagship at the battle of Navarino and is
the only (398) 3 decker that has crossed the equator.


        There are 8 or 9 large gun boats for going up the river, etc., and chas-
ing the numerous Chinese pirates1                  two corvettes, one at Shanghai, and one at
Yokohama for the winter, and the flagship "Iron Duke", Admiral Shadwell: she
is a sister ship to the "Invincible" and "Audacious" and has been out here


                                                    135
four years.        She is the largest and heaviest ship that ever came through the
Suez Canal, being towed by a smaller man-of-war, and grounded 17 times on the
mud.   The "Audacious" is now on the way out to relieve her.


       Soon after we anchored here, scores of small Chinese junks and sampans
swarmed around us, containing tailors, shoemakers (399) washermen and women,
dealers in curiosities, provision boats, one of which was nominated to the
ship   all   the    time we   remain here.       These boats are called in the      navy
"Bum-boats" and supply the men with provisions from the shore.              The Chinese
bum-boats had bread, all sorts of fruit, foreign butter and cheese, fried fish
and prawns and boiled and fried eggs, the eggs are very large, being all tur-
keys and ducks and they have been a 1/2 each all the time.


       Very sweet mandarin oranges and bananas are the principal fruit,              the
oranges run 3 a penny, other fruits are dearer for it is the winter season
now.   All these provisions and those sold on shore come from the mainland and
are brought by the numerous junks, etc.           These boats come (400) alongside the
ship every meal hour, so also do the other boats containing washer women,
tailors, etc.        I should think there were 500 people in these boats when we
came in, and other ships were similarly surrounded.             These boats as well as
the largest junks, are built in the shape of a Chinese slipper.              The reason
for this is reporte~ by tradition to be as follows -- Some 3000 years ago the
people of China began to build their vessels after all sorts of patterns and
shapes, so the Emperor was consulted concerning this innovation against pre-
cedent, and asked to furnish a model for all future generations in naval arch-
itecture, so he threw down his slipper for a design and it has been adhered to
to this day, even their steam war junks are built on this fashion, (401) and
looking at these vessels from the stern, you see an exact likeness                 to a
Chinese slipper.       The smallest boats are decked over, and there is a sort of
bamboo hood built over        the stern,     after    the style of a gipsy's caravan.
Between the deck and the bottom of the boat is the sleeping apartment, and the
smaller ones generally carry one man, two women and any amount of children,
the larger boats carry several families.             They live on fish and rice chiefly,
but nothing comes amiss to them.       At meal times they come alongside and send
all the children on board with bags to pick up the scraps and broken victuals.


                                           136
      About 10 boats attended the ship day and night to take anyone on shore
who wished to go, the fare is 10 cents at night and 5 in the day.            (402) The
money here is in dollar banknotes and Mexican silver dollars, value 4/3 and
100 cents to the dollar.    There is also Chinese and Japanese copper money.


      The floating population of China is estimated at over 15 millions, the
total population 400 millions.     Before arriving here I considered this a gross
exaggeration, but can quite believe it now.         Canton has a million and a half
of people within its walls, Peking has more, and there are dozens of cities
with over a million inhabitants.      Still this immense number counts for noth-
ing, for they can scarcely be called a united nation.             There are distinct
languages and religion among them and not the slightest fellowship or national
feeling whatever.    If the people here were to hear that Canton had been des-
troyed by fire, or any other cause, they would send no relief or help whatever
to the sufferers, and evince not the least concern unless it touched their own
pockets.   Human life is considered of no account, during the recent typhoon
scores of people were drowned in sight of           their   countrymen,   without   the
slightest notice being taken of it.      The Chinese have a very numerous army and
navy and their government is even more despotic than the Russian, but to say
that our empire in India is in danger from them is all moonshine.             They are
well able to defend themselves, but as an offensive power they count for noth-
ing,. they have no 'ambition, no curiosity and very few of them know there is
such a country as India.     I mention this (404) because I read an article in a
leading magazine the other day, wherein their designs on India, in the future
were distinctly foretold and also that of the Japanese.           The Chinese do not
recognize such a division of time as a week, and have no Sabbath, if anything,
they appear to be busier on Sunday.        They are idolaters, and each household
and   junk has   its own peculi ar de i ty •   Notwithstanding this       is a British
colony, they have not adopted a single custom of ours, nor introduced any art-
icle of European dress.       They live in the same style as their forefathers
2,000 years ago and use the same mechanical tools.          Their motto is to "adhere
to all that is established and to reject all that is new·.              They have con-
descended to erect sign boards (405) over their shops in English as well as
Chinese characters and this is the only innovation I could detect when I have
been on shore.      There   is   no alphabet   in   their   language,   each character


                                        137
represents a distinct word and this is what makes it so difficult to learn.     I
enclose you my washing bill written in Chinese characters, as a sample, they
write with a small brush, and wonderfully quick they do it.


     I need not descr ibe their dress, the long cotton blouse and very wide
trousers     white gaiters and clumsy looking shoes.    Their dress is generally
blue and costs very little, their pigtail reaches nearly to the ground.       The
women dress and look very similar to the men, they generally wear earrings,
and all their hair, which is the only means of distinguishing the two sexes.
The men (406) and women afloat wear no shoes or stockings.       I saw scores of
women with the proverbial small feet, on shore, they are bound up and com-
pressed into shoes about 3 inches long, and they amble along with great diffi-
culty, "like a cat on hot br icks n •     This cruel custom, I think, is falling
into disuse, for I saw no children being sacr ificed to this queer national
fashion, and imagine it is now confined to the upper ten thousand.     The women
work terribly hard, on the water they invariably do all the rowing and steer-
ing, it is nothing unusual to see a boat full of men being rowed by two women,
and they can navigate one better than the men.        They car ry their babies on
their backs in a sort of gipsy sling and nurse and work just the same.        The
baby's nose is compressed close to the mother's back (407) and this is what
causes the Chinese to all have very flat noses.     They are a dirty but very in-
dustrious, and, in many things, a clever people.     I have been more struck with
this country and people than with any other we have vfsited, and it is the
only one that has exceeded my expectations.       provisions, clothing, etc., are
cheaper here than in any other part of the world.       Any sort of manual labor
can be performed at about half the European price, and in many articles they
can compete with machinery.   Rice is the principal food, and they can exist on
a halfpenny a day and a whole family of the middle class will subsist on three
shillings a week.   Their vegetables are the best I ever tasted, they eat very
little animal food, though fish and game are very (408) plentiful, they drink
nothing but water, and their only vice is opium smoking, and eating, which is
too expensive for    the majority to indulge     in , but they smoke tobacco and
cigars.    All our carpentering, plumbing, repairs, etc., have been effected by
Chinese mechanics and nearly all the workmen in the government dockyard are



                                        138
Chinese. They are good citizens and very little trouble in the town, but are a
mercenary and treacherous people and would do anything for money.      During the
Chinese war they attempted to murder all the European community by putting
arsenic in the bread, but they used too large a quantity that its presence was
detected and they were discovered.      They do not scruple to rob a drunken man
in the streets, or even murder him, and piracy is still very (409) prevalent
on their coasts, although the penalty is death.     We get good meat, vegetables
and bread here and also English beer in the canteen at night.       All sorts of
provisions are cheap, especially poultry, eggs, etc.      We often have geese for
dinner and sometimes a Chinese dinner of curry and rice from the bum-boats.
Cats, dogs, etc., are great delicac ies in this country and have no doubt I
have tasted both since we have been here.     You can get a good suit of clothes
for 30/, the cost of making is only 6/-, and a pair of English-style boots and
shoes from 3/ to 6/, made of kid or catskin and they will wear a long time if
not wetted, and are very comfortable.


     Scores of artists come on board every time the men's wages are paid, who
do oil paintings from photographs, very tolerable, for from 8/ to 10/ each,
also ship's landscapes, etc.   The Chinese invariably ask twice as much as they
expect to get and are wonderful fellows at driving a bargain.       Their English
is very peculiar, they say, "can do" and "no can do" for "yes and "no"7 in-
stead of saying "this is good", they say "this number one piece", and they
always pronounce the letter "r" as "1".      In jewellery, carving, etc. they are
                                                            -
very skillful and can imitate things to a nicety.       If you go to a tailor and
order a suit of clothes, he will scan your figure, and say "can do", without
measuring you at al17 fit you to a nicety, and in a very short time, for they
are so eager to get the money.     Washing is only 1/6 per dozen and they will
take it ashore one day and bring it off the next.       Any rubbish, ashes, etc.,
thrown overboard is eagerly collected, and nothing in the shape (411) of food
is thrown away as refuse.      On the day they paid us our money the ship was
swarmed with traders of all sorts and a good deal of money was spent.     An art-
icle worth a dollar,   they will ask       2 1/2 for,   and say "No have got two
tongues, only one price-7 and then if you offer them a dollar, show them it,
and walk away, they yell out "can do" and its the same in the bazaars on
shore, if they only see the money, they will sell you something.     I have spent
a lot of money here in cur iosi ties, oil paintings, clothes, etc., and have
bought a fine large camphor wood chest to keep my clothes in, only cost 3


                                     139
dollars and would fetch two pounds in England.    The wood smells so nice and no
moths or insects will come near it.     A man could soon spend a fortune here in
silks,    fans,   ivory goods, cabinets, etc., and when you (412)    visit one of
their bazaars, you can't come away while you have money in pocket.     r intended
going up to Canton, but have spent so much that r can't afford it.


       Lots of our officers and men are up there now, for it is the race week,
and r must get a description of that wonderful city from some of them.        You
can get a box of good tooth powder here for a penny, the box would cost that
in England, for it is made of wood with a sliding lid, like a slate pencil
box.     Our officers have played several cricket matches here, and everyone is
enjoying himself as much as possible.


       Our photographer who was engaged at Cape Town left us here, making the
third we have had, but we have got another.


       The carpenter of the ship has deserted, and also a boy, but we have taken
in (413) 6{) new men and boys, the latter just out from England, and are now
full up again.     Some have been invalided and r don't think there are more than
60 hands left of the original 240 that commissioned the ship.       But the great-
est alteration of the lot happened a few days ago, when our Captain Nares re-
ceived a telegram from England to say that he was appointed to the command of
the new arctic expedition that leaves England in April, and was to proceed
home at once, Lieutenant Aldrich, the 1st lieutenant, was also to accompany
him.     The Captain would have preferred remaining in this ship until the cruise
was finished, but he could not refuse it.


       Professor Thompson was in a great way about it, and talked of throwing up
the whole affair and coming home, but the Captain (414) persuaded him not J
however, he will go long before we get back.       The officers gave a farewell
dinner, and made the Captain a handsome present, who made a short speech and
said "how sorry he was to go", and "how he should often be thinking of his old
shipmates, and that he hoped to be back nearly as soon as us".        They will be




                                       140
away one winter and two summers and return about September 1876.       The recent
Austrian expedition is, I think, the reason for the present hurry in getting
away.


        Captain Nares said he owed his command to the zeal of his officers and
men in the present expedition, and their great success, and he said it was an
off-shoot of the ·Challenger· cruise.    I don't think he is quite strong enough
for such a voyage, he suffered from rheumatics in the Antarctic, and he is
(415) rather a timid man, not enterprising enough for such a command.      He was
up in the Arctic 16 years ago, in the nResolute· and another ship after Sir
John Franklin, he was a Lieutenant at that time, and they were frozen in so
hard that they abandoned the ship, and made their way to a settlement over the
ice.     Some years after the -Resolute" was found in the North Atlantic by an
American whale ship, having floated there, nearly 2,000 miles from where she
was frozen in.    She was taken to New York, and put in a thorough state of re-
pair, and presented to the Queen at Portsmouth, by the American Government. On
December 10th the Captain and Lieutenant left in the mail boat, and will be
home long before you get this.   They go overland from Alexandria. (416)


        The Captain took with him his steward,     and his coxswain, one of the
finest and most popular seamen we had in the ship.      He was rowed on board the
mail boat by eight of the junior officers, all hands mustered on the rigging,
and gave him 3 good cheers, and the band played nAuld La~g Syne·.      We are all
sorry to lose him, for he was a very kind and good man.


        A new Captain has been appointed and will be here in two days from
Shanghai, where he is in command of HMS nModiste".      His name is Thompson, and
bears a bad character on this station.      He plays the fiddle, and I believe, is
a preacher of his own sermons, but will tell you more about him by and bye.
(417)    His coming will probably make our commission longer.      We have a new
lieutenant from the "Iron Duke" named Carpenter.




                                      141
     The Transit of Venus was distinctly visible here, but there was no party
of observation hereabouts.    I wonder how they got on at Kerguelen's Land.   We
generally go on board the "Princess Charlotte" to church, she is a roomy old
ship with 5 decks; she carried 110 guns and 1,200 men. I have been on shore
several, times but the first was the greatest novelty.     The town of Victoria
extends from east to west for four miles, but is of no great extent from north
to south.     The houses are mostly of stone, three and four story's high, with
open balconies, and they are wonderfully thick and overcrowded, and fires are
very frequent here.    The population is estimated (418) at 110,000, but if you
could see the immense crowd in the streets, you would, like me, fix it at over
250,000.    There are no cabs or omnibuses, so the traffic is not confined to
the road sides, instead of cabs, there are hundreds of sedan chairs carried on
bamboo poles by four chinamen; you can hire them for a dollar per day or for
5d an hour.     Very few white people ever walk, and soldiers and sailors in-
variably use these chairs.    It is a very common occurrence to see two or three
sedan chairs coming along the streets, each containing a sailor with cigar in
his mouth, and one foot out of each of the small windows.     When they reach a
public house they sing out "shorten sail" and out they all get, keeping the
chairs waiting until they have got pretty well "three parts seven-eights"     as
they call it, then mounting and off again. Very often they will meet an oppo-
sition party of Yankee seamen, and there is generally a fight until the patrol
comes and separates them.     The Russian and American seamen generally fight
also, and last Christmas day there was a regular pitched battle between the
"Iron Duke's" and the Yankees, and several were killed and severely hurt.     The
"Iron Duke" always sends a party of seamen and an officer armed with cutlasses
to patrol the streets whenever they give leave.     The police of Hong Kong are
Sikhs from India, they wear a blue uniform, and a white linen turban, and are
a very fine body of men.     The Chinese never mingle in these street quarrels,
and take no notice, (420) but walk on about their business as solemn and staid
as can be, and give the police very little trouble, except for stealing and
quarreling in the gambling houses.    The people dry their clothes on long bam-
boo poles thrust out from the balconies,     and if you look down a street you
will see nothing but these flags of blue clothes.




                                      142
     Besides being lighted with gas, each house and shop burns a large paper
lamp like the Chinese lanterns you see in England and the streets look very
br illiant at night and thronged with people.    On each side of the road are
fruit stalls and movable Chinese restaurants, where you get a good dinner of
ice and sundries for a halfpenny.


     The streets and houses are very dirty and smell very disagreeably.    There
(421) are but few European shops or bazaars, as the Chinese can undersell most
of the trades.   There are among the Chinese a great many shops where they sell
silk, ivory goods, jewelry, cabinets, and curiosities of all sorts, in which
you could easily spend a small fortune.


     There are scores of artists, photographers, printers, book binders, car-
penters, coopers, cabinet makers, stonemasons and above all barbers.       About
every 10th shop is a barber's, and they do gossip in them while they are get-
ting their heads shaved and their pig-tails dressed.    The undertakers make a
fine show of cOffins: these are made something like a slipper in shape, gen-
erally of camphor wood.    The manufactures are chiefly silk, cotton,       (422)
paper and porcelain, but the great export is tea.       There are some immense
stone quarries here worked by a small army of Chinamen, and there are several
docks round at Aberdeen on the other side of the island, and also at Kowloon
on the opposite peninsula, there is also the prison.   There are three British
regiments here and one Lascar regiment from Bombay.     There are several fine
public buildings and merchants houses, there is a fine sailor's home for the
benefit of the numerous merchant seamen of all nations.       There is a Roman
Church, and a Protestant Cathedral -- for Hong Kong, Canton and Shanghai form
a Bishopric.


     I was at St. John's cathedral the (423) other Sunday afternoon.      It is a
very pretty one, and so neat inside, there is a fine organ, and the singing
was good.   There are several monuments in it to the memory of crews of diff-
erent British ships that have been wrecked      in the China Seas at var ious
times.   In the grounds is a large granite monument to the memory of the brave
Captain Thornton Bale R.N. who was killed under the walls of Canton in 1859
when the city was taken by the English and French.      There is a fine public
botanical garden in which is situated the Bishop's Palace.     No other people
                                     143
could have made such a garden on the steep slope of a mountain some 600 feet
above the sea.    The women work at many manual trades as hard as the men.



December 22nd.
     Our new Captain has arrived from Shanghai, with his servants, his fiddle,
and his piano -- he seems a nice sort of man, but it is too early yet to form
much of an opinion, as the old saying is "New brooms sweep clean", but if he
proves equal to his predecessor, we shall have no reason to complain.


     There was an awful wreck here last week of the steam ship "Mogul" just
off the island, but must tell you more particulars next time, also of another
terrible disaster     near   here,    the destruction by     fire of     the   steam   ship
"Japan".     She was the American mail boat from San Francisco to Hong Kong (425)
and Japan.     There are only seven survivors out of about 700 so far, but the
two American men of war, and a British gun boat have gone to the scene of the
disaster to look for survivors.


     The English mail has just arrived, and we shall receive one more here be-
fore leaving for the south and Japan.            I hear that we shall leave on the 8th
of January for the Phillipine Islands, Caroline Islands, and New Guinea, and
we shall be at Jap~n early in April, and all future letters must be addressed
to Yokohama.

result, but can see several bales and packages on their decks.                 H.M. troop

                                                      Hong Kong.      December 28, 1874.


Dear Tom:
        I am afraid we shall be going to sea before the next English mail comes
in, January 7th: if so, shall get no more letters until April.                 The ship has
been inspected today by Vice Admiral Sir. Chas. Shadwell, and we expect to
leave here on the 4th.      Our address until May is Yokohama, Japan, and a tele-
gram will appear in the English papers, about the beginning of April to an-
nounce our future destination, expect it will be Vancouver's Island.


        Christmas is over again and passed away very pleasantly with us, but the
(428) weather was so warm that it seemed less like an English Christmas than
our two previous ones, in the Bay of Biscay, and the southern ocean.                  As far
as provisions go this is as good a part to spend it in as any foreign place in
the world, and expect the Chinese did a rare trade with all these men-of-war
here.      The Pruss ian ship "Arcona" is here again, I believe there was some
fighting on shore on Christmas Day between the Russians, Prussians, British
and Americans.      I was at St. John's cathedral yesterday afternoon, it was very
nicely decorated with evergreens and reminded me more of home than anything
else.


        Our new Captain's name is "Thomson".         He has not given us any of his ser-
mons yet, and does not even read the service, so the Commander does it.                    He
has two (429)      fiddles, and a piano, and seems a rather gentlemanly sort of
man.     He also brought with him his favourite tom cat, a very good ratter, the
men get him up on deck at night to fight with the old tom we brought from the
Cape, and Thomson's generally gets licked, "as the sayin is".


        I think I told you of HMS "Adventure" arriving here on the 23rd from
Sydney,and bringing three of our old deserters back, they were imprisoned
there     for   three months,   and   said    they   had   returned   for   their   Christmas
dinner.     You would see in the papers of the wreck of the steamer "Mogul", and




                                             145
the total destruction by fire of the American mail boat "Japan", one of the
steamers running from San Francisco to Japan and Hong Kong.                    Another of the
same line the "Alaska"        (430)    is on shore on the other side of the island,
driven there by the typhoon.           Our men who have been to Canton described it as
the dirtiest and most overcrowded city in the world,                   there are exactly 2
millions of people within its walls and the streets are so narrow that only
about four people can walk abreast ..Ttlere are no vehicles in the city, the
heavy work being done by porters who tearry loads across a bamboo pole, and
also by the river and numerous canals.                 The walls are high and wide, and you
can't pass out of the gates after 6:30 p.m.


       The river is more crowded than the streets, thousands of people live on
the water entirely, where there are shops of all sorts and even theatres.
There are lots of European merchants there, also at Shanghai, 700 miles north.
Yokohama is(43l) 1,600 miles northeast and steamers run every week.                    Pekin is
about 1,000 miles north,         and    inland;    but you can get to         it up the   river
Tientsien.     It was taken by the British soon after Canton and concluded the
war.     The   Chinese,   then   according        to   Treaty,   threw open    five   ports   for
European commerce,     since then they have voluntarily opened several others;
still,   in social progress and          enter~r.ise     they are far behind the Japanese.


       The bamboo is the most useful tree in this part of the world, and is put
to an incredible number of uses.              The other day I was watching some large
junks unloading fat pigs from CantoD'-# which they did without any bustle or
noise.    A sort of cradle was slung across two bamboo poles, and carried on the
shoulders of two men, two pigs were placed on their backs in the cradle, and
carried away to be killed.


       At the street corners here are professional ear cleaners, whose stock in
trade consists of a three-legged stool, and a wooden skewer, this latter is
bored into the patient's ear and twisted round a few times, so as to extract
any cockroaches,     etc. ~   the charge for which           is about a halfpenny for         both
ears, and very picturesque these groups look at the street corners, almost as
well as the barbers at the road sides.                 I have had supper once or twice at a
Chinese resturant (European fashion):::as they call it.               There were about eight
dishes, consisting of fish, ham, eggs.7 steak and onions, mutton chops, grilled
                                             146
fowl, curried cats, etc., tea or coffee, tarts, bananas,      orange~   and cigars.
The whole affair for one shilling.       If you are not too particular you may do
very well, and the (433) eggs, fish and fowls are always wholesome and to be
depended upon.     Our Christmas dinner comprised geese, turkeys, ham and plum
pudding (made by our joint efforts and a great success) also a rum cake made
by the Parsee baker of Hong Kong -- "Nowrojie Dourojee".      Some of the English
sign boards over the Chinese shops read very funny, one over the door of a
stone mason read as follows, "Sun Wong Hing will erect a most handsome monu-
ment over the grave of any person".       This shop is on the way to the cemetry,
and the sign is both appropriate and impartial. When I was on shore the other
day I looked into a Chinese Joss House, or place of worship.      The building was
similar to others, but on the roof were a lot of ugly porcelain gods.       Inside,
facing the door was a sort of alter of gilt work covered with carved ivory and
wooden gods,     (434)   and all sorts of queer animals and reptiles.       Several
lights were burning, and the whole affair reminded me of the Transformation
scene at a Christmas pantomime.       There was one worshipper kneeling before the
altar, and a priest officiating.      In front of the worshipper was his offering,
consisting of a large dish of roast pork.      The priest kept pouring some liquid
out of a teapot into some small glasses and handing them to the worshipper,
who placed them on the alter, and prostrated himself to the ground. Neither
spoke a word,     the pr iest wore a particular dress and appeared to take it
pretty cool, but     kep~   a hungry eye on the roast pork, and looked rather im-
patient for at the door was another devotee, with an offering of oranges and
bananas.   These offerings are the priest's perquisites, and would account for
his being such a stout party.      They (435) sell sticks of scented wood, similar
to cinnamon sticks, to the people for burning in their houses and junks to
their own particular gods.        The Chinese worship the moon, and have special
services when it is at the full.      I had a walk the other afternoon to the top
of Victoria Peak, there is a fine zig-zag road leading to the very top, and it
is so cleverly made that a horse can go up, you can ride up and down again in
a sedan chair for a dollar.       This road was made by the Chinese, and must have
taken a long time, and cost a lot of money, these sort of jobs they can do
better and cheaper than any other people, and the Great Wall of China, and the
Grand Canal will testify to the stability of the work.         On the summit is a



                                        147
signal staff and a telegraph (436) leading to the town, so that as soon as a
vessel is sighted and made out, it is known long before she arrives.             A gun is
fired from the summit on the arrival of the English mail.            There are several
houses up there and a cottage for           the governor during the sick         and   hot
season.   There is also a barracks for sick soldiers, a fine breeze is always
blowing up there.      The view is wonderfully str iking, you can see the wild
mountainous coast of China for miles and miles, and away inland the peaks of
mountains over 8,000 feet high.       Looking out to sea you can count scores of
lofty ster ile looking islands belonging to the "Ladrone" group.                 From the
mouth of the great Canton river you will see scores of junks standing across
for Hong Kong, loaded with provisions and merchandise.            Right under your feet
(437)   is the city and bay, with its numerous shipping, and opposite is the
barren, desolate looking peninsula of Kowloon.          Altogether it is one of the
most wonderful panoramas you can conceive.        Although the coast of China has
such a forbidding appearance, there is no country in the world so fertile and
well cultivated.      Victoria Peak is 1,875 feet above the sea, but I would
rather go up there four times than ascent that volcano of Goomong-api once.
All the roads of Hong Kong are in beautiful order for there are no vehicles of
any sort to break them up.        About one mile from the town of Victor ia is a
gully between two ranges of hills, called "Happy Valley", here, vegetation
flourishes and the whole aspect of nature is changed.         No one, to look at the
general barren (438) appearance of Hong Kong, would imagine there was such a
pleasant spot on the island.     Out this way is the cricket ground, and a small,
but well kept race course, on which is a grandstand.        The horses that run are
principally   those   of   the   military   officers.     Here,     also   are   all   the
foreigner's cemeteries, the Chinese being on the other side of the island and
nothing to look at.    The first and largest cemetry is the Mohammedan, which is
surrounded by a good wall and looks very bare, the stones are all lying down.
There are many Mohammedans in Hong Kong ~ the Sikh policemen, and the Lascar
troops are all of that sect, and there are lots of priests knocking about.              On
the other side of the Mohammedan wall is the Catholic cemetry, also surrounded
by a wall, (439) and just beyond that is the Protestant, the best kept of the
three, and in which are buried a great many brave soldiers and sailors, who
were killed during the long Chinese war, and there are scores who died on the
station from the effects of the climate, and there are many stones to seamen


                                        148
who have been killed by pirates on the coast.    There are a great many American
men-of-war men bur ied there and scores of merchant seamen of all flags and
nations.    Some of the monuments erected by the different regiments and ships
are very large and handsome.     The "Calcutta" (flag ship dur ing the Chinese
war) has one to her officers and men, to the memory of over 100 of them.         The
favorite walk of the European community on Sunday afternoon is out this         way~

when I say walk, it should be ride in a sedan chair, merchants, hotel keepers,
clerks,    (440) soldiers and their wives, all use these.      They dress and live
very extravagantly and generally above their means.        It is a common thing when
a seaman volunteers for    the Chinese service, to hear some old sailor say,
"There goes another candidate for the Happy Valley."           I have not yet seen
anything in the papers of ,the new arctic expedition.       I hear the English mail
has left Singapore this morning, so we shall probably wait for her, it is 1450
miles from here and they generally come in five days, if the monsoons are not
too strong against them.     There is a fine line of French mail boats running
here and to Shanghai, via the Suez Canal,        Bombay,    etc.,   from Marseilles,
calling at the French possessions of Saigon, Cochin China. (441) The fare from
here to England by the mail boat-1st class, is 98 pounds.              Opium is the
principal import here, it chiefly comes from British India, and there is an
immense profit on it, fortunately it will not grow in China.        The weather here
is very dry, and generally warm, with very sudden changes.


                                                December 29th.


     We have been outside the harbour today to adjust compasses, and have a
little dredging, and about 40 ladies and gentlemen accompanied us to witness
operations, but they appeared to enjoy the luncheon and dancing most.         We are
just steaming back to our anchorage again, have had a good view of the Ladrone
Island and the mainland of China.     It is very cold up in Japan now, but will

letters for 3 months and I shall get none either.       One of these British reg-
iments here is going to the Fij i Islands in the troop ship "Adventure".           I



                                      149
expect the natives there will decrease rapidly during the next 10 years.        I
don't think we are going to Petropavlovsky at all now, or anywhere north of

                                               December 31st.


        Another Russian man-of-war has arrived flying an Admiral's flag, and the
Prussian frigate "Arcona" has left here for the south.    We were paid a month's
money again yesterday and the Chinese traders, with that sublime pecuniary in-
stinct, got scent of it and swarmed alongside with curiosities, etc.     Half the
men are on a day's leave and the rest are going when they return and we shall
then be ready for sea.


                                               January 1st, 1875


        The French ironclad ram "Monteulieu" came in yesterday afternoon, and

and he saluted the Prussian Admiral.


        The American ship had gone out, or the saluting would have been more in-
