                                                       Hamboldt Bay~ New Guinea
                                                       February 24th, 1875
Dear Tom
         I had not time to wr i te you from Mani lla, as we only had a few minutes
notice that there was an opportunity for sending letters.


         We left Hong Kong on the 6th of January for there, and had pretty good
weather across the China Sea: during the voyage we sounded at an average depth
of 2,000 fathoms.       On Sunday the lOth, we sighted the large and mountainous
island of Luzon, at about 100 miles north of its capital, Manilla.           The wind
falling we got up steam, and when about 60 miles from the town, we sighted a
small dismasted (446) vessel, and went out of our course to examine her.           She
proved to be a small Spanish coasting schooner, and from her appearance looked
as if she had been plundered by pirates.       We towed her in to Manilla, and be-
ing of no value, she was given back to her owner, who lived there and had been
out looking for her for some time.      Her name was the "St. Mayana" and proved
to have been robbed by Chinese and Malay pirates, and her crew murdered.


         We anchored for the second time in Manilla Bay on the 11th.         The place
looked as pretty and sleepy as ever, and on going on shore one evening found
the same stagnant peculiarity which all Spanish and most Catholic countries
seem to exhibit -:- soldiers, priests, ladies in carriages,         bands playing,
church bells ringing, natives hard (447) at work and whfte folks doing nothing
but smoke, perspire and drink coffee.         There are a great many Chinese in the
Phillipine Islands, and they work harder than anybody: but a Chinaman does not
labour for society, or for anybody's good but his own.         He wants the appro-
bation of no man, and cares not what you think of him so long as you pay him.
They will work very hard in such countr ies as America and Australia and are
invaluable, if not too numerous.


         Our ship brought the news per telegram received at Hong Kong the day we
left, of the elevation of Alphonso to the Kingdom of Spain.       The government at
Manilla refused to credit this information, or to allow of its being published
in the papers until they had received two telegrams of their own (448) con-
firming the same, which will probably reach them during the present year.
                                        151
     We found a Spanish frigate, a Prussian corvette and a Russian frigate ly-
ing in Manilla Bay, and the British gun boat "Elk" which sailed the next day
for Singapore and took a small mail for us to be forwarded to England.            The
Prussians are well represented in their navy in this part of the world; lots
of their officers, as well as Spanish and Russians visited our ship during the
stay, and our officers gave the usual dinner party before we left.            Our new
Captain is a regular ladies' man, and a frightful old growler, and spinner of
incredible yarns, commencing "When I was a midshipman 20 years agone           He is
also fond of his cigars and good living.


     We left Manilla on the 14th for          (449) Cebu, another of the Philippine
Islands,   300 miles further   south.    We steamed through some very intricate
str ai ts, with small islands spr ink led about like mushrooms.      Lots of lofty
islands were passed and the weather got warmer every day, over 90         0
                                                                               in the
shade.


     On the 17th we passed hundreds of sea serpents averaging 2 feet long,
floating on the surface of the sea; they were beautifully marked with black
and yellow stripes, and were so active in the water, that it was not an easy
matter to catch them.    On the 18th we sighted Cebu and Matan an adjoining
island and steamed through the strait between the two, the scenery on either
side being beautiful, anchored off the town of Cebu the same day.        The strait
is only half a mile wide near the town. Cebu is a volcanic island, tolerably
high and (450) Matan is of coral formation, scarcely above the sea level, but
very fertile.   Magellan discovered the Philippine Islands, and was murdered by
the natives of Matan in 1521, and lies buried where he fell, on which spot
there is a large monument erected to his memory; our photographer went to
Matan on purpose to take a view of it and I have managed to obtain one copy.
There was a large monument to Magellan in the great square at Manilla.


     Cebu is about 100 miles long and 30 broad, and is a great tobacco growing
island, it being sent on to Manilla to be made up into cigars.          There was a
fine British merchant ship at Cebu from Sydney with coal, enroute for China
for a cargo.    It seems strange that Sydney should be sending coal to such
places as the Philippine Islands, where it lies almost on the surface of the


                                        152
earth 1    There was also a French barque at anchor, and she sailed the next
(451) day for London with a cargo of cigars.             There was a British, American
and German Consult at Cebu, as it is a place of considerable trade.                 We ob-
tained fresh meat and vegetables there from a German contractor.                Fruit was
very plentiful, and cigars could be bought by hundreds for old clothes, knives
or razors -- these article being luxuries and unobtainable by the natives.                I
got 1100 there for a few knives and fancy articles, i f it were not for the
custom house I should br ing them home.            The people are much handsomer than
those of the other Philippine Islands we have been to and were more like
Polynesians than Papuans.        The women were very fond of dress, without being at
all overburdened with it.         (452) The bottom of the sea round Cebu is covered
with gauze looking creatures called ·Venus Flower Baskets·, which are spun by
a sort of water beetle. and look like columns of frozen lace.             I went on shore
one evening and had a very pleasant walk into the inter ior •               The town was
nothing attractive; there were the usual Catholic churches, in front of which
quantities of fireworks were sent off every evening, for the amusement of ad-
miring crowds of natives, while the bells of all the churches discoursed sour
music, like those at Bahia, Brazil.


      I was in conversation with a Spaniard on shore, belonging to Cadiz, who
had been in Australia and America.          He said the Philippine Islands were the
oldest European co19ny in the east, and almost in the world, and it (453) was
the   most    backward;   this   he   attributed   to   the   inherent   laziness   of   the
natives.     If he had also said to the strange deterioration of the Spaniards
since the days of Cortes, he would have been nearer the mark.


      On the 20th we took in 75 tons of coal and on the 23rd a Spanish steamer
arrived from Manilla with news of the political changes in Spain, and owing to
them, appointing the following day a general holiday.              So on the 24th flags
were streaming from all the houses, the church bells rang louder than ever,
and   firewor ks were going off        in the evening to a fr ightful extent.            The
natives seemed very well satisfied with their new king and would be ready for
any further political changes at a very short notice. We left Cebu on the 24th
for Mindanao, the second sized of the Philippine Islands, and about as large
as England.


                                           153
     On the   25th,    we passed the large island of Bohol, and on the 26th,
touched the small volcanic isle of Camuiguin, and landed a party thereon.         It
was about 5 miles     long~   one end was flat, fertile and inhabited, the other, a
black sterile burning cinder, rising 1,500 feet above the sea level and smok-
ing night and day,      it was far more active than any other volcanos we have
seen, and dense clouds of smoke ascended from caves level with the water's
edge, without affecting the temperature of the sea.          We left again the same
evening and sighted Mindanao the next day.


     For 12 days we sailed parallel to the western side of the island and on
the 29th dropped anchor for the second time off the capitol, Zamboanga.           We
brought despatches to the Governor (455) of Mindanao from Cebu concerning the
new King, and the following day the six Spanish gun boats lying there, and the
town itself, were dressed with flags.          The same evening we steamed across to
some small islands, 10 miles to the south, and the next day landed an ex-
plor ing party thereon, while the ship steamed away to make some magnetic
observations, returning to Zamboanga the same night.         On Sunday, the 31st, I
went on shore and had a nice walk into the country, and found that the rice
crop had been gathered in since we were there last, and it being the rainy
season, the fields were under water.       Cock fighting is the great Sunday amuse-
ment at Zamboanga, which takes place in the centre of the principal street,
most of the Spanish military and naval officers looking on, and betting on
their pet birds. The' birds belong to the natives, and to the (456) Chinese,
and the owner backs his bird for so much.           Cock fighting is about the only
amusement I ever saw the Chinese engage in, but as they are great gamblers,
this is not to be wondered at so much.


     I was on shore again before we left, and looked at the old fort,            300
years old, but think I described the place in a previous letter.          A party of
our officers, seamen, naturalists, etc. went on a 4 day's excursion into the
interior of Mindanao, but as they only penetrated about six miles, they can't
know much more about its capabilities and resources than we who stayed on
board.   They shot some monkeys, and other queer animals, and (457) brought a
tiny monkey back, whose mother they had shot, but in about ten days it pined



                                         154
away and died.        Fire flies were very numerous there.      On the 23rd of February
we got up anchor, and steamed to Port Isabel on the same island, to coal.              In
getting up the anchor we brought up from the bottom, two other old anchors,
and long lengths of cable attached, which, from their corroded appearance must
have been there many years.       Port Isabel was a convict settlement for natives,
and they carried the coal on board,             and were rigidly overlooked over       by
Spanish soldiers.       We took in 100 tons, making 240 on board to take us all the
way to Japan, via New Guinea, etc., against the N.E. trade wind.


        We returned to Zamboanga on the 4th and          found a Spanish fr igate at
anchor,     (458) with an Admiral's flag flying.        On the 5th, we took in some
breeding goats and pigs for landing on uninhabited islands, and left Zamboanga
for New Guinea.         On the 6th one of the pigs foolishly committed suicide by
jumping out of the cabin into the sea.           On the 8th, we sounded close to the
S.E. point of Mindanao at 2,025 fathoms, and on the 9th we lost sight of the
Philippine group altogether.       On the lOth, we sighted the Mianclin Islands and
trawled off Luboc the largest of them.          The depth was only 500 fathoms and the
trawling very successful.         Luboc was 2000 feet above the sea level in its
highest part, the island looked fertile.          A canoe came off from it flying the
Dutch     flag,    and brought several beautiful birds which were bought by our
naturalists.


(459)        The natives were almost black, and seemed of pure Papuan origin.           On
the 12th, we trawled at 2,550 fathoms, but got nothing, the bottom being of
pumice stone.        On the 13th, we were getting close to the equator, and were out
of the trade winds region into that of constant precipitation, which region
extends for about 40° on either side of the line, and is one of the most un-
comfortable and depressing portions of the world.            Evaporation is going on day
and night         to an incredible extent.      The vapour    after   ascending   into the




                                          155
cloud region is met by an icy current of air from either pole, which condenses
a great deal of it again, and causes these constant rains that are here met
with, which every few hours comes in torrents.     I never saw it rain to such a
degree elsewhere (460) and mariners have described the surface of the sea
immediately after a heavy down fall of rain, as being almost fresh enough to
drink for a short time.     Some times it rains one side of the ship and not the
other, and you can see the squalls coming for miles before it reaches you.
But it is not only the rain that makes it uncomfortable but the damp oppresive
nature of the air, which seems to take all the energy and life out of a man.
The atmosphere looks hazy and you can scarcely see 10 miles, your clothes and
boots get covered in blue mould and require airing every day.      Men subject to
rheumatics suffer terribly and can tell when the rain is coming long before it
does.   The sun does not seem so hot as the air, and the inside of the ship is
(461) like an oven, especially if we are under steam.      Strong squalls of wind
come with the rain, and these assist ships across this region in a few days,
but we are not like other vessels, as we shall be in this part for the next
month, steering east when we leave.      On the 17th, the temperature of the sea
on the surface and the air in the shade was exactly the same -- 86°         that of
the sea seldom reaches higher and varies if you are steering north or south 4
or 5 degrees a day.       We were seven days sailing 200 miles and crossed the
equator in longitude 138°E on Sunday 21st at 9 a.m.        I might say we flopped
across it, going ab9ut half a knot per hour, and it rained all day.        The same
night we got up steam as there was no sign of any wind- and proceeded to New
Guinea, 100   (462)   miles distant south.    On the    22nd, we sounded at     2020
fathoms and passed enormous masses of dead mangrove trees and bushwood, etc.
Dolphins and sharks also became very numerous.         Yesterday at 12   0' clock   we
sighted New Guinea out of the fog about 12 miles away.       The land was high and
covered with vegetation and as the weather cleared a little, several mountain
peaks appeared above the clouds.      They were at least 6,000 feet high, but on
the opposite side of the island there are ranges whose peaks exceed 16,000
feet and what there may be in the interior no man knows.      At 6 p.m. we steamed
into Humboldt Bay, and dropped anchor about 3 miles from the shore.         We soon
saw some lights dancing about on the beach, and at 8 p.m. two canoes came off
to the ship, (463) but for a long time they would not come alongside. A blue



                                       156
light was lit and though it startled them a bit at first,             they soon gained
confidence,    and came close enough      to    receive   several little presents,    and
bundles of cigars.        They were entirely naked, and tattoed and painted in a
most horrible manner.       They were armed with bows and arrows, spears and stone
hatchets.     They could all say "Segar, Segar" and smoked away with great de-
light.     At 9 p.m. they returned to their village to fetch others,           and all
night    long we could hear     them gathering round the ship and       jabber ing like
magpies.


        New Guinea or Papua was discovered by Torres in the middle of the 16th
century and the strait which separates it from Australia is named after him.
It is 1200 miles long and averages 250 broad, and is more than three times as
large as England.     It is the headquarters of the Papuan or Austral negro race,
which on this island alone is supposed to number several millions.          Of its in-
ter ior nothing definite      is known,   one or    two travellers have   succeeded    in
penetrating a short distance from the western side of the island, but the de-
termined hostility of the natives prevented any connected exploration.                The
natives being broken up into different tribes hostile to each other proved the
greatest drawback.        One German traveller estimated the mountains in the in-
terior    as exceeding 20,000 feet     in altitude, and of course where there are
such mountains,     there must be rivers of considerable extent.           The western
portion of the island being contiguous to the (465) Dutch and Spanish posses-
sions, has been visited by their ships at intervals for-the last 200 years,
and it is certain that the Chinese were acquainted with it much earlier.               In
exchange for iron and fancy goods, they obtained from the Papuans ambergris,
tortoise shell, small pearls, and birds of paradise, of which country the lat-
ter are natives.     No   permanent settlement has ever been made onthe island, and
even its coasts have not been properly surveyed.


        Bouganville, the French navigator, surveyed Humboldt Bay and other parts
of this side in 1769, and the Russians have also visited it during the present
century.     One or two British men-of-war have been within the last 20 years,
one the "Basilish" has just gone home from making a survey of the coast (466)
opposite Australia, with a view to making a settlement in that direction.               A




                                          157
year or two ago a report was spread in Australia that gold had been discovered
in New Guinea, so a party of ,diggers and adventurers started from Sydney as
the pioneers of the new El Dorado, and some of them never returned,                      the
climate and natives killing them, so the expedition came back again to Sydney
without seeing a sign of the precious metal.           The place where they landed is
over 1,000 miles southwest of Humboldt Bay.         Those missionaries we saw at Cape
Yorke make occasional visits to the southern portion of the island, but as yet
their progress has been small compared to that confined space, and the work of
evangelizing the Papuans will be one of difficulty and danger and will neces-
sarily take a long time.


(467)       The natives in the interior are supposed to be a very different race
to these near the coasts, where they are frequently mixed with the Malays.                By
daylight this morning about 30 canoes were alongside, containing some 150
natives.     They were of a dark brown colour, tall, well built men with long
wooly hair, were entirely naked, and most of them were tat toed and painted
with red and blue ochre1 a great many had spear wounds and arrow holes in var-
ious parts of their        bodies, which had evidently been received in battle.
Their canoes were something similar to the Fijians and they brought off cocoa-
nuts, bananas and native war implements for trading purposes.


        Cigars and iron hoops were most sought after by them, not caring much for
clothes, beads, or fancy articles, and had no idea               o~    tobacco or pipes. I
should     think   they   have   been   visited   occasionally    by    vessels   from   the
Philippine Islands trading with cigars, etc.           The iron hoops they straighten
and sharpen, and grind them into fighting hatchets.          Their own knives and axes
are made of a hard green stone sharpened, it is exactly like that you see
brooches made of occasionally.          The noise they made alongside was deafening
and trading in Papuan war implements has been going on all day long to an in-
credible extent.      Most of them had bones through the nose and ears, and orna-
ments of bone round their arms and ankles, a row of cock's feathers round the
crown of the head, and a necklace of human teeth.           No women or children have
been near us, but can we see them down on the beach.                   Their huts are neat
(469) looking conical structures, over 30 feet in height and apparently built



                                           158
of bamboo and grass, etc.       They all chew betel root to a frightful extent, and
have no teeth or voices, owing to this habit, still they were a finer looking
race   than   the    Arroo   Islanders,   and    far   superior   to   the   aboriginals    of
Australia.


       At 7 a.m. we got up anchor and steamed in towards the settlement, the
band playing all the time, which startled them at first but they soon ceased
to notice it.       They yelled with delight when the anchor came up, but evidently
could not make out what it was that moved the ship.                All the boats were got
out at 9 a.m. preparatory to a week's stay, surveying, exploring, etc.


       Steam was got up in the steam pinnace and the boat's crew were all armed,
and at 10 a.m. the Captain left the ship for (470) the native settlement, tak-
ing several presents of hatchets, fancy gear, etc.                Just as he approached a
crowd of naked women rushed down to the beach, armed with spear s, bows and
arrows, etc., and frightened our brave Captain on board again in very little
time, after seizing everything in the boat they could lay their hands on.


       The women were much uglier than the men, and quite able to look after
themselves.     Another boat tried to land at a village near, but was served in
exactly the same manner.       They evidently knew the use of fire arms, and it was
the sight of these alone that prevented them from active measures.                         This
afternoon the steam pinnace with an armed party effected a landing in an unin-
habited part of the bay and the naturalists shot several cockatoo parrots,
etc.



                                                 March lOth, at the Admiralty Islands
                                                 Lat. 20·S.
       These islands are 400 miles due east of Humboldt Bay.                 On the 26th, we
lost sight of the mountains of New Guinea, and passed Fiju and Matty Islands,
made the usual slow passage across, and had wet miserable weather.                    On the
28th we passed Bertrand Island and sounded at 1,025 fathoms.                     We sighted
several of the group on the 2nd instant and anchored on the 3rd in our present



                                           159
position.     In 1642 Tasman visited these islands, but they were probably dis-
covered by the Spaniards at an earlier date.        Bouganville visited them in
1767.     They are a considerable cluster situated to the W.N.W. of New Ireland,
only one is over 100 sq. miles in extent, this is tolerably elevated and (472)
of volcanic origin.    The remainder are small level islands of coral formation,
they are all fertile, and several are inhabited.      The total population is not
over 4,000.     We are anchored in a bay between the large island and several
smaller ones, surrounded by extensive coral reefs, over which the sea rushes
and roars tremendously, especially during the night.      Our officers have sur-
veyed this bay and called it "Nares Bay".


        Several canoes full of naked warriors came out to meet us, and numbers of
them have been alongside all the week, trading with their native war imple-
ments, cocoanuts, bananas, yams, etc. for iron hoops.


        They had no idea of tobacco or cigars, but the hoops and hatchets were
prized above anything and there is scarcely one left on board now.        They are
great thieves, and are (473) not at all afraid to come on board to have their
portraits taken.     They are something like the Papuans, but not so fierce look-
ing.     They are evidently mixed with the South Sea Islanders, and is a great
diversity of features and colour amoungst them 7 are more used to the sea than
the Papuans, and swim and dive like fishes.      They chewed betel nut, and their
weapons are similar to the Papuans, only made of       diff~rent   material.   They
fight among themselves, one island and tribe against another, and there is no
sign of any missionary ever having been here.     They wear large mother-of-pearl
shells round the neck as a charm, and do not care to part with them.


        The islands are out of the track of regular navigation, and are seldom
visited.     The natives are tattoed and wear bones through the ears and nose.
The disease called     (474)   elephantiasis is very prevalent here.    I bought a
cocoanut the other morning wi th a young palm tree growing out of it, and on
opening it was never so surprised with anything before: the young tree holds
the nut suspended by several long white fibres, which completely envelope it
and their province is to supply the young tree with nourishment until it no




                                        160
longer requires it.     On opening the inside I found the whole of the milk ab-
sorbed and the nut quite dry but full of a sweet pithy substance.          The cocoa
palm flourishes in a sandy soil, and the young tree bears fruit in about 3
years.     Shooting parties have been away every day to the large island and shot
enough pigeons (of a parrot species) to last all hands twice.      The natives act
as guides and lie down (475) when the gun is being fired and yell with delight
on seeing the bird fall.


        The Admiralty Islanders are Polygamists.     One of the chiefs offered our
Captain two of his best looking wives for a hatchet.      Yesterday two couples of
breeding goats were taken over to the main island and landed there to remain
to increase and mu1tip1Y1 lots of pigs are there already, but being no cocoa-
nut palms,     there are no natives residing on the island.        I    was on shore
yesterday for a few hours.       The island is about 2 miles long, and a half
broad, and contains about 600 inhabitants who live in large huts, and chiefly
on cocoanuts, yams, fish and pigs1 which are very numerous.      The women are the
ugliest human beings I ever saw and are horribly painted and tattoed.         The men
are quite handsome compared to them.


(476)        They wear nothing but a branch of palm leaves round the middle, and
when about 50 of them danced a war dance to the music of tom-toms, anything
more suggestive of the "Infernal Regions", I never saw.        In a physical point
of view they are superior to the aboriginal women of Australia.


        At the entrance to one large hut, were two life size,          roughly carved
figures, representing a naked man and woman, but the natives did not appear to
pay any reverence to these deities.          Last night we fired off several shell
rockets which frightened them a great deal.


        We are just leaving these islands for the Caroline and Ladrone group fur-
ther north, and we hope soon to be in more pleasant weather again.         At present
it is raining very heavily.

        On Good Friday, we signalled the first ship for six weeks, the "John

(479)                                                       H.M.S. "Challenger" at
                                                            Yokoska, April 30th, 1875
Dear Tom
        We arrived here at 6 o'clock on the night of the 12th and received our
letters and papers soon after and all were most eager to read the news.                           The
railway accident was a most terrible affair and I think the English companies



                                               162
might learn a great deal            from the Japanese, although the railway between
Yokohama and Yedo is on the American system.             The marine disasters of the "La
Plata" and "Cospatr ick" were pitiful events, as regards the latter, I hope
more survivors may turn up and that we may learn more particulars as to the
cause of the fire, and the means taken to overcome it.                   How the newspapers
gloat over the details and horrors of the events!


        Since my arrival here I have been "up to town", for Yedo is a town, and
excepting London and Paris there are no European cities larger; however, I am
not going to give a description of its wonders in this letter, the next one
must be reserved for        that.     We are now in the Japanese Imper ial Dock at
Yokoska, a town and bay in the Gulf of Yedo, 18 miles east of Yokohama, for
the purpose of refitting, etc.


        This letter is a sort of introduction to the descriptive one which is to
follow, containing an account of European progress,                etc.,    in Japan,     up to
1856,    when    the country was opened for           commerce and   intercourse with all
nations.     It is gathered from various (481) books.             In the year 1278, Marco
Polo the great traveller of Venetia was at Pekin soon after Kublai Khan had
over-run China, on his return to Europe in 1295, he pointed to the eastern
margin of the Yellow Sea,            and said there was a great island there named
"Xipango" or "Cissango", peopled by a highly civilized and wealthy race, who
had 'bravely rolled back the tide of Tartar conquest in the days of Kublai
Khan. His countrymen smiled with incredulity at this wondrous tale, and for
several subsequent centuries Europe knew but very little more about Japan.                   It
was to search for the mythical land, that Columbus sailed from Spain in 1492,
and discovered the great American continent, which, he for a long time thought
was the same fabulous xipango.           Before Europeans found their way round the
Cape of Good Hope, China (482) was allowed to send 15 junks annually to and
from Nagaski, a port at the extreme south of the Japanese Empire, for trading
purposes.       The Japanese group was inhabited long before the commencement of
authentic       records,   whether    peopled    by    refugees   from     China,   The   Corea
Peninsula, or from the great deserts of Scythia is not certain.                     The ancient
history of Japan says that 650 years B.C. a hero known as the divine warrior,




                                           163
firmly established a dynasty which has flourished to the present day, in a
line of 122 male and female monarchs.            Of their reigns, far better records
exist than the oldest European Empires can boast, the early monarchs combined
in their persons the double office of high priest and generalissimo.              Chinese
historians    assert   that   Japan was     voluntarily tributary     to the    Celestial
Empire, but (483)      this may be doubted.       Rublai Khan after he had subjected
China, sent envoys to the Emperor of Japan demanding his submission, which was
refused, and when the great Tartar conqueror invaded the country with a Mongol
Chinese army, he was boldly met by that of the Japanese, and totally routed
and driven back. The "Mikado" or Emperor, was assisted at this juncture by a
"Tiegoon" or assistant emperor, who took the command of the armies while the
Mikado performed his spiritual part of praying for their success.              The office
of Tigoon was then made hereditary and since then there has always been a
"Spiritual" and a "Temporal" Emperor in Japan, until 1868, when the present
Mikado defeated the reigning family of usurpers, and ascended the throne as
sole Emperor.


     After the Mongol hordes were dr iven back,             the Japanese retaliated by
(484) ravaging the coast of China, and for several subsequent centuries, their
bargues were the terror of the China Seas.             The Portuguese were the first to
rediscover Xipango,      when Fernando Mindes Pinto accompanied a Japanese bargue
from Ning-po, Chin,a,       and    reached Kin-sin, Japan.     His report on reaching
Europe in 1542 was hardly believed, but from then to- 1579, and after                 the
Spaniards were     firmly     established on     the   Phillipine   Islands,   numbers of
Spanish and Portuguese missionaries under the great Francis Xavier, who was
afterwards martyred in China, visited Japan, and converted one million of the
natives.     In the year 1579 Saiko Sama, was the Temporal Emperor, who one day
asked a Spaniard how it was that the King of Spain had managed to possess him-
self of half the world?           -- The reply was -- "He first sends priests to win
the people, his soldiers then are sent to join the native Christians, and the
conquest is easy".      Saiko Sama was so much struck and alarmed that he swore
"no priest should be left alive in his dominions". In 1587 the first edict for
the banishment of the Catholic missionaries was issued, the native Christians
were sent away to fight in the Corea, and were decimated.              In 1596 the edict
was reversed against Christians. All missionaries were ordered to quit the


                                           164
country, twenty-three disobeyed and in 1597 suffered death at Nagaski, and
were duly canonized in 1627 by Pope Urban VIII.         Saiko Sama's warrant has been
preserved, which reads as follows - "I have condemned these prisoners to death
for having come from the Phillipine Islands to Japan,                under the pretended
title of ambassadors, and for having persisted in (486) my land without my
permission, and preached the Christian religion, against my decree.                 I order
and wish that they be crucified in my city of Nagaski".             A few Portuguese were
allowed to remain in Japan, but they were obliged to disown their religion and
conform to the native habits and laws.            In 1767 the Abba Sedotti learnt the
Japanese language from refugees at Manilla and sailed from thence with several
missionaries to make another attempt at converting the Japanese.               He was land-
ed on the coast and from that hour has never been heard of.                    Chr istiani ty
never flourished in Japan after this.


      In the year 1600 the Dutch made their appearance there, notwithstanding
the hostility of the Spaniards and the bulls of the Pope, and were allowed to
establish a factory at Fesando, and from that time until within (487) the last
30 years, they have remained master of the field, as regards trade with Japan.


     The pilot on the Dutch ships on their first per ilous voyage was "William
Adams n a native of Gillingham, Kent.  They were two years on their passage
out, the fleet bei,ng separated and dispersed near the Straits of Magellan.
The   "Erasmus",    Adam's   ship,    was   the   only one   tha~    reached     Japan.    The
Portuguese misrepresented the character of the new arrival, and endeavored to
have the crew treated as thieves and robbers saying "that if justice was
executed upon them it would terrify the rest of their countrymen from coming
there anymore".      Adams, and one of the Dutch sailors was brought before the
Emperor in whose presence Adams spoke up manfully -- "I showed him" says he,
"the name of our country, and that our land had sought out the                    (488) East
Indies for a long timen, and after explaining the purely mercantile purpose of
the voyage, the King asked him whether our country had wars?              "I answered him,
yea   with   the   Portuguese   and   Spaniards,    being    at   peace   with    all     other
nations". This was the best reply he could have given and probably saved the
lives of the whole party.       They were treated kindly by the Emperor, but they
and their stout bargue were never to leave Japan.             The "Erasmus" was ordered


                                            165
to the city of Yedo, the temporal capitol of Japan.              Adam's merits were so
appreciated that he obtained great influence and when in 1649 the next Dutch
ships visited Japan, considerable privileges were conceded them through "the
good offices of Will Adams".        By those ships he sent letters to England, and
had been 15 years in the country when he learnt that (489) a vessel bearing
the red cross of Old England had reached Firando.              She was the "Clive" of
London, belonging to the East India Company (then in its infancy) and com-
manded by Captain John Faris, furnished with a letter from King James I, and
suitable presents for the Emperor.       The "Clive" left the Thames on April 11th,
1611 and reached Firando on the 11th June, 1613, having spent two years trad-
ing on the way.        Adams was sent from Yedo to Firando to greet his long
expected countrymen.      Thirteen weary years the old man had looked forward
hopefully, and at last his prayer was heard. He, with Captain Faris, and 10
Englishmen started for Yedo, bearing the royal letter and presents, and the
influence of Adams soon obtained from the Emperor a favorable treaty granting
(490)    to England the most important privileges ever conceded by Japan to a
foreign country.


        In 1613 an English    as well    as    a   Dutch   factory   was   established   at
Firando.    The English for political reasons very soon withdrew and so avoided
the trouble that overtook the rest of the European residents in Japan.               Will
Adams was employed at Yedo in building ships for the Emperor and was advanced
to the rank of Imperial Tutor, being acquainted with geometry and mathematics.


        He acted as   interpreter    to the East India Company, and possessed an
estate about 2 miles from where we are lying in dock.                 He left about 800
pounds in his will to be divided between his English and his Japanese family.
There are people in this neighbourhood who claim to be his descendants.             About
3 years ago, his tomb and that of his (491) Japanese wife, was discovered by
an Englishman living at Yokohama, and all Europeans visiting Japan endeavor to
see the grave of the first Englishman who reached the country.               It is on the
summit of a hill on his own estate, being buried there at his own request, and
the Japanese Mrs. Adams lies beside him.           I went yesterday to visit the tomb.
There is a Budhist Temple near it, the priest of which says that Adams used to
worship there.     The hill commands a splendid view of the Bay of Yedo and of


                                         166
the surrounding country, the scenery is magnificent, and is considered the
finest in this part of Niphon.      There is a religious feast observed at Yedo in
June to the honor of Will Adams, the "Man of Kent".           After his death the
English factory at Firando was abandoned and in the following year the (492)
persecution against the Christians again began, and ended in the withdrawal of
the English, the expulsion of the Spaniards and imprisonment of the Dutch to
the island of Decima, Nagaski, where they were not allowed to worship accord-
ing to their religion, or even to observe the sabbath.      Under these conditions
the Dutch factory continued at Decima until the recent treaties with European
powers.


        Nagaski is at the extreme south of the Japanese empire.      Firando is a
little further north.       The empire of Japan or Niphon as the natives call it,
consists of four large islands and about 300 small ones -- many scores of
which we passed coming into Yokohama.         The large island of Niphon, or Japan
proper, an island over 800 miles in length.


        From the shores of Japan to those of China is 450 miles in a direct
line.     (493)   The area of Japan is about 160,000 sq. miles (one-fifth larger
than Great Britain and Ireland together), and the population is estimated at
30 million.       It was formerly governed by some 200 Daimios, or native princes,
who were tributary to the Emperor, but very turbulent and independent, but in
1866 this feudal system was abolished and the present Mikado is sole Emperor
(temporal and spiritual) and he frequently sees the ambassadors at Yedo or
Tokio, as the natives call it (sic), which means eastern capital.        It has only
been the metropolis since 1690 before which time it was a paltry fishing vil-
lage.     The ancient capitol of Japan was Kamakura, an insignificant little town
about 8 miles from Yokoska and which I could see from Adam's tomb yesterday.
In the 16th century according to the Jesuit priests,          it contained 200,000
houses.      (494) Japan is fertile and beautifully cultivated.     It   is rich in
minerals,     including coal, possesses plenty of magnificent harbours and its
seas abound with fish.        Agriculture is the principal native pursuit, rice is
largely cultivated and exported.      The chief manufactures are those of silk and
cotton, lacquering or japanning, and porcelain.         The internal trade is very



                                        167
extensive and rigid regulations are in force for protecting and encouraging
home industry.     Foreign trade was far from being popular until the last few
years.     In 1853, the American fleet under Commodore Perry forced its way up
the Gulf of Yedo, and after proceeding to active measures forced a treaty in
1854 between Japan and the United States.        The ports of Osaka, Kanagama,
Yokohama, Nagaski and Kakodeki, were (495)     thrown open for foreign trade in
1859, when all the great European powers arranged separate treaties with
Japan.    The second treaty between Great Britain was concluded by Lord Elgin in
1859 soon after the fall of Canton.     There was a "Spiritual" and a "Temporal"
Emperor of Japan at that time.      The former lived at Micao, a city 350 miles
further    south and according to Japanese etiquette the "Spiritual" Emperor
never leaves his palace.


        Our government in 1859 presented him with a fine steam yacht to travel
round his palace and grounds.      Osaca is the sea port of Micao.     Micao has
nearly a million inhabitants.      The Japanese are of a yellowish complexion,
with thick black hair, are not much like the Chinese in appearance and quite
different to them in temperment, being a cheerful, contented, jolly people.


(496)       I consider them the most wonderful and interesting race we have yet
met with, their curiosities and manufactures in wood and bronze work are in-
finitely more arti~tic and pretty than anything the Chinese ever produced, but
                                                          -
must tell you more about them in my next letter.      The weather here is rather
warmer than England in the middle of the day, and certainly colder in the eve-
nings and early mornings.     Volcanoes, hot springs, sulphur springs, etc., are
very plentiful in Japan and earthquakes are thought nothing of. The atmosphere
is wonderfully clear here and the peak of Fusi-Hamu, 60 miles inland, looks
scarcely more than 6 miles away at sunrise and sunset.


        Fusi-hama or the "matchless mountain" of Japan, is the prettiest mountain
in the world.     It is 11,500 feet high and stands (497) in the middle of an im-
mense plain, so that we can see it two-thirds of the way from the summit,      it
is covered in snow more than half way down.     In August, there is scarcely any
snow on it and then you can easily ascend it.          Lady Parkes,   the British
Ambassador's wife has been to the top.       It can be seen 100 miles out at sea


                                       168
and was sighted a        few weeks ago by the Captain of the "Sylvia", English
man-of-war, from the summit of another mountain, 140 miles further north.                It
 is quite a baby among mountains, having made its appearance according to re-
liable Japanese authority one evening about 500 years ago.                   Its birth was
accompanied by a tremendous earthquake, and for 400 years, Fusi-hama was a
volcano of the most active kind, but at present it is only a moderate smoker.
The British Ambassador here, Sir Harry Parkes, lives at Yedo.               He has been out
here many years and has done more towards opening the country for trade than
other European.       The Gulf of Yedo is one large harbour, 40 miles long and 12
broad, containing scores of beautiful little coves and bays, where ships can
lie securely.


       About 30 miles down the Gulf, on the southern shore, stands its seaport,
Yokohama, where ships lie that could not get up to Yedo, which great city is
on the opposite side.          It is 12 miles from Yedo by water and 18 by rail and
contains    over     300,000    inhabitants     including   about   3,000    Europeans   and
Americans, and about the same number of Chinese, who are considered foreigners
. in this country.     There are not as many vessels lying in Yokohama Bay as at
Hong Kong, but still (499) a large number, the British, French and American
flags being most numerous.         There are 8 good sized Japanese men-of-war lying
there, 6 here at Yokoska, and others elsewhere.               The flagship was built at
Aberdeen and is      nea~ly    as large as the "Audacious".         Most of the Japanese
men-ot-war were built in England or America, as their dockyard has not got in
proper swing yet, it is very compact and situated in an impregnable and secure
position, has been made by French engineers and the leading hands are French-
men.    The ships are manned entirely by Japanese sailors, trained at the naval
college at Yedo, by English men-of-war's men, who receive from 300 pounds to
 500 pounds a year.      The officers arae partly English and American, as well as
natives.    The scenery round here is magnificent, something like the Isle of
Wight on a larger and grander scale.           Will continue by next mail.

                                                      Joe Matkin

                                                 Yokohama, May 4, 1875


Dear Tom
        I   find we shall be leaving here     in about a week   for our cruise   in
Japanese waters, so will commence another letter.


        We do not have such a crowd of junks round us here as at Hong Kong and
there is no floating population at all, the sailors and fishermen all live on
shore the same as other countries.      The Japanese junks are built more substan-
tially than the Chinese, but something after the same style, they are rigged
differently, having only one square sail, and they are propelled at a good
pace by sculls.      You see (501) no women or children in the junks, working like
horses: if there are any afloat, they are passengers.      Neither do you see the
Japanese women working       in the fields or doing any kind of rough work at
all: their duties are domestic and confined to spinning, cooking, nursing and
smoking, which habit they all indulge in this country, but their tobacco is
very mild and the pipes only hold about 2 grains. The married women have their
teeth blackened and their eyebrows shaved off.      In appearance the Japanese are
a small clumsy looking people, with heavy regular features and a look about
the eyes and mouth as if they had just woke from a comfortable sleep: st ill
they have a much healthier and fresher appearance than the Chinese.       They seem
to be of Tartar and Chinese extraction and yet (502) there-is something of the
Malay about them.      Their dress is a long dark woolen robe, fastened round the
waist, with sleeve holes and open in front.        If it is cold weather they wear
two or three of these, one over another.       The women dress exactly the same as
the men, only it is opened round the neck and wear a sort of panier behind.
Their hair is differently dressed.      In this country no shoes or stockings are
worn indoors, but wooden clogs in wet and dirty weather, and in fine, neat
straw sandals.       The poorer classes wear no underclothing whatever.     In the
towns the men have tight fitting pantaloons, exactly like the harlequins in a
pantomime, and both sexes wear a small, tignt-fitting stocking, shaped like a
mi t ten, wi th a thumb hole for the big toe, wh ich holds the sandIe on by a
loop.       Neither sex use any (503) head covering, except in cold weather, when



                                        170
they tie a scarf round the head.           When it is wet or hot, they have pretty
umbrellas for shelter, made very ingeniously of bamboo and prepared paper.


        In Yedo and Yokohama, many of the better class of men are dressed in
European costume, and several in a sort of half and half, like the native
priets at Tongatbu.          But they seldom look well in European dress and their
clothes have a Jewish appearance.


        None of the women use the European style, and their clothes are generally
of a plain dark colour, and wear no jewelry to speak of, unless in their
hair.     They paint very much, but seldom are improved by it as they have very
fine rosy complexions.


        Bread and meat are rather dearer than at Hong Kong, but the meat is much
better and the prices are lower than in England. (504)


        The vegetables in this country are something wonderful, even superior to
those in China.     There are carrots and turnips 3 feet long and the same thick-
ness from the root to the head.


        Green peas, etc., are just coming in, but there will be no fruit for an-
other month.      We have provision and cur iosi ty boats alongside every day and
you may see some wonderful cabinets, workboxes, tea-caddies and knick-knacks
of all sorts tolerably cheap.         If we were only allowed space to keep things,
we might bring wonders home from the different places, but, as it is, we have
to stow everything into our chests.         The Japanese have the same system of ex-
tortion as the Chinese, but are always good tempered and civil.              They are very
clever and ingenious in imitating anything, and are not so prejudiced against
innovations and improvements as the Chinese.


        Such   things   as    locomotive   and     mar ine   engines   as   large   as   the
"Challenger's" are already constructed in this country, and you see lots of
sewing machines-American, of course.             Labour is not so plentiful in Japan as
China, and there are not so many helplessly poor people, have never seen a
professional beggar in the country.        A few years ago the Japanese seemed as if


                                           171
they were going to adopt European habits and dress entirely, and-English and
American newspapers began to speculate as to how long it would be before they
learnt the English language and altered their own national systems, but a re-
action appears to have lately set in, and they are fast falling back into
their own customs and usages.      The Japanese are a more united (506) people
than the Chinese and better governed, but they are still frightfully and dis-
proportionately taxed, the burden all falling on the poorer classes.     However,
there is a great reform going on, and there are already native newspapers
printed at Yedo, which are commencing to agitate, and to "want to know, you
know" and ask "why such things should be?"    I learnt this from translations in
the English papers printed here.    They wash and get up linen beautifully, even
better than the Malays or Chinese and do everything so neatly.     The shores of
the Gulf of Yedo look more like England than those of any other country we
have visited.     There are lots of batteries on the commanding points, and some
immense earth forts in front of the city of Yedo, built on small and conve-
niently situated islands.     The town of (507) Yokohama stands in a hollow and
we cannot see much of it from the ship.      More of Kanagavu is visible on the
opposite shore.


     The Japanese sailors are dressed like our men and their officers similar
to ours.   Their national flag is white with a red ball in the centre.    They do
not wear pigtails but most have the crown of the head shaved, have no sign of
any beard or whisker and a long beard is greatly admired in this country,
especially by the fair sex.    Lots of leave has been given to the crew since we
arrived -- more than they have money enough to take advantage of.      A few days
after we arrived two clerks belonging to the French bank here absconded with
37,000 dollars, and bought a small vessel and hired a crew to take them to
Manilla.   As soon as their absence was discovered a steamer (508) was sent
after them, as it was known the wind had been unfair for their getting out of
the Gulf of Yedo.     The steamer took with her a sub-lieutenant and 10 armed men
from HMS "Thalia" which is stationed here, and came up with the schooner the
same night -- becalmed.      Before the vessel was boarded the two clerks went
down to the cabin and shot themselves -- one through the head and the other
through the heart, after which they shortly died and the money was recovered.
One was an Italian, the other an Englishman.      They had been several years in


                                       172
the bank and held a very considerable position in the European Society of
Yokohama, but gambling and betting proved too much for their integrity.      The
Europeans here, like those at Hong Kong, live very extravagantly and try to
cut a dash.     They must have their horse racing, club house, etc., the same as
in England, only about 10 times dearer, and they are little gods in their own
tin pat way, but on returning to their native country many of them find that
they are rather ordinary personages after all, and not infrequently return
again to the place of their former glory.


        On the 19th of April I went on shore for the first time, and returned
again on the evening of the 20th.     There are three daily English papers print-
ed in Yokohama and one weekly, also a "Japan Punch n for the select few which
is a feeble imitation of its English prototype, for unless you know everybody
of consequence among st the Europeans, you don't see exactly where the joke
lies and soon get bewildered.


        There is an English, a French, an American, (510) a Dutch and Japanese
Imperial Post Office.       Also an English and a French landing quay and an
English and French quarter of the town -- called English and French Hatoba.
There is also a Chinse quarter, where the celestials may be seen scraping
money together and minding their own business, for they are under the same
regulations as other foreigners.      The English community and the foreign con-
suls, etc., live in the most healthy part of the town, on some heights called
the Bluffs, from where a fine view can be obtained of the town and the Bay of
Yedo.     Their houses are built almost entirely of wood, for earthquakes are not
rarities in the country, but most of them are very pretty erections and have
nice flower gardens attached.      Japan is a fine country for wild flowers and I
have gathered lots of violets in the fields.       There are about twice as many
hotels in Yokohama as there ought to be -- English, French and American (511)
-- very large buildings too, considering that all Europeans of any standing
have private houses, it is a mystery to me how they are supported.      There are
only three churches, an English, Roman Catholic and a Presbyterian, which is
an Amer ican.      In   this respect Yokohama   is scantily supplied compared to
Lisbon, Bahia and Manilla.      The first thing that strikes one in Japan, after
visiting China is the beautiful roads, and clean streets, there are none of


                                       173
those fearful smells that you find in Hong Kong or Manilla.       The streets are
wide and straight and kept clean by the people, each householder sweeping and
watering his frontage.


(512)        Proper labourers mend the roads and there is an efficient police
force, but they appear to have very little to do.       There is no drunkenness in
this country and everyone can read and write the Japanese language, so one of
the girls at the tea gardens told me -- who spoke English and said they went
to school until they were over 13.


        The Japanese houses are built almost wholly of wood and plaster, gen-
erally two storys in height, with carved gable ends and roofs.      The fronts and
backs of them can be opened and closed at pleasure for ventilation, etc., and
the interior is kept beautifully clean.        The rooms are partitioned off with
wooden partitions, sometimes only paper, and the windows are made of thin but
strong paper which will keep out wet, and yet admit light.      (513) The floor of
the house is raised about two feet and covered with beautiful white rush mats
on which cushions are spread at night for sleeping.        The Japanese pillow is
simply a small wooden trestle which they cover over with a roll of cloth or
paper.     The pillow itself is exactly like those used by the natives of the
South Sea Islands.     There is a porch inside the door before you mount on to
the raised floor, in'which they leave their shoes or sandals, wearing either
their socks or going barefooted indoors.    They expect all visitors to take off
their boots unless they are very clean indeed,        though they admire European
boots and shoes more than any other article of dress. They are the most hos-
pitable people I     ever met with.    Paper    enters largely into the   use   and
domestic wants and arrangements of the Japanese, and they are unrivalled in
their manner of utilizing straw and paper to the best advantage.       You can buy
a Mackintosh made of prepared paper, and capable of keeping out wet, as well
as another, for about 2s/ and you could not distinguish it from an ordinary
one.     Over these capes the fishermen spread thick straw overcoats to keep out
the cold in winter, and by spreading a bamboo frame from the head to the stern
of the boat, they make it water tight and warm by fixing movable sheets of
straw.    They have a charcoal fire in all the boats, and when hauling in their
nets they beat a wooden rattle to charm the fish.      The fires in the houses are


                                      174
all charcoal;    the fireplace   is a movable one and generally st-ands in the
middle of the room.    The charcoal comes from the great interior forests where
many thousands are employed in its preparation.     Of course there are no chim-
neys to the Japanese houses.


     The horses, which appear to be (515) very scarce in Japan, are shod with
plaited straw shoes.   Oxen and sheep are far from plentiful as there is no de-
mand for them.    Pigs are met with everywhere, and poultry and game there is a
good supply of. You seldom see a butcher's shop, but fishmongers are numerous,
as the natives live chiefly on fish, rice and eggs.      There is a great number
of ravens, may be seen on half the housetops in Yedo.     Except European private
carriages, there are scarcely any horse conveyances, the passenger traffic is
performed by neat little cars called in Japanese "Jinrickshaws" (our sailors
thought "Jenny Rickshaws" best).     They are drawn by one man who stands between
the shafts, and trots along very much faster than a London cab horse.       These
cars are cushioned, have hoods for wet weather, lanterns at night, and are
numbered like cabs. (516) They are an American introduction and have appeared
within the last 20 years, and are far more comfortable and proceed faster than
the Hong Kong sedan chairs.      Their number in Yokohama and Yedo alone exceeds
200,000, and the men who draw them are mostly from the country, so that the
agricultural pursuits have suffered in consequence.      You can ride about five
miles for a (shilling).


     Money here is principally Mexican and American silver dollars, Japanese
silver, and copper and paper money which is very difficult to understand and
is being withdrawn for a more convenient system of coinage.        The Europeans
here, as at Hong Kong, invariably ride if they have many yards to go.        Soon
after I landed I went to the railway station, a large stone building with
every convenience for passengers and directions printed in English, French and
Japanese.   The (517) railway is 18 miles long, and is, I believe, the only one
open in Japan,    but they are now talking of making one from Yedo to the
northern part of the island.      The present one was opened about 12 years ago,
is a double line, and winds round the shores of the Gulf of Yedo all the way.
It calls at 4 towns on the journey and is greatly patronized by the Japanese,
there are no tunnels, but lots of bridges.        The station-masters and engine


                                       175
drivers are mostly Englishmen, but the clerks and all the other officials are
natives, these and the police all dress in European clothes.            The fare to
Yedo, 1st class is 3/, 2nd class 2/6 and 3rd class 1/3.         No European travels
by the latter, and are only used by natives, but many of them occupy 2nd and
even 1st.     The car r iages are constr ucted on the AIDer ican pr inc iple, the en-
trance (518) being at the ends, and not at the side as in England, and as they
are of glass, the guard can see every carriage interior as far as the engine~
and there is a platform running the whole length of the train, so that if he
is wanted in any particular carriage, he can walk outside the cars and not
through the doors of each.      The seats are all round and the centre is open for
traffic, without disturbing the rest of the passengers.        As both sexes smoke,
there are spittoons let in the floor of the carriages.        The sides as well as
the fronts     are all glass,    so that the carriage is entirely open in fine
weather, and there are venetian blinds to keep out the sun and dust.              The
trains run every half hour from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. and take an hour to accom-
plish the journey to Yedo.      You have a fine view of the gulf on one side and
the (519) surrounding country on the other~ which is another advantage you do
not have in English carriages, unless they are empty and then you only catch a
glance as you shoot past.        The country is richly cultivated and there are
houses and market gardens all the way.        Rice is the principal cultivation and
the fields are under water at present.        The men working in them are entirely
naked except for a strip of linen round the waist.


     The religion of Japan is Buddhism and Confucianism chiefly, the latter,
with Chinese letters, writing, etc., was introduced A.D. 285.         Buddhism found
its way through China and Corea, from India, about the year 552 A.D.               In
travelling in Japan the tourist will continually meet with saint            shrines,
Buddhist temples, wayside idols, images and tablets of various kinds, the out-
ward (520) evidence and superstition of the Japanese people.          In a Buddhist
Temple are drums, bells, candles, images, books and a variety of alter orna-
ments.      There are many ·off-shoots· and • schools·     etc., off the original
doctrine.    They worship Buddha and a host of minor deities, and pray to a vast
number of saints.     They believe in the transmigration of souls, have a high
moral code and are influenced in their actions by the fears and hopes of the
future.     You will often come across a shrine with candles burning in front of


                                        176
it, at the corner of a street, and each household appears to have one favorite
deity, the same as in China.      There are Buddhist temples allover the country
generally built on an eminence, surrounded by trees or else in the midst of a
garden.   There are temples in all the towns, and of course priests (521)        to
look after them, who are generally rich and are unfavourably looked on by the
government on that account.    The largest and finest of the temples at Yedo was
burnt down a few years ago by government -- completely it is thought, as it
was getting enormously rich.      Besides temple gardens, there are large tea gar-
dens on the outskirts of the city, where there are nice walks and all sorts of
amusements for the people, and scores of tea houses for refreshment.          Every
day they are thronged with holiday makers and the temples with worshippers,
and on special saint I s   days    (which occur   about   as often as   in catholic
countries)   half the population is to be found there.        I took a Jinr ickshaw
from the station to the largest existing temple, about five miles from thence,
but still in the city.     The building stood in a garden, at the bottom of an
avenue, (522) and was an enormous structure of carved wood, gilded and lac-
quered beautifully, and would be a great wonder in Europe.         In shape it was
like no other building I have seen, and seemed to be all projecting gables,
something after the style of a Swiss cottage on a large and elaborate scale.
It was about 100 feet in height and covered 3,000 sq. yards of ground.          The
wood carvings about it represented all sorts of griffins, dragons fabulous
serpents and birds' etc., carved and gilded very· beautifully.          There were
several gilded idols to be seen inside, and priests capering about as bad as
your ritualists at home.    There were steps leading up to the temple on which
the people knelt and prayed to their particular gods, and put their offerings
in a large receptacle for the purpose.        The interior could only be (523) seen
from a distance, as it is fenced round with lattice work and only opened on
special occasions.   I could see therein all sorts of pictured allegories, rep-
resenting the effects of different cr imes and their punishment, etc.           The
temple grounds are fenced in and at the entrance you may see from 500 to 600
Jinrickshaws waiting for the return of their passengers.        About three-fourths
of the people in the gardens are women and children in holiday dress.        Occas-
ionally you may see the father and mother with all their family drive up to
the entrance, looking as if they had come to enjoy themselves and meant to do
it.   Everyone looks cheerful and contented, and always ready to laugh even


                                        177
against themselves.     In front of the temple was a large carved and gilded Dove
Cote, and hundreds of the most beautiful pigeons I ever saw flying round the
roof of the temple and amongst the people as tame as chickens.            The visitors
bring all kinds of food for them, corn and rice principally, but am not able
to say whether they are held peculiar ly sacred, or are only tolerated as
pets.    The people are not at all bowed down to their religion, and if they see
a foreigner laughing at their devotions, they join in it quite heartily.              In
one place there were figures of wax and bronze images, representing all sorts
of torture and horrible punishments,           executions, monster demons, etc.      and
everybody seemed to laugh at these.          One was an enormous dr agon (someth ing
like S. George's) attacking and trampling under foot a whole Japanese armYJ
another a minotaur attacking a fleet in the baYJ one represented a tiger about
to devour a women for doing something (525) wrongJ and a still more remarkable
one of an enormous bird flying away with a queen on its back.


        The metal work and building of the creatures was beautifully done, but
the wax figures were not equal to Madame Tussauds.          There were also live mon-
keys climbing up poles, archery tents presided over by pretty young ladies,
children's toy shops (greatly patronized), and lots of Tea shops.               From the
temple I went to some large tea gardens, which were thronged with holiday
makers, and here the same arrangements were to be found.              There were penny
peep-shows,    the   pictures   of   which   were   beautiful,   representing   splendid
scenery and temples inland, the Mikado's Palace, and himself in his state
robes; the Tykoon (office now obsolete) or "Spiritual Emperor" in his palace
at Miado; Japanese armies besieging castles, and all sorts of native scenes
and personages.      The tea garden was situated on an eminence from which a great
part of the city could be seen, but not the whole, by a long way. You must re-
member that there is no smoke hanging over Yedo, the fires being all charcoal,
so that the atmosphere is very clear, there are no factories or large build-
ings in the way anywhere.       Yedo covers a larger space of ground, in proportion
to the inhabitants than any other city.         The streets are on the average wider
than those of London (excepting the larger thoroughfares) and there is not
more than one family occupying a single house.            The city covers over 70 sq
miles of ground and the population is about a million and a quarter.             Some of
the streets are as much thronged as the (527) great London streets, but as


                                         178
there is no carriage traffic, the passengers move along much quicker in such
wide throughfares.      Those of Yedo would be very suitable for tramways, and
they are talking of adopting them.


      These gardens are so pleasant and rural that you could fancy yourself in
the country, but for the busy hum to be heard all round, and the dense crowds
moving under your feet are features that indicate convincingly to the tra-
veller that he is in one of the largest cities in the world.               The houses of
the richer Japanese are in the suburbs, most of them are finely carved and
have nice gardens attached.        The girls at the tea-houses are very sedulous
in soliciting customers and very kind and attentive in their manners.             The tea
is very nice and almost colourless being newly gathered, it is drunk without
(528) milk or sugar, and in the tiniest china cups imaginable.             They bring you
a teapot to yourself, with fancy cakes, eggs and fruit, if it is in season.
If you choose they will play the guitar and sing to you, but their music is
not inspiriting and I fancy they charge extra for it.            The cost of a good tea
is about 9d, but they will get more if they can, appearing to think it an ex-
cellent joke if able to impose upon you.          I forgot to mention that there was a
large bronze god in the temple gardens, which seemed to be credited with
extraordinary      healing   powers,   as    mothers   would   bring    their   scrofulous
children, and after rubbing their affected parts stroke the corresponding part
of   th~   deity, but without any visible result.       The old gentleman's brass face
was partly smoothed down with constant rubbing, giving to the features a most
benevolent appearance.


      There are several salt water canals at Yedo, spanned by good bridges, and
the bay facing the city is crowded with fishing smacks, the fish-mongers liv-
ing in the adjacent streets, and are very numerous and you can buy almost any
kind of fish.      Enormous porpoises weighing half a ton, great turtles over 300
lbs in weight, and all sorts fo shell fish, including good oysters.              Near the
railway station was the Japanese Naval Training College, and in this neigh-
bourhood are a few European hotels, and here live those Europenas who are
allowed to reside at Yedo, their number is very small.                 I did not see them
from the time I left the Yedo Station until I returned again at night, reach-
ing Yokohama at 6 p.m. after having spent a most wonderful day.


                                            179
     There is a telegraph from Yokohama to Yedo, and a cable to Europe and
America via Shanghai and Singapore, and across the Atlantic, another via Pekin
and across Siberia to St. Petersburgh, but the Pacific has none yet.                I stayed
at the Temperance Hotel at Yokohama all night, and spent the following day
looking round that place, returning on board at night, have not been on shore
again yet, but shall do so before we leave.


     We have refitted and are now provisioning to last us to Vancouver's, have
taken in our coal, and are almost ready for sea again.               We were a week down at
Yokoska, and I was on shore several times, and visited lots of little vil-
lages.     In that vicinity there are plenty of temples, particularly one at Dai
Butsu of Buddha, in which there             (531)   is one of the largest images in the
world, except perhaps the famous Colossus of Rhodes.


     It represents the god Buddha, and is cast in bronze, it stands over 44
feet high, and will hold 60 people inside. There is also the ancient capital
of Japan, Komagawa, and in that neighbourhood have been fought some of the
most terrible battles recorded in Japanese history, to which people the town
and district is classic ground.             Not less interesting to us is the solitary
grave of Will Adams, the one Englishman whose name and memory stands out from
the obscurity of 250 years, as the representative of our nation in Japan, and
who, ,when     such   meh   as    Francis   xavier,    and    th~   numerous   Spaniards   and
Portuguese who were contemporary with him are utterly -forgotten, still has
descendants, who are proud to (532) claim him as their progenitor.                  From his
tomb you can see the beautiful island of                     • Yokosha is a good sized town
and the people very clean.           There are eight bath houses, where both sexes
bathe promiscuously: their sense of propriety being sacrificed to that of
cleanliness.     The natives could speak French: at Yokohama they spoke English,
and down at Nagasaki they speak Dutch, as well as Japanese of course.
