                                                                  Kobi, June 1st, 1875


Dear Tom
     We left Yokohama on May 12th and arrived here on the 15th, after a rather
stormy passage round.      The coast of Japan is very rough and not unlike that of
Barbary.    We had to anchor on the 14th in Osaka Bay, a pleasant anchorage off
the mainland of Niphon.        The bay contained 13 good sized villages and the
cultivation all round them was wonderful.           The fishermen in Japan tie their
nose up at night to prevent ague, fever, etc.


     We entered the "Inland Sea" of Japan at 1 p.m. on the 15th, and were at
once in smooth water.       This sea or strait is over 300 miles in length, and
separates (536) Kin Sni from Sikoki at its south eastern extremity, and Sikoki
from Niphon in the north.      It varies in breadth from a quarter of a mile to 20
miles, and contains therein some 2000 islands of all sizes,                between which
there are hundreds of different channels where small vessels can push through,
and of course plenty of good bays and harbours.                 The navigation for a ship
like ours is very intr icate, and large ships always anchor every night and
generally take a Japanese pilot.      It is only with the last 15 years that large
vessels have adopted this passage, and it took several years properly survey-
ing by the British,'French and American vessels.           It cuts off about 100 miles
of the voyage from Yokohama to Nagasaki and Shanghai, and enables the numerous
junks to run      (537)   from Nagasaki,    etc.,   to   Kobi    in comparatively     smooth
water.     Kobi is just inside the northern entrance of the inland sea and is 330
miles from Yokohama, and 400 miles north of Nagasaki.                It is situated in an
enormous gulf or bay in the main island of Niphon, called the Bay of Osaca
which is about as large as Hobson's Bay, Melbourne, and contains the ports of
Hiogo, Kobi and Osaca, besides scores of fishing villages.                Osaca stands at
the extremity of the bay, Kobi is 20 miles to the south and Hiago is close to
it, the two towns running into each other, but Kobi was substituted for the
latter as an open port, on account of its better anchorage,                  the     same as
Yokohama for Komagawa.      The two towns look something like Wellington and Cape
TOwn, as to position, being situated at the foot of an amphitheatre of hills,
but they look more like English than those places, and the population together


                                           182
is about 200,000.       Osaca contains about 300,000 and with Hiogo was one of the
Treaty Ports opened in 1859, but the anchorage is bad, and ships have to lie a
long way from the town, so in 1867, Kobi was opened as it afforded better
facilities for shipping.        There are a good many Europeans here, but it is not
such a place for trade as Yokohama.         The early ports opened by the Japanese
for foreign trade were the worst they could choose, and they did all in their
power to disgust foreigners from coming.         The pilots were encouraged to run
the ships aground,       and an extraordinary system of espionage was practised
towards them.        Officials were set to watch them wherever they went, and the
shopkeepers were not allowed to take foreign         (539) money, or pay away the
native coin.       If a foreigner purchased anything, he, and the shopkeeper went
with the goods to a government official, who priced them and received the
money,    paying     the poor   trademan again in native money,    and cheating him
frightfully, until they dreaded to see a foreign customer enter their shops.
Officials boarded ships long before they came into port ,and had to find out
why they were coming, and how long they meant to stay, etc.             If it was a
man-of-war they had to report all particulars concerning the armament, number
of men carried, and what was her object in coming.        They had to write all this
down, and another set of officials kept a check on them, and if there was the
slightest sign of anything suspicious in their reports, or behaviour, they
were handed over to the executioner.


(540)       The captain of an American man-of-war writes in his book an account
of his entry into the port of Nagasaki about 20 years ago.        Long before he was
near the place a two-sworded official was seen coming out in a small boat, and
making signals with his face to be taken on board, but the "Stars and Stripes"
sailed on and took no notice of his frantic gestures, until after the ship had
left him behind when he was seen to kill himself by falling on his own sword,
rather than survive his disgrace, which by the law of Japan, would have in-
cluded his family, as well as himself.          The Amer ican captain remar ks, "that
the most awful sign of despair he ever saw depicted on a human face, was on
that of this poor baffled man, as the ship shot- past him-.


        Soon after    the Treaty with the Americans in 1853, there was a        (541)
terrible typhoon along the Japanese coast, accompanied by an earthquake, which


                                          183
destroyed an immense amount of shipping and property, as well as lives.                       A
deputation of Japanese officials waited upon the European residents to inform
them that such sort of occurrences were very common in Japan, and that a
repetition might be shortly expected, so that if they would avoid the catas-
trophe,    they had better        leave the country as soon as possible and never
return.     The deputation was as civilly received, and was about as successful
as that of the three Quakers who went to St. Petersburgh to advocate peace,
just before the Crimean war.         Since that time a real change has corne over the
Japanese people, and they are encouraging foreign trade more and more every
year.     They are undoubtedly of an inquisitive and commercial                (542)    turn of
mind, and only want a few missionaries to make them a great people.                    There are
now a few in Japan and China, but it will be many years before Christianity
has established a footing in either country.                  I think the English language
will be taught in the schools of Japan for the future, as well as the native,
for the latter is not sufficiently copious to allow anyone to express himself
on any subject unconnected with Japan, without                  introducing a host of new
words.     It would not be possible to translate the Bible, without first arrang-
ing a grammar, and making many new words.                So it is highly probable, that our
language will eventually be spoken.


        The new Japanese silver and copper money is very pretty and similar to
our's at Hong Kong.           I   am a great believer         in the future of this        (543)
country, but until Christianity is taught, I don't think the people are pre-
pared     for    such   radical   changes   as     the   American   and   English   newspapers
presage.        These writers seem to forget that the people are influenced and con-
trolled by the priests, more than by the ruling powers.


        In 1867 just before the present Mikado ascended the throne there was a
general rising in this neighbourhood against Europeans ip general, which was
doubtless incited by the priests.           A boat's crew belonging to the French man-
-of-war "Duplex" was murdered (cut in pieces) and their bodies sent off to to
the ship.        This occurred at Osaca, a port 20 miles down the bay, but the men
were buried at Kobi.         The French Admiral demanded from the Japanese author-
ities 500 dollars for the friends of each of the men, and a certain number of
heads as satisfaction for the outrage (544).                 The heads were forthcoming in


                                             184
any quantity,       collected promiscuously from the different pr isons,          and the
money was also eventually paid.        The British Ambassador, Sir Harry Parkes, was
at Osaca at the time, and had to fly for his life, some of his mounted body
guard being wounded by the excited Japanese people.          Sir Harry has had several
narrow escapes of his life in Japan and China, but he is a very courageous
man, and not easily intimidated.


        Just before the China wars he was carried naked round Japan in an iron
cage.     He was secretary at that time to the Br itish Ambassador and was then
Mr.    Parkes.


        On May 17th, I went on shore here and looked over Kobi and Hiogo which
are something like Yedo on a smaller scale.          There are Consuls of all nations
here, lots of Europeans and Chinese, a few European hotels, a catholic and a
protestant church, and railway from Kobi to Osaca.             It is more of a country
place than Yokohama, and there are some fine walks here.                Lots of cur iosi ty
shops abound in Kobi, and the goods were quite different in design to those at
Yokohama.        The town will soon be lighted with gas.        There are not so many
Jinrickshaws here, but there is a race course for the fashionable Europeans,
and a daily paper printed.        In the vicinity of Kobi there are two beautiful
waterfalls situated in a deep gully between the highest hills.                  There are
scores of tea houses up there which command beautiful views of the waterfalls,
the bay and the city of Osaca, and several islands at the entrance of the
"Inland Sea". Every fine day these islands show out most distinctly, and the
tea     houses   are   crammed with   people   chattering,   smoking,    tea-drinking and
studying nature.       I have been up there several times and always enjoy it.          The
weather is much warmer now and the people wear brighter garments, and all use
pretty painted parasols to shelter themselves from the sun, so that a crowd of
Japanese holiday makers forms a very picturesque scene.                 The waterfalls are
each about 150 feet in sheer descent and are the prettiest of the kind I ever
saw.     There are several gardens and temples near Kobi -- all of which I have
visited.     There is a temple of the sun at the foot of the hills, crowned by an
enormous gilded globe representing the sun.            There is also a Temple of the
Moon built on the summit of a steep hill, over 2000 feet high, however it was
erected up there I can't (547) imagine, as most of the materials would have to


                                           185
be brought up from below by manual carriage, for the road is narrow and steep
and there are 250 stone steps leading up to the temple after you have almost
reached the summit.     The building itself is of carved wood, but the interior
is magnificant.     We had to take off our boots before entering, but were allow-
ed to touch and examine all the altar ornaments, which, with the altar itself
were of bronze and gilt work beautifully carved, and there were massive gilded
candlesticks weighing 400 or 500 lbs., any amount of candles and tapers burn-
ing, as well as beautiful smelling wood which scented the whole place.          A
large steel mirror stood on the altar which was supposed to represent the
moon, and any amount of food offerings in the shape of rice, fish, etc., were
placed on shelves near the altar, which affair loked something between a Royal
Throne and a large state bed and near it was the finest sounding bell I ever
heard.   It was a sort of large metal vase on another hollow metal vessel, with
a large silk cushion between the two, and it was beaten with a wooden mallet.
A journey up to this temple is considered a sort of salutary pilgrimage, and
you see lots of old women toiling up this road every day most perseveringly.


     The Japanese have large burying grounds outside the town.        Their monu-
ments are solid stone pillars standing on a flat base, and another flat stone
fixed on the top, the column bears the inscription in deeply engraved (549)
characters.   The   Chin~se   grave stones are generally shaped like a horse-shoe
and occupy more space than the Japanese.       The European cemetery contains the
graves and monument of the murdered French seamen, and also those of the crew
of an American Admiral's barque who, with himself were drowned at Osaca in
crossing the bar, about the same time as the French massacre.     There is an up-
right tablet for each of the lO seamen, and a large monument in the centre to
Admiral Lee, whose body, a few days after he was interred, was taken up again
and sent over to America in a man-of-war for interment.


     I have been on shore several times here.     One afternoon I visited a large
tea roasting shed belonging to a company of Chinese merchants.     The sheds con-
tained some 300 small coppers in rows, and I thought at first the women were
washing clothes, for they were half naked.       Each copper had a charcoal fire
burning underneath it, the inside of the copper was black leaded, and I fancy
that has something to do with colouring the leaf.     Each copper contained about


                                        186
4   lbs.    of    green   tea   leaves,   which     the    women   shook     up     with    both   hands
continually.          Chinese overlookers    superintended         the     firing    process,      after
which      it was weighed and packed for          export to San Francisco.                 Most of the
Japanese tea is consumed in America, but it is not so good as the best China
tea.       The tea shrubs are like small gooseberry bushes, and bear about three
crops of leaves a year, the leaves are like those of the sloe.                              Our ship's
band     (551)   used to land sometimes of an evening, and play in front of the
British Consul's house,          causing a   great gathering          of    natives        to   hear   the
music.


        The Japanese have a native spirituous drink called Saki,                           which tastes
like strong cider with a dash of spirit in it, and will produce intoxication.
In some of the Japanese temple grounds there was a white horse, which had a
carved      stable,    and a man to look after            it,   and seemed to be greatly ven-
erated, the people fed it with small plates of beans, which were sold by the
man who looked after it.           Every Japanese house contains a shrine and a part-
icular deity shut up in a sort of cupboard, in which offerings of fish, rice,
etc., are placed and changed daily.                 (552) The family pray in front of the
shrine whenever they feel disposed, but I think the women do the praying for
their husbands, who smoke approvingly in the background.


        On the 20th of May I went on shore with two shipmates and took the train
to Osaca, which railway has only been opened 12 months, and is still a great
source of amazement and admiration to the people hereabouts.                               It is only a
single line with sidings at each station for the trains to pass each other.
The same regulations and pr ices are              in force       as on the        Yokohama and Yedo
line,      the engine drivers are all Englishmen, and the rest of the officials
Japanese.        The carriages are English (built at Birmingham) and are not half so
comfortable as the (553) American built cars.                    The railway is 22 miles long,
winding round the shore of the bay,               and calling at 4 stations.                    The train
occupies over an hour running the journey, and passes through a beautifully
cultivated and very populous country.                 There are villages everywhere and I
should think this part of Niphon is more populated than any part of England.
Wheat and barley are almost ready for cutting and also rice, but they get two
crops of that every year.           The rice fields are under water for several weeks


                                              187
after being sown, but at present they look like an ordinary barl~y field, the
ear is exactly like that of barley only shorter and twice as thick.              When
ripe, all the corn, rice, etc., is pulled up by the roots, and threshed almost
directly.    The grinding is accomplished by water mills, on quite a different
system to ours in England.     The force of the falling water raises a large up-
right beam which falls into a small pit and crushes the rice.         This is a very
rude and primitive contrivance, and I have no doubt it will very soon be
superseded by steam crushing mills.     The country people seem to grow a suf-
ficient quantity of tea for their own consumption and dry it in the sun, the
firing process described previously is only effected on that which is intended
for export and is done, I am told, to prevent the tea from getting sea sick.
If it were not served in this manner it would lose its virtue entirely before
it reached England.


     Osaca proved to be a very large and dull sort of place.             I have been
there twice. The streets are long and rather narrow compared to those at
Yedo, some of them were five miles in length and there were lots of large
wooden br idges over the numerous creeks.       There are scarcely any Europeans
there, and the people stared at us as if we were great curiosities.


     There were scores of public bath houses conducted on the same principle
as at Yokosaka.     Few.vessels go to Osaca now as they are unable to get close
up to the town.       About 40 miles from i t is the old   n   spiri tual capital n of
Micao, which contains nearly a million inhabitants, and beyond there some 50
miles,    is another large city called Kiola.    The new railway which is being
made from Osaca to Yokohama, a distance of 320 miles, (556) is nearly finished
as far as Kioto.      The European and the native name of the Japanese towns is
frequently different.


     There was a large Japanese citadel at Osaca, a really strong fortress
surrounded by very thick high walls, encompassed by a deep wide moat,              and
flanked at each angle by a large pagoda-shaped tower.            It covered some 200
acres of ground and was guarded by Japanese soldiers armed with long swords.
I saw no sign of any cannon on the walls, and the soldiers seemed to have no
rifles.     I and my friend entered one large temple at Osaca, which was crowded


                                      188
with worshippers, but we had to come away quickly or should have disturbed
them with laughter.       About 30 yellow-robed skull-shaved priests were singing
the (557) most doleful, monotonous slow music I ever heard in my life, com-
mencing with a single voice pitched very high and ending in succession of deep
howls and groans in which the congregation joined with loud fervency.           It
takes a good deal to make me laugh in a foreign country, for I generally wear
my features screwed up into an unconcerned indifferent sort of focus, but on
this occasion had to run for it although I stood it better than my friend.


        Every   fishmonger's    shop in this country contains stewed "Devil-fish"
which are considered great delicacies in Japan and are very numerous in its
seas.      Our ing the   last   few days there have been many process ions in the
streets of Kobi, for May is a sort of festival month.          Two enormous carved
wooden cars      (558) have been dragged about the streets by hundreds of young
children of both sexes in fancy costumes of cotton, silk and paper.       At night
each child carried a red paper lamp and the cars were lit up.       The carving on
them was magnificent, and there were some splendid embroidered silk curtains
to them.        The cars are kept at the temple and are dragged by a long rope.
There were also processions of young girls in fancy silk dresses, straw hats,
flowers in their hair and painted faces, and were accompanied by a native band
of fiddles, gongs, and tom-toms, and in each street, they went through a queer
sort of posture dance, moving like marionettes.       There were other processions
of women dressed as men, and men as women, but they were of a noisier char-
acter. I don't know what these affairs all mean but the streets are crowded
with people and everybody seems highly delighted and interested, except the
Chinese community who appear to take no notice.        In walking along a street in
Japan you will see in the porch of each house all the clogs and sandals be-
longing to the inmates, as the people never enter in their shoes.         Occasion-
ally you may see a few pairs of flash English (sic) shoes among the group, and
you can conclude they belong to some British sailors taking tea up-stairs.


        On the Queen's birthday, our ship was illuminated, and the British Consul
gave a ball.       This afternoon our officers gave a luncheon and dance party and
the old Japanese governor and his native interpreter came.           They wore the



                                          189
usual (560) black dress clothes, and white chokers, sitting up on the bridge
in arm chairs the whole time, trying to look as if they enjoyed it.


        On the 25 May we left Kobi for a four day's cruise in the Inland Sea, re-
turning again on the 29th.    We did not go to Nagasaki after al17 it being too
far, but went about 120 miles through it and came back, having anchored every
night and landed parties of officers at the settlements.         According to the
Treaty, no one is supposed to land except at the treaty ports, but these
orders are not so strictly carried out now.      Everywhere we anchored boat loads
of native men and women with children came off to the ship, and seemed vastly
pleased and astonished with what they saw.         Of the scenery in the • Inland
Seas·, I can truly say that it is the finest I have ever seen.          There are
nearly 2000 islands sprinkled therein of all sizes and shapes, and the main
islands of Niphon and Sikota, which are tolerably high lands, are generally
hidden from view by the smaller ones.        The narrowest part we passed through
was about 4 miles broad, but lower down it is less than a mile.      The number of
junks and fishing vessels to be seen on the Inland Sea is something enormous,
and exceeds anything I have seen off the coasts of England or China.       The men
in them are almost naked and of a copper colour, to see them sculling their
boats along and hear them singing their wild discordant choruses, is to be
irresistibly reminded of the South Sea Islanders, and the Malay fishermen, but
there the similitude (sic) ends.


(562)        The marvellous and unrivalled cultivation to be seen in every direc-
tion around, affords abundant testimony to the superior industry and civil-
ization of the Japanese people.      Some of the islands are very lofty and at
every point rounded, the secenery seemed to change like a grand moving pan-
orama.     At one moment we seemed to be passing one of the tropical islands of
the South Pacific, and before the ship had fairly got past it, some miniature
Kerguelen's Land would start up -- a mass of sterility and desolation!      In the
morning one could imagine that he was ste.aming through Cook's Straits to
Wellington, and in the evening he would find himself at anchor in the counter
part of the Bay of Naples -- scenery more varied (563) and diverse in char-
acter it is impossible to conceive.      The number of villages passed during a
run of 50 miles is extraordinary, and the cultivation is something wonderful.


                                       190
Islands rising quite abruptly to a height of 1500 feet, were cultivated, to
the very top and the produce would support 50 such little villages as were
situated at their foot, whilst others similar in size, shape and altitude, and
scarcely a stone's throwaway -- were pictures of solitude and sterility!       We
leave Kobi tomorrow for Yokohama.      We have on board now an amphibious animal
called a ·salamander", purchased from the shore, I believe there are some in
the Crystal Palace Aquarium.      They are something between an alligator and a
sea serpent, and would astonish most people.




                                                     Yokohama, June 16th.


     We arrived here on the 6th after a very rough passage round, and received
our mail.     The other evening our ship's company were invited by the Temperance
Society of Yokohama to an entertainment of songs, recitations, etc., with the
addition of refreshments, in the shape of sponge cakes and tea, strawberries
and cream, which were provided by the ladies of Yokohama.      The other British
and Amer ican ship's companies were invited, but the affair was got up spe-
cially for the "Challenger's· crew, and our band was in attendance.


     Yesterday we went out to sea for three hours with a large party to show
them how the dredging and sounding (565) operations were carried on.         There
was a grand luncheon and dancing on the quarter deck.       Besides a large party
of ladies and gentlemen resident in Yokohama, there were among the company the
French and the Japanese admirals,       with other   naval officers,   the British
ambassador,    Sir   Harry Parkes and Lady Parkes,    and several Japanese state
officials,    including the Prime Minister of Japan.       The latter party were
dressed in European costume, with Wellington boots outside the trousers.       Sir
Harry Parkes is a fine looking man and so is the Japanese admiral.


     We have taken in seven more hands to fill up our complement, they came
from the ·Audacious· which ship came in on Saturday from Shanghai (566) and is
now in the Imperial Dock at Yokoska.

(567)                                                H.M.S. "Challenger"
                                                      North Pacific,   July 13, 1875


Dear Tom
        We are within 900 miles of Honolulu,           so must commence my letter as
usual.     At 3 p.m. on the 16th of June we left Yokohama for England with the
homeward bound pennant flying and the band playing "Home, Sweet Home" as we
steamed past the other ships.         I can't say that I felt particularly "homeward
boundish" or cheerful, thinking how altered everything seemed since we sighted
Japan on the 11th of April previous, and were so eager to get our letters,
from which I first heard of my paternal loss at home, casting a gloom over
everything now.


        Fusihama stood out above the clouds long after the coasts of Japan had
disappeared, and when that had also faded away, I suppose I had seen the last
of that interesting country with its queer people and quaint customs.                  Miss
Midgi Maru said as I paid her the night before we left for my 55th cup of tea
that nShe very much sorry when Challenger go."              Miss Maru and her marr ied
sister kept a tea house on the highest hill near Yokohama, which commanded a
splendid view of the town and bay.               Miss Maru could speak very tolerable
English and was on that account a martyr to every nintelligent traveller" like
myself.     I calculate that I asked her several thousand questions as to stat-
istics and customs etc. of Japan, and think I pumped her pretty dry, and was
able to tell her more about the productions, position and population etc. of
the cities of Japan than she herself knew.              The Japanese are very ignorant
about everything of this sort, and scarcely know the size and extent of their
own country.        Miss Maru was quite in a fog about everything 10 miles from
Yokohama, and concerning the history of Japan could only relate her own ex-
perience and her papa's.         If I asked about her religious views, she would only
laugh and point to a large neighbour ing Buddhist Temple, and to the English
Church and say, "That is my church and this is yours", after which she would
change the subject to the price of ladies clothing in England.              Of course, I
was particularly well up on that subject.               I think I told her a complete
costume     (570)   for   a   respectable English    lady would cost something     under



                                           192
£2,000 including a set of teeth and some back hair.          Miss Maru was very pretty
and genteel, her manner of bowing and receiving payment for refreshments, I
have never seen equalled.         I have her portrait, and find about 50 others in
the ship have it also.     Her ideas of the position of the Sandwich-Islands, and
of most countries were very vague, and could only jerk my hand out to sea and
say, "It's a month's journey out there."        On the day before we left Yokohama,
the   American   ship   nKearsage"   arrived,   she was     the vessel   that   sunk   the
"Alabama" off the coast of France.         One of our men deserted just before we
sailed and one died the day after we left from the effects of poison taken by
himself, whilst in a state of intoxication.         (571)    He was a Scotchman named
James Macdonald, was sick berth steward, and had been many years in the Navy,
and joined the "Challenger" at Sheerness.         He was an intemperate man when he
could obtain liquor,      and was the man who was robbed whilst drunk at St.
Thomas, West Indies, and wished to be brought off (sic) in a newspaper and an-
alyzed to see what kind of drink they had sold him.            When at sea he was all
right, and a very steady, saving and industrious man, he earned over 30 pounds
by a sewing machine which he bought at Melbourne and used to work in his spare
time.     In harbour he would squander away an incredible amount of money, and
was never quite sober, but at sea he was more careful over a penny than the
generality of Scotchmen, and to hear (572) him holding forth to the sick sea-
men about the evils and lamentable effects of intemperance and immorality, you
would have thought him a paragon of excellence and self-control.            He was also
a dabbler in scientific pursuits, and of an inquiring disposition, and was a
great admirer of the poet Burns.         I could not help thinking as they lowered
his body into the sea, of the epitaph that Burns wrote for himself and how
applicable it was to the deceased -


        "Is there a man whose judgment clear
        Can others teach the course to steer,
        Yet runs himself life's mad career,
             Wild as the wave
        Here pause - and through the starting tear
             Survey this gravel

     The poor inhabitant below,
    Was quick to learn, and wise to know,
     And keenly felt the friendly glow,
           And softer flame:
     But thoughtless follies laid him low,
           And stain'd his name!


He was buried on the 18th and directly after the funeral we took soundings at
the enormous depth of 3,900 faths. 4 1/2 miles, the second deepest sounding we
have ever obtained.     We have come nearly 3,500 miles since leaving Japan, as
we have not steered direct for the Sandwich Islands, but nearly due east, and
tomorrow the course will be altered to south as we are already in the longi-
tude of the Islands, so shall soon be in hot weather.    We have 980 miles more
to run and are at present under steam, with calm pleasant weather.      We have
taken a fine line of soundings, having sounded about every 200 miles.      From
Japan the depths have been 17th June 1875 faths, - 18th 2,900 faths - 19th
3675 faths - 21st 2900 faths - 23rd 2300 faths - 24th 2575 faths - 26th 2800
faths - 28th 2900 faths - 30th 2775 faths - July 2nd 2050 faths - 3rd 2550
faths - 5th 2950 faths - 7th 3000 faths - 9th 3050 faths - 10th 3000 faths -
12th 2675 faths.      The dredging and trawling have been very unlucky, for the
bottom of this part of the Pacific is very rough being of volcanic formation.
Several trawls and some 10,000 fathoms of line have been carr ied away, the
value of which is nearly £ 500.


     A few good specimens have been obtained, and lots of great boulders of
pumice stone which contained the fossil remains of animal life.    Serial (sic)
temperatures have also been taken, and the strength of the current (when any)
has been ascertained.    We have had good winds, but damp, wet, unpleasant wea-
ther: this we shall leave behind shortly and pick up the dry north east trade
winds.    Our lat. today is 380 N. long. 1580 W.    We are rather ahead of our
time for reaching Honolulu, and the Captain says he will drive the ship home,
by the first week in May 76.       We have only seen one vessel on the journey
across~   the American mail boat "Mohawk" from San Francisco for Yokohama on the
1st of July.    We are now on the Pacific Admiral's station, which extends to
the 180 0 of long. and includes the coast of America from Alaska to Cape Horn.


                                      194
      (576)   Last week with us contained 8 days, and we had two Sundays as the
Admiralty allow us no pay for the extra day, one of the Sundays (your Sunday)
was kept as a holiday.   Of course, we are now twelve hours behind England, but
that we shall gain again on the homeward voyage through Magellan's Straits.      I
see   by the papers that the Americans have managed to obtain one of           the
Sandwich Islands as a naval station for their Fleet, and persuaded the King to
refuse this privilege to any other power.        This is another smart piece of
Yankee diplomacy and I expect before long they will succeed in annexing those
islands.


      July 24th - We expect to reach Honolulu on Tuesday the 27th as we are
only 300 miles away.     We have picked uup the N.E. Trades, and the weather is
much warmer (577) but pleasant.    The depth since the 15th has been about the
same, but we have lost another 1500 fms. of line in dredging.    We shall prob-
ably sight land on Monday night, for most of the islands are lofty, being of
volcanic origin.    The Pacific Islands generally lie in groups and clusters.
The Sandwich group numbers 13, 8 of which are inhabited.      Their   (sic)   total
area is about 6000 sq. miles and the population 60,000.      The group was dis-
covered by Captain Cook in 1778 and named after Lord Sandwich, 1st Lord of the
Admiralty.    Cook estimated the population at 400,000, so that in all prob-
ability these people will have entirely disappeared before the lapse of an-
other century; and like the aboriginals of Tasmania, who also numbered several
thousands when Cook visited there.    The Kanakas as they are called, were des-
cribed by Cook in his journal as the finest, the most civilized, and the best
disposed of all the South Sea Islanders.    I believe Captain Cook treated them
fairly and was a good, humane man, but the conduct of several of his officers
and crew was cruel and disgraceful, and in a squabble at Owhyee in 1779 caused
by the impolicy of some of his crew, Captain Cook fell a victim to the sudden
resentment of the natives.    Owyhee, or Hawaii, is some 200 miles S.E. of Oahu
and the other islands, and was not discovered until 1779 when Cook returned
from the Arctic to the Sandwich Islands again.


      It is the largest island, its. area being over 4,000 sq. miles, and the
population (579) 27,000, and it contains the stupendous volcanoes of Mauna Loa



                                      195
and Mauna Rea, each over 13,000 feet high, and still active.         The Kanakas be-
long to the same family as the Maories and Tongans, but are unmixed with the
black Papuan race.   The present king is Kalakua, elected in 1874.       The islands
are just in the tropics, and very fertile, growing sugar, coffee, cotton,
rice, arrowroot, cocoas, breadfruits, and various West Indian fruits.            The
islands are well situated and the seat of considerable commerce, with America
chiefly.


     Honolulu, Oahu, is the capital, which we reached on July 27th.        We sight-
ed land at 3 a.m. in the morning and at 5 a.m. the islands of Molokai and Oahu
were in sight.   We dredged between the two all the morning, but got nothing,
so proceeded (580) onward under all sail and steam.         The islands were lofty
and very irregularly shaped, and looked about as large as Fayal, Azores.        At 2
p.m. we passed Diamond Head at the south eastern extremity of Oahu, and at 3
p.m. anchored outside the reefs in front of Honolulu and made signal for a
pilot to take us over the bar.    A native pilot soon came out and took the ship
through the narrow shallow channel between the reefs and we anchored again by
4 p.m. within a stone's throw of the town, when the mail was at once sent on
board, and another is expected tonight from San Francisco for Sydney.           There
are a few whaling vessels lying here and the American flag ship "Pensacola."
The usual contractors, washermen etc. came on board at once.         Fresh meat, veg-
etables, and bread are very (581) cheap considering - only 2 1/2 each per lb.


     Provisions in general are cheap.       Butter made on the island is only 1/3
per pound, and this is a great rarity in the tropics.         The meat is quite as
good as in Australia, but fruit is not so cheap as it ought to be, and washing
is 5/ per doz.   About half the population of Honolulu came down to the wharf
to see the ship moored, and after seating themselves as comfortably as pos-
sible, gave a half holiday, apparently, and took a good long view of us for
about 2 hours - then went home to supper.       From my short experience I should
say that the Kanakas are about the most cheerful, good tempered, indolent and
impulsive people under the sun.     One old gentleman came on board and intro-
duced himself to me (582) as Mr. John Williams, shook hands and said he had
had the pleasure of seeing me in Calcutta.          I   told him I    had never been



                                      196
there, so he shook hands again, and said it must have been my brother, and
told me to come on shore and see him at any time.            The Kanakas in appearance
are the very counterpart of the Maories of New Zealand, and much darker than
the friendly islanders - being as brown as Malays.            Still, they have pleas-
anter features than the Maories, and look very different to the Fijians, and
Admiralty Islanders.       They are a fine made people and wear European dress.        I
have not seen any ladies yet except at a distance.           Of course the Kanakas are
Christians converted by American missionaries chiefly, and they are undoubt-
edly the most civilized of the         (583) Pacific races, but unfortunately it is
this civilizing process that is killing them so fast.           They are a very sensi-
tive people and one of our seamen, who has been here before, assures me that
they can lie down and die whenever they feel disposed, so unless they inter-
marry    "say   the Chinese"    or   unless    they introduce the Mormons     into their
country they will soon belong only to the past.             I saw that the measles had
carr ied away about one        third of the Fij ians since we were there, so the
English and Chinese will soon have it all to themselves in that group.             There
are lots of Chinese at these islands, and a very hard-working race of people
they are, too.       The island of Oahu has a very pleasant rural appearance, but
the scenery is certainly not tropical, as seen from the ship (584) and if it
were not for a few cocoa palms dotted here and there, one could fancy the
island to be one of the Azores.         It is not to be compared to Tongatbu or the
Fij i   islands,    and the   town of Honolulu has      a   very straggling   unimposing
appear ance.       The weather is much hotter here, thermometer 85 0 in the shade,
and over 1200 in the sun, and the ship is already full of flies, whilst the
ravenous, but playful mosquitos are only waiting for us to turn in before com-
mencing their onslaught.        I shall tell you more about Honolulu after I have
been on shore.       Themail for Sydney is in sight, but will not be in before 11
p.m. so shall not get our letters until tomorrow morning.


        July 28th - The mail has just arrived and have received our news, shall
have to wait (585) for another until the 1st of November, the day we are due
in Valparaiso.        This one left England July 1st and as they only leave San
Francisco once a month, shall get no more while we are here.           We are now tak-
ing in 240 tons of coal and as soon as it is in, leave will be given to each
watch for 48 hours.


                                              197
        The American Admiral was on board here today, quite a rough looking
chap. The men's wages were paid today in American dollars - value 4/2 ster-
ling.     H.M.S. ·Petre1· arrived today from Panama.    I see by the Illustrated
papers that the Arctic Expedition has gone: and also saw a portrait of Captain
Nares which was very good, indeed.     I hope they will be successful, I should
much like to have gone.       Last night we heard of the death of Lady John
Franklin, per telegram received at San Francisco on the 19th of July, and
their papers of the same date announced it, and as the death only occurred in
London on the evening of the 18th, it was very quick work.      Honolulu is 2200
miles from San Francisco.


        August 4th - There were some pictures in the Illustrated London News of
the Admiralty Islands, and New Guinea, which were sent by our artist, and very
good.     They appeared in the middle of June.   I have been on shore here twice
and went horse-riding both times.     Honolulu is quite a civilized place, more
like England than any town we have been to since leaving Wellington.       There
are some fine shops of all kinds, and a very considerable white population,
principally American settlers (587) and merchants.      Consuls of all nations,
missionaries of all sorts, and invalids from America.    There are several chur-
ches, native, American, Wesleyan, Methodist, Roman Catholic.       The native is
the largest, and is just like an English Dissenting Church: is nicely seated
and contains a good organ.     The King's seat was under a crimson velvet canopy
and in the centre .stood a large spitoon, containing several ends of cigars:
other pews contained the same, so I suppose the Hawailans smoke during ser-
vice.     It was a week-day when I looked in, so of course, I can't say that is
the case, but they certainly smoke there some time or other.      There are only
four hotels allowed in Honolulu, and they have to pay a very heavy tax to the
King, which makes the drink very dear and promotes temperance.    There are lots
of Chinese shopkeepers, and they have native wives and generally very pretty
children.     They work hard, and on that account are looked down on by the nat-
ives.     Of course, the natives do work, but in a desultory sort of manner, and
they want very high wages.    About 40 of them helped to coal our ship, under an
American overseer.    Their pay was 5/ per day and the overseer offered them an-
other 4/ to work until 10 p.m. one evening, they laughed at him but refused



                                      198
the job, and told the Yankee to do it himself.             The natives can nearly all
read and write the Hawaiian language, and most of them speak English.                   Their
books etc., are printed in the native tongue, (589) and they only talk English
to foreigners.      They live in nicely furnished houses, and are altogether quite
as comfortable as the working classes in Europe.          Their living costs them very
little, and they work when they like, and on a Sunday they dress in the latest
fashions, and strictly observe the Sabbath.           They are straightforward and re-
ligious, without being at all gloomy or strait-laced.              The town is laid out
exactly like an English one, with good horse-roads for there is a large car-
riage traffic.      On week days the men wear shirt and trousers and go bare-
footed.    The women wear a         long coloured loose night gown reaching to the
knees, no shoes or stockings, and their long black hair hanging either in two
long plaits, or loose down the back, in it they wear natural flowers, and also
in their little straw hats.         This is their weekday rig1 on Sundays they dress
rather more expensively than an English lady bound to a flower show, are very
fond of high laced up French boots.          The real native women are not so handsome
as the Tongans, but the half-castes are generally very pretty, and many are
married to Europeans.


     There is an upper, a middle, and a lower class even amongst the Kanakas.
The principal amusements are swimming and horse riding1 all the natives can
ride and swim.      One may see mothers bathing and throwing their children into
the sea to teach them to swim before they can walk.              I believe there are more
horses on the small island of Oahu than in the county of Yorkshire.                     ( 591)
They breed so fast that every native who likes can have one, and, of course,
every white person keeps a horse and carriage, and they are to be found graz-
ing allover the island.       The women ride astride the animal, the same as men,
and to see them on a Saturday afternoon in their long white muslin dresses,
galloping along the streets by scores, with their long hair streaming behind,
and a baby sitting in front, is to see a very pretty sight.                Saturday after-
noon is a general holiday with them and they dress up, trim their hair and
their horses with flowers before starting out.            They generally use the clumsy
Mexican   saddle,    which   with    the   bridle   costs more    than   the   horse,   which




                                            199
animal you may buy for a pound, but unable to hire one for a short time under
2/6.    (592) The last horse I rode was a donkey at St. Michael,_ Azores, but
have had two long rides here and am going again tomorrow.    Honolulu has been
thronged this week with sailors on horseback and am sure it's a great mercy no
one has been killed.    I must not forget to remark on the number of cats, dogs
and pigs there are on the island, especially the former, which you may see in
all the houses, on all the roofs and walls, and in every garden, and even fol-
lowing people about the streets.   Pigs are to be met with everywhere.   I saw a
party of natives cooking one, of which they invited me to partake, but not
being hungry preferred to decline, as they cooked him whole, just as he was
killed in a pit full of red hot stones, and when he was sufficiently roasted
they poured buckets of cold water over him.   Cocoanuts are rather scarce here
but bananas, melons, guavas, oranges, native apples and mangoes are plentiful,
but come from the large island of Hawaii.


       The natives are very fond of elaborate funerals.   I met one on Saturday
afternoon with hearse and plumes in grand style, and the natives all in the
deepest mourning, but chattering loudly and affable as they marched along.
The cemeteries are very pretty and the natives are very fond of gravestones.
The finest building on the island is the King's palace, built in 1872 by
Kamehameha the 5th.    It is something like a gentleman's hall in England, with
a square tower in the centre.      The state officials here, officers etc. are
mostly Americans, there is a native cavalry regiment, one of infantry and a
military band.    The population of Honolulu is 70,000, abOut one-third of whom
are foreigners.   You can't hire a horse, buy a glass of ale, or do any sort of
bartering with the natives on Sunday, it is the Sabbath with men and beast,
and they considered ita great sin, sometime ago when an English, a French,
and an Amer ican Man of War all sailed from the island on a Sunday morning.
They don't mind a ship coming in, but detest to see one sail.      Our men who
were on shore last Sunday could buy nothing or get any dr ink anywhere, and
they say they walked about the town all day with their pockets full of money
like a lot of codgers.     For such a large town I   (595) never saw quieter or
more orderly streets,    the shops are nearly all shut after 7 p.m.      and the
streets are as quiet as on Sunday evenings in England, and there is evening
service in nearly all the churches.


                                      200
        Most of the houses are built of wood, nicely painted, with pleasant gar-
dens surrounding them.        Water is very plentiful on the island, but still it is
not fertile for the soil is all lava cinders, and everything has to be culti-
vated.      I consider     these natives far          super ior to those of the Philippine
Islands in civilization, and social improvement etc. although they were can-
nibals but a short time since.           The first missionaries landed here in 1820, in
the brig "Thaddeus" from Boston, U.S.                 The white ladies here, of course, ride
horses as they do in Barrowden, but where everybody                      (596)   sits astride,    a
side-saddle looks ridiculous.            Lots of the native women are over 6 ft. high.
As compared with a          similar     sized town      in China or Japan,        there   seems a
scarcity of children in Honolulu and the girls seem twice as numerous as the
boys.     Of course, there are newspapers printed here, and even a monthly maga-
zine, but they are after the American style, and the tone is not equal to our
own local papers.          Yesterday we had a lot of the native ministers etc. on
board, and today we have had King Kalakua himself with his son, and several
officers, etc.         Kalakua is a stout man about 40, almost black as a negro, and
in figure like a small edition of Sir Roger.                  He was dressed in an old dark
suit of clothes and a straw hat, but his son, and his officers (597) were ela-
borately dressed.         All our officers were in full uniform, the yards were man-
ned and the band played the "Sandwich" anthem, and he was received with as
much honor as we show Queen Victor ia.                   He stayed to luncheon and had his
portrait taken afterwards.


        I should like very well to live in Honolulu, and should keep a horse with
a litter of cats, dogs and pigs,                the same as other Christians here.               The
founder of the Hawaiian Kingdom was Kamehameha the 1st who conquered and ruled
the islands for 20 years.             He was born 25 years before Cook discovered the
islands, and was a very remarkable man.                  His memory is still regarded by his
countrymen and he is often called the Napoleon of the Pacific Islands.                     Before
his time they were broken up into petty kingdoms like the Fij i Islands.                          He
was succeeded by four other Kamehamekas in succession, then Lomailo, who died
last     year,   and    should   have    been    succeeded    by   his    Queen   Emma,   but    the
Americans, after a serious riot had occurred among the natives, succeeded in
getting Kalakua elected to the throne.                  King Kamehameha II with his favorite




                                                201
wife visited England in 1820, in a British merchant ship, and were very kindly
received by King George IV.         He and his Queen both died while - there of the
measles, within 8 days of each other, and their bodies were brought back to
Honolulu     by   Captain   Lord    Byron,      in   H.M.S.   "Blonde"    and   buried   here.
Kamehameha    IV also visited England and France               in 1849 when he was heir
apparent.     We expect to leave here on the 10th for Hawaii, Tahiti, Marquesas
Islands before reaching Valparaiso.          We received today from H.M.S. "Petrel" an
animal called      a   "terrapin"   or   land    tortoise,    brought    from   the Galapagos
Islands.     They have several which are to be sent to the Zoological Gardens
London.     Ours is dead, and weighs nearly 300 lbs, but they have been known to
be 1200 lbs in weight.        They are not amphibious and are found only in that
group of islands, and will soon become extinct, as the whale ships kill them
for food.


     August lOth - We sail in the morning for Hilo, 200 miles distant.                      On
Sunday I went to the English Church, a very poor one for a bishop's, and the
service was burlesqued by that mixture of mom millinery and tom foolery called
nRitualism. n      In the even to the American Free Church, which was quite a
healthy change in an opposite direction from the "posture" and "imposture"
practiced (600) at the Cathedral.


     The American Illustrated Papers I have seen here are full of copies from
the "Graphic" and n'London News, n and the local papers contain the novels of
the best English authors, printed in chapters and without the author's per-
mission.     I mentioned this to an American and he said, "Of course, they do the
same in England with ours, or they can do if they like.
