                                                                 Hilo, Hawaii      August 19/75
Dear Tom,
        We left Honolulu on the 11th Aug for this island distant 200 miles, and
arrived on the 14th having to steam against a head wind.                             Before leaving we
received from H.M.S. npetrel" two of the Galapagos turtle, which I told you of
in my last letter, one weighs nearly 300 Ibs,                          and the other, a small one,
about 50 Ibs.        The larger can walk away with a man on its back.                      They are very
ugly creatures,          the    head   is   like a         serpent,   the   hind   feet   similar    to an
elephant's, and forefeet like the flippers of a seal.                           They have five toes on
(602)    each   foot ~    live entirely on green stuff,                 but do not masticate their
food, swallowing it whole like a large python would a monkey.                             If possible we
shall bring them home alive, the men polish their shells with bees wax and
oil,    when cleaning          their guns        in   the morning.      We sounded on our           passage
across about 12 miles from the island of Maui at the depth of 2,075 faths.
Maui was a lofty island but inferior in altitude to this of Hawaii, which is
the highest in the Pacific.




        On the night of the 12th, the blazing volcano of Mauna Loa was visible,
hut we were 90 miles away and were steaming parallel with the island of Hawaii
all day on the 13th, for the town is on its eastern side, and the prettiest of
all     its ports.       The     island     is    about 75 miles        (603)    in length,   and 55     in
breadth, and seen from the sea has a beautifully verdant appearance owing to
the large amount of rain it receives through the attraction of its high moun-
tains.     In the manner that it sloped upwards from the sea, it reminded me very
much of Madeira, but the great rents, fissures and upheavals everywhere in the
soil were more indicative of a volcanic origin.                       On the morning of the 14th we
anchored in the Bay of Hilo,                 about a mile from the town and close to the
American flag ship npensacola."                   The natives who came out to us with a pilot,
were wear ing H.M.S.            Repulse's hat ribbons round their straw hats, and they
told us that the "Repulse" had gone round to Kalikahua Bay on the other side
of the     island,    and the place              (604)    where Captain Cook was murdered.             They
abused the Americans frightfully, said they never had any money to spend, and
that the "Repulse's" men were rolling in dollars,                           that Admiral Cochrane had


                                                         203
behaved like a father to them, had thrown his ship open, and found boats to
bring them off, and refreshments when they were on board.               The "Repulse" is
homeward bound, so I suppose the Admiral wished to leave behind a favorable
impression.        He    is the grandson of the    famous but   ill-used Admiral Earl
Dundonald.


       The Americans here, through their great political influence, succeeded in
getting King Kalakua elected to the throne, against the wishes of the majority
of the natives, which caused terrible riots at Honolulu at the time.                They
have settled down          (605)   now to their new King, but after his return from
America he tried to pass a law for the cession of Pearl River, Oahu, to the
U. States for a naval depot, which they fiercely refused to part with, or a
foot of their soil, and the discontent and distrust of foreigners in general,
gave   rise   to    their    new rallying cry           "Hawaii   for    the Hawaiians."
"America gave us the light" said a native pastor in a sermon at the time, "But
now that we have the light, we should be left to use it for ourselves."            There
is no doubt that the Americans have had all the work of civilizing and edu-
cating these people, and have done it well, but this does not establish their
right to the island, if the natives would prefer "British protection."               The
ancient chiefs          (606) are all dead, and foreigners here seem to think there
will be no more kings after Kalakua' s death, but the remnant of the people
will then decide what form of government they would prefer.               When that time
comes there will probably be rows about the matter •. Since the last election,
the Americans here do not feel quite safe unless one of their ships of war is
cruising round the island.


       The town of Hilo is much prettier than Honolulu, the houses are generally
white, and surrounded by trees and gardens.            There are about 3,000 inhab-
itants,   including a couple of hundred white people, and plenty of Chinese.
There are Americans, English and Roman Catholic missionaries and churches.


       The Chinese work chiefly on the sugar (607) plantations, which are very
numerous on this island: at the back of the town are some sugar mills where




                                            204
     the cane is crushed.   Sugar growing and cattle and sheep farming are the prin-
     cipal pursuits here, but the planters are losing because the native laws do
     not permit them to make rum, which article is the most profitable item in a
     sugar planter's income, but there will be plenty made here by and bye.       This
     island is as large as Mauritius, and that produces half the sugar and rum con-
     sumed in Europe.    The cattle farms are on the slopes of the mountains, where
     grass is plentiful and the climate temperate.     Some of the farmers have 20,000
     sheep and thousands of cattle, the main profit of them being the wool, tallow
     and hides, for meat is so abundant and cheap, (608) that it hardly pays for
     bringing in from the station.    We paid 2d per lb for beautiful beef, and the
     regular inhabitants pay even less.    Fruit is plentiful, especially pineapples
     and mangoes, a delicious Indian fruit.      We had one good view of the mountains
     the day we arrived, they are 25 miles apart, the extinct volcano Mauna Kea,
     was covered with a small patch of snow, but the active one of Mauna Loa was
     free from snow.    They are each over 13,000 feet above the sea level, and slope
     upwards so gradually that a mule can climb to their summits.        They are not
     conical shaped like Teneriffe or Fusihama, but merely rise from a chain of
     mountains which is 10,000 feet high for      (609) several miles near the culmin-
     ating point.    There is an active crater near the summit of Mauna Loa, and an
     immense burning lake of fire in its side, about two-thirds of the distance
     from the base.     This wonderful lake of fire is what all travellers coming
     hither try to go to see.     Nearly all our officers have been, but as it is a
     two days journey, and you require horses and native guides, none of the ship's
     company have been able to go, and I was much disappointed, but to compensate
     for this, last Sunday night, the upper crater of Mauna Loa burst out bril-
     liantly, burning more than it has done for the last six years, and we had a
     splendid view of the strange subterranean fire.       We have not seen it since,
     and the (610) people say that you may be here for months without seeing it
     burning.    It is the upper crater the inhabitants fear most for when it bursts
     out the burning lava rushes down the sides of the mountain toward Hilo.     There
     have been about six eruptions during the present century, the last and worst
     being in 1868.      A good many of the      foreign settlers then left Hilo for
     Honolulu thinking their town was about to be buried like the "Cities of the
     Plain."    Those who could not leave sent men out on horseback towards the moun-
     tain to see what course the stream of fire was taking.         It came direct for
.!



                                           205
Hilo burning and destroying everything in its course, but about 10 miles from
the town, it entered the earth, and flowed underground until it reached the
end of the town, when it burst out of the ground, and ran into the sea, form-
ing a long narrow peninsula nearly a mile in length, which is now covered with
cocoa palms and beautiful vegetation.


        Horses are as plentiful here as at Honolulu, and every native seems to
possess one.     I was on shore yesterday afternoon with two ship-mates, and we
went horse-r iding, but there are no good roads here like those at Honolulu,
the whole surface of the island is lava rock and cinders, overlaid with a thin
soil, which is very productive on account of the abundance of rain.             Water is
very plentiful and there are scores of creeks and rivers in which groups of
natives may be seen bathing all day long.          We bathed and rode, ate fruit and
sugar cane, and joked with the natives.         They are about the (612) most hospit-
able race we have seen, and so cheerful and pleasant.            The young ladies decor-
ated our horses and us with flowers, and brought us fruit to eat, while they
had a gallop themselves.        We saw lots of children surf-bathing or riding into
the beach on the top of the great rolling waves, which break all along the
shores of the island1 they balance themselves on these waves, and shoot into
the beach at the rate of 40 miles an hour or more. We are just steaming away
from Hi10, and shall soon have seen the last of the Hawaiians,                 and their
pleasant     land.   We   are    bound   for    Tahiti,   distant   2,200   miles   south.


                                                September 15th
                                                South Pacific, Lat 10 S0




        We are some days behind time again (613) and are still 300 miles from
Tahiti, owing to the light wind, and the numerous soundings we have had to
take.      We have sounded about every other day and the aver age depth               from
Honolulu has been about 2,700 fathoms, the dredging and trawling have also
been successful.     We had the usual unpleasant and hot weather in the rainy
latitudes near the equator, but caught the S.E. trade winds 300 miles north of
the line, and have them now, though very light. The equator was crossed at
midnight on the 5th in Long. 1510 w. We have had another sad death on board
since leaving Hilo, and this time it was one of the scientific staff, a fine


                                          206
healthy looking man, too.      Dr. Von Suhm joined the ship at Sheerness as a
naturalist, under Professor Thompson and (614) was very clever in his profes-
sion, quite an enthusiast in hunting up rare specimens of natural history at
the different countries we have visited.    About a week ago he was laid up with
a severe cold which produced Erysipelas in the head and caused delirium.       On
Sunday he was so bad that we could not have church and the bells could not be
struck1 was worse on Monday, and in his wanderings he gabbled away in German,
which Mr. Buchanan, the chemist, could understand and answer.        He talked of
the battles he had helped to gain during the late war, in which he served as a
common soldier, and was wounded.      On Monday evening he got out of bed, and
said he must pay a visit to his father and mother, and he died at 3 p.m. the
next day.    He was buried yesterday morning at 9 a.m. (615) the ship's company
being dressed in white, and the officers and scientific gents in full uni-
form.     We sounded in the afternoon at 2,650 fathoms.      Professor Thompson
helped to carry him to the gangway, and was very much cut up about it as were
all the scientific staff.    On the day before he died the anchor was got ready
for anchor ing at a small group of islands called the Carolines, so that he
might be kept more quiet, but we passed over the exact spot - according to the
chart - where they should have been, without seeing any sign of them, so we
proceeded onwards for Tahiti.     Several groups of islands in the Pacific are
positioned incorrectlY1 we found the Admiralty Islands a long way out.


        Dr. Van Suhm had a brother at Manilla who used to be constantly with him
during our two visits there.     He was a native of German Holstein and about 26
years of age.     All his books and effects will be sent home from Valparaiso to
his father, but letters will be forwarded to his friends from Tahiti.


                                               Sunday, October 3rd
                                               At Tahiti


        On the 16th of September we brought up from a depth of 2,350 fathoms the
head of a harpoon, and sever al whale's teeth 1 so we must have dropped our
dredge on the skeleton of some hundred whales.          On the 17th evening we
witnessed the most beautiful sunset I ever remember seeing in my life, and at



                                      207
4 a.m. the next morning we sighted Tahiti and Moorea, another of the Society
Islands at the distance of about 60 miles.      (617)   Both islands were lofty,
the highest peak of Tahiti called the Diadem, being over 8,000 feet above the
sea level.    The elevated portion of both these islands is very irregular - a
mass of pinnacles, ridges and gullies,       thrown up by volcanic agency in a
wonderfully cur ious and str iking manner.    We sounded between the islands at
1,525 fms. then steamed in towards Tahiti, and anchored within 200 yards of
papeete, the capital of the island.


     Tahiti or Otahiti was discovered in 1767 by Captain Wallis R.N. and in
1769, Captain Cook came to observe the Transit of Venus.      He visited it four
times, and discoverd the surrounding 7 islands, which he called the "Society
Islands" after the Royal Society, which was the instigation of his coming hit-
her, as it is of the voyage of the "Challenger."        The appearance of Captain
Wallis at this island in 1767 did not create among the natives so much sur-
prise as you would imagine, for it was but the realization of a prophecy of
one of their sages.    This personage had foretold "that at some distant period,
a canoe without outriggers would come to their shores."       I think I told you
that a Polynesian canoe was balanced in the water by a framework           like a
hurdle~    so of course a vessel without this appendage was a great curiosity,
and when it did appear in the shape of H.M.S. "Dolphin," the Tahiti islanders
soon made friends and traded with its crew.      They and the natives of the ad-
joining islands, have. always had the name of being the handsomest of the (619)
Pacific races,     they are also the laziest, the most cheerful, and the most
immoral.     They are lazy because there is nothing to induce them to        work~

their island produces spontaneously everything they require for sustenance,
and is naturally the most fertile island in the Pacific or elsewhere.           The
Tahitians are wonderfully like the Hawaiians,       but are whiter,    taller   and
better featured.     They are just as kind in disposition, of a similar temper-
ament and speak nearly the same language, but are even lazier, fonder of gay
clothes and music, not so well educated, and far more immoral.        Their island
is frequently called the "Gem of the Pacific," which it undoubtedly is, and is
also termed the "Corinth of the South Seas" on account of the universal immor-
ality (620) and the inherent lightness and gaiety of its people.




                                      208
      This island and people have caused more desertions and punishments in the
British Navy than all the rest of the Pacific Islands together.         Captain Cook
lost several men here for some weeks, and the natives stowed them away, until
he recovered them by stratagem.    It was this island, and the pleasant memories
it excited among the harassed and oppressed crew of the WBounty,W that caused
that ship's company to mutiny in 1789 near Tongatbu, set their wretch of a
captain with 19 of his officers and men adrift in an open boat, 3600 miles
from any European settlement, and return with their vessel to Tahiti again.
Here many of them settled down and married native women, while the remainder,
nine in (621) number, taking with them some Tahitian men and women, sailed
away to the southeast and found a home on Pitcairn Island, 1,000 miles away,
where they remained undiscovered for 20 years.         Meantime their Captain Bligh
had after suffering incredible hardships, succeeded in reaching the Dutch is-
land of Timor, by way of Torres Straits, from whence he proceeded to England
and gave his own version of the mutiny.


      The "Pandora w frigate was sent in search of the mutineers, and discovered
the portion who had remained at Tahiti.   They were torn from their wives and
children, and put in irons on board the wPandora w for passage to England. The
frigate was totally wrecked on the great coral reef near Cape York, but the
whole of her crew reached Batavia in the ship's boats, and eventually arrived
in England.    The mutineers were tried, and and several of them hanged.             The
Pitcairn mutineers   included   the    ringleader    Lieutenant Fletcher      Christian:
they destroyed the "BountyW and after getting settled on their fertile and al-
most inaccessible little island, lived comfortably and peaceably together for
about 3 years, after which a great quarrel took place about the women.              Five
of the mutineers, including Lieutenant Christian, were killed by the native
men, and the latter from motives of self defence were also killed by the re-
maining 4 seamen.     Soon after      this two of    the   seamen succeeded    in manu-
factur ing a   native spir it and were continually intoxicated:            one of them
killed by a fall from a (623) cliff, and the other was killed by his comrades
for   the sake of quiet7 leaving but two of the original mutineers, a mid-
shipman, and an able seaman.       A great change then took place in the moral
character of these two men, they discovered an old Bible, .and a prayer book,
which led them to alter their mode of life.         They observed the Sabbath, taught


                                        209
their wives and children and began to lead honest Christian lives.         At this
juncture Young the midshipman died leaving John Adams, a rough uneducated
English seaman, only 24 years of age, the sole protector of a helpless colony
of women and children.     How he did his work, all the world now knows: he suc-
ceeded in establishing such a community as had been the dream of poets, and
the aspiration of philosophers, and he died in 1829 at the age of 65, Chief
Magistrate and Pastor of Pitcairn Island, in the presence of his children and
the flock he had guided so well.


     His youth had been marked by terrible and unusual events, but his end was
peaceful and noble, and I think there are few lives in history so strange and
instructive   as    that of John Adams,   the mutineer.    In 1831 the Pitcairn
Islanders having increased to 87, a great number of them removed to Tahiti,
where they were very kindly received by Queen Pomare, now reigning here: but
the manners and morality of their Tahitian cousins proved quite repugnant to
them, and they soon returned to their old island: but in 1856, when they had
increased to 130, the colony was removed, with the general consent, to Norfolk
Island, near New Zealand - the convict establishment having been previously
removed.   There the majority are now, but a few returned again to Pitcairn,
and we shall probably visit them on the way to Valparaiso.     In 1842 the French
Government took forcible possession of the Society and Marquesas Islands, and
established their seat of government at Tahiti.      This transaction was nearly
the cause of a war. with Great Britain, but the storm blew over, and the two
powers bound themselves by treaty to respect the neutrality of the Hawaiian
Islands.   Prior to the French occupation, Tahiti had been visited by British
and American missionaries,      who had converted   the natives,   and   introduced
schools, etc.      Even now the majority of the natives are Protestants, although
there are any amount of Sisters (626) of Mercy, and Catholic Priests on the
islands.


     In most of the houses I visited, there were Bibles, and other books prin-
ted in London by Spottiswoods.      Queen Pomare was not dethroned by the French,
for they found her influence very great, and her authority useful, so she re-
ceives a pension from the French Government, and has a palace guard, etc. but
no real power - that is centred in the French Military Govenour (sic).


                                       210
     There is a coral reef in front of Papeete harbour, and an island at the
narrow entrance of the tiniest size, but covered with cocoa palms, etc. and
being further adorned by a small battery of guns.      This small island is set
apart for the isolation of lepers, for leprosy is as prevalent here as at the
Hawaiian Islands, and there is the same fearful decrease of population (627)J
that of Tahiti is now under     10,000 and Captain Cook estimated it at over
200,000 in 1778, and he also describes in his journal, a grand naval review he
witnessed at this island, where there were 150 large canoes manned by 7,000
warriors.    Tahiti is about 50 miles in length and about 12 in breadth, and in
Lat. 17°S it is well watered, being mountainous and wonderfully fertile.     The
general productions are about the same as at the Hawaiian Islands and Fij i
group, but the indigenous fruits and roots are much more plentiful.    Sugar and
cotton are produced, but in no great quantity.


     When we got close into Papeete, I thought I had never seen such a beau-
tiful place in my life, and now as we are leaving it, I think so still and the
longer we stay, the more we seem to like it, (628) and the people - natives as
well as Europeans.     The houses are all hidden by cocoa palms, bread-fruit
trees, orange and banana trees and tropical greenery of every kind, and the
great mountains which rise just behind the town, are covered with vegetation,
with the intervening valleys and plains richly cultivated, and watered by num-
erous creeks in which the natives seem to be bathing and washing clothes the
whole day.    Right opposite Papeete, about 20 miles distant, is the mountainous
island of Mooree, from which the most beautiful oranges I ever tasted in my
life are brought and sold in Papeete, 50 for a shilling.


     Behind this island the sun sets every night, painting its mountains every
imaginable colour for about 10 minutes.     There were two French warships at an-
chor in the bay when     (629) we came, one of which sailed the other day for
Brest, with time expired soldiers, prisoners, etc.     I omitted mentioning that
immediately after sunset, it is at once as dark as with you at 9 p.m.


     There is a military governor, an Admiral and any amount of officials and
soldiers stationed here, but of working Frenchmen of the agricultural or in-
dustrial class,    there are none.    Either   they are too fond of   the parent


                                      211
country or are not encouraged to emigrate, and this is the great cause of
French failure in colonization.       They failed   in Canada,   in Louisiana,   in
Madagascar and the East Indies, and also at New Caledonia, at the Marquesas
Group and here also.    The French possessions in the Pacific must cost the home
government a lot of money every year, here at Tahiti, there are scores of
officials, soldiers, priests and Sisters of Mercy, all drawing money and yet
there is nothing to show for it.       There is scarcely anything exported from
these islands, and no shipping trade to speak of, whereas if the British or
Americans had them, they would be the West Indies of the South Pacific.           I
should think the Fiji Islands are already producing and exporting more cotton
and sugar   in one year than these islands have done since they were under
French protection.     Papeete is not to be compared to Honolulu for business and
fine shops, etc.     What trade there is, is in the British and American hands,
the richest merchant and shipowner here, being an enterprising Scotchman named
John Brander, who is married to a princess - Queen Pomare's cousin, one of the
handsomest women I ever saw.     There is no newspaper printed here, the people
get their news and mails at uncertain intervals from San Francisco, in sailing
brigs belonging to Brander and Co.      The French people here make no pretence
about working, there are a few French cafes and restaurants, but they have no
shops.    However they enjoy themselves as much as possible, and are very hos-
pitable to strangers.     I looked over the soldier's barracks and was very much
pleased with everything, the soldiers seemed so comfortable, civil and con-
tented, was very sorry I could not converse with them in their own language,
but hope to master it by and bye.      Some of the French soldiers came on board
our ship and I showed them round, and were much interested with the curi-
osities from Japan, China, etc.      I also got acquainted with some very nice
English, American, Danish and French people on shore, who all spoke English.
I and a few of my messmates went to meet them every evening at their houses,
and they entertained us first rate with music, dancing, etc.         They came on
board the "Challenger" and saw the ship's albums, containing photographs of
all the countries and people we had visited.


     One evening we all went to a grand baIlout in the country and we did en-
joy ourselves.     Have felt more at home here than at any place since we left
Sydney.   We have had the French Governor, and other grand officials on board,


                                       212
as well as Queen Pomare and      (633)   the Royal Princes and Princesses to an
afternoon dance and luncheon.     Queen Pomare is quite an old woman now, and
rather reminded me of grandmother - if she were about two shades darker, and a
good deal stouter.    Her Majesty was received with the usual honors, the yard
being manned, and the officers and ship's company in full uniform.        As she
came over the gangway the band played "God Save the Queen," and the old lady

Governor and officials came with her, but she seemed more at ease when they

plainly and seemed a nice old    lady~   her sons and daughters are fine looking
persons, speak English and French, and play the piano first rate.      They were
dressed in pink muslin generally, their dresss made like those of the natives
of all these islands and the Hawaiian group.     They are what used to be worn in
Europe many years ago, and were called Sacques I think - being shaped like a
dressing gown with no waist, they were introduced here by the missionaries
wives, and many of the European ladies here wear them.      I should not be sur-
prised if they were to become fashionable again, for they look very nice and
comfortable in hot weather.     Before Queen Pomare left the ship, she asked to
see a sailor's hornpipe danced.      She is much liked by the natives and very
partial to English people.


       There is an English church here, where the service is (635) conducted in
English in the morning and French in the evening, also, two Roman Catholic
churches~   and the only schools on the island are managed by the priests and
sisters.    Nearly all the British and American girls speak French, having been
educated in these schools, and they also speak the native language.      They re-
minded me a good deal of the Australian young ladies, but they grow much
quicker than they even~ at 14 they are as tall and fully developed as girls of
20 in England, and there are several under 16 who were married, and had child-
ren.    When a lot of them are together, and they don't want you to know what
they are saying, they jabber away in the native tongue - which seems to me to
have no backbone to it.




                                         213
      The   natives        here    dress   more   like    the    Tongans,    than   the    Hawaiians,
resembling the former people very much, but are fonder of pleasure, and more

      Coral is very plentiful here, and so (637) is fruit, especially oranges,
plantains and bread fruit.             The bread fruit tree is as large as a walnut tree,
and covered with fruit, which when ripe is much larger than a cocoanut, and
covered with a rough serrated skin.               It eats (sic) something between new bread
and custard, and I like it very much.                   An English merchant captain is now in
pr ison here for kidnapping round the islands, and his vessel lies close to

muchy work there, Tahiti plenty food, plenty wife, no work."                          There are no
horses here like there were at the Sandwich Islands, neither are there any

cattle and sheep for qonsurnption here are brought from Honolulu, and we pay
lOd per     lb    for     very infer ior beef.          Other things are much dearer          than at
Honolulu except fruit and drink.


      At the French Police Court the other day, a Chinaman for breaking into a
house,    was sentenced to 10 years transportation to New CaledoniaJ                           another
Chinaman for deliberately murdering his fellow countryman, only received six
months impr isonrnent.            All the roads here are shaded by palm and bread frui t
trees, and it is certainly a lovely island.                     There are lots of mosquitos, but
no noxious animals.


      These natives are wonderfully fond of music, and when our ship's band
(639) used to play on shore, they used to dance until they dropped, and got so


                                                  214
excited.       They all asked eagerly what the nChallenger" had come for, and seem
to have some vague idea that the Br i tish will one day come and dr i ve the
French away, who they hate wonderfully.               Were greatly struck with the nDuke of
Edinburgh" when he came here a few years ago in the "Galatea."                   At one large
native house they showed me his portrait, where he sits leaning on some native
young ladies in a manner that the Duchess would not like.                    At this house I
dined with the family in the open air, off roast pig, baked in a hole under

modated me with a knife and fork, refusing to accept (640) any money I offered
them.     They had a large picture of Queen Victor ia in her state robes before

grandchildren she had.         This family consisted of an old grandfather and grand-
mother~       their married sons and daughters and a host of children - about 50 -
all living in one large two-roomed house, and very happy they all seemed.
After dinner one of the young women asked me if I was a Mormon and what I
thought of Mormonism?         I told her there were never any Mormons in England and
that the faith was dying away in America - the only country where the exis-
tence of such a community was possible.                 They seemed rather disappointed at
this and after a bit, one of the men dressed in a black                      (641)   shirt, and
silver mounted spectacles, and of a generally clerical appearance, brought me
a piece of parchment to read which explained it all.                      It ran as follows -
"This is to certify that Taranei has been duly elected a member of the Mormon
brethren, and is hereby authorized to preach the gospel of Jesus Christ, as it
was revealed to his servant Joseph Smith" - signed by two of the original 70
elders of that church.          He then told me that all the family were Mormons, but
this the young women denied,             though I believed they spoke falsely.             They
brought me Brigham Young's portrait to look at and to write his name thereon~
so I endorsed it "Brigham Young, American Impostor."                  I    (642) presented the
grandfather       with   a   Sheffield   razor    and came     away very much amused.        We
received a mail here, but there were no letters for me as usual.


        Are    just leaving Tahiti       for    Valparaiso -    distant    5,000 miles and in

sighting on the way the island of Tubuai, one of the Austral Group.                      Before we
had been 3 weeks from Tahiti we were in Lat. 40 0 S. and found it very chill in-
deed.     This island and settlement reminded me very much of Tristan D'Acunha,
and rises quite as abruptly (643) from the ocean to a height of 3,000 feet.
The hillsides are covered with vegetation and forest, and large flocks of wild
goats may be seen feeding on the steep slopes of the hills.                    The island is 10
miles long and 5 broad, well watered, but far from fertile, the soil being
wretchedly poor: the island has a very solitary appearance.                   It was discovered
in 1563 by Juan Fernandez, and in 1703 Alexander Selkirk was left here on
account of some quarrel with his captain, and was not rescued until 1709 by a
Bristol privateer.        From Selkirk's journal De Foe pinched the materials for
his interesting romance of Robinson Crusoe.               Omson touched here in 1765, and
his crew caught several goats, the ears of which were supposed to have been
clipped by Selkirk.           (644)   Soon after Omson's visit,              the Spaniards from
Chili settled here ,and built the fort of which the remains are still stand-
ing.      When the Chilians gained their independence at the beginning of the
present century,      they claimed      the    island as      an appendage       of Chili,        and
established     a   convict    settlement     here    which   has    since     been     removed     to
Magellan's    Straits.,       At   present    the    island   is    rented    from     the   Chilian
Government for a term of years by Don Fernandez Lopez, a Chilian who employs
about a dozen families of Chilians in seal fishing and the rearing of cattle.
Their chief trade is with the numerous Arner ican whale ships that call here
during the year for fresh provisions, etc.


        There are lots of fine cattle, horses and goats here, but very little
cultivation, and the people seem very lazy.               They charge (645) very dear for
everything - 1/ for meat per Ib, and they are very independent.                       The working


Note:     Their spelling of "Chile" is always spelled "Chili."




                                              216
     men look to me like convicts, the women have an Indian cast of countenance,
     and the children are very healthy looking.         There is no priest of any sort on
     the island and they can only communicate with Chili about thrice a year.          The
     sea round this island abounds with fish, especially fine crayfish, and hun-
     dreds have been caught by our crew.        Our botanists, naturalists, photographers
     etc., have been hard at work here, there are some very rare humming birds in
     the forest here.     We have a young kid, and a young tame seal, which we shall
     take away as pets from Robinson Crusoe's island, the latter animal cries just
     like a child.      The island has a wonderfully (646) wild and deserted appear-
     ance.     I was on shore yesterday for a few hours, and mounted the elevated
     promontory,    whereon   poor   Selkirk   used   to gaze seaward   in search of   that
     friendly vessel which was to bear him to his distant home.           I could not help
     thinking of Cowper's beautiful poem - "0 solitude where are the charms, which
:;   sages have seen in thy face?       Better dwell in the midst of alarms, than reign
     in this horrible place."        At the back of this settlement are some enormous
     caves in the hillsides and in one of these, Selkirk is supposed to have lived
     in in winter.     Many suppose them to have been made by bucaneer s as a hiding
     place for their treasures7 but I think they are natural, or nearly so.             The
     largest is about 50 feet long, 20 broad, and 20 high, and the (647) sides and
     roof are covered with green ferns and stalactites, which give them quite a
     fairy-like appearance.      Hundreds of English and American names are carved on
     the sides of these caves and, of course, added my own to the number.          I dined
     today off a descendant of one of Selkirk's goats, which ate very tough.


             We are just leaving for Valparaiso, distant 360 miles, and the captain
     has issued wine to all hands as this is the third anniversary of the ·Chal-
     lenger's· commission.      The average depth across from Tahiti is about 2,000
     fathoms and tolerably level bottom.

(649)                                             H.M.S. Challenger
                                                  Valparaiso, December 7th, 1875


Dear Tom,
        Since writing your last I have received your October letter, and expect
no more until we reach Sandy point, which will be about xmas day (sic).            I
also received another letter from home, and think that all my missing ones
have now reached me.       I was greatly surpr ised to hear of the loss of the
"Vanguard," having served in two of her sister ships, and knowing them to be
such fine vessels.


        We are having beautiful weather here now, and fruit of all kinds is in
season.     Chili is a great country for cherries and strawberries and is not a
bad place to live in, although there is an earthquake about every other night.


        After a longer stay I find Valparaiso much better than I thought, and the
people more tolerable also; they are certainly a little more lively than the
Spaniards or Portuguese, and not such bigotted Catholics - especially here in
Valparaiso where there is a very numerous foreign community.          I believe the


                                       218
people up at Santiago and      inland are more   "priest-ridden"   and prejudiced
against Protestants.     Religious processions are very common in this city,
there was one the other day half a mile long which completely stopped all
ordinary traffic for more than an hour.     A short (651) time ago if you met one
of these processions you had to take off your hat until it passed; but this is
not insisted upon now, and the Protestants have their own places of worship,
and enjoy the same privileges as their Catholic neighbours.        I believe Chili
is the best governed, and the most prosperous of all the states in South
Amer ica and its history has not been so turbulent and sanguinary as that of
the other little republics.     In these Spanish settled countries there is al-
ways a party fighting against the government and a war on hand.          Peru and
Bolivia have been the worst for this, and I believe the priests are the insti-
gators and fomenters of all these quarrels.


        There were never such upstirs in America or Australia, or even in India
where so many different races are peaceably and quietly governed by British
laws and impartial policy.     I think the Chilians are beginning to see these
things, and to keep the priests in their proper position.      In a young country
like this, I did not expect to find so many poor and uneducated people as
there are, in which respect it is very different to Australia and America.      In
Valparaiso there are just as many poor as there are in Lisbon, and they are
quite as ignorant, except for the better classes; schools are rarely to be met
with.


        Chili was conquered from the Incas of Peru by two lieutenants of piz-
arro, the famous conqueror of Peru in 1532.       The Indians have dwindled away
(653) by degrees, but as they intermarried with the Spaniards, there are many
half-castes.    Some pure Indians may be met with at the back of the Andes, and
also in patagonia, but they won't work like the natives of the Philippine Is-
lands, and as there are no Chinese here as yet, the Spaniards have to work
themselves, so there are many poor people.


        The Chilian Revolution broke out at Santiago in 1814, and after many
years fighting, the Spaniards were compelled to acknowledge the independence
of Chili.      About the same time Peru and Bolivia and other Spanish states


                                      219
obtained their independence, but have been fighting amongst each other ever
since, and are only now getting settled down.     The great influx of foreigners,
the railways, telegraphs, and numerous mail boats constantly running now from
England, have done more to establish stability in these countries than any in-
ternal influence and improvement, and newspapers have done more than priests
for the people.


     I have noticed in the shop windows here Dicken's works translated into
Spanish, and also those of many other British authors.       That popular period-
ical the "British Workman" is also translated and republished out here, and
has a great sale, I believe it is also translated into Russian and Italian.


     The   two leading figures   in obtaining    the   independence of Chili were
Admiral Cockrane,    Earl of Dundona1d,     and General O'Higgins,   an   Irishman.
Cockrane commanded the Chi1ian (655) navy and O'Higgins the army against the
Spaniards.    Cockrane's great exploit was the cutting out of a treasure ship
from Callas, and at the conclusion of the war the Chi1ians quarreled with him
about some money he had advanced from his private estate, and he left them in
disgust.     Cockrane was one of the most daring admirals we ever had, his feat
of destroying the French Fleet in Basque Roads, with fire ships, is said to
have determined Napoleon against his meditated invasion of England.


     Cockrane was dismissed from the British Service on account of some stock-
jobbing panic he is said to have caused, but it was proved many years after
that he was quite innocent.    After fighting for the Chi1ians he commenced the
command (656) of the Greek Fleet against the Turks until the independence of
Greece was established and recognized.       He then remained unemployed for some
thirty years when his innocence was established and acknowledged everywhere
but at the Admiralty.    The Americans and other nations began to cry out about
his ill-treatment, and at length he was re-instated by Queen Victoria and made
an Admiral.     He died in 1861 at the age of 92, and was buried in westminster
Abbey with all honours, but it was the Americans, I believe, who, by writing a
correct account of his life effectually cleared his good name, and pointed out
to his countrymen and the rest of the world, that the bravest of British



                                      220
Admirals, and the man who had wasted his fortune in obtaining (657) the liber-
ties of others, had been driven by harrassing creditors from his country and
died in debt.     However bad the Chilians treated him when alive, they are very
kind of his memory, and proud of his exploits.     Here in Valparaiso there are
Cockrane streets, squares and hotels, there is a fine iron-clad ship, built in
England for the Chiliean government called the "Admiral Cockrane", and in the
centre of Cockrane Square is a fine statue and monument of him in the attitude
of declamation, erected last year with splendid ceremony.        I think he and
O'Higgins have done more for the British name and credit in this country than
most people imagine.     The British residents, although Protestants, are more
liked, and get on better with (658) the Chilians than their Catholic neigh-
bours, the French or Italians.


        The richest two merchants in Chili are Englishmen, and the greater part
of the busiest portion of this city is owned by an English banker, resident
here.     In no other city we have been to were there so many foreign residents,
a great number of whom are British and German, also lots of Italians, French
and Dutchmen, but scarcely any Americans, not being nearly so well represented
as in China and Japan.     The richest of the merchants are British and Germans.
The French and Italians are generally hotelkeepers, some of which are first-
class houses.     The harbour here is more crowded with shipping than any other
we have anchored in.      There are some splendid mail boats running direct to
Liverpool, and a whole fleet of coast steamers, nearly all of which fly the
British flag and are manned by English crews.      The railway employees and the
mechanics on the docks are mostly English also.


        There are two fine streets in Valparaiso over two miles in length, for
the city is built at the foot of a range of hills, and, like Hong Kong is
about four times as long as it is broad.     In these two streets there are some
splendid shops, and tramways extend the whole length of the city.      There are
three large squares and some public gardens7 but although the business portion
of the city is very tolerable, the remaining larger part is miserable and
wretchedly dirty.     The houses are mean and built of wood, the streets (660)
are narrow, and the people naturally very unclean in their habits and ways.
There are some fine Catholic churches, one, the finest I was ever in, though


                                       221
nothing to be compared with our English cathedrals, there were some fine oil
paintings on the walls, and at the service the solo singing was very good,
there was a large organ and three small ones.       I   always notice in these
Catholic churches that the congregation is nearly all ladies.


     I have been on shore a good deal, on duty, and on pleasure, and like the
place much more than I did at first, if I were staying on this station, should
certainly learn Spanish.     Valparaiso is a much better place than Bahia or
Manilla, and more like an English city than any we have visited, since leaving
Sydney.   (661)   The Chilians dress very extravagantly, especially the ladies
who are tolerably handsome, they have fine dark hair and eyes, good teeth and
very small feet, but a cheerless impassive sort of countenance.     They wear no
bonnets and many of them smoke, dancing is their chief amusement.    There is a
British consul here and a resident minister at Santiago.     I think it is the
most expensive place we have been to, a dollar won't go as far as a shilling
in England.   Wages are very good, especially for mechanics, but there are an
awful lot of idlers and loafers about the wharves.       The landing wharf is
crowded by them all day, and directly a passenger lands, they fight over him
and his luggage, and demand to take him somewhere or (662) anywhere for half a
dollar.


     There are no police to check, for they are the smallest, sleepiest and
most miserable looking ·lot of policemen and soldiers I ever saw anywhere, and
the sailers are not much better.    The other evening I went to a circus, on
purpose to have a good look at the Chilians of all classes, and to see how
they took their amusement.     The principal feature in the programme was an
allegorical representation of the Republic of Chili~ it being represented by a
painted young female in scanty classical garments who galloped about the ring
and kept the Chilian banner in the most insane manner, whilst a small army of
Chilian soldiers, gentlemen and ladies rode round her with drawn swords (663)
and kept the rest of the world at a respectful distance.    The band played the
Chilian anthem, and red fire added to the sublimity of the edifying spectacle,
which was re-demanded by the patriotic but excited Chilians, about six times,
until the foreign portion of the audience could stand it no longer -         the
Frenchmen coughed scornfully, the Germans and Dutch grunted impatiently - and


                                     222
the British portion winked at each other and shouted "Encore" after everyone
else was tired.                Directly this was over for the last time a very large mer-
chant sk ipper, we ighing some 20 stones, and fr ightfully intoxicated, made a
rush across the ring after the procession.                 Three Chilian soldiers averaging
about four feet in height fisted him and forced him back, but every now and
again he would make another dash, and the people would hiss and yell at him
until you would have thought he would be glad to get away: but all he did was
to make an elaborate bow to each part of the house and sing out pitifully,
"Once more, do let us have it once more."                 He was either an Englishman or an
American, and was fined 10 dollars next day.


        The population of Valparaiso is over 200,000 and it covers a large area
of ground.               Santiago is 70 miles inland by rail, and is a very fine laid-out
city; most of our officers have been up. Sub Lieut Lord Campbell and Balfour
left the "Challenger" on Thursday for Santiago, thence across the Andes to
Buenos Ayres, and Monte Video, where they will catch the steamer that brings
this letter.                (665)   The journey across the Andes is rather a dangerous one,
but more interesting than that by Magellan' s Straits.                  We have a new sub-
lieutenant Lloyd, from H.M. Ship "Teredos" out here.                The "Repulse" is expect-
ed in here shortly with Admiral Cockrane, son of the famous Dundonald, and the
Chilians will make a great fuss with him.                 We have taken in all our coal and
provisions to last us to Ascension, and expect to sail on the 9th for Sandy
Point.


        I   was on shore on the 2nd (my 22nd birthday) and had a good ramble all by
myself.             I    also posted the second volume of my Journal to mother, which      I

think will be more interesting than the last, as it describes a less known
part of the world.                  Some day I hope to copy the three volumes (666) into one
book.       I       climbed the hills at the back of the town for a view of the snow cov-
ered Andes - the noblest range of mountains we have seen.                    There are many
peaks over 20,000 feet high and one Aconcagua is nearly 24,000 feet above the
sea level, and the highest mountain in the world that can be seen from the sea
level.          I       am going on shore again tomorrow, as it is a grand religious festi-
val day, being the anniversary of the burning down of the great cathedral at
Santiago some 10 years ago, when so many ladies were burnt to death.                     The


                                                   223
shops    will    all be closed and there will be special services        in all the
churches.       We have lost a few men here by desertion, and some are also to be
invalided, for this voyage is very trying to weak constitutions, but don't
think I ever felt better than I do at present and like the prospect of a cold
weather trip better than a repetition of the tropics.        We have taken in a fine
bullock for xmas, and shall be about in the same latitude as on xmas Day /73
off Pr ince Edward's Island.          The land round Valparaiso is very bleak and
sterile, but soon improves as you get clear of the sea.


        The mail leaves tomorrow so shall write again from Sandy point, and you
will get letters more frequently now, as our long voyages are pretty well
over.


                                                    Yours sincerely,


                                                    Joe Matkin


(668)                           H.M.S. "Challenger" in Messier Channel, Patagonia
                                January 5th, 1876


Dear TOm,
        We are gradually getting nearer to Sandy point, so will begin to get my
Patagonian letter ready.         After closing your last I received no more from any-
one, but of course shall get some at Sandy Point.


        We lost six men by desertion at Valparaiso and sailed from there on the
10th of December but had to return the same day as it was too rough to take
the magnetic observations required.         We made a fresh start on the 11th and had
a head wind which blew us right across to Juan Fernandez, so we sounded and
(669) trawled off that island, but did not go in again.          The wind still being
ahead, we were, by xmas day in Lat. 42°S and Long. 89°W, and the weather began
to get very chilly.        On   xmas Eve we had a concert which proved a great suc-
cess, and is to be repeated once a fortnight for the remainder of the com-
mission.        In addition to the ship's band, there were 4 violins, violoncello,
piano and harmonium. and of course there were readings, recitations, dances
and laughable farces.       The captain played a very nice solo on the violoncello
                                           224
with piano accompaniment, and several of the officers and scientific gents
assisted as well as the crew.


     Great cooking preparations were made the day before Xmas, in the shape
(670) of plum puddings and cakes, and as we had brought a fat bullock along
with us, we did very well in the provision line.


     After dinner there was dancing on the main-deck, and in the evening wine
was issued to all hands.              The paymaster sent me a bottle of madeira for my
dinner.      This Xmas passed as pleasantly as any of the four we have had in the
"Challenger;" all the more so, I think as it will be the last, but the pleas-
antness only lasted until tea-time, for the seamen had managed to smuggle a
great deal of        liquor    into the ship before        leaving Valparaiso, which was
brought out on Xmas night, and soon did its work.                More than half of the crew
were helplessly drunk, and the quarreling and fighting was something awful,
especially among (671) the Irish portion of the crew, and one poor fellow had
his jaw broken in three places.               Since leaving England we have lost a great
many men by desertion and have demanded others in their places from any men of
war we have fallen across, who have invariably sent us their worst characters
- generally Irish; so of course they are pretty numerous.                  An old German at
Valparaiso, who spoke good English, and had been in Australia and America, re-
marked to me that the worst class of men he had fallen across were the Irish
of America, and I think the Irish of London and Liverpool are equally as bad,
and much worse than the native.              They are nearly all Roman Catholics, and when
in   liquor    are   very     noisy    and   eloquent   (672)   about   the wrongs of   "Ould
Ireland. "


      On the last day of the old year we sighted the coast of Patagonia, and
anchored in a bay off the peninsula of Tres Montes, or three mountains.                   The
coast of Patagonia has a very dismal forbidding appearance even in that lati-
tude; the land being high and covered in interminable forest, without exhibit-
ing a sign of human being or habitation.


      The country is inhabited by wild romantic tribes of Indians, who live by
hunting and fishing,          some of whom we shall see by and bye.             Chili claims


                                                225
sovereignty over the whole of this country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific
down to Cape Horn, but there are no white settlers south of Cape -Tres Montes,
except a Chilian convict settlement down at (673) Sandy Point.      On the 1st
January we crossed the Gulf of Penas and entered this channel to do some sur-
veying.


     Messier Channel is about 150 miles in length and averages 3 in breadth,
so that it is more like a canal than a strait, on the east side it has the
mainland of South America, and on the west Wellington Island, which is 130
miles in length and uninhabited.    The scenery through the strait is very bold
and striking, but presents the same monotonous aspect everywhere, and is very
different to the beautiful Inland Sea of Japan.     The land on each side runs
abruptly from the water to a height of more than 1,000 feet, so that very lit-
tle of the interior of either the mainland or the island can be seen.      This
channel is completely sheltered from the wind, and the sea is as calm as the
WeIland.



     The hills are covered in forest and those over 1,000 feet high are clo-
thed in perpetual snow, although this is the middle of summer, and we are only
in Lat. 49 0 S.   The interior of the country seems a mass of undulating forest
clad hills, and snow covered mountains, and by the way it is broken up it is
easy to see that volcanic eruptions have been very active here at some distant
period.


     The land too seems strangely destitute of animal life.     You see nothing
but wild ducks and geese, and at night everything is as still as death, and
seems even more forsaken and uncanny than Kerguelen's Land.    The channel var-
ies in depth from 500 to 50 faths (675) in the centre, and there are scores of
splendid bays and harbours, but as the strait has not been properly surveyed
as yet, very few vessels come through, but the passage is far preferable to
that in the open sea outside Wellington Island.


     Sailing vessels could not come through as there is scarcely ever any wind
and the channel is very winding.       On New Year's evening we anchored in a


                                      226
splendidly sheltered bay, and the var ious exploring, botanizing and shooting
parties landed, but obtained nothing except wild seafowls, and some splendid
kingfishers.       Fish are not plentiful except shell fish.


     We left again on the 2nd and anchored that night in a bay under the lee
of the mainland, which was one of the most secluded and romantic looking spots
in which we have ever anchored.              (676)     We lay close under the land which
seemed    to    rise   right    above our   mast      head,   and was covered    in beautiful
forest.        Early the next morning several exploring, shooting, botanizing and
photographic parties landed, and leave was also given to the crew to wash
their clothes in a fresh water creek.              Some of the parties managed to set fire
to the bush, which spread so rapidly that by 5 p.m. the whole country was in
flames in all directions, and after sunset the scene was grand beyond des-
cription, the fire being even more extensive than that we saw at Cape York,
North Queensland.


        The different parties returned in the evening, bringing in various spoil,
but Mr. Wild, the artist, who generally rambles (677)                 about by himself was
found to be missing, and his non-appearance up to 7 p.m. caused great anxiety,
as the fire seemed to be spreading over the whole country, and several search
parties of officers and men went out to look for him, taking with them rifles,
bugles, etc., and guns were fired at intervals from the ship.                   All hands were
on deck to see the fire, and listen for any tidings of the missing gentleman.
One of the parties went round the coast in a boat, and the crew landed at the
back of the burning tract of countrY1 here they found the old gentleman, and
very pleased he was to see them.            It appears that he lighted a fire before go-
ing sketching to a distant spot, to serve him as a beacon on his return, but
the flames spreading           (678)   so rapidly, completely frustrated the object in
view, and compelled him to make a long detour whereby he lost himself alto-
gether.     They brought him alongside at 9 p.m. and the ship's company gave him
three cheers for being so kind to relieve the general monotony by getting
lost.     When we left the next day, the fire was burning as fiercely as ever,
and the ship was covered with ashes.                 We proceeded about 60 miles and passed
through the "narrows· where the channel is only 240 yards across, and the
navigation is very ticklish.            We anchored last night in another well sheltered


                                              227
bay and shot four seals.       In this bay, we found a Peruvian steamer which had
been abandoned by her crew.       She was bound from Callas, I think, to Hamburgh
with copper ore, hides,       leather and a     (679) general cargo, and in coming
through the "narrows" in Messier Channel, she ran on a rock and knocked a hole
in her bottom.


        Her crew managed to bring her into this bay and run her aground.         Soon
after a French surveying vessel came along and the Peruvian crew are supposed
to have gone away in her, but this is not certain.              Anyhow the Frenchmen
appropriated all the steamer's boats, sails, and various deck fittings, as her
share of the spoil, and sailed southward.        SOme 10 days ago, a British steamer
came this way and found her, which of course became her prize.           She left her
chief officer and 3 men in charge and went on to Valparaiso, whence she will
send assistance to repair her and bring her to that port.           with her cargo, I
fancy    (680)   she is worth nearly £10,000, and the crew of the vessel that
picked her up only numbers 24.        The chief officer came on board our ship to
dinner last night, and attended the concert which was afterwards given.            We
exchanged some flour and preserved meat for beer, butter and walnuts, part of
her cargo.       The patagonians came down to her the night before we arrived, but
were soon frightened away by firearms.


        We heard from her that the French surveying vessel was wrecked somewhere
lower down, but it may not be true.


        We left that bay at 4 a.m. this morning, and have come about 50 miles, to
the end of Messier Channel.      We are now anchored between the Madre Archipelago
and the mainland, and shall remain two or three days.


(681)                                          January 12th
                                               In Magellan's Straits
        We passed a Chi1ian man of war on the 6th, and a merchant steamer yester-
day bound nor th.      We remained two days in the bay off Madres Island, to do
some surveying in the different channels.         On the   night of the 6th it came on
to blow with tremendous force, and steam had to be got up at midnight as there
was great danger of the ship dragging her anchor.          The stern of the ship swung


                                         228
within 20 yards of some large rocks, and 40 of a small rocky island.       The wind
was blowing right onto these rocks, so that it was impossible to get up the
anchor and move until the wind lulled; it was about the most dangerous posi-
tion the ·Challenger· has ever found herself in.


     We left on the 8th and steamed        (682) through Innocent's Channel, into
Sarmients Channel, where we anchored for the night.      The next day, being Sun-
day, we remained at anchor and on the lOth steamed through into Smythe Channel
where we anchored, steaming through that yesterday and entered Magellan's Str-
aits, anchoring at night in this bay, Port Tamar.     A ship entering these stra-
its from the pacific, does so at Cape pillar, some 30 miles west of our en-
trance from Smythe Channel.     We have come all the way from the Gulf of Penas,
through a series of channels separated from the Pacific by a continued chain
of islands, the largest being Wellington, Hanover, Madre and Queen Charlotte
Islands.     The generality of ships keep outside these for the channel navi-
gation is very intr icate, and must anchor every night.       The (683) mountains
that rise so abruptly from the sea in this part of the Patagonian coast are a
continuation of the great chain of the Andes, which, rising to a little of the
north of the equator, extend southward for        4,000 miles, and passes through
Colombia,    Peru, Bolivia,   Chili   and Patagonia, disappearing finally in the
Fuegan Archipelago.     The coast of Patagonia south of the Gulf of Penas, is in-
dented with deep and narrow inlets, which penetrate within the mountain masses
in a similar manner to the fiords on the west coast of Norway.


        Since we have reached above Lat. 50 S, the scenery has changed again, the
                                              0



land is now destitute of trees, and almost of vegetation of any kind.            The
islands and mountains present the same bleak (684) aspect - bare lava and bas-
altic rock, and except from the numerous cataracts which fall from the hills,
you hear no sound anywhere.      Of course snow is more abundant, for we are now
in Lat. 52°S.


        Latterly we have fallen in with a new kind of duck called the ·Steamer W
which in its manner of locomotion is a ,perfect masterpiece.      It weighs from 20
to 30 lbs and its feathers are so thick that ordinary shot will not penetrate
them.      They are splendid divers but cannot fly.       Their   wings   are double


                                        229
jointed and they move them backwards and forwards like a beam-engine in the
old steam boats.   Our steam pinnace chased one the other day, but as she could
only steam 10 knots an hour, and the duck 17, the latter won the race.         It
generally takes about (685) a dozen close shots to bring one down, they are
not good eating, but our men had a taste of them.        We had a heavy thunder
storm the other night with frequent lightening and snow and hail all at the
same time.    We passed through some very narrow places yesterday, and are now
anchored in a bay of King William IV's Land, and Desolation Island - part of
the Euegan Archipelago forms the southern side of the Strait, which here, is
about five miles wide.     This morning our anchor broke clean in two by dropping
on to a hard rock when let go, and the ship dr i f ted wi thin 50 yards of the
rocky shore before the other anchor could be let go, or steam got ready.       We
are now anchored in a bay which is completely surrounded by mountains, and
must at some time, I should (686) imagine, have formed the crater of an ex-
tinct volcano, like xmas Harbour, Kerguelen's Land.     In this latitude it rains
and snows every few hours and a dense fog continually hangs over the land,
which weather we shall have until we reach the Falkland Islands next month.


     Ferdinand Magellan, the discoverer of these straits, was a Portuguese by
birth, but sailed in the service of Spain.      In 1519 the Molucca Islands being
claimed by the Portuguese and Spaniards also, Magellan thought he could reach
them by sailing round the southern part of America and started from Spain with
five ships and succee"ded in reaching these straits.      They are 360 miles in
length and he lost two vessels on the passage through.     He was 110 days cross-
ing the Pacific, (687) when he discovered the large group afterwards called
the Philippine Islands: at one of which - Matan - he was murdered by the
natives.     (We saw his tomb and monument there.)    Only one of his fleet, the
"Vittoria," succeeded in reaching Spain, by the way of Cape of Good Hope, and
this vessel was hauled on shore and long preserved as the first ship that cir-
cumnavigated the globe.       She was 3 years, and 14 days on the voyage, and
Francis Drake's ship, the "Golden Hind," was about the same time, performing
the voyage 56 years later.      He, however, had over a million pounds worth of
Spanish gold in his hold, plundered from Valparaiso, Lima, etc. and after re-
fitting his ship at Temati in the Moluccas (visited by "Challenger") reached
Plymouth in safety.      His voyage so troubled and terrified the Spaniards that


                                       230
they resolved to fortify Magellan's Straits, and thus forever keep the English
and Dutch from the South Seas.     For this purpose an expedition left Spain in
1581 under Sarmiento, who built and fortified a city near Sandy Point, but
disease, cold and famine soon caused it to be deserted, though not before
three-fourths of the settlers had per ished, for when, three years later, an
English adventurer, Candlish, came through the straits he found the city in
ruins.


     In 1615, Schonteu, the Dutch navigator found his way round Cape Horn,
which he named after his native town, Horn, in Holland.     I forgot to mention
before, that H.M.S. "Challenger" was totally wrecked in 1838 near the Gulf of
Penas, on the Patagonian coast and many of the crew were drowned.


     (689)      The Archipelago of dreary, barren, mountainous islands to the
south of these straits was called by the Spaniards - Terra-deI-Fuego (land of
fire) on account of the volcanoes which appeared at distant intervals to illu-
minate the perpetual snow which prevails in this region.       Narrow channels,
strong currents, and boisterous winds render it unsafe for a sailing vessel to
enter this dangerous labyrinth.


     The Atlantic side of the straits is more favored by nature than the Paci-
fic and there, a few trees and animals are to be found.      Penguins and other
Antarctic sea-birds flock to these shores and pursue their prey without moles-
tation.      The Terra-del-Fuegan natives are said to be the filthiest and most
depraved of (690) all the races under the sun.    They are undoubtedly the least
favored by nature as regards country, climate and subsistence, but shall be
able to tell you more about them by and bye, as we shall most likely see them,
and also the Patagonians as we proceed towards the Atlantic.    We are 200 miles
from Sandy Point where I expect to post this.

January 14, at Sandy Point.


       We anchored here this morning and received a mail.    Two of our deserters
are here, having been sent on from Valparaiso by mail boat~ they were captured
by the Chilian police three days after we sailed.


       On the 17th we sail for the Falkland Islands.     Our Captain has just re-
ceived a letter from the (691) King of Spain, thanking him for towing into
Manilla that derelict schooner which was worth about 10 bob.         He calls our
vessel "The Werder" which is very much like "Challenger".


       We have just missed the homeward mail, so it will be some time 'ere this
reaches you.    Will tell you about Sandy Point in my next, it appears a mis-
erable looking place.     There are two Chilian men-of-war here.      Our next ad-
dress is Ascension or St. Vincent.


Yours sincerely,
Joe Matkin.
