Dear Tom:
       We remained four days at Sandy Point, and I was on shore several times.
Sandy Point, or Punta Arenas, as the Chilians call it, is the most southerly
inhabited place    on   the globe,   excepting of course the opposite coast of
Terra-deI-Fuego.    The settlement stands on a flat sandy point of land,        and
consists of about 80 rough wooden houses,       a wooden fort, Catholic chapel,
etc.    The place has sprung up within the last 10 years~ was originally a con-
vict settlement, but the discovery of (693) a coal mine in the neighbourhood
proved the making of the place and       induced other   settlers   to come.    The
Liverpool Pac i f ic Mai 1 boats call there once a·· week   for   coal, and remain




                                       232
six hours.     A German line of steamers, as well as casual steamers passing
through Magellan's Straits also call occasionally.      The coal mine is six miles
inland, but there is a tramway and a steam engine which drags the coal right
on to the "apology" for a pier which the Chilian government has erected, and
the coal is shot through holes in the pier into barges underneath.        The mine
is owned by a company, the shareholders being mostly British and German.       The
employees at it and on the tramway are all Br itish getting enormous wages.
The coal is not to be compared to English, being very small (694) and found
almost on the sur face of the ground.        There is a Chilian Governor there, an
English surgeon in charge of the hospital, a British Consul who flies the flag
on a clothes prop stuck out of the roof of his house, also a considerable
force of miserable looking Chilian soldiers.        There are a few convicts, but
are only exiles, and do no hard work.         There is a gold mine in the vicinity
worked by two or three old Australian diggers,         but they say they are not
making much out of it.


        The population is about 500, mostly Chilians of very dilapidated and
miserable appearance, but there are a good many British and Germans, and a
roving population of hunters, mostly British who go on horseback immense dis-
tances inland to hunt on the great pampas, or plains (695) of South America,
they also trade with the Indians in tobacco and fire-water for skins, which
fetch a pound each at Sandy Point, and when they have gathered sufficient
skins to load two or three horses, they start for Sandy Point to dispose of
them.     This they call "coming to town".      Puma, Emu, Guanaco and other skins
are the most plentiful.    The Patagonians make periodical visits to Sandy Point
themselves for trading, and a tribe was expected there every day, but had not
arrived when we left.     There were several grog shops and stores there, and we
used to get fresh beef and vegetables every day; meat was 7d per pound, other
things dearer in proportion.     There are any amount of cattle near, but sheep
will not thrive, there are settlers now 50 miles inland, and they can grow
(696) potatoes, turnips and cabbages, but no grain.




                                       233
        The country at the back of Sandy Point is tolerably well wooded, and
abounding with various wild animals and birds,      particularly ducks,    geese,
ibis, and snipes.


        Sandy Point is in 53°S and the climate at these islands is very much
colder in summer than England in spring, but still although the winters last
nearly six months the cold is not so severe as in England, and the ice on the
lakes is seldom strong enough to bear a man.       The grass there, and also at
these islands is very coarse and large, but suitable for cattle and horses:
near Sandy Point there are plenty of wild horses, all the Patagonians have
them.    Mushrooms were very plentiful near the settlement, and also wild cran-
berries.     Lots of shooting parties landed (697) there every day with great
success,    and the Governor presented our   naturalist with a young      puma or
American lion, which he had captured, but it died the other day, and has been
stuffed since.


        There were two Fuegan girls and a woman at Sandy point picked up in the
straits by a steamer, and left under the care of the hospital surgeon, who was
trying to civilize them a little before sending them back.    I saw them once or
twice in a hut, crouching over a smouldering fire: they were washed, and part-
ly dressed, and I must say they are not half so ugly or degraded as they have
been represented by various travellers, particularly by Commodore Wilkes, USN
the discoverer of the mythical Termination Land.     They were over 5 feet high,
and their limbs were (698) as well formed as those of other races, were very
broad across the shoulders, and had wonderfully large flat faces, and stiff
coarse locks of hair: their eyes are something like those of the Chinese, and
altogether look between Chinese, Malays and Indians.


        The youngest girl had quite an intelligent appearance,     and were   all
queens compared to the aboriginal women of Australia, the Papuan, or Admiralty
Island ladies.      We took in a li ttle coal and left Sandy Point on the 18th,
anchoring again the      same day at Elizabeth Island,   25 miles further east.
There we stayed two days shooting geese, ducks and tern,        which were very
plentiful.



                                      234
       I was on shore with a shipmate and we shot nine wild geese.            They build
their nests in the grass in the interior (699) of the         island~   the young ones
were nearly ready to fly, and could run like partridges.         The English mail to
Valparaiso went past while I was on shore, but our ship could not communicate
with her, as she was a long way       off~    the straits being 18 miles wide just
there.   The birds called "Tern" lay their eggs on the bare ground close to the
sea~   they are something between Kingfishers and Swallows~ on that part of the
island where they were breeding it was impossible to walk without treading on
their eggs or young, and the noise they made when we intruded on them was
exactly like the roar of the surf on a coral reef.


       We had another concert on the 18th and sailed on the 20th for these
islands, which are about 230 miles east of Cape Virgin, (700) the Atlantic en-
trance to Magellan's Straits.


       The depth across here was only 50         fathoms;   we sighted one of these
islands on the 22nd and anchored on the 23rd, Sunday, off this settlement
which is on the eastern side of the eastern island.         This group was discovered
in 1592 by Davis, and named in the reign of James 1st after Viscount Falkland~
it comprises two large islands, east and west Falkland, and over 200 smaller
islets and rocks, the whole area being not less than 7000 sq. miles, of which
East Falkland comprises 4000 and West 2000 sq. miles.


       There is not a tree on the whole group but abundance of coarse grass upon
which feed enormous herds of half wild cattle and horses,               and    flocks of
sheep.    Of course they have been introduced recently. Albatrosses, wild ducks,
geese,   snipes   (701)   penguins, etc.,    are wonderfully numerous,     and rabbits
which have been brought quite lately are more plentiful than in England.


       The coast round these islands is very rough, but there are numerous good
harbours, the soil is boggy~ the land of moderate elevation, with an undulat-
ing surface.




                                        235
     Of course grain will not grow here, and there is not a fruit or any other
tree to be seen, but potatoes, cabbages, and the hardier sorts of vegetables
are successfully grown.


     The principal exports are wool, hides, tallow, horses, etc., and the
islands   are    frequently visited   for     fresh   provisions   by whale   ships,   and
vessels bound round the Horn. The French were the first to colonize these
islands, after losing Canada in 1763, they abandoned them a year or two after,
and the British formed (702) a settlement here. The French turned over their
colony to the Spaniards, and in 1770 these islands were nearly causing a war
between Great Britain and Spain.       Dr. Johnson wrote a pamphlet against push-
ing the matter to extremity on the ground of the worthlessness of the disputed
territory.      Both countries forsook them as useless in 1774, and in the early
part of the present century the Governor of Buenos Ayres occupied them, and
formed a settlement at Port Louis, on this island, but his was destroyed in
1830 by the Americans, and three years later the Governor of Buenos Ayres sur-
rendered their claim to Great Britain.            The whole of them were then annexed,
and this settlement of Stanley establishedJ the harbour of which would be one
of the finest in the world i f the hills (703) which encircle it were only
higher J it is completely land-locked, and has a lighthouse at the entrance.
The settlement is built on the slope of the hills, the houses are two storys
high, and generally whitewashed, some are of stone, others wood, they stand in
blocks, and are laid out in tolerably regular streets.                It looks far more
clean and pleasant than Sandy Point, but the surrounding country is even more
dismal than patagonia, there is not a tree or scarcely a sign of vegetation to
be seen -- it is a second Kerguelens Land.              There is a small detachment of
marines here, and barracks, the present Governor is Col D'Arcy whose salary is
£1000 per annum, there is also a Bishop and two or three missionaries who make
periodical visits to the Fuegan Islands to try to civilize and convert the
poor (704) outcasts of those desolate regions.           They have brought some of the
men over here, taught them English, and are now teaching them farming, garden-
ing, etc.    By and bye they are to be sent back with presents of a few cattle,
sheep, horses, garden seeds, and implements to see what they can accomplish in
                                                                                             ...


                                            236
     the way of social improvement among their countrymen.                 We had one of the men
     on board here, quite a well made man, spoke English and laughed at everything;
     so after this I shall consider the Fuegans as nothing inferior to their anti-
     podean     fellow-creatures,      the    Samoides   and      Laplanders   of     the   northern
     hemisphere,    although    they    are   by   nature   the    least   favoured    of   all   her
     children, as regards their land and the means of subsistence.


             There is a Dissenting Chapel here (705) as well as a Church of England,
     and also a Catholic Chapel for the Governor's wife is a Roman Catholic, and
     insisted upon having one.         I have been on shore several times, and if there
     were but nice gardens and fields could fancy Stanley was an English village.
     The people wear real English working dress, the children are so numerous, and
     healty looking.      There are horses and carts, any amount of stray poultry,
     cows, cats and dogs, and for the first time since we left New Zealand have
     found English money.       Copper coin we have been strangers to for more than a
     year.


             Outside of every house is a peat-stack instead of a coal shed, the same
     as in the south of Ireland, and this peat burns better than wood, and is won-
     derfully abundant.     There are several stores (706) and more public houses than
     in Barrowden, here also, as in your place, everybody knows everyone else, and
     his business. The best of beef, pork and mutton may be bought for 3d per lb.
     and geese, ducks, snipes and rabbits in any quantity may be shot at the back
     of the settlement; we have never lived better since we left England than at
     this place; still everything is dear except meat.                Butter is 2/      per lb. and
     eggs 4/ per dozen.        Many of the houses have vegetable gardens attached and
     there are tolerable roads here.


             Our concert party gave a very successful entertainment on shore one eve-
     ning, which was well attended, being a novelty; the proceeds were given to the
     school funds.     We have taken in 150 tons of coal, and given leave to all (707)
     hands, when of course the grog shops were extensively patronized.                      A month's
     money was also paid in English silver.              Themail here is brought from Monte
     Video every six weeks, by small schooners, which also do all the trading to
'i   and fro.

     Our band played on shore once or twice, and the Captain and officers have
given several partiesJ one afternoon there was a dance party on board, but the
ladies are a very sleepy lot compared to those in Australia, and other places
we have been to.       Last Sunday, Dr. Stirling Bishop of the Falklands, conducted
the service on board, and preached an excellent sermon.         He said that we had
all done our duty to our country on this remarkably interesting voyage, and he
had heard that the crew of the ship (708) was one of the most united company's
ever afloat ("especially the deserters" JM).        He did not doubt but that there
were many scores of people in England who were counting the weeks and days
that would elapse before we could arrive: and hoped we all should find friends
well on our return, and the money that we shall have so hardly and honorably
earned will not be squandered in the first English port we touch at, but spent
pleasantly among our own friends and people.         Dr. Stirling comes of a naval
familYJ one of his brothers was a Commander with me in the -Audacious" and was
married at Hull, one is a Commodore and another, a Captain R.N. was drowned
with his wife in the "City of Boston", on his way out to join his ship in
North America.        His father was (709) Admiral Stirling, so he knows all about
the sailors.     On   Jan. 31st we took in a lot of wooden piles brought from South
America, to form a fence round the cemetery of Port Louis, where we were to
arr ive on the day following.         The same evening the Officers gave a large
dinner party, and the visitors left the ship at 11 p.m. in the steam pinnace.
When the boat returned several of its crew were the worse for liquorJ just as
it got close to the ship one of the men Thomas Bush,        abl~   seaman, fell over-
board and, being intoxicated, was perfectly helpless in the water.         Lieutenant
Carpenter at once jumped overboard, and succeeded in the darkness in finding
the drowing manJ after great exertion he brought him along side the boat, and
they were both rescued and brought on board.         The water (710) was very cold,
and Lieutenant Carpenter was quite exhausted,         but recovered after a time.
Although the promptest measures were taken by the surgeons, and numerous vol-
unteers to restore animation to the unfortunate seaman they were of no avail,
and after persevering for upwards of an hour in the usual method for the re-
suscitation of the apparently drowned, they were compelled to decide that life
was extinct.          The next morning we steamed round to Port Louis, 25 miles fur-
ther north and anchored off the small settlement of about half a dozen farm-
houses.   We landed the timber for the cemetery fence, and sent a party to dig

    the grave, of him who only 12 hours before had helped to get the wood on

            Yesterday all the school children of Stanley, Protestant and Catholic to

            It was quite a novelty to us to see so many English children around us,

    band played "Homeward Bound", and "The Girl I Left Behind Me" as we steamed

            The population of the Falklands is about 1000: we are now nearly out of
    sight of the most southerly, as well as one of the quietest, and pleasantest


                                                 239
of Her Majesty's foreign possessions.          For a ship in want of fresh provisions
after a long sea voyage, there are few better places to touch- at than the
Falkland Islands, and although the country is naturally sterile and unpro-
ductive,   being   three   degrees   further    south   than   (794)   Kerguelen's   Land,
British settlers and industry have managed to utilize it to the best advan-
tage, and to turn what was only intended at first as a military and naval

February 16th at Monte Video:


     We arrived here yesterday after a rough but quick passage of 10 days from
Stanley, sounding etc., by the way, average depth across 1200 fathoms.                  We
received our letters last night dated up to December lOth but shall get two
other English mails before we leave.       We leave here about the 29th, and shall
reach Ascension by the end of March.           Letters to S. Vincent only take 10 days
from England.


     The difference of climate here, and at the Falklands caused a good deal
of (715) sickness, rheumatic fever, etc.           This place being in 35°S latitude
and now is the middle of summer, it is hotter than that season in England.
There are all kinds of fruit, but I have not been on shore yet.



February 24th:


     I have been too busy since we came in here to get my regular descriptive
letter ready, but shall have lots of time on the way across to Ascension, and
as everything is written down in my Journal, shall have no trouble about               it~

the reason for my extra work is owing to the long sickness of the Ship's
Steward -- my opposite number.       He contracted a dangerous illness at Hilo and
Tahiti, and has been confined to his hammock almost ever since, and is no
better yet, so have his duty to do as well as my own, which, as my Paymaster
tells me is a great honour, but of no material benefit to me7 if he were to go
to Hosptial, I should receive four times as much pay as I am now doing, and he
would also receive his; but as long as he is borne on the ·Challenger· books
he alone takes it.


                                         240
     We invalided home on the last mail boat, a Sub-Lieutenant dangerously ill
from a sickness also contracted at that southern paradise -- Tahiti.               His
father is, I believe, domestic chaplain at Windsor Castle, and don't know what
he will think when he learns the nature of his disease.         He, Sub-Lieut. Swire,
was the tallest, strongest and finest looking man we had (717) in the ship,
but now, through bad surgical treatment, he is physically ruined.            We sent
home in the same vessel a seaman, who was with me in the "Invincible" and
"Audacious".     He seemed a strong man then but the peculiar voyage of this ship
as regards climate has brought on a galloping consumption, and am afraid the
poor fellow will never see England again.            I have been on shore, but shall
tell you all about that in my next.         The weather was intensely hot, much more
so than where we are lying, about 3 miles out in the Rio-de-la-Plata1 it is
about the same as in Melbourne and Sydney at this season.           We have received
two other mails here.


     A rebellion is expected to break            (718) out next week, but as this is
the normal state of Uruguay, it creates very little anxiety among the people
unconnected with the government.         The English papers seem strangely unsettled
in . their   tone as   regards   the general     peace of Europe.   The Buenos Ayres
Standard of yesterday (English paper) contains a telegram from Lisbon, assert-
ing that enormous naval preparations were going on in the English dockyards.


     We sail tomorrow morning for Tristan d'Acunha, and Ascension, and shall
reach the latter in about six weeks, when I shall write again.
Your sincerely,



Joseph Matkin.

Dear Tom:
      I will now commence my Monte Video letter, which I            hope to post at
Ascension a month hence.


                                           241
      We sighted the mainland of South America, near to the entrance of the
River Plate(sic) on the morning of February 15th and as soon as we were fairly
within the river, full steam was got up, and we proceeded full speed for Monte
Video, which is 90 miles up the river. The land was low and very similar to
the South American coast        (720)   near Pernambuco and Bahia.            In steaming down
the La Plata, you would almost think you were in the open sea, if it were not
for   the freshness and turbid color of the water f the immense body of fresh
water which it pours into the ocean is perceptible for more than a hundred
miles out at sea, and causes a powerful current among its waters.                        The La
Plata is formed by the union of the rivers Parana, Par aquay , and Uruguay, as
well as many tributary streams, and ranks second among the rivers of South
America.


        The Parana has its source in the Bolivian Andes, and is navigable for
vessels of light draught for more than 1800 miles.                    The river La Plata is
2,350 miles       in length,   the area of    (721)    its basin being 1,240,000 square
miles.     It is over 150 miles wide at its mouth,               and about 90 up at Monte
Video: at Buenos Ayres, 100 miles above Monte Video, it is about 15 miles in
breadth.    It was discovered in 1514 by Juan de Salis, who was murdered by the
natives in making a descent into the country.             For some time it was called the
river    Salis,    but   in 1526,   Sebastian Cabot,      then   in    the    Spanish   service,
visited it,       and having procured much silver from the natives, he called it
"Rio-de-la-Plata" --. "River of Silver".              It is comparatively shallow and we
passed lots of vessels at anchor as we proceeded.                At   l~     a.m. we passed the
lighthouse of Maldonado, a small sea port 50 miles east of Monte Video.                    (722)
It was near this port that the British line of battle ship "Bombay" was burnt
with over 70 of her crew in 1863.           She was Flag Ship of Vice-Admiral Eliott,
who remained on shore at Monte Video whilst the ship steamed down the river
for target practice.        She caught fire whilst the crew were at dinner, it was
supposed    in the Spirit Room,         and was burnt to the waters edge in a short




                                            242
time. The Captain (so I have been told by men who were in the ship) called his
Galley away as soon as the fire was discovered and laid off from the ship.
There were not boats enough to save all hands, and when some of the drowning
men swam alongside the Captain's galley, he ordered his coxswain to chop off
their hands if (723) they attempted to get into his boat.


     Commander Stirling who was with me in the "Audacious" was a lieutenant in
the "Bombay", and was promoted to Commor. for his efficiency on that occasion.


     From Maldonado down to the anchor age off Monte Video, we r aced with a
French Man-of-War, and beat her by a mile.     We were obliged to anchor about 2
1/2 miles from the city on account of drawing over 20 feet of water, but it is
possible to go in nearer.     There were nearly as many vessels (merchant) lying
close into the town as at Valparaiso, and several Mail Boats -- Spanish,
German, French, and British.     There were two British Gun Boats alongside the
town, and about 15 gunboats of nearly all nations.      Monte video derives its
name (724) from a small mountain in the vicinity of the town, upon which is a
lighthouse.   Seen from the sea it looks very compact and imposing -- something
like Manilla, being built on a level plain -- but like all foreign places it
disappoints on a closer inspection.     There is a wall round the older portion
of the city, for it has stood more seiges than any other in the New World.    It
is the only good port in the La Plata, for vessels drawing more than 12 feet
of water cannot approach within about 12 miles of Buenos Ayres, which is the
parent city and greatest enemy of Monte Video, but fortunately on the opposite
shore of the river. The city of Buenos Ayres was founded in 1535 by Pedro
Mendoza: and Monte Video was founded by a colony from Buenos Ayres: (725) for
a long time it was a bone of contention between Spain and Portugal, as the
Portuguese claimed the whole of South America, north of the La Plata to the
western boundary of Brazil.    Soon after Brazil was erected into an independent
kingdom,   the people of Buenos Ayres threw off the Spanish yoke,        and the
Brazilians seized on that event as a pretext for taking forcible possession of
Monte Video which was recovered again by Buenos Ayres in 1814 after a long
siege, and after that retaken by the Brazilians in 1821, when it became what
it now is -- the capitol of the Republic of Uruguay, by Treaty.     Buenos Ayres
is   the capitol of   the   Republic of that   name, which   is the head of the


                                      243
Argentine Confederation of States.                  It is a remarkably fine and (726) well-
built city, so our Officers, who visited it, said, -- with a population of
over 200,000.          Monte Video has over 120,000 inhabitants, and although they are
of Spanish descent, the same as the Buenos Ayrians, they hate each other.                         The
City was besieged in 1852 for more than 9 years by Rosas the despotic ruler of
Buenos Ayres, who did great damage to the city, and almost ruined the commerce
of Uruguay.       Since the restoration of peace however, the city has rapidly in-
creased in size and importance, and the country has made great progress: the
city is now well fortified, and there is a Uruguayan Army and Navy in perspec-
tive,     so    that     the    people    consider    themselves      quite    a   respectable    and
formidable power.             Buenos Ayres was (727) taken by the British in 1806, but
retaken soon after by the citizens, and the British were driven away with con-
siderable loss, owing chiefly to the impossibility of naval cooperation, on
account of the shallowness of the river -- there being no gun boats at that
time.      Buenos Ayres and Monte Video were visited a few years ago by that
scourge of South America,                Yellow Fever,       which   almost put    a   stop to    all
business and foreign intercourse.               There will probably be a row before long
between Chile and Buenos Ayres concerning Patagonia as both those Republics
claim the eastern coast of that large country.                   The area of Uruguay is about a
sixth    greater       than    that of     England,    and     the   total    population   is    about
500,000.       It is more of a grazing country than any other in South America, and
the chief wealth           (728)   lies    in its     immense herds of cattle,         horses,     and
sheep.     The chief exgorts are wool, hides, tallow, and the famous Liebig's (?)
Extractum Carnis works near Monte Video.


        Uruguay has a national debt of over                   £9,000,000.      There used to be a
British Minister          residing at Monte Video,            but at present there is only a
Consul.        There was a rebellion only a few weeks ago which was with difficulty
suppressed.       Our Steam Primace used to do all the running between the ship and
the shore, on account of the long distance.                   Meat was only 2d per lb. at Monte
Video, but everything else was dear: fruit of all kinds was very plentiful but
expensive.        The weather was to us, coming from the Falkland Islands in 10
days, intensely hot in the day time, as much- so as Sydney and Melbourne.




                                                244
        (729) On the 17th of February a German Frigate called the "Gazelle n came
in, and remained two days before sailing for Kiel.                         She went to Kerguelen's
Land with a party of Astronomers, etc., to observe the Transit of Venus in
1874,    and since that time has been on a various cruise taking occasional
soundings, trawlings, etc., at moderate depths. She was fitted up after the
manner of this ship, and her scientific instruments for soundings, etc., were
borrowed     from    Plymouth    Dockyard.            Most    of     her    officers      visited    the
"Challenger", before she sailed.              Uruguayan paper money is at present worth-
less    in its capitol city,          and as there is no native coined money except
copper,    all    kinds of gold and           silver    coins       are    taken;   but   Spanish    and
Brazilian money bring         (730)   the best value; on French, Dutch, English, and
American you lose considerably; an English sovereign was worth 4 dollars 70
cents, and a shilling would only pass for 20 cents.                        A month's money was paid
to us in English sovereigns, and the first leave given on Sunday the 20th when
most of our men went on shore.              I did not go that day, but all who did attend-
ed the bull fight, which takes place outside the city every Sunday afternoon;
entrance 2 dollars to the seats in the shade, and 1 dollar to those in the
sun.     If the fight had been on a week day I should certainly have gone, for
the say of the thing; as it was I had to get a description from some of my
mess    mates.      Eight    bulls    and    six   horses      were       killed,   and   two   of   the
"Matadores" or bull fighters were within (731) an ace of being killed.                               Our
men describe it as cruel and brutal sport; some of the horses were literally
ripped open, and the poor maddened bulls are pricked with spears and knives,
irritated by coloured flags, and terrified by combustibles made fast to the
handles of the spears, which explode as soon as the spear is thrust into the
animal's body.       The combatants consisted of eight men on foot armed with sharp
prods, and carrying coloured flags to irritate the beast, and three men on
horseback    armed    with    long    spears,      which     they    try    to   thrust   between    the
animal's shoulders, so as to reach the heart, avoiding at the same time the
headlong charges that he makes.              One bull which was very much cheered by the
audience         especially the numerous (732) ladies -- succeeded in killing three
horses, one after another, tossing one with its rider completely into the air,
and taking away the whole side of the horse with its horns.                          This bull before
he received his final thrust exhibited a horrible appearance, bleeding from
scores of wounds.


                                                245
        The Matadores are gaily dressed, and loudly cheered when they make a
particularly successful thrust.          If they bungle at it, they are h~ssed, and if
unlucky enough to get gored by the bull, the audience applaud the animal,
singing out nBravo Toro".       My informants assert that when a matadore is killed
he is buried with disgrace on the spot where he falls, but this statement must
be received with caution.       Only one bull is let into the arena at once, (733)
and if he does not exhibit sufficient ferocity then and there, he is lassoed
and slung out to make room for a ngamer" animal.             When the bull is killed,
four white mules come in and drag him out, as well as any horses he may have
gored.     At the conclusion a very small bull was let in and killed by amateurs,
many respectable looking gentlemen presenting themselves as candidates for the
sanguinary honour.      This very edifying national Sabbath amusement lasted over
three hours.


        On the 22nd we received six supernumary seamen from the Gunboat whose
time of foreign service /3 years/ had expired, for passage to England.          I went
on shore that afternoon and spent the day rambling about the city and neigh-
bourhood.     When you get close into the place, Monte Video (734) has a much
meaner and dirtier appearance than Valparaiso, but             it is   in reality much
cleaner,    and   of   course   better   laid out,   being   built on tolerably level
ground. There are fewer idlers and loafers to be seen on the wharves, but
still Valparaiso is the busier and finer city in the business part of the
town.     No two buildi.ngs seem alike in Monte Video, but the streets are very
regular, and there are more tramways laid down than at any other place I have
visited.      The tram cars are not so comfortable, nor so showy as those at
Valparaiso 1 they are drawn by 4 mules, and the prices for riding are very mod-
erate.     There are one or two fine squares in which Military Bands play every
evening, and crowds of remarkably well dressed ladies and gentlemen promenade
(735) until 11 p.m.


        There were several large Catholic churches of the regular stereotyped
Spanish stylel most of them were undergoing repairs, and the interior of them
exhibited more tawdriness as regards images, paintings, ornaments, etc., than
any of the Catholic Churches we have seen anywhere.              The waxen figures of
various male and female saints were so outrageously ugly, and unlifelike that


                                            246
an audience at a penny peep show would have scoffed at them.                           One figure,
gaudily decorated, of a female saint (apparently the Virgin Mary) was repre-
sented as a daughter of Ham -- she was as black as a crow, and so were many of
the surrounding worshippers, for colored people and half-castes are very num-
erous in Monte Video (736).           There are no slaves in Uruguay now, and you see
lots of nicely dressed colored ladies~ the colored people of Uruguay seem far
more comfortable and respectable than those in Brazil.


     The generality of the shops were not so large or so fine as those in
Valparaiso, but the public buildings are finer, and there are many splendid
residences    in    the    suburbs.        Monte   Video    is     not    so   well   fortified   as
Valparaiso, for the country is very poor on account of the frequent political
disturbances,      and    the   generally    turbulent      and     unstable    character   of    the
people.    There was a rebellion there a few weeks ago, and the Foreign res-
idents    report   that     another   is    brewing.        There    is    a   very   numerous    and
influential     Foreign     population,      British,      German     (737),    American,   French,
Italian and Spanish residents, but there are more Americans and fewer Germans
than in Valparaiso.


     There is an English daily paper printed at Buenos Ayres, and brought to
M.V. by train three hours after publication; but it is very feebly conducted,
and its foreign information is seldom reliable, the European telegrams being
copied, apparently from the native newspapers.                    The railway which runs paral-
lel to the La Plata until opposite Buenos Ayres, is owned by a company, the
shareholders being mostly British.


     The soldiers and vigilantes of M.V. are about on a footing with those in
Valparaiso and Brazil, their clothing, accoutrements, etc., being of the most
common descr iption.        Their manner of (738) marching and going through their
evolutions is peculiarly their own, being totally unlike anything I have ever
seen before.       When they are on duty the drums are always beating, and the
buglers play the most original "calls", each performer appearing to have his
own peculiar tootle.




                                               247
        There are three fine spacious markets in different parts of the town1 the
meat, vegetable, and fruit supply being splendid.       A quarter of -mutton weigh-
ing 15 lbs. cost half a dollar 2/.


        Everything is much dearer in M.V. than it was a few years ago, on account
of the recent disturbances, and the worthlessness of the paper money.         There
are several fine Hotels,      one,   the "Or iental" being   the largest   in South
America.     Most of the Hotel keepers are Frenchmen (739) and Italians.        The
weather    in the middle of the day was as hot as Melbourne and Sydney.          Of
course Monte Video, Bahia, Manilla, Valparaiso, etc., are not to be compared
to Melbourne and Sydney for general business and convenience, neither are they
laid out so well, nor do they possess the comforts and luxuries that are ob-
tainable in our large Colonial Cities.        The great majority of the population
of these Spanish settled countries are apparently wretchedly poor, ignorant,
and isolated from those above them.       There seems no prosperous lower trading
class in these cities, and the Catholic religion and style of education does
not appear     to conduce anything towards drawing the various       local classes
nearer together.     Most of the Officers, naval and military, serving in these
South American states are Americans or British, and the children of the upper
classes are frequently sent to Europe or America to be educated or "finished
off".     The public officials of most of these little states are invariably in-
competent men, and notoriously venal and corrupt.      Only a day before we sailed
the Uruguayan Chancellor of the Exchequer was kicked unceremoniously out of
office 1 still in the present state of Uruguayan finance, that is not a very
satisfactory situation.     The windows of all the houses in M.V. are protected
with thick iron bars1 those who cannot afford them have wooden ones.            The
houses are almost all of stone and brick -- there is an English Church, and
Clergyman attached to the Consulate.      The week after we sailed was "Carnival"
week, and great preparations were being made for it, especially by the sellers
of masks, dominos, and fancy dresses, some of which were wonderfully quaint
and ridiculous.      Fightings, quarrelings,    and even assassinations are very
frequent during Carnival time, and the predicted rebellion is expected to show
itself during that delectable period.         Foreign residents and people uncon-
nected with the Government take these little political explosions very calmly.



                                        248
     On the 25th February we steamed down the La Plata, and had seen the last
of the Spanish settled cities we shall visit in the "Challenger".    Our course
was to "Tristan-d-Acunha, thence (740) to Ascension, a distance by our neces-
sary route of 3700 miles.    We have to sound every day until we reach our old
track of soundings from Bahia to Tristan-d-Acunha in 1873.   We have also taken
dredgings, trawlings, and serial temperature: have lost a lot more line and
discovered an undercurrent of very cold water travelling from the S.E. towards
the Equator.   We are about 1200 miles from Tr istan today: the average depth
across has been 2,800 fathoms so far: on the 2nd we caught a shark over 10
feet long.


March 15th.
     On the 13th we sounded over the same spot where we sounded 2 1/2 years
ago, on the voyage from Bahia to the Cape.     It is not often that a ship sails
round the world and reaches the (741) same latitude and longitude again --
after having ploughed a nearly straight furrow round: we are only 40 minutes
behind English time today and about 200 miles N.E. of Tr istan-d-Acuhna, but
the wind has shifted dead ahead, and as we have not much coal in the ship, the
Captain has decided on not going to that island again, but on proceeding
direct for Ascension.


April 3rd at Ascension.
     We arrived here on March 26th and received a few letters and papers.     We
have provisioned, etc., to last us to England and coaled to supply us to S.
Vincent: have also received several seamen for passage to England making our
total number borne 254.     This island was discovered by a portuguese navigator
on Ascension (742) Day 1511, and taken possession of by England as soon as
Bonaparte was sent to S. Helena.      It is only 34 square miles in extent, and
one of the most desolate, rugged, and inhospitable looking spots on the globe,
is nothing but mountain, cinders and land, and except on the top of Green
Mountain, where the hospital is situated, there is not a tree or sign of veg-
etation visible.


     The island produces nothing, and everyone on it is on an allowance of
provisions and water, the same as on board ship.         It is used as a Naval


                                      249
victualling and refitting depot for the Fleet on the African station.                   There
are about 200 people on it all under government 1               the Governor of the island
is a Naval Captain, and the discipline, regulations, etc., are something like
a convict prison, only the people need remain but 2 years.                Being so close to
the equator, the climate is fearfully hot, and it only rains hard about once
in three years.        There are no springs or wells of fresh water on the island,
that for drinking, etc., has to be condensed from the sea.


        There are no shops or hotels, and there are sentries and boards of reg-
ulations    stuck everywhere,        so    that   altogether   the general   routine   is   so
irksome to all but officers, that the place may be said to merit the name it
bears of the "Sailor's Hell".              Turtles are more plentiful here than at any
other place in the world1 they land at certain seasons to lay their eggs in
the sand, and are then caught and placed in ponds for consumption or export.
The Mail Boat generally takes some to England.


        (744) We had four given us averaging 300 Ibs in weight, two of which we
have eaten.       They often weigh 600 Ibs. and when first hatched are no larger
than frogs1 the flesh is as good as beef and makes most excellent soup.                     The
eggs are quite white and round, as large as a hen's, the shell is as supple as
parchment 1 one of our turtles contained 300 eggs, which were all eaten before
it was dead, for they are several hours dying.                 They had over 100 turtles in
the pond when I was there.


        On one part of the island the sea bird called (Wide-Awakes) have their
rookerY1 it covers several acres of ground, over which it is impossible to
walk without treading on the eggs or young 1 the place is called RWide Awake
Fair R, and is one of the sights of Ascension. We found HMS "Supply" at anchor
here1     she   took   stores down    to    Kerguelen's   Land,    in   connection   with   the
"Transit of venus", the year after we were there.                  Her officers report that
they experienced the worst weather they have ever known on the voyage to that
island.     Such a fearful surf breaks all round the shores of Ascension that it
is impossible to land except in one particular place, and the rollers are
something awful.        Seen from the sea, the island looks like a great red and
black cinder, and after you have landed find it nothing but a mass of lava


                                              250
     rocks and clinkers, thrown up without shape or form, and the whole surfce is
     broken up more strangely than S. Vincent, for which island we are just (746)
     starting.     You most likely remember my account of that rugged spot; it was
     where our schoolmaster was accidentally killed.


     April 11th, Saturday, Latitude SON, 180 miles west of Sierra Leone.
             We crossed the Line for the sixth time in the ·Challenger·, on the 7th in
     longitude 14°W.     The average depth from Ascension has been 2,200 fathoms and
     we reached our old track of soundings on the 10th, so between this and England
     very little more sounding or scientific work remains to be done.            Yesterday
     morning I saw one of the most wonderful sights I ever saw in my life -- an
     enormous water-spout, said by our old seamen to be the largest they had ever
     seen.     It was a cloudy morning, but no rain fell near us; it was first (747)
     seen at 6:30 a.m. about 10 miles away, and travelled slowly for some 4 miles,
     and disappeared finally at 7:00 a.m.       The column looked like an enormous semi-
     transparent    factory chimney,    its   base resting    in the sea, and its sununit
I,   enveloped in a black cloud, out of which came frequent flashes of lightning;
     the sea at the base was in such a violent commotion that it looked like a ship
     on fire without flame.       The water could be discerned ascending the column
     spirally in dense volumes, and the spout was almost perpendicular until the
     wind caught it, and bent it in the centre, when it looked like the trunk of an
     old tree, breaking soon afterwards.        It disappeared in the centre first, and
     the lower part (748) seemed to sink in the sea, and the upper part to vanish
     in the clouds very slowly.        A smaller one was also formed close to it, which
     travelled parallel with it, but with much greater rapidity and disappeared in
     about S minutes.      Some scientific men say that these water-spouts are formed
     in the clouds, owing to their being greatly overcharged with rain, but the
     general opinion is that they are columns of water raised by an ordinary whirl-
     wind from the sea to the clouds, but the amount of water is very small, being
     nothing but the spray from the agitated spray.          My own observation leads me to
     believe that immense volumes of water are carried up from the sea, but should
     like to know more of it, (749) you will probably read accounts of this won-
     derful phenomena in the papers from our scientifics.




                                              251
April 19th at S. Vincent.
        We arrived at this dismal looking spot last night from St. Jago, where we
stayed 24 hours for fresh provisions, etc., that place and St. Vincent I des-
cribed in 1873, but since we were there, the latter has greatly increased in
size on account of the frequent calling of various line of Mail boats for
coal.     A telegram was sent to England last night to announce our arrival, as
we sail for Portsmouth on the 26th, so this will be the last letter from the
nChallenger" before reaching "Horne, Sweet Horne".


Yours Sincerely,
Joe Matkin.

Spithead, May 25th, 1876
Dear Tom:
        We arrived here at 9 p.m. last evening and must commence my description
from leaving St. Vincent.


        On April 26th the anchor was got up at 5 a .m. and proceeded out from
Porte Grande Harbour, under sail for England, having no further places to call
at according to the projected route.     The distance is 2,300 miles.   There was
scarcely a breath of. wind, and the ship was in sight of St. Vincent all day,
sailing round the southern point of the opposite island- of St. Antonio on
account of the wind.


(751)     May 20th.
        We have had nothing but headwinds since we left St. Vincent, we were
blown to the westward of the Azores, and then right onto the coast of Spain,
when, being short of provisions and coal, the Captain decided upon putting in
to Vigo.     The Spanish coast was sighted at about 10 a.m. ten miles ahead, sev-
eral steamers and small sailing vessels were passed during the morning, and
the entrance to Vigo Bay was passed at 2 p.m. when the British channel fleet
were discovered lying at anchor off the town.        As we steamed past the Fleet
the band of the "Defence" played "Home, Sweet Home".       The Fleet consisted of


                                       252
the "Resistance", "Monarch", "Iron Duke", and "Lively" Despach Boat belonging
to the (752) Channel Fleet and the "Hector" and "Defence", part of the Coast-
guard Fleet, under the command of Captain Charles Webley Hope, late of the
"Invincible" and "Audacious".    The other division of the Channel Fleet are ly-
ing at Lisbon.   The anchor was let go at 2:30 p.m. about half a mile from the
town, and some English papers were sent on board.       Lots of contractors, bum-
boats, etc., came alongside as soon as we anchored, and did a good trade as
everyone was hungry.     Eggs were only 6d per dozen and the other things were
cheap in proportion.     Vigo is a favourite rendezvous of the Channel Fleet arid
when here, trade is pretty brisk with only half of it, as at present the shop
keepers have the victualling of nearly 4000 additional people.          Vigo is a
quaint, old fashioned, but pleasant looking town (753) of the regular Spanish
pattern.   It is very irregularly built on the slope of a range of hills, and
looks like a poorer edition of Lisbon.       Judging from the size, the population
is about 30,0001 there is a very dilapidated ancient looking Moorish castle on
the summit of a high hill overlooking the town.      The houses are very lofty and
ugly, and the streets seem narrow and crooked.        The country round the shores
of the Bay looks beautiful, and is apparently fertile and well cultivated.
There are white houses visible through the trees in all directions, and in its
general aspect the country looks very similar to that in the neighbourhood of
Lisbon, only there are not so many windmills for crushing the grapes.           An
English merchant ship, and several small (754) Trading vessels are at anchor
in the bay, but Vigo is not a place of any considerable export trade.       During
the summer months great numbers of cattle and eggs are sent to Falmouth and
Plymouth from this port.      It was just outside this port that HMS "Captain"
foundered in 1870.     After getting close to the land very little wind could be
felt, and the sea was quite smooth 1 the sun seemed to strike warmer, and by
the time we came to an anchor, we appeared to be in a different climate1 in
the evening the seamen of the other ships were bathing overboard, and this
morning our men were wearing winter clothing.


May 21st, Sunday.
     Took in 100 tons of coal to last us to England, the hands working all
(755) night, and finishing cleaning ship by 10 a.m.




                                       253
     The five-master Ironclad "Minotaur" arrived at 8 a.m. and anchored close
to us.      She is a splendid looking vessel bearing the flag of Rear Admiral
Beauchamp Seymour, commanding the Channel Fleet.


     Fresh meat, vegetables, and bread sufficient to last us four days were
taken in during the morning, and an officer and one seaman joined us from the
"Monarch" for passage to England.     At 2 p.m. the anchor was got up once more
for another attempt at reaching England.     Our band played "Homeward Bound" and
"Auld Lang Syne" as we steamed through the Fleet, and the "Monarch's band res-
ponded, but we could not hear what tune they played.        After getting two or
three miles down the bay (756) the splendid ironclad "Black Prince" was met on
the way to join the rest of the fleet at Vigo.     It was a beautiful warm day at
the anchorage, but as soon as we got outside the Bay, the cold wind began to
be felt.     The distance from Vigo to Plymouth is 520 miles -- to Portsmouth
about 650; when the "Captain" was lost, HMS "Inconstant" took the news to
England and was 29 hours steaming and sailing to Plymouth.


May 24th.
     Sighted old England once more at 7 a.m. when Start Point hove in sight
about 15 miles north;     stood away up channel under     all possible sail and
stearn. The wind was very light, and the weather beautifully cool and clear.
There were more vessels passed during the day than (754) we have seen at sea
since we left the channel in December 1872.      The Bill of Portland was passed
at 4 p.m. within signalling distance~ the distance from Portland to Portsmouth
is 60 miles so it will be late before we can arrive at Spithead.      The Needles
were passed at 7 p.m. and soon after 9:00 the anchor was let go and the mail
came on board as well as lots of officers' friends, etc.


May 25th.
     We find it very cold today almost like winter to us.     The ship is full of
people, friends and relatives of the officers, crew, etc. -- among others,
Mrs. Captain Nares and family.     In addition to these there were scores of out-
fitters, burn-boatmen, Jews, and sharpers, selling sham jewellry, boots, and
every conceivable (755) article.



                                       254
        Most of the scientific staff landed and went on leave, and the crew and
officers had leave to go on shore, until 10 p.m.       Close to us are lying the
"Valorous" and "Sultan".     The latter, a splendid ship of war, under the com-
mand of the Duke of Edinburgh.      The supernumary seamen, invalids, prisoners,
etc., were discharged to the "Duke of Wellington" today, and orders were re-
ceived for the "Challenger" to proceed to Sheerness to-morrow to payoff all
standing, that is without shipping, ready for recommissioning.


        In the evening the officers of the "Pandora" dined on board.       She is
about to sail again for the Arctic regions, and will take mails, etc., for the
(759) "Alert" and "Discovery·, to be left at the entrance to Smith' s Sound,
should the ships not be met with.       At 6 p.m. thirty-six supernumary seamen
came on board for passage to Sheerness, and the ship was ordered to proceed to
that port as soon as possible.       The anchor was got up at 10: 30 p.m. and we
steamed from Spithead up channel: about a dozen of the ship's company who were
not able to get on board in time were left, and will have to join the ship by
rail.


Yours sincerely,
Joe Matkin.



(760) HMS "Challenger".
Chatham, June 11, 1876.


Dear Tom:


        This is the last letter you will receive from this famous discovery. ship,
and shall conclude the descr iption of our long voyage by retracts from my
"Journal" since leaving Spithead.


        On May 26th we were under full steam all day: the weather wet, cold, and
miserable completely shutting out all view of the land.        A Swedish Gun-boat
was passed, and any amount of merchant shipping.       Dover was passed at 2 p.m.
and at 6 p.m. the anchor was let go at the great Nore about 8 (761) miles from
Sheerness, the fog being too dense to allow us to proceed with safety.
May 27th.
       Got up anchor at 5 a.m. and proceeded into the Medway, anchoring about 4
miles below Sheerness.            Thirty supernumeraries were discharged to the "Duncan"
flagship of Vice Admiral Chads, one of the finest line of battle ships in the
service.     This being kept as the Queen's Birthday was a general holiday in
Sheerness, all the Men of War were dressed with flags, and the "Duncan" fired
a royal salute at 12 o'clock.             The ship was full of visitors and we discharged
powder and shell.


       On the 28th, Sunday, all hands went on shore to the Dockyard Church.
Leave was given to the ship's company. (762) Ship was crowded with visitors of
all classes -- Lieutenant Lord G. Campbell, late of the "Challenger" being
among the number.


       On the 29th the ship was inspected by Vice Admiral Chadd, Commander in
Chief at the Nore, who expressed himself highly satisfied with the appearance
of the ship and her company.              All the deep sea sounding, dredging and trawling
apparatus was rigged for his inspection, and will remain in position, as the
ship is to be thrown open to the public for the next few days.                      Crowds of vis-
itors came on board during the day from London and elsewhere, but there is
very little for them to see as all the marine curiosities, etc., have been
sent away.     The next day a grand luncheon party was given by the officers to
some    of   the   Loros     of     the    Admiralty,   (763)     Members   of      the   Royal   and
Geographical Societies, etc.               The ship was crowded with visitors all day,
special trams running from London for their convenience ~ the ship was moved
yesterday from her         moor ings of Queensboro'         and towed close alongside             the
Sheerness Town Pier, which is near the Railway Station.                       HMS    "Duncan" lies
close to us.
June 6th.


       Since Wednesday crowds of visitors have daily visited the ship, and today
orders were received from the Admiralty for                     the ship to· be taken down to
Chatham ready for paying off.              We left Sheerness at 7 p.m. and entered the re-
pairing basin at Chatham dockyard at 11 a.mJ the Ironclad "Rupert" coming out
to make room for       us.         In the afternoon other orders            (764)    were   received


                                                256
for the ship to be taken out of the basin, further down the Medway alongside
the dockyard jetty, to be ready for paying off on Monday at 9 a .m.                 Nothing
but the provisions and scientific stores have to be taken out, as she is to be
recommissioned again shortly for coast guard service at Harwich, the crew of
the "Penelope" turning out to her from that ship.


        Another very distressing occurrence took place at about half-past six
this    evening    when   Sub-Lieutenant Henry C.E.       Harston committed suicide by
poisoning himself.         He was subject to fits of despondency, and on this part-
icular evening refused to come to dinner and retired to his cabin, where he
was heard to make a peculiar snoring noise, and found on inspection to be
black in the face.         The (765) surgeon was fetched as soon as possible, but he
was already dead.         The body was removed from the ship, and an inquest held,
when after hear ing the evidence the Jury decided that the deceased poisoned
himself by drinking chloral hydrate whilst in a state of temporary insanity.


        Wm. Harston was a fine looking you man, and a son of retired Captain
Harston, R.N. who was dreadfully grieved when the news reached him.                 The de-
ceased left a letter to the surgeon apologizing for the trouble he had given,
and giving a few weak reasons for his act.



Sunday, June 11th.
        All hands are busy clearing out storerooms, etc., ready for paying off.
On     the   8th   we   were   returning   stores   and closing   books   and   accounts
Professor Wyville (766) Thomson presented several of the leading hands of the
scientific and surveying party among the crew with silver cups as a souvenir
of the voyage.
June 12.


        Ship inspected by the dockyard authorities1 the savings bank money was
paid at 11 a.m. and the wages due to the ship's company at 2 p.m. when the
ship was paid off, and the crew granted 8 weeks leave.              Several of those who
were entitled took their discharges from the Navy -- myself among the number
-- finding sea life nought but vanity, and vexation of spirit, especially the


                                             257
latter -- my opinion of it coinciding with that of Dr. Samuel Johnson's A.D.
1776 -- with which quotation I will conclude my long series of letters from
(767)   HMS   "Challenger".


        "A ship is worse than a jail.          There is in a jail, better air, better
company, better conveniency of every kind; and a ship has the additional dis-
advantage of being in danger.            When men come to like a sea-life, they are not
fit to live on land.


        Men go to sea before they know the unhappiness of that way of life; and
when they have come to know it, they cannot escape from it, because it is then
too late to choose another profession; as indeed is generally the case with
men, when they have once engaged in any particular way of life."


        Hoping to see you to-morrow,
        Believe me,
        Sincerely yours,


        Joe Matkin.
