                                                  Series XIV: House/Senate: Campaigns, 1946-1976
                                                   48 linear feet

                                                   This series covers a broad range of topics relating to Mansfield's personal campaigns for both U.S. House of
                                                   Representatives and the U.S. Senate. The series also contains significant material relating to other
                                                   Congressional campaigns in Montana and to presidential campaigns throughout this time. As Mansfield grows
                                                   more prominent in national politics, the files grow more extensive and cover a broader spectrum of races from



http://nwda.orbiscascade.org/ark:/80444/xv87911[24/05/2014 20:10:41]
Guide to the Mike Mansfield Papers 1903-1990


                                                   across the country.
                                                   There are oversize copies from the Office of Montana General Election Results for both primaries and the
                                                   general elections. These returns cover the even-year elections from 1946 to 1972, with the exception of 1968.
                                                   There are numerous letters from constituents to Mansfield concerning his campaigns. They include many notes
                                                   of congratulations, offers of assistance, letters of support and opposition, advice, requests for inaugural tickets,
                                                   and requests for help and support on various issues. The series also contains Mansfield's letter and telegrams in
                                                   reply to this correspondence. Mansfield's press releases and copies of his speeches are scattered throughout the
                                                   series. There is also significant correspondence from congressional colleagues and from prominent fellow
                                                   Democrats. In the 1960s and 1970s there were many letters from presidential hopefuls seeking Mansfield's
                                                   endorsement. Democratic leaders routinely requested Mansfield's help in stumping for candidates, so there are
                                                   a number of personal letters from Adlai Stevenson, Hubert Humphrey, George McGovern, Jimmy Carter, and
                                                   Sargent Shriver. A copy of the McGovern-Shriver Handbook for the 1972 election is in Box 90, and there are
                                                   folders containing information relative to the Stevenson, Kefauver, Fjare, Eisenhower, and Nixon presidential
                                                   campaigns.
                                                   A number of folders also contain information on Montana campaigns, including letters, booklets, newsletters,
                                                   and bumper stickers for Arnold Olsen, Lee Metcalf, and James Murray. There are also candid Democratic
                                                   assessments of the Montana political climate. The series is rounded out with other campaign-related materials.
                                                   These include background information on candidates, correspondence relating to the Watergate and "dog
                                                   named Nixon" controversies, and Mansfield's nominating speech for Sargent Shriver. There are numerous
                                                   document requests and newspaper clippings from constituents, generally that reflect prevailing attitudes but
                                                   also support Mansfield and oppose Nixon. Finally, there are invitations to Eisenhower's inaugural ball, other
                                                   candidates' press releases, and guidelines to selecting delegates to the 1976 national conventions for both
                                                   Democrats and Republicans.

                                                   The series contains boxes specifying time periods like "U.S. Senate Fourth Term 1971-1976" and boxes with
                                                   vague designations like "House and Senate: Campaign," and is in no coherent order. There is no box 1.

                                                  Series XV: Senate: Correspondence, 1953-1976
                                                   168.5 linear feet



http://nwda.orbiscascade.org/ark:/80444/xv87911[24/05/2014 20:10:41]
Guide to the Mike Mansfield Papers 1903-1990



                                                   This series contains all of the outgoing correspondence from Mansfield's office during his tenure in the Senate.
                                                   The folders contain copies of the letters and telegrams sent by the office.
                                                   The letters cover all aspects of Mansfield's job in the Senate. They include reply letters to constituents on a
                                                   variety of topics, numerous condolence letters to constituents, and thanks to various Montanans for campaign
                                                   assistance. The constituent topics include correspondence relating to pending legislation, military personnel
                                                   issues like court martials, concerns about Social Security and inflation, job applications, labor disputes, the war
                                                   in Vietnam, hippies, farm conditions, and Academy appointments. Besides the constituent mail, there is
                                                   significant correspondence with Congressional colleagues, various federal agencies, the White House, and
                                                   foreign dignitaries. These letters also cover a broad range of topics including pending legislation, informal and
                                                   formal Committee meetings, the House Committee on Un-American Affairs, agricultural subsidies, and civil
                                                   rights. The vast majority of the letters are a single page, though matters of particular importance sometimes
                                                   cover two or three pages.
                                                   In general, Mansfield's replies are not particularly substantive, and many are variations on standard form
                                                   letters that appear repeatedly throughout Mansfield's files. Nevertheless, the subjects and volume of mail
                                                   provide insights into the political concerns of the era. Specific issues, like passage of the Wilderness Act in
                                                   1964, can be traced through letters sent daily from Mansfield's office. Particularly volatile political issues like
                                                   opposition to the Vietnam War are reflected in voluminous correspondence on the subject. Mansfield's rising
                                                   political importance is seen in the increasing volume of mail his office replies to and the prominence of the
                                                   correspondents. The letters also provide an excellent overview of the overwhelming array of concerns a Senator
                                                   copes with and the affection that Mansfield elicited from Montanans.

                                                   The typical box holds four or five weeks of letters broken into folders containing a week of correspondence
                                                   each. The folders are arranged chronologically, with all of the communications for a single day grouped
                                                   together. The series is arranged in four chronological subseries: First Term, Second Term, Third Term, and
                                                   Fourth Term, and proceeds from November 1953 to the end of Mansfield's fourth term in 1976. The series is
                                                   arranged strictly chronologically; after box 190 the folders shift from containing a week of correspondence to
                                                   holding a single day. Many of the copies in this series appear elsewhere in the collection in a subject area. Some
                                                   of the boxes have pink inserts highlighting particular topics and issues. These inserts do not seem to follow any
                                                   pattern and often mark a single letter.

                                                  Series XVI: House/Senate: Academy Appointments, 1943-1977
                                                   31.5 linear feet

                                                   The material contained in this series relates to Congressional appointments to the various service academies,
                                                   particularly West Point and Annapolis. Most of the series relates to Mansfield's files on specific candidates for
                                                   appointments from his home state. Besides candidate files, there are a number of boxes containing general
                                                   information about the particular academies such as civil service examination requirements and guidelines for
                                                   nominations. Most of this series holds a predictable repetition of documents.
                                                   The series is divided between boxes with general information and boxes of candidate files. The bulk of the
                                                   series is comprised of a chronological listing of academy candidates from Montana, filed alphabetically by year.
                                                   For example, Box 30 has all the folders for candidates in 1966 beginning with the letter I. Accompanying
                                                   candidate files are letters of recommendation, test scores, nomination forms, and Mansfield's replies to
                                                   candidate inquiries. Many files contain other, unofficial letters supporting various candidates and offer a
                                                   glimpse of a whole generation of each Montana community's leading sons. The more general files relate to
                                                   specific academies including the Coast Guard Academy, the Air Force Academy, the Merchant Marine Academy,
                                                   the Military Academy, and the Naval Academy. There are catalogs beginning in the early 1940's regarding
                                                   admissions standards. Mimeographs for medical examinations forms, results of candidates' medical exams,
                                                   information about the Civil Service exam, newspaper clippings about candidates, studies of the success rates of
                                                   different candidates, and progress reports of appointees occupy the rest of the general files in the series. As
                                                   mentioned above, this series is more descriptive than substantive, containing a shallow sample of information
                                                   about each candidate and Academy.

                                                   The organization of the series is coherent. The opening boxes of general information are followed by a
                                                   chronological sequence of candidate files leading to the year of Mansfield's retirement from the Senate in 1976.

                                                   This series is restricted.


                                               ^ Return to Top

                                                  Series XVII: House/Senate: Projects, 1943-1977
                                                   180 linear feet

                                                   This series contains information relating to federal projects in Montana during Mansfield's entire tenure in
                                                   Washington. Almost every aspect of life under the Big Sky is referenced in these files and the series gives an
                                                   indication of the breadth of federal involvement in the state. The folders include a dizzying array of documents
                                                   that represent every step in a government project from letters supporting creating new policy to documents
                                                   about Congressional appropriations to maps and blueprints to newspaper clippings announcing the new
                                                   facilities and programs. This series focuses more on the administration of projects than on the legislation
                                                   involved, though there is overlap with the Federal Agencies, the Montana Files, and the Legislation series.
                                                   The specifics of this series are especially difficult to quantify since the series covers so many subjects for such a
                                                   long time span. The materials represent Mansfield's time in both House and Senate, though the majority of the
                                                   folders seem to center on his Senatorial career. It appears that the series proceeds alphabetically by subject or
                                                   supervising agency but this is only a rough frame of reference. The organization is confusing and adheres to no



http://nwda.orbiscascade.org/ark:/80444/xv87911[24/05/2014 20:10:41]
Guide to the Mike Mansfield Papers 1903-1990


                                                   particular chronology. For example the folder titled "City Project Billings: Relocation of the Northern Pacific
                                                   Tracks" has papers dating from 1959 to 1975, while an adjacent Billings folder has documents from 1971 to
                                                   1973. There are multiple boxes that contain only city project information, appropriations material, and reports
                                                   on Montana industries, schools, and Air Force bases. The industry folders hold reports from the Forest Service,
                                                   the Commerce Department, and government investigations of trucking practices. There are also letters
                                                   supporting various industries, especially timber, from voters, workers, and lobbying groups. Timber sale
                                                   revenues, newspaper clippings, reports to Senate committees, and papers from industry conferences round out
                                                   this portion of the series. The files on public works projects range from political concerns to the practical
                                                   problems of administering specific programs. The Master Plan for Helena includes letters from constituents,
                                                   maps of the city, historic preservation information, Housing and Urban Development applications, reports
                                                   concerning drug and alcohol abuse, photographs of proposed improvement areas, and information about the
                                                   municipal golf course. Similar information appears for many of Montana's cities and towns. Other boxes have
                                                   material concerning the Economic Development Administration, the Montana Department of Public
                                                   Instruction, bussing issues in schools, teacher contracts, and cutbacks in school sports to meet Title IX
                                                   requirements. There are newspaper stories, reports from the Army Corps of Engineers, and Mansfield's own
                                                   notes about water rights in the Missouri River Basin. Development schemes to promote tourism and federal
                                                   help with airports, health care, and employment problems are documented here. The series is completed with a
                                                   staggering array of more government reports, letters from Montana voters and local boosters promoting plans,
                                                   and Mansfield's replies to correspondence.

                                                   Finding specific information in this series can be time-consuming, but given the extent of the series any federal
                                                   project in Montana that concerned Mansfield is probably referenced. The Appropriations Boxes are particularly
                                                   interesting because they demonstrate the level of federal spending in the state for any given year. There are also
                                                   some very complimentary letters to Mansfield for his efforts on his constituents' behalf. As mentioned above,
                                                   some related material appears in other series, especially Federal Agencies.

                                                  Series XVIII: Senate: Intergovernmental Correspondence, 1953-1977
                                                   27 linear feet

                                                   The material collected here primarily relates to the internal affairs of the Senate. The volume of correspondence
                                                   grows markedly after Mansfield's selection as Majority Leader. Most of the documents concern fairly mundane
                                                   matters like assigned parking spaces and requisitioning typewriters for the office. The series begins with several
                                                   boxes of miscellaneous personal files arranged chronologically. These are followed by other Senate affairs boxes
                                                   and boxes relating to Majority Leadership. Beginning at Box 40, the remainder of the series is composed of
                                                   folders for specific senators, listed alphabetically. There are newspaper clippings, government reports, copies of
                                                   the Congressional Record, voting record tallies, and telegrams, but the majority of the folders contain letters.
                                                   Mansfield's arrival in the Senate is marked by routine administrative documents including letters from the
                                                   Sergeant at Arms and a copy of Senate Rules. There are copies of Mansfield's letters regarding committee
                                                   appointments and his radio broadcasts. Later there are letters regarding Senate employees, reservations in the
                                                   Senate dining room, security clearance notices, Mansfield's staff, scheduling of hearings and meetings, and
                                                   unofficial advocacy of pending legislation. Odds and ends included here are directories of the Congressional
                                                   Secretaries Club, maps of the Senate Office Building, reports on restoration of the Capitol, press releases from
                                                   President Johnson, and plans for plaques in John F. Kennedy's old Senate office.
                                                   The files on Majority Leadership also proceed chronologically but contain a more repetitive collection of
                                                   documents. The folders are divided by Congressional session and focus on record-keeping. The folders contain
                                                   copies of voting records from the session and attendance lists for each Senator. There are letters to all Senators
                                                   at the end of most sessions, letters informing Senators of imminent key votes, thank-you letters to the Assistant
                                                   Senate Whip, Democratic Policy Committee reports, letters regarding legislative oversight, and information
                                                   regarding Mansfield's responsibilities as Senate Whip. The files for individual Senators vary greatly; those for
                                                   important Democratic Senators are the most substantial. For example, there is extensive material for Hubert
                                                   Humphrey and very little Harrison Williams, Jr. Some folders contain policy information like military strategy
                                                   reports and specific legislation. Others hold requests for autographed pictures for colleague's staffs and press
                                                   releases. The letters between Senators are very interesting and provide a glimpse of the personal relations
                                                   among Congressional members. There are a number of very complimentary letters to Mansfield from his
                                                   Senate colleagues and from constituents regarding their general happiness with his performance in
                                                   Washington.

                                                   The overall organization of the series is fairly clear. Most of the material here does not overlap with other
                                                   series, though references to particular legislation may appear across several series. The primary value of these
                                                   documents is to provide a good background for understanding the behind-the-scenes machinations of Senate
                                                   business.

                                                  Series XIX: House/Senate: Personal, 1943-1977
                                                   304 linear feet

                                                   This voluminous series is focused on correspondence and scheduling; the material contained here is
                                                   considerably less intimate than the title implies. It covers the entire time that Mansfield spent in Washington
                                                   and becomes broader as his Senate career progresses. There are huge portions of the series that contain



http://nwda.orbiscascade.org/ark:/80444/xv87911[24/05/2014 20:10:41]
Guide to the Mike Mansfield Papers 1903-1990


                                                   nothing but Christmas cards received or copies of condolence letters sent by Mansfield's office to constituents.
                                                   It is easy to divide the series into coherent blocks and then follow chronology within those blocks, though
                                                   locating information in individual boxes can be difficult.
                                                   The first one hundred and thirty boxes hold copies of condolence letters sent to constituents. These are
                                                   cataloged chronologically beginning in 1943. Sometimes the folders are divided alphabetically within a given
                                                   year. Generally, a folder contains all the letters either a single month or half a year. The letters usually follow
                                                   the same basic outline, though there are some very personal letters. Of note is Mansfield's letter to Mrs.
                                                   Roosevelt upon the death of the President in 1945. All of the letters manage to be individual and the volume of
                                                   letters sent increases dramatically as with Mansfield's importance and a growing staff. Most of the letters are
                                                   addressed to Montanans who have lost a relative. Condolence letters to the families of servicemen in World War
                                                   II, Korea, and Vietnam are mixed into the folders during the appropriate time periods. Reply letters from the
                                                   bereaved and newspaper obituary clippings fill out the folders here and most of the "Miscellaneous" folders
                                                   contain replies and thank-yous for condolences. Following the condolence letters are almost one hundred boxes
                                                   of Christmas cards. These include both thank you letters from recipients of Mansfield's cards and the hundreds
                                                   of incoming cards the Senator and Maureen Mansfield received every year. Most cards are from Montana
                                                   voters, though congressional colleagues, trade associations, corporations, interest groups, and citizens all over
                                                   the country are also represented. Thank-you letters for gifts received by the Mansfields are also included here
                                                   and dozens of Christmas photos sent by constituents appear throughout the series.
                                                   The Christmas correspondence is organized chronologically, though some boxes contain no dividing folders.
                                                   Despite the clear chronological divisions, locating material inside the boxes is quite difficult because of this lack
                                                   of order. The remainder of the series deals with scheduling and invitations. The invitations are organized
                                                   chronologically and include designations regarding whether they were accepted or declined. Invitations from
                                                   Montana are filed separately. The sheer volume of invitations indicates the demands on a Senator's time and
                                                   the range of people interested in having him appear. The functions range from black tie affairs for ambassadors
                                                   in Washington to birthday parties in Montana. After Box 302, the invitations are accompanied by daily
                                                   schedules for both Senator and Maureen Mansfield through the end of the his career in the Senate. There are
                                                   also schedules for their driver, requests for appointments from constituents and non-constituents alike, and
                                                   invitations to keep in mind.

                                                   While the series is not particularly substantive in some ways, it provides insight into the quantity of mail a
                                                   Senator receives and the array of social duties that are expected of an elected official. The larger organizational
                                                   scheme for the series is clear and can be derived from the index. Unfortunately, inside the boxes are thick
                                                   packets of cards and letters that require considerable time to investigate. Little of the information here appears
                                                   in other series, though this series also provides valuable background for documents elsewhere.

                                                  Series XX: Senate: Secretary to Majority, 1961-1977
                                                   14 linear feet

                                                   The parameters of this series are unclear but appear to consist of reports on a variety of government projects
                                                   during the time that Mansfield was Senate Majority Leader. Almost all of the contents are focused on projects
                                                   inside Montana, though there are national programs represented also. Boxes typically contain information on a
                                                   single large project and individual folders divide the information chronologically. The series holds letters,
                                                   official reports, clippings, excerpts from the Congressional Record, copies of legislation, and testimony from
                                                   Mansfield and Metcalf supporting specific projects.
                                                   Boxes contain documents relating to magnetohydrodynamics, Glasgow Air Force Base, and the National Center
                                                   for Appropriate Technology, among others. Supporting materials include numerous letters from interest groups
                                                   and constituents to Mansfield. Other letters include those from Senate colleagues, federal agencies like the
                                                   Office of Coal Research, and Montana State University-Bozeman. Accompanying specific projects are status
                                                   reports from the governing agencies including an update on Emergency Energy Conservation Programs by the
                                                   Community Services Administration. There are fourteen copies of the Technical Data Sheet for the Glasgow Air
                                                   Force Base's proposed National Human Resource Center that were prepared by Mansfield and Metcalf's offices.
                                                   These share a box with twenty-seven copies of a 1975 report on using Glasgow Air Force Base as a
                                                   transportation hub for supplying the Alaskan pipeline construction. In addition there is testimony from Senate
                                                   Appropriation Committee hearings, legislative amendments, and fact sheets on proposed research. Some of the
                                                   boxes are divided into several bound notebooks on a specific topic. For example the box on
                                                   magnetohydrodynamics is split into two books, each of which is carefully labeled with numbers corresponding
                                                   to a detailed index included in the front of the book.

                                                   Despite clear organization and helpful indexing in individual boxes, there is little indication why this material
                                                   appears here and not in already existing series on similar topics. All of the information here could fit into either
                                                   Federal Agencies or Montana Projects. If a program does not appear in the two larger series it is worth checking
                                                   here as well, and material here may provide more depth to subjects found elsewhere.

                                                  Series XXI: House/Senate: Speeches and Reports, 1942-1977
                                                   36.5 linear feet

                                                   This series is primarily documentary and is evenly divided between collections of clippings and copies of
                                                   speeches. The series covers Mansfield's entire tenure in Washington. The organization of the series is clear and
                                                   coherent. The first thirty-three boxes contain clippings, and the speeches listed chronologically beginning in
                                                   1952 start at Box 35. The clippings are from newspapers, magazines, and the Congressional Record. They
                                                   appear to have been compiled by Mansfield's staff and include a broad range of subjects. The boxes initially
                                                   begin with folders divided by subject, with all the clippings on a given topic grouped together. These include
                                                   topics like foreign affairs, Berlin, Asia, and H. H. Adberson. Though subject divisions help locate information, a
                                                   "Montana Affairs" folder might hold information on local news, federal projects in the state, and editorials from
                                                   newspapers around Montana. The boxes shift to chronological divisions and contain unsorted clippings for any
                                                   given month in a single folder. For example the "July 1973" file holds stories about cloud seeding, library
                                                   funding, real estate sales, and a Butte fire. It is unclear why some categories of clippings like Asia appear here
                                                   and not in the Foreign Relations series, but it is worth checking both places for information. The clippings do
                                                   show both what news interested Mansfield's office over more than thirty years and a progression of news
                                                   highlights from Montana over that same span.
                                                   The collected speeches begin in 1952 and proceed chronologically to 1976. They include drafts and copies of
                                                   speeches Mansfield made. Testimony for House and Senate hearings, transcripts of radio and television
                                                   broadcasts, and press releases from Mansfield's office also appear in these boxes. Many of the speeches and
                                                   addresses were printed in the Congressional Record and copies are in the files. There are also copies of




http://nwda.orbiscascade.org/ark:/80444/xv87911[24/05/2014 20:10:41]
Guide to the Mike Mansfield Papers 1903-1990


                                                   speeches, testimony, and press releases from other members of Montana's Congressional delegation. The
                                                   speeches portion of the series serves as a nice complement to the rest of the collection by providing Mansfield's
                                                   actual words on a plethora of topics documented in other series.
                                                   There are also many of Mansfield's speeches and materials related to them located in Series XIX: Personal.
                                                   In 2012 this series was reviewed in advance of digitization. Duplicates were removed; folder titles cleaned up
                                                   when needed; and untranscribed folder titles were added resulting in some renumbering of folders in boxes 36-
                                                   51.

                                               ^ Return to Top

                                                  Series XXII: Senate: Leadership, 1961-1977
                                                   72 linear feet

                                                   This series includes an amalgamation of information relating to Mansfield's time as Senate Majority Leader.
                                                   The documents range from voting and attendance records for Senators during a Congressional session to
                                                   memorabilia from Maureen Mansfield's trips abroad with the Kennedys and Johnsons. The bulk of the series
                                                   focuses on boxes relating to legislation, foreign affairs, and other policy business in the Senate. There are also
                                                   files on weekly Majority Conference meetings and files for individual people including constituents,
                                                   ambassadors, General MacArthur, and Jacqueline Kennedy. The series holds letters, reports, press releases,
                                                   clippings, survey results, minutes for informal Democratic leadership meetings, and memorandums from the
                                                   Central Intelligence Agency.
                                                   The structure of the series is inconsistent, though parts of the series are clearly organized. The first boxes in the
                                                   series contain basic housekeeping documents from the Senate. These include voting worksheets on various
                                                   bills, absentee lists, attendance records for each senator, and copies of the Congressional Record. The boxes are
                                                   not arranged chronologically but individual folders are labeled by Congressional session. Following these boxes
                                                   are about fifty that contain material on a wide variety of topics. There is no clear organizing principle and most
                                                   of this information overlaps with other series. For example the folder "Legislation-Gun Control (Firearms)"
                                                   holds letters from interest groups, copies of Mansfield's letters and statements on the issue, a working draft of
                                                   the bill, and newspaper clippings. Generally these folders are titled by legislative subject or foreign affairs area.
                                                   Individual nations have their own folders, though there are regional folders as well. For example, there are
                                                   extensive files on the Middle East concerning the 1967 Egypt-Israeli war. Some of the legislation files do have a
                                                   specifically leadership slant and contain documents analyzing legislative strategies for passing pending bills.
                                                   Progress reports on President Johnson's legislative agenda, synopses of Senate activity for a given
                                                   Congressional session, and letters from the Democratic Policy Committee also reveal leadership issues. The
                                                   foreign affairs folder tends to be general but also contains information like choices for Great Britain's
                                                   bicentennial gift that concern Mansfield's leadership position in the Senate. The synopsis reports from the
                                                   weekly Majority Conference meetings are especially interesting because they chronicle candid policy discussions
                                                   among Congressional Democratic leaders. These reports are collected chronologically by Congressional session
                                                   and also include meetings on particularly important topics like the nation's economic situation in 1970. The end
                                                   of the series has a number of folders labeled "personal" and containing correspondence and reports relating to
                                                   the person on the title. Typically the letters pertain to business connected with Mansfield's majority leadership
                                                   and many are on purely partisan matters. The folder on Charles Ferris provides an interesting glimpse into the
                                                   importance of party workers in determining the practices of elected officials. Some of the folders contain
                                                   nothing more than thank-you letters for helping a constituent gain contacts abroad while others hold
                                                   information about Senate scandals like the resignation of Secretary of the Majority Baker.

                                                   The series is divided into seven subseries: Attendance Records; Domestic Affairs; Foreign Affairs; Leadership
                                                   Functions; Speeches, Trips, and Reports; Policy Committee; and Majority Leaders Office. The attendance
                                                   records and voting tallies are easy to follow. The following foreign affairs and legislation files show no particular
                                                   structure and adjacent folders might contain a bill from 1966 and another from 1974. The Majority Conference
                                                   meetings follow chronologically but the personal files have no apparent order. Finding specific information here
                                                   is difficult and folder names are probably the best guide to the hidden treasures about the real workings of
                                                   American government.

                                                  Series XXIV: House/Senate: Clippings and Scrapbooks, 1903-1982
                                                   316 volumes and 0.25 linear feet

                                                   This series contains albums and folders of newspaper and magazine clippings about Mansfield or collected by
                                                   his staff. The clippings are from Montana-based, national, and international publications. There are numerous
                                                   profiles of Mansfield and of his close political associates, news articles on crucial issues and events, and
                                                   analyzes of legislation and political events. Dates are occasionally added to the articles. Most of the albums are
                                                   simple chronologies, but some focus on particular events, including John F. Kennedy's assassination,
                                                   campaigns and elections, Kennedy's 1963 trip to Montana, the 1964 Montana floods, trips to Mexico and that
                                                   Far East, and the Mansfield Lecture Series at The University of Montana. There are index volumes for 1963 and
                                                   1964. The albums also contain campaign materials, a few photographs, programs, and certificates. There are
                                                   also presentation albums given Mansfield on important occasions, including Olivet College commencement and
                                                   several informational binders put together by the Park Service and the Forest Service to inform Mansfield of
                                                   issues of interest. Most are from Mansfield's congressional period, but there is a bit of overlap with his term as
                                                   Ambassador.

                                                   Materials are divided into two subseries: Clippings and Scrapbooks. They are arranged chronologically within
                                                   each category.

                                                  Series XXVII: House/Senate/Ambassador: Moving Images, 1956-1987
                                                   132 pieces

                                                   This series consists of 55 reels of 16 mm film and 77 videotapes in 3/4', VHS, Beta, and 2' formats. Most were
                                                   recorded by the major television networks, the Senate and House recording studio, or other professionals.
                                                   Venues include interviews, single and joint presentations, campaign materials, video conferences, and
                                                   ceremonies and events. There are also tapes that focus exclusively on other individuals, including Ronald
                                                   Reagan. Several tapes and films were made during events at The University of Montana, including the
                                                   establishment of the Mike Mansfield Endowment Lecture Series and subsequent lecturers and other events at
                                                   the Mansfield Center. There are numerous recordings of Mansfield's appearances on television programs,
                                                   including Face the Nation, Washington Conversation, Eyewitness to History, 60 Minutes, and Good Morning
                                                   America. There are also numerous materials relating to John F. Kennedy, including the eulogy delivered by
                                                   Mansfield. Other materials focus on Mansfield's time as ambassador, and include President Reagan's 1983 visit
                                                   to Japan and interviews of Mansfield on Japanese television. Materials are mostly in English, but there is some
                                                   Japanese.

                                                   Materials are arranged in five Subseries by format: 16mm film, 3/4 Inch Video, VHS Video, Beta Video, and
                                                   Two-inch Video. Within these Subseries, materials are arranged chronologically.

                                                  Series XXIX: House/Senate/Ambassador: Awards and Memorabilia, 1937-1986 and
                                                  undated
                                                   40 oversize boxes

                                                   This series contains a wide variety of awards and memorabilia that Mansfield owned or was given as gifts and
                                                   recognition. It is distinct from the Art Objects series because most objects are of a more documentary than
                                                   artistic nature. Objects of note include badges from Democratic National Conventions, a piece of marble from
                                                   the U.S. Capitol taken during remodeling, and many souveniers of the ambassadorial period.

Guide to the Mike Mansfield Papers 1903-1990


                                                  Series XXX: Ambassador: General Correspondence, 1977-1988
                                                   21 linear feet

                                                   This series consists of Mansfield's correspondence during his ambassadorship, and includes mostly letters to
                                                   and from U.S. congressmen; embassy associates; constituents about concerns; businesses; and people in
                                                   Montana. The letters are generally personal, not form, letters, and a carbon copy of Mansfield's reply is usually
                                                   included. Most materials are in English, but there are a few things in Japanese.

                                                   Materials are arranged chronologically, then alphabetically within years. Letters are alphabetical by
                                                   correspondent name in most folders; the full name of the correspondent was typed on the long edge of the letter
                                                   by Mansfield's staff for easy location of individual pieces.

                                                  Series XXXIV: Ambassador: Scrapbooks and Albums, 1977-1985
                                                   12.5 linear feet

                                                   This series consists of scrapbooks and albums compiled by Mansfield's staff. They contain mostly newspaper
                                                   clippings, letters, program, and invitations. Most are professional, but a few are personal materials relating to
                                                   wedding anniversaries, birthdays, and other important events. Most of the materials are in English, but a few
                                                   are in Japanese or French. Mansfield's staff often annotated the materials as they assembled albums, adding
                                                   last names when only the first name was signed to a letter, for example.

                                                   Materials are arranged chronologically.


                                               ^ Return to Top

                                                  Series XXXV: Ambassador: Art Objects, 17th century-1988
                                                   600 pieces

                                                   This series consists of art objects that Mansfield collected or received as gifts during his terms as representative,
                                                   senator, or ambassador, mostly the latter. Most of the art objects are from the Far East, including Japan, China,
                                                   Burma, and Thailand. However, there are also numerous objects from Mexico, the Middle East, and the United
                                                   States, particularly gifts from Montana constituents.
                                                   The objects are divided into fourteen Subseries: Boxes and Incense Burners; Dolls and Masks; Cartoons,



http://nwda.orbiscascade.org/ark:/80444/xv87911[24/05/2014 20:10:41]
Guide to the Mike Mansfield Papers 1903-1990


                                                   Caricatures, and Drawings; Knives and Swords; Medals and Jewelry; Musical Instruments; Other Objects;
                                                   Paintings; Paper Arts; Prints and Posters; Sculpture; Tableware; Textiles; and vases.

                                                   Objects are arranged in their subseries according to accession number.


                                               ^ Return to Top

                                                  Series XXXVI: House/Senate/Ambassador: Photographs, 1942-1988
                                                   approx. 7500 images

                                                   The photographs in this collection were gathered by Mansfield's office from a variety of sources. A few
                                                   snapshots were produced by Mansfield himself, but the bulk of the images were taken by news and commercial
                                                   photographers at official events and ceremonies. Maureen Mansfield appears in many of the images with the
                                                   Senator or by herself. Not all of the photographers are identified; researchers wishing to republish the images
                                                   should be aware of the difficulty of clearing copyright. There are no photographs of the Mansfields taken before
                                                   his election to the House in 1942, nor are there images that postdate his ambassadorship. Many of the images
                                                   are official portraits; there are autographed portraits from several presidents and high officials in the United
                                                   States government. There is especially complete coverage of Mansfield's Asia trips beginning in 1944.
                                                   Most of the images were originally housed in albums assembled by Mansfield's staff and by persons who gave
                                                   him the albums as gifts. The titles of the albums have been retained, but the photographs have been removed
                                                   and listed individually. Identifications and dates were transcribed from the albums as available; many of the
                                                   photographs, particularly those from the ambassadorial period, are not well identified.
                                                   A few albums have been left intact because of the mix of materials inside or the intrinsic value of the album.
                                                   These are mostly from the ambassadorial period, and are listed at the end of the series.
                                                   A portion of this series includes small framed photographs with individual numbers. Many of these are
                                                   autographed as well. These are listed at the beginning of the series.

           Poetry (By Howard
           McCord, unless stated
           otherwise.)                     Biographical Note                    +/-




                                           Howard McCord was born on November 3, 1932, in El Paso, Texas. After a hitch in the U.S. Navy during the Korean
          Series 3: Published Works
                                           War, he returned to El Paso and attended Texas Western College receiving a Bachelor of Arts degree in Business. The
           from Journals (By
           Howard McCord, unless           following year he received a Master of Arts degree in English from the University of Utah. In 1960, he began teaching
           stated otherwise.)              at Washington State University offering courses in Poetry and Eastern Civilizations. He also began the graduate
                                           program in Creative Writing. In 1965 he was awarded a Fulbright scholarship which allowed him to travel extensively
          Series 4: Monographs by          in India and Nepal and study for a year at the University of Mysore. In 1971, he was appointed Professor of English
           Howard McCord                   and Director of the MFA program at Bowling Green State University. The North Carolina Poetry Circuit selected him
                                           as visiting poet for the fall of 1971, and he gave readings at campuses throughout the state. Besides his studies in India,
          Series 5: Monographs by          he also traveled through Iceland and published a book of poetry about his trip. His published works include poems in
           Others                          over 15 collections of poetry, as well as inclusion in numerous journals and monographs. From 1960 to 1977 his Tribal
                                           Press published many works of poetry in various formats.
          Series 6: Miscellaneous
           Materials

    Collection Overview                                                                                            Table of contents


    Description          This collection of stereographs compiled by Charles L. Camp consists of 181               Collection Overview
                         photographic prints from circa 1867 to circa 1895. The photographers include              Collection Details
                         Eadweard Muybridge, Carleton E. Watkins, M. M. Hazeltine, Walker &
                                                                                                                   Collection Summary
                         Fagersteen, William Henry Jackson, J. J. Reilly, Barkaiow Bros. (Omaha),                  Information for Researchers
                         Kilburn Bros. (N. H.), Halsey and Coffin, Hayward & Muzzall, C. W. J. Johnson,            Administrative Information
                         T. J. Norton, H. T. Payne, A. J. Perkins, J. Pitcher Spooner, Andrew Price, W.            Biography
                         N. Tuttle Photo, C. R. Savage, Savage & Ottinger's, William Shew, Chas.                   Scope and Content

                         Weitfle, R. E. Wood (Santa Cruz), Underwood & Underwood, Edward De Froffs
                         (Sitka, Alaska), T. W. Ingersoll, J. D. McAuliffe (Tucson), and Thomas                        Container Listing
                         Houseworth & Co. Included are images of mountains, hot springs, rivers, falls,
                         mining, trains and train tracks, a few California Indian images, city views,
                         camping, and the 1868 and 1906 San Francisco earthquakes. Locations
                         featured include San Francisco, Berkeley, Yosemite, Stockton, Los Angeles,
                         Pasadena, Santa Barbara, the counties of Sonoma, Lake and Napa,
                         Yellowstone National Park, Salt Lake City, Wyoming, Sitka (Alaska), and others.

    Background           Charles Lewis Camp was born in 1893 in Jamestown, North Dakota. Camp
                         attended the University of California, Berkeley and received his M.A. degree
                         from Columbia University. He served in World War I before returning to
                         Columbia to teach and earn his Ph.D. He then went back to Berkeley and
                         became a Research Associate at the Museum of Paleontology at U.C.
                         Berkeley, where he remained for the rest of his career. Known for his collecting
                         of fossils in Nevada and elsewhere, he became a professor of Paleontology
                         and head of the Department as well as director of the Museum.

    Extent               181 photographic prints ; stereograph, some albumen ; various sizes 182 digital
                         objects

                               Special Collections and Archives

                                   William D. Taylor, Papers, 1938-71

                                   Inventory

                                   Prepared by Leslie Warren, Mar. 17, 1977
                                   Prepared for World Wide Web by Barbara Bass, May 30, 1997
                                   4 rsb's, 3 document boxes, 5.75 cubic ft., 11th floor

                                   Biography

                                   William D. Taylor was born in Hartford, Kansas on Dec. 5, 1903. He received his Master and Bachelor of Arts degrees from the University of Washington where his family had
                                   moved when Taylor was at an early age.

                                   Taylor began his journalism career as a reporter for the Spokane (Washington) Daily Chronicle. He taught at Arizona State University and Northwestern University before coming
                                   to Kent State University. Taylor was the first Chairman of the School of Journalism from 1936-1963. The new architecture and journalism building was named for Taylor after
                                   Pres. White learned that he was to retire during the year (1967) that the new building would be opened.

                                   He was given a commendation for pioneering leadership in education for press photography by the National Press Photographers Association in 1949. In 1950 he was awarded
                                   the Governor's Award for advancement and in 1952 he won the Crusade for Freedom Citation. In 1961 a journalism alumni award was established and named the William Taylor
                                   Award and has been presented to an alumus each year since.

                                   Taylor served on boards for the Canton Art Institute and the Canton Symphony Orchestra and many other community organizations including the Kent Rotary where he held the
                                   position of president at one time.

                                   Taylor retired in 1967 and kept in contact with his students and they with him. He served on the Inauguration Committee for President Robert I. White and Presidential Search
                                   Committee in 1971. He served as a trustee from 1969 until his death on Nov. 3, 1975 at the age of 71.

                                   Scope and Content

                                   This collection contains materials relating to Kent State University and the activities in which Taylor played a major role especially in the area of journalism and performing arts
                                   such as the Ohio Arts Council contained in box 3.

                                   Box 1, folder 1 contains correspondence on the proposal of a land purchase in 1966 next to Blossom Music Center for use by the university for the College of Fine and
                                   Professional Arts. The Historical correspondence and subject files in Box 1, folders 5-43 relate to the early days of Kent State including listings of names and dates of early
                                   buildings.

                                   The collection is divided into three categories:

                                              Correspondence/subject files - Boxes 1-4
                                              Artifacts/Photographs - Boxes 5-7
                                              Oversized materials - in Horizontal File

                                             Historical Abstract:                      Deutsche Guggenheim Berlin opened on November 7, 1997 as a partnership
          Grant
                                                                                       between the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation and Deutsche Bank.
          Digitization of Wright's                                                     Designed by American architect Richard Gluckman, the space was
          Papers                                                                       established to organize and present exhibitions of modern and contemporary
                                                                                       art. The exhibition space hosted three to four important exhibitions each
                                       GO                                              year, many of which showcased a work specially commissioned by an artist.
                                                                                       The exhibition program and the day-to-day management of the museum
                                                                                       was the joint responsibility of the two partners. The museum closed in early
                                                                                       2013.

                                             Scope and Content Abstract:               The Collection on Deutsche Guggenheim Berlin contains materials collected
                                                                                       by the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum Archives to document exhibitions
                                                                                       and events at Deutsche Guggenheim Berlin. The bulk of the collection
                                                                                       consists of non-unique materials, such as press kits, press clippings, slides
                                                                                       and digital photographs, brochures, and the Deutsche Guggenheim
                                                                                       Magazine. Documentation within the collection begins with the opening of
                                                                                       the exhibition space in 1997.

                                             Location:                                 OS, IA, TSB

                                             Language:                                 Collection is primarily in English and German.

                                             Arrangement:                              Organized into 4 series: 1. Administrative; 2. Exhibitions; 3. Deutsche
                                                                                       Guggenheim Magazine; and 4. Commissions.

                                             Restrictions:                             Series 1, 2, and 3 are unrestricted unless otherwise indicated at the folder
                                                                                       level. Series 4 is open to qualified scholars only.

                                             Publication Rights:                       Requests for permission to publish material from this collection should be
                                                                                       discussed with the Manager of the Library and Archives.

                                             Preferred Citation:                       Collection on Deutsche Guggenheim Berlin. A0054. Solomon R. Guggenheim

          Summary Information
                  Title: Collection of H.J. Heinz Company (Pittsburgh, Pa.),
                  Collection Number: MSS#57
                  Creator: H.J. Heinz Company
                  Collection Dates: 1867-1996,
                  Collection Dates: 1920-1940,
                  Collection Dates: 1950-1970
                  Extent: 67.5 cubic feet (33 boxes)
                  Abstract:

                          The H.J. Heinz Company was founded in 1869 by Henry John Heinz (1844-
                          1919). The collection contains advertisements, correspondence, label
                          books, pamphlets, scrapbooks, programs, postcards, and other sundry
                          items. The collection primarily documents the products manufactured by
                          the Company between 1920-1939 and 1950-1960.


                  Language:

                  The material in this collection is in English.
